problem: Minor: chess rests on a single active-control study (0.10), and WM g=0.01 is for nonverbal ability in groups of 20 or more with treated controls; all other numbers verified.

ARN figures verified (near 97.9 vs 75.0, far 94.1 vs 39.6) but they are averages over 11 systems incl. SBERT and old UnifiedQA/FlanT5/Llama-2, 'halfway between random and human' is not 'fine' on near, and GPT-4 scored 57.1 on (far,far) and 29.1 only on (far,near); the 39.6% mixes both far partitions; 2024 LLM letter-string study shows steep drop on unfamiliar alphabets but not chance.
fix: On ARN narrative analogies (Sourati et al. 2024), the average over eleven tested models, mostly 2020-2023 systems, was 75.0% on near analogies (humans 97.9%) and 39.6% on far ones (humans 94.1%, chance 50%); GPT-4 was near humans on near analogies (about 93%) but 57.1% on far analogies against far distractors and 29.1% against near distractors. A separate letter-string study (Stevenson et al. 2025) shows four LLMs losing accuracy as the alphabet becomes less familiar while adults and children do not.

problem: Minor: adults' Latin value is 0.88, so the range is 0.88-0.91; children N is 41 in Table 2 (42 in the evidence note).
Minor: the 33.9% is the average of 11 systems (GPT-4 got 29.1%).
Minor: ExpeL ALFWorld ReAct baseline of about 40 is read from a figure/earlier note and not re-confirmed exactly; AWM +51.1% is WebArena relative, ReasoningBank +8.3/+7.2/+4.6 matches paper text.

Numbers verified (MTL insight +3.7 vs trajectory +1.1 over zero-shot 0.523; Hu ALFWorld A to B raw -9.5 vs insight +6.5; LifeMem airline Synapse 0.26 vs ReAct 0.32), but in the same LifeMem table the insight-based baseline ExpeL also fell below no-memory (airline 0.26 vs 0.32; FEVER with DeepSeek 0.32 vs 0.39), and in Hu's reverse direction raw and insight were similar (+7.0 vs +7.5), so 'abstracted lessons transfer more safely' is not uniform.
fix: In LLM-agent memory studies, abstracted insights and skills usually transferred better than raw trajectories (Memory Transfer Learning, GPT-5-mini: insight +3.7 vs trajectory +1.1 average points over zero-shot; ALFWorld A to B: raw -9.5 vs insight +6.5 points; LifeMem on tau-bench airline: the trajectory-memory baseline Synapse 0.26 vs 0.32 without memory), but not uniformly: LifeMem's insight-based ExpeL baseline also fell below the no-memory agent on airline (0.26) and on FEVER with DeepSeek (0.32 vs 0.39), and raw and insight memory gained alike in the reverse ALFWorld direction. Differences are small and not token-matched.

problem: Minor: the LifeMem below-baseline example (Synapse 0.26 vs ReAct 0.32) is one of two baselines; ExpeL also fell to 0.26, so it is not raw-trace specific.

Minor: PI-LLM says most models show a quasi-log-linear drop and the largest (L tier) stay relatively high at 400 updates, so 'collapse' applies to mid/small models; the 39-LLM study reports PI collapsing bimodally.

Chattaraj and Raj numbers verified (PI errors 56.1% same-key intrusion, 42.5% retrieval failure, 0.2% hallucination; RI hallucination 0.9%), but Wang and Sun report the opposite trend at high interference (a three-stage progression ending in hallucinated values never shown plus primacy bias), so 'not hallucination' rests on one study's classifier and the sources disagree.
fix: In one 54-model study (Chattaraj and Raj 2026, 9,753 proactive-interference errors), 56.1% of errors were same-key intrusions of earlier values and 42.5% were retrieval failures (no value returned), with only 0.2% hallucinated values absent from the sequence (0.9% for retroactive errors); an earlier study (Wang and Sun 2025) instead reports a growing share of hallucinated values and a primacy bias toward the first updates at the highest interference loads, so the hallucination share depends on load and classifier.

problem: Xiong et al. numbers verified (add-all vs strict: EHRAgent 13.05 vs 38.50, RegAgent 55.48 vs 70.95, AgentDriver 32.32 vs 51.00, CIC-IoT 59.90 vs 85.40; fixed memory 16.75/67.53/40.11/71.50), but this is one study with GPT-4o-mini agents on four tasks, the comparison is to a small fixed memory (50-180 records), and Kerestecioglu et al. measure retention precision and on LongMemEval find forgetting does not beat plain retrieval (70.1 vs 71.2), so 'in agents' is wider than the evidence.
fix: In one study of four GPT-4o-mini agents (Xiong et al. 2025), adding every experience to memory scored below a small fixed memory (e.g. EHRAgent accuracy 13.05 vs 16.75), while adding only experiences passing a strict evaluator scored above it (38.50 for EHRAgent; 70.95 vs 67.53 RegAgent), with history-based deletion helping further when the evaluator is reliable; a separate memory-architecture study found forgetting only matched, not beat, plain retrieval on LongMemEval (70.1% vs 71.2%).

problem: Minor: the two figures measure different things (evolveQA: outdated open-ended answers from parametric knowledge, 23-54% in text and 'as high as 55%' in the AWS appendix; STALE: overall accuracy of agents on implicit memory conflicts), and the 6-31% drop is accuracy relative to non-conflicting controls.

Chroma technical report supports distractor harm and the focused (~300 token) vs full (~113k) gain, but Arjmandi's distractor removal helped only Haiku 4.5 (+0.083) and Sonnet 4.6 (+0.104) on BABILong, was neutral for Opus 4.7 (+0.008, ns) and GPT-5.5 (+0.017), and was negative on MRCR v2 for Sonnet (-0.112) and Opus (-0.060); the focused-vs-full comparison also changes length and distractors together.
fix: Distractors similar to the needle or question lower long-context accuracy beyond length (Chroma technical report: more distractors, lower needle-question similarity and longer inputs all degrade accuracy across 18 LLMs, and ~300-token focused prompts beat ~113k-token full histories on LongMemEval), and removing distractors while keeping the evidence raised accuracy for smaller models on BABILong (Haiku 4.5 +0.083, Sonnet 4.6 +0.104) but not for the strongest models (Opus 4.7 +0.008, GPT-5.5 +0.017) and was mixed on MRCR v2 (Sonnet -0.112, Opus -0.060) in a single-author preprint.

problem: Minor: Keppel and Underwood .99 to .58 is quoted second-hand via Loftus and Patterson; the 91% vs 74% are single early studies (Wickens, Born and Allen 1963 vs Kincaid and Wickens 1970) cited in an undergraduate thesis, which says content release is 'typically greater' than time release, so they are illustrative, not a pooled effect.

Baeuml and Kliegl 2013 study list-learning release via a forget cue, testing the earlier list or an internal context change (not a category change), report 'almost complete' release for the forget cue only as a non-significant difference (no-PI vs forget p=.173, N=24), and conclude release reflects a smaller memory search set; PI build-up and category-shift release come from secondary pages (Wikipedia, a thesis), and Peterson and Peterson found no PI build-up in their own check.
fix: In list-learning experiments (Baeuml and Kliegl 2013), proactive interference lowered recall and slowed responses, and three release methods (a forget cue, testing the earlier list, an internal context change) restored recall and speed, with the forget cue giving almost complete release (14.58% lower recall with remember cue vs no-PI, n.s. difference to forget, p=.173), consistent with a smaller search set; the classic buildup over trials and release by a category change (Wickens paradigm) are documented here only through secondary sources.

problem: Numbers verified (LoCoMo retrieval failure 11.4-46.3% vs utilization failure 3.9-8.1%; MINTEval evidence in pool 58.3%), but MINTEval also finds that answering errors add a 25.2% drop even when evidence is present, far above LoCoMo's 4-8% utilization failure, and the 41.7% loss is attributed to memory construction as well as retrieval, so 'retrieval quality dominates' holds in LoCoMo but is weaker in MINTEval.
fix: On LoCoMo (GPT-5-mini, 1,540 questions) retrieval failures were 11.4-46.3% of questions versus 3.9-8.1% utilization failures; on the multi-target interference benchmark MINTEval the needed evidence reached the retrieved pool in only 58.3% of cases (a 41.7% loss from memory construction and retrieval), but even with evidence present answering errors added a further 25.2% drop, so utilization is a smaller but not negligible bottleneck there.

problem: Minor: Zhu and Simon's control group was taught by lecture in the normal way (not conventional problem solving), numbers verified (School A 93.13 vs 75.50, p<.001, n=32 each; School B 97.23 vs 95.08, n=39/38, ns); it is an unreviewed 1987 technical report, and Sweller 2023 notes the effect failed to replicate in geometry and physics when the examples had high split attention.

All listed sources are Sweller's own reviews (Sweller 2023 appears twice under two URLs, Sweller 2011 chapter twice); the underlying primary studies (Kalyuga et al. 2001, Chen et al. 2015-2017) were not opened, and Sweller 2023 states the reversal as a cognitive load effect without pooled sizes.
fix: Cognitive load theory (Sweller 2011, 2023, citing Kalyuga et al. 2001 and Chen et al. 2015-2017) holds that the worked-example advantage shrinks and can reverse for learners with more prior knowledge, because the examples become redundant; the evidence listed is one author's reviews and no independent replication or pooled effect size was opened.

problem: Minor: 'analogue of worked examples' is the researcher's interpretation; Wang et al. also show invalid-reasoning exemplars (39.5) keep most of the gain, unlike what the worked-example effect would predict.

In Yasunaga et al. the GSM8K 75.0 for GPT-3.5-turbo is fixed hand-written 5-shot CoT (no retrieved baseline on that model), self-generated is 75.8-77.8 across variants; retrieved vs self-generated appears only on the text-davinci models (001: 11 vs 9; 002: 47 vs 48; 003: 54 vs 61), and curie scores 2-3% for all methods, a floor, not evidence about exemplar source; Sarukkai (agents) does not test this.
fix: On GSM8K (Yasunaga et al. 2024) GPT-3.5-turbo reaches 75.0% with fixed 5-shot CoT versus 75.8-77.8% with self-generated exemplars; against retrieved exemplars, self-generated ones roughly tie on text-davinci-002 (48 vs 47) and win on text-davinci-003 (61 vs 54) but lose on the weaker text-davinci-001 (9 vs 11), while text-curie-001 is at the floor (2-3%) for every method.

problem: Minor: the 36 iterations without library succeeded in only 2 of 3 runs, and the three results come from different agents and benchmarks, not a common baseline.

Minor: the diagram result rests on small groups (analog+diagrams 23% vs analog-only 40% before hint, ns; 26 and 25 subjects) and the claim's numbers are all from one paper (Gick and Holyoak 1983) with Gentner et al. 1993 supporting the retrieval-bias side.

Minor: the 182.6% Tulu figure is measured after the DPO stage for the poem task, not at a final RLVR stage; Mohammadi gives no numeric entropy in abstract but text says base entropy significantly higher.

Laban's 35-39% is the total average drop from single-turn to sharded multi-turn (aptitude -15%, unreliability +112%), not a cost isolated to early guesses; early premature answers are only one identified cause.
fix: LLMs show anchoring: a number or hint in the prompt pulls answers and chain-of-thought and reflection did not remove it (Lou and Sun 2024); in multi-turn chat models average 35 to 39% lower performance than with the full task at once, partly because they make early assumptions, attempt answers prematurely and overly rely on them (Laban 2025); restating all information in a final turn (recap) or each turn (snowball) recovers some but not all of the loss.

problem: Minor: Xia et al. call the dropped terminations give-up or uncertain-answer endings (not 'low-confidence'), and report the gain as 2.6% to 4.9% across aggregation rules.
Minor: the 22 LLMs' mean originality was slightly higher than humans (0.711 vs 0.695 on AUT) rather than identical; 'comparable' is fair.
Minor: Terwiesch table lists the CoT arm and independent-session arm separately; the Opus 0.24 vs 0.80 and 0.33 vs 0.21 values come from Wadhwa Table 12/11 on scientific ideas, not product ideas.

The numbers match (Hu 71.6 to 68.0; Ferreira CSQA -2.1 to -4.4 and temperature spread -0.11 to -0.41pp), but 'diversity helps only as strategy-mode coverage' is not shown by any source: Wu et al. show mode-conditioning helps pass@k on math in 0.5B-7B models, not that nothing else helps.
fix: On correctness tasks expert personas cost accuracy and temperature spread does nothing: MMLU 71.6% to 68.0% with an expert persona (Hu et al. 2026); maximally diverse persona teams lost 2.1 to 4.4 points on CSQA versus plain debate and temperature spread changed accuracy by only -0.11 to -0.41 points (Ferreira et al. 2026, small open models). Separately, Wu et al. argue that splitting a sampling budget across distinct reasoning modes beats sampling from one mixed distribution (0.5B-7B models). No Claude model was tested.

problem: Zhou et al. 2019 Table 3 values -3.21 (p=.003) and -2.38 (p=.029) are for ideas in the total 20 minutes, not the late window; last-10-min differences are -2.48 (p<.001) and -1.75 (p=.010); also Sio and Ormerod say high-demand filler gives a smaller incubation effect, not that it hurts.
fix: Human incubation: exposure to others' ideas did not hurt in the first 10 minutes but did in the last 10 minutes (exposed-immediate produced 2.48 and 1.75 fewer ideas than exposed-relax and exposed-task in the last 10 min; over the full 20 min -3.21, p=.003 and -2.38, p=.029); a relax or unrelated-task break removed the deficit. Meta-analysis (Sio and Ormerod 2009): positive incubation effect, divergent tasks gain more than insight tasks, longer preparation gives a larger effect, high-demand filler tasks give a smaller effect. The agent analogue (context truncation or reset) is untested for fixation.

problem: Shidara et al. report Claude 4.1 Opus (0.751) is not significantly different from physicians (0.66, CI 0.55-0.75) and wrong or indeterminate on 45% of the human-miss items; 'largely avoids' overstates 'human-level'. Minor: GPT-4 solved 3 to 7 walls depending on shots (6 at 0-shot).
fix: Current Claude with reasoning reaches physician-level performance on the mARC Einstellung benchmark: Claude 4.1 Opus 0.751 vs physicians 0.66 (difference not significant); on the 20 items most physicians missed it was decisively correct on 55.0%, decisively wrong on 25.0% and indeterminate on 20.0%. Earlier models failed (o1 48% on mARC; GPT-4 solved only 3 to 7 of 494 red-herring walls vs 285 for humans).

problem: Both findings (faculty beat graduate students; graduate students overestimate novices) come only from Singh's Pittsburgh group (Singh 2009, Mason and Singh 2011); Wolf et al. 2012 (listed twice, arXiv and the APS version are the same paper) only reports them secondhand, so there is one primary lab, not independent replications.

All accuracy numbers check (GSM-NoOp -65.7/-32.0/-17.5; GSM-IC macro under 30%; R1 1.50% to 4.50%; Haiku 4.5 -1.3), but the token cost is misstated: CatAttack reports the share of responses exceeding 1.5x/2x/4x original length (R1 28.0%/16.2%/4.8%) and lengths up to 3x in some cases, not a uniform 1.5x to 3x cost.
fix: LLMs are pulled by irrelevant surface content: one irrelevant sentence cuts GSM8K-style accuracy (GSM-IC: fewer than 30% of base problems solved consistently; GSM-NoOp drops up to 65.7 points, GPT-4o -32.0, o1-preview -17.5). The drop is smaller in absolute size for reasoning models: a searched cat-trigger moved DeepSeek R1 error from 1.50% to 4.50%, Claude Haiku 4.5 lost 1.3 points on GSM-Symbolic name/number variants, and triggers made reasoning models write longer answers (28.0% of R1 responses exceeded 1.5x the original length, up to 3x in some cases).

problem: Minor: BoT and ReasonFlux share a first author/lab; the Dynamic Cheatsheet AIME comparison is on 30 questions as stated.
Minor: the Yasunaga GSM8K table is garbled in extraction; 76.7 (5-shot CoT) to 77.8 (self-generated) for GPT-3.5-turbo is the best reading and matches the paper's reported 77.8.

In ARN the 39.6% far-analogy figure is the mean over all tested models (the two far-analogy partitions average 45.3 and 33.9), not GPT-4; GPT-4 scored 57.1 and 29.1 on those partitions (humans 94.1% on far analogies). Counterfactual-alphabet figures (humans 75.3%, GPT-3.5 35.0%) and Webb's story result check out.
fix: LLMs rely on surface similarity in analogy: on far analogies in ARN the tested models averaged 39.6% (chance 50%; GPT-4 57.1% and 29.1% on the two far-analogy partitions) against 94.1% for humans; in counterfactual letter-string alphabets humans scored 75.3% vs GPT-3.5 35.0%; on story analogies GPT-3 was weaker than college students.

problem: Minor: Chen's over-30% drop is on logical-reasoning tasks (R-GSM drops are smaller); the table in Williamson is garbled but Gemma-7B 37.76 +8.26 = 46.02 on GSM8K is right (the evidence note's Mistral +11.68 is actually Granite).

Minor: 'expert identity wins only on judge-rated open answers' generalises from one GPT-4-judged ExpertPrompting result; Zheng reports in-domain persona coefficient 0.004 (p<0.01) and most personas non-significant.

The numbers are right (Smith 2013: faculty n=23 deep 71.7% vs non-majors n=101 29.2%; Bissonnette 2017 entering vs advanced majors did not differ in free sort) but both come from the same SFSU/Smith group using one instrument, and Hoskinson 2017 reports no faculty comparison, so the expert-novice gap is one lab's result, not an independent replication.

Wolf et al. support stacker/spreader (PC1) outweighing expertise (PC2 only; first two components 87% of variance) and Veldhuis sets 3-4 agreeing with Chi while sets 1-2 were inconclusive, and Smith's crossed-feature biology task splits faculty from non-majors, but no source shows that ONLY crossed-feature designs give a clean split; Veldhuis is reported secondhand.
fix: Human card-sort results depend on sorting style and item design: in Wolf et al.'s data stackers versus spreaders (PC1) outweighed expert versus novice (PC2 only), and in Veldhuis's work (reported secondhand) the crossed-feature sets 3-4 agreed with Chi while the natural sets 1-2 were inconclusive; the crossed-feature biology task (Smith et al. 2013) also separates faculty from non-majors.

problem: Scope note: DAGGER is evaluated on Bangla math with 3B-12B models, and the tuned Gemma-3 12B (69.4%, 359 tokens) does not quite match Qwen3-8B reasoning (71.4%, 3,128 tokens), so 'recovers' means most, not all; CatAttack share exceeding 1.5x is 28.0% for R1.

Claim describes Shah et al. 2003 only; all formulas and weights (10/6/3/1, 0.944, 0.624 post and 0.591 a priori vs peers) verified in the paper; the second listed source (Sankar and Sen 2024) is not needed and its abstract does not mention Shah.
Minor: Si et al.'s 4000 ideas are per topic (seed-generation within a topic), and the Hivemind figure is for 100 queries x 50 samples at top-p 0.9, temperature 1.0.

Scope note: Terwiesch also finds a composite pool across four vendors matched humans (B=-0.010) and random personas reached 0.757 vs humans 0.773, so the gap holds for default single-model pools only.
Minor: the two comparisons come from different studies and metrics (Meincke: cosine similarity on GPT-4-1106 pools, base prompt 0.386; Terwiesch: diversity = 1 - similarity on GPT-4o pools).

Terwiesch 0.575 vs GPT-4o 0.679, BSR duplicate rate 0.022 to 0.238, and Dong and Yakura refinement b=0.007 (ns) all check out, but the MUTATE Self-Refine datapoint is about interactive path discovery for Claude Sonnet 4.6 (25/56 vs 30/56), not pool diversity, and Self-Refine matched or beat base for the other three models (GPT-5.4 29 vs 27, Llama 13 vs 13), so it is not a clean 'one more data point'.
fix: Iterative self-refinement of an LLM-made idea pool lowers diversity: in Terwiesch et al. the refine-twice (Bold Ideas) arm ran on GPT-4o and scored 0.575 vs 0.679 for GPT-4o zero-shot (a 0.104 drop); uniform refinement of a pool raised the near-duplicate rate from 0.022 to 0.238 (Budgeted Subset Refinement, preprint by one independent author); refining a person's own seed ideas did not compress diversity (Dong and Yakura). In the MUTATE agent benchmark Self-Refine lowered Claude Sonnet 4.6's path discovery (25/56 vs 30/56) but not the other models'. Frontier-2026 models at equal tokens are untested.

problem: Minor: Anderson compared ChatGPT to an Oblique Strategies card deck (N=33), not to no tool; Dong and Yakura's individual ratings rose for aptness/explanation for both groups.

Minor: the 'over 50 points' prompt shift is for one judge (gpt-5.4); the 'expert-level' VLM result uses the paper's own rule (kappa at least 0.80x expert-expert, 0.52 vs 0.54) and used in-context examples.

Minor: StructSim whole-text accuracies are 0.511-0.524 (0.562 is the keyphrase variant); Sankar and Sen's 10-of-12 is the two cases where near/same labels were swapped (far labels still matched); the headline that metrics 'disagree with each other' is inferred from several papers rather than shown in one.

Minor: both papers say returns diminish (Ueda: a fourth turn 'negligible gains'; Chen: three to five agents or more than eight rounds 'minimal improvement'), not that gains stop completely; the two use different metrics and task setups.

Minor: the heading 'context-aware avoidance' is interpretive; all Terwiesch figures (0.679, 0.452, 0.575, 0.757, 0.735, 0.698, 0.773) match Table 3 and the second paper (Deng et al.) independently shows personas closing the gap.
Johnson 1987 supports it for generator/auto technicians; Steinberg and Gitomer only broadly (explicit mental models, physical clues).

Lesgold et al. give one expert (7 steps) vs. three trainees (14, 20, others similar) on a single sample problem and say most trainees also try to be systematic by space splitting or sequential tracing; the contrast is not general.
fix: In Lesgold et al.'s Sherlock task analysis, the expert solved one sample problem in 7 steps by splitting the suspect space, while one trainee took 14 steps and another 20, tracing circuit paths end to end; the authors say what differs with expertise is which space is split, and Johnson (1995) found strategy type did not separate high from low performers but range of strategies did.

problem: The theory-knowledge null comes from one student sample (Johnson et al. 1993, n=34, t(32)=0.073) that the author hedges as 'may not be as important', and a null test is not proof of no prediction.
fix: In one student study (Johnson et al. 1993, n=34) systems-exam scores did not differ between high and low troubleshooters (19.82 vs 19.88 of 24), suggesting theory knowledge may be a weak predictor of troubleshooting skill; range of strategies (Johnson 1995) and strategic and system knowledge (Katz et al. 1997; Steinberg and Gitomer 1992) were what separated skilled from unskilled technicians.

problem: Numbers match, but Katz et al., the Gott et al. report and Parker are all the Sherlock developers' own evaluations (Katz summarises the same data as Gott), so there is no independent source.
Numbers are right, but Cloud-OpsBench's 0.76/0.68 is the best joint RCA accuracy (a high score, not a failure), and ITBench tested 2024-era models (GPT-4o, Llama) rather than strong current agents.
fix: ITBench found agents on 2024-era models resolved only 13.8% of SRE scenarios, ORCA-bench's best RCA accuracy was 25.3% on Medium and 10.0% on Hard tasks, and Cloud-OpsBench's best joint RCA accuracy was 0.76 (OnlineBoutique) and 0.68 (TrainTicket) but with evidence closure of only 0.38 and 0.15.

problem: SREGym drop is for Claude Code (Sonnet 4.6); the 'like novices' link is the researcher's analogy.
ORCA 9-16 pts is right, but GALA+ 74.44% vs 48.35% compares a whole multi-phase system with a different published method (Flow-of-Action), not a with/without dependency-graph ablation.
fix: Removing source code cut RCA accuracy by 9-16 points across models in ORCA-bench, and GALA+, a method that bounds exploration with the service dependency graph, reached 74.44% AC@1 on Online Boutique against 48.35% for the best prior LLM method (Flow-of-Action), though this compares whole systems and is not a dependency-graph ablation.

problem: Only SREGym supports it (63.7% to 17.9% is Stratus/Sonnet 4.6, n=13 new-failure problems); the second source is a human transfer study that says nothing about LLM agents.
fix: On SREGym, end-to-end success of LLM SRE agents fell on its 13 new failure scenarios compared with ported problems (Stratus/Sonnet 4.6 63.7% to 17.9%, Claude Code 60.8% to 28.2%, Codex 57.8% to 15.4%), while similar-failure problems stayed near ported levels; this is one benchmark.

problem: OpsHarness numbers match, but Trace2Policy found one-shot distilled rules (69.2%) no better than no rules (70.3%) and worse than few-shot (73.3%); only error-refined rules (78.9%) won, and OpsHarness's 59.0% bundles knowledge, skills, tools and a cold-start substrate.
fix: In OpsHarness, a harness that mines past diagnoses into knowledge, skills and tools reached 59.0% final A@1, against 38.4% for in-context retrieval of three correct past rollouts and 36.1% for the bare agent; in Trace2Policy only error-refined rules (78.9%) beat few-shot examples (73.3%), while one-shot distilled rules (69.2%) did not.

problem: The no-verify ablation removes the whole verification gate (inner and outer), not the held-out gate alone; the 37% rejection rate is with the gate on.

The two-stage design is described accurately, but only the whole gate was ablated (no stage-by-stage test), and the second source (Trace2Policy) uses a single validation regression gate in a different domain, so 'should pass a two-stage gate' is not shown.
fix: OpsHarness verifies each proposed memory or tool change with an inner gate (no accuracy or cost regression on the source cases) and an outer gate (no regression on a freshly re-sampled held-out testbed stratified by fault family and time); removing the whole gate made accuracy decay (final-window A@1 0.33 vs 0.43 for no-evolve) and hurt weak backbones most, but the two stages were not ablated separately; Trace2Policy independently found a regression gate necessary, in a different domain.

problem: Lu's 'up to 11.4 more rounds' is a correlation between failure and length, not proof that extra rounds fail to help.

Only Zheng et al. (one paper, listed twice) tests it, on factual MMLU questions with open models, and finds small domain-alignment effects; Borchers et al. is about LLMs simulating novice students, not expert personas.
fix: In one large study (Zheng et al. 2024: 162 personas, 4 open LLM families, 2,410 factual MMLU questions) adding a persona, including expertise-domain roles, to the system prompt did not improve accuracy over no persona on average, and picking the best persona per question was about as good as random; domain-aligned roles helped only slightly.

problem: The 65.48 vs 34.21 score is the mean over all 15 participants (students, faculty, professional engineers) on embedded development tasks, not novices only or debugging only; HypoCompass is software debugging and Hu and Ash is qualitative.
fix: In a 15-participant study of embedded-system development and debugging, participants using GPT with a structured workflow scored 65.48 vs 34.21 without GPT (t(38)=2.73, p<0.01), with all five users on the environmental-sensor task scoring 100% (including some with no hardware experience) against 25% without GPT; the models also hallucinated hardware facts (e.g. wrong I2C address from pin voltage in 38% of trials, a wrong register or configuration value in 100%).

problem: Westermo paper reports no consistent quality advantage (scenario-dependent) from 2 scenarios and 6 practitioners; Bi et al. compares simple harnesses with published agents, not single vs multi-agent.
fix: In an exploratory Westermo case study (2 failure scenarios, 6 practitioners, 120 runs) neither the single-agent nor the orchestrated multi-agent RCA configuration showed a consistent practitioner-rated quality advantage, and the single agent was faster and cheaper.

problem: Slips: Ko et al.'s 35% is navigation time in a 10-person lab study (Xia et al. recast it as comprehension), and Xia's 58% covers all development work, not debugging only.
Alaboudi and LaToza state '5 times / 6 times more likely', not odds; AutoSD compares only roughly level with its LLM baseline (Defects4J v1.2: 76 vs 87 correct, v2.0: 113 vs 110).

debug-gym numbers match but the table shows Llama-3.3-70B and GPT-4o gaining with the debugger, and on Aider GPT-4o gains while o3-mini slips, so 'helps strong, hurts weak' is the authors' text rather than what the cited numbers show; in Debug2Fix, optional debug tools were flat for GPT-5 (+1.0%) and Haiku (-0.8%) and fell 14.8% only for Sonnet, whose 9% usage rate is the cited one.
fix: In debug-gym on SWE-bench Lite, an instruction-following pdb debugger lifted Claude 3.7 Sonnet from 37.2 to 48.4 (52.1 when enabled after the fifth rewrite), with the authors reporting that weaker models (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.3-70B) gained little or were harmed; on the easy Aider benchmark debugger access made no clear difference (GPT-4o 69.7 vs 72.9, o3-mini 95.2 vs 94.2). In Debug2Fix on GitBug-Java, forcing a debug call through a subagent raised GPT-5 from 60.2 to 73.1, while giving the main agent debug tools alone was flat for GPT-5 and Haiku and cut Sonnet by 14.8% (it used a debug tool in 9% of instances). AutoSD found 73% of runs plausible with a real debugger vs 63% with LLM-imagined output.

problem: Olausson's 1.05x figure is at equal token budget in the np=10, nfr=1 cell; the 33.30 vs 52.60 is repair success on failing programs only.
The 72-81% file-found figure is for SWE-bench Lite only (Majgaonkar et al. report 35-40% of failed Verified trajectories miss the file and call file localisation a bottleneck there).
fix: On SWE-bench Lite agents located the correct file in 72-81% of failed trajectories (on Verified 35-40% of failures miss the file); 60-69% of failures of capable models (GPT-5, GPT-5-mini, Qwen3 variants) on SWE-Agent and OpenHands edit the right functions yet give a wrong patch; and 12 never-solved SWE-bench tasks needing only simple patches defeated all agents because of gaps in architectural reasoning and domain knowledge.

problem: Loc-Bench and Lite gains compare whole systems, not a with/without graph ablation; CogniGent is not a structural-map method.
Differences come from single runs on 300 tasks (SWE-agent reports about +/-0.5 run-to-run noise on one config); Agentless 'element recall' is the related-element contains-GT metric.

Source numbers are right, but REval's 44.4% averages mostly small 2024 models (GPT-4-Turbo scores far higher), and the Abdollahi paper cited for the 58% tool fix reports 85-98% execution-simulation accuracy for newer reasoning models, so 'LLMs are weak at tracing runtime behaviour' is too broad.
fix: Earlier code LLMs traced runtime behaviour poorly (REval average accuracy 44.4% across mostly 2024 models; CRUXEval GPT-4 63-67%, 75-81% with CoT; CodeSense Python no model above 50%), but newer reasoning models simulate execution at 85-98% accuracy on short snippets (Abdollahi et al.), where a calculator tool fixed 58% of the remaining computation-error category; reliability on real repository code is still limited.

problem: Slip: 7.8% is the share of plausible patches that fail the full repo tests (inflation of resolution 4.5 pts from that alone, 6.4 pts with PatchDiff); SWE-bench+ figures are for SWE-Agent+GPT-4.
29% to 3% is correct but the drop is sharp only at 256K (Claude stays relatively high at 64K and 128K) and LongCodeQA accuracy peaks at 64-128K; the note-beats-files line is untested speculation.
fix: On LongSWE-Bench, Claude 3.5 Sonnet solved 29% of issues at 32K context and 3% at 256K (staying relatively high at 64K and 128K), and Claude 2 on SWE-bench performs worse as total context length grows; whether a compact running note would beat dumping files was not tested.

problem: Numbers match, but Reale et al. say RPD was found in every study that looked while analytic strategies were also common and surgeons used RPD only about half the time, and the sport 60-81% is Macquet (2020) cited second-hand; 'dominant across domains' is too strong.
fix: Recognition-primed decisions were reported in every one of the studies in a 32-study review of high-risk decision making that examined strategy (e.g. naval AEGIS officers: 95% of 77 actions recognitional vs 4% choosing among multiple options), though analytic strategies were also common when time pressure was lower and surgeons used RPD only about half the time; a sport review citing Macquet (2020) reports 60-81% of expert decisions as simple matches, 13-28% diagnosis and 3-24% evaluating a course of action.

problem: Numbers check (6 of 12, 11 of 24 one option; pumping fire mostly deliberated in consultation, non-expert crews), but the review does not show single-option use dropping with less routine tasks or less expert groups (two studies found time pressure had no effect; the comparison with other groups is the note's own inference), and only one sport study (Basevitch) ties more option generation to more time; a18 and b13 are the same review.
fix: Surgeons in two interview studies reported recalling only one option in about half of the challenging cases they described (6 of 12; 11 of 24), the non-expert crews in the pumping-station fire mostly deliberated in group consultation, and one sport study (Basevitch et al.) found generating more options worked better when more time was available; these separate observations are consistent with, but do not test, a drop in single-option use for less routine tasks or less expert groups.

problem: Fireground numbers (12 vs 12, 18%, novel options, almost twice as likely to consider contingencies) match Klein & Calderwood 1990, but the sport half rests on a single study (Basevitch, via the review): Musculus found only less-is-more support and Raab & Johnson (equal option counts across expertise) say nothing about time.
fix: Experts and novices both used recognition, but experts built novel options and weighed future contingencies more (12 vs 12 fireground commanders; only 18% of decision points fit classical concurrent comparison); in sport, one study (Basevitch et al.) found generating more options worked better when more time was available, while another (Musculus) supported only less-is-more.

problem: Minor: R-CAST result is for human-agent teams in a simulation (6 vs 6 teams, 9 speeds), attributing the gain to expectancy monitoring specifically is the authors' framing; the 16 s figure in a34 was not checked (8 s in the paper's text for the diagnose case) but is not used in the claim.

Numbers all match (87.5->64.4 = 23.1; 36.3 is o1-preview 57.7 vs GPT-4o direct 94.0 on 440-problem subset; AMC23 700 tokens 51.3 vs 28.9; Sprague: commonsense nearly no CoT gain). The NoThinking result is on math/proof/code tasks, not pattern-like tasks, so the 'pattern-like' framing is the note's.

Ma et al. show NoThinking beats Thinking at pass@1 in the low-budget regime with no selector at all (Thinking wins pass@1 only at higher budgets, and on LiveCodeBench throughout), so the advantage does not wholly 'depend on' a selector; selectors/verifiers matter for turning pass@k into accuracy at matched latency. Sprague part is supported. Sources are two papers each listed twice.
fix: Fast no-think tries beat thinking at low token budgets even at pass@1, but at higher budgets thinking wins pass@1 and the fast-try advantage needs many samples plus a verifier or confidence-based selector (Ma et al.); on symbolic multi-step tasks CoT beats direct answering and tool-augmented solvers beat CoT (Sprague et al.).

problem: Numbers match Ruoss et al. Table 1 and dataset text (95.4%, Elo 2895 vs humans, 2299 vs bots, 15.3B action values, AlphaZero 56.1 vs 95.6); caveat that the action-value labels come from Stockfish, a search engine, so 'recognition-only' is amortized search.

Thinkless 50-90%, Dualformer 80 vs 30, 96.6 with 59.9% fewer steps, and DART 13 of 14 pairs with 32-73% fewer thinking tokens all verified in the papers (the miss is Qwen3-8B OlympiadBench, -1.7); the 'no head-to-head with Thinkless' statement is a search-gap remark that cannot be verified from sources.

Numbers match DART Table 2 and Think When Needed (Self-Select well under Ideal); slip: the 4% and 24% token savings are on MATH-500 where accuracy held, the HumanEval collapse (10.4, 8.5) comes with -7% and 44% savings, so the sentence merges columns.

Supported by Lamparth (214 experts, agreement on about half of 21 actions, no significant persona effect) and Rivera (all five models show forms of escalation; GPT-3.5 10.15 to 26.02); caveats: Rivera says most escalation-score changes are not statistically significant, and the two studies use different setups (human-vs-LLM teams vs LLM nation agents).

All numbers match Huang et al. Table 3 and Valmeekam et al. (38 of 45 invalid plans passed, 40/100 to 88/100 with VAL plus backprompting); note the 88% includes backprompting iterations and Blocksworld only.

Numbers verified (1,953% more tokens on 2+3; over 92% of cases first round already correct, under 60% of tokens), but 'nothing helps' on hard puzzles goes beyond Shojaee et al., who show accuracy collapse at high complexity and no gain from giving the explicit algorithm, not that no intervention helps.
fix: Task complexity moderates keep-first in LLMs: on easy items the first solution is usually enough (in over 92% of cases the first round already holds the correct answer, and o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models on 2+3) and later rounds add little; on hard puzzles models fixate on early wrong attempts, accuracy collapses, and even supplying the explicit algorithm did not help in the tested puzzles.

problem: Numbers match (GPT-4o-mini 98% Ideal vs 21% Harsh first-listed; 13-75% gap in Pezeshkpour); the primacy-when-good, recency-when-poor pattern differs by model (Claude 3 Haiku already prefers the later option at Fair), and the 'no study' / 'reasoning models not tested' statements are search-gap remarks not checkable here.

Numbers match (18.8, 34.5, up to 40% fewer thinking tokens in low-compute settings; Adaptive-Consistency up to 7.9x with average accuracy drop under 0.1%); slips: the 0.1% is an average over datasets, and short-1@k matches majority voting only in low-compute settings.

Russo et al. show greedy 'does not always converge' on a 3-arm Bernoulli bandit and TS fixes it; Krishnamurthy et al. show basic-prompt GPT-4 had suffix failures in over 60% of replicates (one failure mode; others are near-uniform picking), with UCB and TS baselines at 0.02 and 0.00 vs greedy 0.47. 'Plain-LLM choice locks on and never recovers' generalises one prompt design on small bandits, and 'never recovers' is stronger than the sources.
fix: A greedy rule can lock onto a worse arm after early lucky outcomes, and a basic-prompt GPT-4 agent showed the same suffix failure (stopping choosing the best arm) in over 60% of replicates of a 5-armed bandit; Thompson sampling (sampling from belief) and UCB (an optimism bonus) did not show it in the same simulations.

problem: Krishnamurthy et al. confirm only one of many configurations (GPT-4, CoT plus externally summarized history) explored well and that unsummarized CoT variants failed, and EVOLvE shows SH 50.2 vs RH 27.5 few-shot win-rate; but these are GPT-3.5/GPT-4/Llama-2/Gemini-1.5 era results, and Harris & Slivkins find reasoning models fix the exploit half on raw history, so 'raw history plus CoT fails' is not general.
fix: For GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama-2 and Gemini-1.5-era models, externally computed summaries of per-arm counts and mean rewards combined with chain-of-thought gave robust bandit exploration, while the same prompt with raw history (even with chain-of-thought) did not; summarised history also beat raw history in EVOLvE; reasoning models are reported to cope better with raw history.

problem: Auer et al. (2002) compare UCB1-Tuned, UCB2 and epsilon_n-greedy, and Kuleshov & Precup (2014) compare epsilon-greedy, softmax, UCB1, UCB1-Tuned and others; neither includes Thompson sampling (no 'Thompson' in Kuleshov & Precup), and softmax/epsilon-greedy are not always ahead (UCB1-Tuned wins at high variance; epsilon-greedy loses on Auer distributions 12 and 14).
fix: In simulations on Bernoulli (Auer et al. 2002) and Gaussian (Kuleshov & Precup 2014) bandits, well-tuned epsilon-greedy and softmax match or beat UCB variants on most settings, with exceptions (UCB1-Tuned best at high variance; epsilon-greedy weaker with many unequal bad arms), and a badly tuned epsilon degrades fast; these studies did not test Thompson sampling.

problem: Noisy-TV slowdown in the Unity maze is confirmed (Burda et al., IDF and RF agents), but 'ICM ... resist it' is contradicted: Savinov et al. report PPO+ICM falling below plain PPO under injected noise (7.7 vs 11.6) and Raileanu & Rocktaschel report ICM performance dropping with a noisy-TV ball; Burda's own IDF agents (ICM-style features) were slowed. ICM resisted only the 40% white-noise distractor test in Pathak et al.
fix: Forward-prediction-error curiosity can be hijacked by noise (noisy TV): in a Unity maze a controllable TV drastically slows IDF and random-feature curiosity agents (Burda et al.); ICM resisted a 40% white-noise distractor (Pathak et al.) but degraded under TV noise in DMLab and MiniGrid (Savinov et al.; Raileanu & Rocktaschel), RND avoids stochastic-transition traps by using a deterministic target, and episodic reachability bonuses degrade less than ICM under injected noise.

problem: Coverage numbers (40/65/65% of 10 arms, with CoT; ~25% without) match Schmied et al., but the 96% is the frequent-action fraction for the 2B model on constructed histories where the last action is repeated many times (up to 100), not its share of picks in ordinary runs; the Binz & Schulz source does not address frequency bias or coverage.
fix: With chain-of-thought, Gemma2 2B/9B/27B cover only 40/65/65% of the arms in a 10-armed bandit (about 25% without CoT), and on constructed histories with many repetitions of one action the 2B model picked the frequent action 96% of the time (27B: 14%).

problem: Simon & Chase text matches (patterns tied to plausible moves, masters notice at a glance then analyse minutes; 3-4 minutes per move; 50,000 chunks); Gobet & Simon say Kasparov's simultaneous play was 'often less than 100 points below' tournament level (worked example 2650 vs 2750), so 'about 100' is a mild rounding.
Karvonen numbers match (legal 99.8% 16-layer, win 46%/64% vs Stockfish level 0, best board probe 99.6%) and Toshniwal supports the general claim; the claim does not say which model gets which figure.

Ruoss Table 1 (GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct 66.5% puzzles, 1755 vs bots) and LLM Chess (reasoning 45.4% vs non-reasoning 0.7% average win rate vs a random opponent) match; the two comparisons come from different papers and tasks.

All figures verified (LLM Chess +15%/+20% from reasoning effort, 3x MoA slightly above and 5x slightly below o4-mini medium on 30+ games; ChessArena no model beats Maia-1100, o3 55.6% and all others under 15% on puzzles; Hwang et al. 25-30% plateau with the authors attributing it to missing pretrained chess knowledge); caveat: the 'wider sampling does not help' point rests on one MoA setup with o4-mini.

Bilalic et al. (three SD, about 600 Elo, candidate masters performing like average players) and Sheridan & Reingold (8 of 17 experts and 8 of 17 novices chose the Einstellung move; all experts avoided it when it was a blunder) both verified; the 3 SD figure is from a single pooled comparison in the 2008 series.

F(5,20)=0.6 (ns) for the group with the familiar solution and F(5,20)=11.9, p<.001 for the group without verified in Bilalic et al.; Sheridan & Reingold replicate the gaze persistence; 'attention bias' is the authors' interpretation, from a small sample (about 5 players per group in the interaction test).

Snell et al. numbers are right (more than 4x compute saving; beam search over-optimizes on the easy bins 1-2 and helps on bins 3-4) but the bins are model-specific pass@1 quantiles, not MATH levels; Yao et al. Table 7 shows ToT's 74% costs about as many tokens as 100 CoT trials, whose best-of-100 reaches 49%, so setting 74% against single-sample CoT's 4% is not a matched-budget comparison.
fix: In LLM reasoning, search beats best-of-N on harder items but not easier ones: on MATH, PRM-guided beam search was worse than best-of-N in the two easiest model-specific difficulty bins and better in bins 3-4, and choosing the method by estimated difficulty cut test-time compute by more than 4x; on Game of 24, Tree of Thoughts (b=5) reached 74% at about the completion tokens of 100 CoT samples, versus 49% for best-of-100 CoT (single-sample CoT: 4%).

problem: Numbers verified (ToT IO 7.3, CoT 4.0, CoT-SC 9.0, b=1 45, b=5 74; Large Monkeys SWE-bench Lite 15.9% to 56% at 250 samples with unit tests as verifier), but Tree of Thoughts selects with the same LM's value prompts, not an external checker, so it is not an example of external-checker selection; its 74% also uses more tokens than single-sample CoT (best-of-100 CoT is 49%).
fix: Sampling many candidates and selecting with an external checker gives large gains (Large Language Monkeys: SWE-bench Lite 15.9% with one sample to 56% with 250 samples using the repository's unit tests as verifier); LM-scored tree search also helps on Game of 24 (Tree of Thoughts 74% at b=5 vs CoT 4.0% and CoT-SC 9.0%, best-of-100 CoT 49%) but selects with the model's own evaluations. Both need an answer that can be checked.

problem: Huang et al. (74.7% retained, more correct-to-wrong than wrong-to-correct) and Stechly et al. (self-consistency with 5 samples generally worse than the original results on table-to-stack) verified; caveats: self-consistency is majority voting not model-scored selection, and Stechly's abstract says 'similar or sometimes even worse'.

Vending-Bench Table 1 matches exactly (Claude 3.5 Sonnet mean 2,217.93, min 476; human 844.05 single run; GPT-4o 335.46) and the paper finds no link between failures and context filling; 'not plan quality' is the note's reading (EcoGym says models are weak at either strategy or execution), and the second listed source (c23) is the same paper.

Girotra (40.4/46.8/49.3% purchase intent, 35 of top 40 from GPT-4, ~800 ideas/h at ~$0.63 vs ~$25 per human idea) and Meincke (human group 0.243 vs 0.255-0.432) verified; slips: in Meincke 0.255 is the chain-of-thought pool and plain-GPT-4 baseline is 0.377, so the 0.255-0.432 range spans all prompts, not plain GPT-4; the Doshi 2024 abstract-only sentence was not checked.

PlanSearch numbers (Claude 3.5 Sonnet 55.6 to 77.0, GPT-4o 60.6 to 73.0, 77.1% at pass@20 with public-test filtering vs 77.0% at pass@200 without), diversity predicting gains, lower pass@1, and the compute-normalised statement are all in the paper (caveat: in the compute-normalised plot PlanSearch pulls ahead only beyond about 10,000 tokens per problem); Meincke and Girotra numbers match; the 'no study links option count to decision quality' gap statement is not checkable.
Chen overthinking paper only loosely supports difficulty-scaled budget; Snell figures match
Doshi part not among listed sources; checked by search summary only, consistent

DEER code results use about 9% to 66% of vanilla tokens (R1-Distill-Qwen-32B: 32.5%, 35.3%, 40.4%), not '34 to 80% of the tokens'; 34-80% looks like a mix-up with the abstract's 19.1-80.1% shorter chains. Chen figures (1,953%, over 92%, under 60%) match the paper text, though its own Figure 5 shows R1 at 89-90% on some sets.
fix: Reasoning models fail to satisfice on easy tasks: o1-like models use 1,953% more tokens than conventional models on '2+3', the first solution round is already correct in over 92% of cases and uses under 60% of tokens (paper text; its figure shows 89-90% for R1 on some sets). All numbers come from one paper (Chen et al.), re-opened and confirmed; a survey frames the same problem. Gap search 2026-11: other groups find the same pattern off the competition-math set. Answer convergence is near step 0 on NaturalQuestions and about 0.8 to 0.9 of the chain on GSM8K/MATH/GPQA/AIME (Liu and Wang 2025). Confidence-based exit (DEER) keeps pass@1 within about +/-1 point on HumanEval, BigCodeBench and LiveCodeBench while using roughly 33 to 66% of the vanilla tokens for the larger models (R1-Distill-Qwen-32B: 32.5 to 40.4%; some Qwen3 cells as low as 9%). The exact first solution right in over 92% figure is still one paper (Chen) and was not reproduced on code or planning.

problem: Minor: the 72% ranking accuracy is for Chat routing, Math and Code are 84% and 74%.

Numbers match, but the GARP result is GPT-3.5-Turbo only (2023), not 'current LLMs'; the .93-.94 and .41/.28 figures are for GPT-4-Turbo/GPT-4o predicting human gamble choices (correlation of predictions with max expected value), a different study and task, not the same models acting as budget optimisers.
fix: In a 2023 revealed-preference study, GPT-3.5-Turbo was near-perfectly consistent on budget-allocation tasks: no GARP violation in 81-95 of 100 runs per domain, mean CCEI .997-.999 vs humans .963-.985. Separately, when GPT-4-Turbo and GPT-4o predict human gamble choices with chain of thought, their predictions correlate .93-.94 with maximum expected value vs .48 for humans (zero-shot only .41 and .28). Consistency is not optimality; framing and temperature matter.

problem: Numbers match, but 'smaller' is wrong: Hagendorff et al. report intuitive errors below 5% for the smallest early GPT-3 models (up to babbage), 21% for curie, 70-90% only for the large davinci family.
fix: Older large models (the GPT-3 davinci family) show human-like intuitive errors on CRT-type tasks (GPT-3 fails all 3 CRT items intuitively in Binz and Schulz; 70-90% intuitive wrong answers vs 55% for humans in Hagendorff et al.), whereas the smallest early GPT-3 models give them below 5% of the time; the effect largely vanishes in ChatGPT-4 (96% correct, 0% intuitive).

problem: The 42.4% and 54.8% are aggregated across all five PUMA benchmarks, not specific to hard items; the hard-item framing is the note writer's inference (Liu and Wang only say consistency stops become less stable on MATH-500 and GPQA).
fix: Answer-level stop signals often fire too early: in PUMA, aggregated over five benchmarks, 42.4% of confidence-based and 54.8% of consistency-based stop failures were cases where the full chain would have self-corrected to the correct answer; PUMA reports that Answer Convergence stops aggressively but suffers severe accuracy collapse; Liu and Wang find label-free stops become less stable on the harder MATH-500 and GPQA. DeepConf notes high confidence on incorrect reasoning paths as a limitation. This is the cost of a wrong stop.

problem: Pilot-vs-probe comparison absence not checkable; 72% is Chat routing, Math 84, Code 74.
Minor: Glebkin dates the first systematic description to Fauconnier and Turner 1994; the 1998 paper is the key expanded statement, not strictly the first.
Glebkin's point is lack of experimental support and unclear principles rather than an explicit 'does not predict'; Gibbs's position is via Wikipedia only.

Glebkin (the second-hand source) actually argues the counterfactual studies show the three-phase schema does not work; the claim's correction that the primary studies do not test operation order is supported by the primary papers.
Negative search claim (no large replication) cannot be verified from sources; sample sizes all match.
Minor: 'more ideas' is measured only in PopBlends; Creative Blends contributes usability (SUS d=0.80) and Scideator creativity-support ratings, not idea counts.
Sato's cited separate quantitative study (2505.00557) was not read; claim is limited to the text read, which holds.
Misty adds no diversity measure; claim is about tools with no quality evidence, which holds. Both sources checked (CHAMELEON via fetch).

Numbers (55%, 59%) match, but 'scratchpads help in distribution only' is too strong: Nye et al. report scratchpad-trained models improve on out-of-distribution 9-10 digit addition with scale; Faith and Fate only find the scratchpad boost diminishes to zero as complexity grows.
fix: Models fail multi-step computation held in the model as size grows (3-digit multiplication 55% ChatGPT, 59% GPT-4; accuracy decays toward zero on larger sizes); explicit scratchpads help, but in Faith and Fate the gain shrinks to zero as complexity grows and fine-tuned GPT-3 does not generalise, whereas Nye et al. find scratchpad-trained models improve out-of-distribution on 9-10 digit addition as model size increases.

problem: Human half holds (Burnett and Richmond abstract: benefit larger when forced; Engeler and Gilbert / Ngai and Gilbert: reminder over-use). But the LLM comparison in Chen et al. is mixed: model-chosen Code Interpreter beat forced all-code for GPT-4o (83.5 vs 80.3) and GPT-4o-mini (80.8 vs 77.4) and lost only for GPT-3.5 (64.5 vs 68.1).
fix: In humans, a meta-analysis (abstract only) finds the offloading benefit larger when forced than when chosen, and people over-use reminders from biased confidence. For LLMs the evidence is mixed: forced code usually beats text, model-chosen code (Code Interpreter) beat forced all-code for GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini but not GPT-3.5, and a program-controlled code+text+summary combination was best overall in Chen et al.

problem: Minor: Ngai and Gilbert 2026 find a different training (5 trials with feedback) modestly lowers reminder bias, so 'partly explained' fits; Engeler and Gilbert figures match.
Higher reward effect appears only as a second-hand citation (Dupont 2021) in Chiu and Gilbert; load, delay and cheap-write findings were checked directly.

Let it go (N=320) shows people given a 100% reliable reminder reduced (not stopped) intention-related thoughts and retrieved worse when it was withdrawn; the removal-costs-more result comes from one route-planning task (Florean et al.), not offloading in general.
fix: In a prospective-memory experiment (N=320), people who had experienced a 100% reliable reminder reduced intention-related thinking and retrieved worse when it was unexpectedly withdrawn; in two route-planning experiments, removing an offloading aid hurt performance more than introducing one helped.

problem: MINJA (Dong, He, Tang, Xiang et al.) and the experience-following paper (Xiong, He, Tang, Xiang et al.) share authors Pengfei He, Jiliang Tang and Zhen Xiang, so they are one research group; numbers 98.2% and 76.8% do match MINJA.
fix: Model-written memory records can be poisoned and agents then follow them (MINJA: injection success 98.2%, attack success 76.8%); a related paper from the same group reports experience-following, where stored errors propagate. No study measured whether agents detect a corrupted store on their own (not verified).

problem: Size-100 figures hold at pB=0.501, n=1000; Rosenstock et al. extend Zollman's model but are different authors.
Debate or Vote says majority voting accounts for 'most' of MAD's gains and the martingale result is theoretical; Stop Overvaluing independently finds MAD rarely beats CoT/SC.
Minor: 3.6-34.4% covers three models in one study (Wu et al.), not all LLMs.
Minor: Li et al. report the larger gain with task difficulty as relative gain within and across GSM8K/MATH, while the quoted absolute ranges (GSM8K bigger than MATH) do not themselves show it.
The sources study post-solution Aha! ratings and perceived difficulty, not felt closeness/warmth during solving; Webb even notes warmth ratings were a different measure.
fix: Aha! ratings (post-solution judgments of insight) behave like inferred metacognitive judgments built from cues such as processing fluency, solution correctness and a correct first move, rather than direct readouts of the underlying problem-solving process (Wiley & Miller 2026, N=377; Moroshkina 2024; Webb 2016).

problem: Numbers match R1-Distill-Llama-8B, but ECE reaches 0.13 for other reasoning models, and the non-reasoning result is a probe trained on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct performing much worse, not a transfer of the reasoning-model probe.
fix: In long-CoT reasoning models (mainly R1-Distill-Llama-8B), hidden-state probes predict correctness of intermediate answers with in-distribution ROC-AUC above 0.7 (about 0.82-0.84) and ECE mostly below 0.1 (0.03-0.10 for Llama-8B; up to 0.13 for other models); transfer between GSM8K and MATH is good but calibration is poor on harder AIME (ECE 0.25-0.31), and a probe trained on the non-reasoning Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct performs much worse.

problem: Token cuts (19-85%) check out, but accuracy changes are not all small: UPAIR reports up to +16.67 points and DeepConf up to about +6 points (86.7 to 92.5), with other methods losing some accuracy.
fix: Confidence/answer-convergence based early stopping and selection methods (DEER, DeepConf, CoDE-Stop, answer convergence, UPAIR) cut tokens by roughly 19-85% depending on method and model, with accuracy about unchanged for some, small losses for others, and gains for several (up to +16.67 points for UPAIR on QwQ-32B AIME 2025).

problem: Both supporting papers (overthinking, underthinking) are from the same Tencent AI Lab group with heavily overlapping authors (Chen, Xu, Liang, He, Liu, Tu, Mi, Yu); the numbers (>92%, >70%) are correct.
Minor: Reflexion heuristic is 'more than 3 cycles' of identical action/response, not exactly 3.
Minor: 25% hint acknowledgement is Claude 3.7 Sonnet only (DeepSeek R1 39%); the CSQA drop is one GPT-3.5 setting.
Wink 5.21%, 2.18%/3.59% and MAST 15.7%/12.4% check out, but DeLoop's compressed-history loop rates are 38.5% (32B), 42.9% (14B) and 57.3% (8B); 26% is not a compressed-baseline rate.
fix: Real agent loops are common: step repetition 15.7% and unaware-of-termination 12.4% of multi-agent failures (MAST); loops 5.21% of coding-agent trajectories at Meta (Wink), but infinite loops only 2.18% (Sonnet 4.5) and 3.59% (Opus 4.5) in the same paper, so the rate depends strongly on the setup; under context compression exact-repeat loops reached 38.5-57.3% of CodeGym episodes (DeLoop, Qwen3-32B/14B/8B).

problem: Nazonazo numbers are right, but GPT-5 fell within the human 95% CI, CresOWLve has no human comparison, and a universal 'no study' absence claim cannot be established from these sources.
fix: Most evaluated models fall well below humans on insight-riddle benchmarks (Nazonazo: non-reasoning models average 7.6% and reasoning models 17.6% vs a human mean of 52.9%, with GPT-5 inside the human 95% CI); we found no study that gives LLMs the classic human progress-monitoring paradigms (anagram solvability, warmth, magic tricks).

problem: Minor: 'matched' OnTrack recall is stated as L1 heuristics and rule baseline matching or exceeding the full system's recall.
Minor: 'at or below chance' for organic failures is length-controlled AUROC about 0.53-0.54, i.e. near chance.
Minor: the 0.048 median SD is across repeated attempts on the same problem, not within one solve; AUC 0.86 is TextCraft Qwen-2.5-7B as stated.

Numbers match Guggenmos 2021 (400 trials recommended; 2.4% negative, 4% above 1.5; 4% and 10% in studies under 200 trials), but b05 and b06 are the same paper and Fleming 2017 does not test the trial-count threshold, so the claim rests on one study.
fix: In one test-retest study (Guggenmos 2021), regular M-ratio needed about 400 or more trials per subject for acceptable reliability (r about 0.7 at 400-600 trials in real data; only about 0.4 at 60% accuracy even then); extreme values occurred in 2.4% (negative) and 4% (above 1.5) of subjects overall, and 4% and 10% in studies under 200 trials.

problem: Minor: Xiong's 54.8 GSM8K baseline appears to be the Top-K (M=1) row, while the CoT verbalized baseline on GSM8K is 74.4; the paper itself states 54.8 to 92.7, and 69.2 to 73.0 is the five-dataset average.
Brewer/Sampaio/Bajsanski/Litvinova are cited within Koriat's review, not opened separately.

Numbers check out (Farquhar 0.790 vs 0.691/0.698/0.687 over 30 combinations; Kuhn 0.77 vs 0.66 CoQA, 0.83 vs 0.79 TriviaQA, where the baseline is the count of semantically distinct answers), but Kuhn 2023 and Farquhar 2024 are one group's (Kuhn, Gal, Farquhar) paper and its follow-up, with no independent replication.
fix: Semantic entropy (grouping sampled answers by meaning) predicted correctness better than comparison baselines in the originating group's two papers: Farquhar et al. 2024 (30 model-task combinations, 10 generations) AUROC 0.790 vs naive entropy 0.691, P(True) 0.698, embedding regression 0.687; Kuhn et al. 2023 CoQA 0.77 vs 0.66 and TriviaQA 0.83 vs 0.79 against the count of semantically distinct answers. The authors state it does not help with systematic errors.

problem: Numbers are correct (Mazancieux 2020: N=181, five of six cross-task meta-d'/d' correlations, only 2 of 6 with nonhierarchical Pearson), but the claim rests on one study; the Fleming and Lau review listed second only mentions Weil 2013 on adolescence.
fix: In one preregistered study (Mazancieux et al. 2020, N=181, four 2AFC tasks), five of six cross-task correlations in metacognitive efficiency were credible under a hierarchical Bayesian model (only two of six with nonhierarchical Pearson correlations), suggesting partial domain generality.

problem: Minor: 'No study yet uses confidence computed from sample agreement' is an absence claim that the sources cannot establish.

Numbers match Anderson and Pichert (+7.1% vs -2.9%, F(1,35)=9.57; -21% in Exp 2, t(15)=5.36), but a11 and a12 are one report and a13 is the same authors' companion report, so it is one lab's work; also the Exp 1 old-perspective loss (-7.2%) was not significant.
fix: In one lab's experiments (Anderson and Pichert), shifting perspective raised recall of newly relevant ideas (+7.1% vs -2.9% for no-shift controls, N=39) and, in a shift-only design without control, lowered recall of old-perspective ideas (-21%, N=16); the Exp 1 loss of old-perspective information (-7.2%) was not significant.

problem: Minor: only OSF abstracts were readable; the 'beats visual similarity' result is conceptual dominance when features compete (equal magnitude in isolation per swy32), and the no-category-arrangement control comes from one lab (Tompary and Thompson-Schill), with Xu et al. reporting it secondhand.

Attractor ordering, toxicity and model differences are confirmed in Perez et al., but the GPT-4-faster-than-humans velocity result is from Kumar et al. on binary grid boards, not text chains, and the claim does not scope it.
fix: Serial-reproduction chains converge on attractors in LLMs: attractor strength Continue > Take inspiration > Rephrase; toxicity the strongest attractor property among the four tested; strength varies by model (Llama3-70B and GPT-4o-mini weaker). Separately, in a binary-grid-board serial-reproduction task GPT-4 chains had higher chain velocity than human chains.

problem: The 86.91-87.17% QuALITY scores correspond to ~2.4-2.8x extension (ReadAgent-P 1-6 pages, ReadAgent-S), the ~3.5x setting scores 86.16%, and the 20x comes from NarrativeQA; the 1-page look-up was below full text (84.13%); the Spens-Burgess paper shows gist stores produce schema intrusions, not accuracy support.
fix: ReadAgent gist memory with look-up extends effective context 3.5x to 20x across three tasks; on QuALITY it scored 86.16% (3.5x setting) to 87.17% (ReadAgent-S) vs 85.83% for the full text, though a 1-page look-up scored 84.13%; gist plus detail retrieval is a plausible schema-like store, with gist reconstruction producing schema-like intrusions in a related model.

problem: Larger-model stubbornness rests on only two model pairs (Llama2 7B/70B, Vicuna 7B/33B) in Xie et al.; fine as stated.

Both evidence lines for the counterfactual-accuracy result are the same Wu et al. paper; McKenzie et al. concerns inverse scaling and does not test counterfactual task variants; Wu says above random on most (not all) tasks, abstract says nontrivial.
fix: Counterfactual variants of familiar tasks lower LLM accuracy consistently while performance stays nontrivial (above random on most tasks) in one study (Wu et al. 2024, 11 tasks), suggesting reliance on default task schemas.

problem: Numbers match STALE; 'core agent failure' is the note's framing, and the Kwon paper's specific percentages were not seen but are not in the claim.

Acerbi and Stubbersfield coefficients match, but it is one study on one model (ChatGPT-3, Jan 2023); the Perez et al. line does not support it (toxicity collapses toward zero over chains), so the general 'LLMs' wording is wider than the evidence.
fix: In five transmission-chain experiments with ChatGPT-3 (Acerbi and Stubbersfield 2023), the model retained stereotype-consistent, negative, social and threat content over neutral content and resolved ambiguity negatively (coefficients 0.058 to 0.523, all P<0.01); other multi-turn work (Perez et al. 2025) finds toxicity decays in LLM chains, so the bias is not general.

problem: Direction misread: Kalyuga's review table gives example-problem vs faded d = 0.28 for novices and -0.26 for experts, and says experts benefited more from faded examples and problem-example pairs, so faded examples were NOT worse than example-problem pairs for experts (they were worse for novices).
fix: Fading alone did not beat a good fixed alternative for everyone: in Reisslein et al. 2006 novices did better with example-problem pairs than with faded worked examples (d 0.28) while experts did better with faded examples (d -0.26 for example-problem pairs); adaptive fading of worked steps beat fixed fading in Salden et al. 2010 (abstract only).

problem: Effect sizes 0.46, 0.55, 0.58, 0.25/0.37 match Kalyuga's 2007 review, but Corbalan's 0.37 load reduction compares shared control with fully system-controlled (also adaptive) selection, not with fixed instruction; the review is mostly the authors' own lab; the Seufert line is a different effect and not support.
fix: Learner-adapted instruction beat non-adapted instruction in several studies reviewed by Kalyuga (2007): knowledge gain effect sizes 0.46 (Kalyuga and Sweller 2004), 0.55 (2005) and 0.58 (Salden et al. 2006); Corbalan et al. 2006 found shared control better than system-controlled adaptive selection (posttest 0.25, cognitive load 0.37).

problem: The 136 study met its own power target (n=125 needed) so it is not an underpowered null, the N=36 'no differences' case has no listed source, and the apprentice study (Gure et al.) is a scaffold-style comparison whose interaction test was not seen in the abstract.
fix: Tests of prior-knowledge interactions often come out null or partial: no prior-knowledge x phase interaction in 136 graduate students (median split; sample met the 125 needed by the authors' power analysis), no effect of pretest in 63 pharmacy-technician students (Gure et al., abstract-level), and prior-knowledge moderation on only one of three outcomes (comprehension, three-way interaction) with N=102 (Herold and Seufert 2025).

problem: SkillsBench (full text) and Commey numbers match; the GPT models in Tang et al. showed no significant drop, and the Qwen 9/30 drop was one prompt condition, so 'peak then decline' holds only for smaller open models.
Numbers match Sprague (14.2/12.3/6.9) and Liu (36.3 point drop); the 95% equals-sign figure is in the Sprague abstract-adjacent text (as much as 95% of MMLU gain).

In Hou et al. the 282 of 515 are fading episodes that followed a learner's answer to the tutor's question (not a tutor 'direct answer'), the paper presents contingency as working, and it covers one tutor design; Macina's 15.5 to 2.2 is the supplying-answers move rate after RL in simulated dialogs.
fix: In a 131-learner study of an LLM tutor (Hou et al. 2026), of 515 coded fading episodes only 282 followed a learner's answer to the tutor's question (the rest followed a pasted plan or code, a bare 'it's fine', or other content), so learner uptake of questions was limited; in simulated dialogs with RL-trained tutors using a solution-handover gate, the supplying-answers move fell from 15.5% to 2.2% (Macina et al. 2026).

problem: Mason and Singh Table 1 numbers match (18/31/44% are for the 7 Chi problems, version II); the Wolf 10.8 vs 11.4 category counts were not visible in the abstract, though the stacker/spreader variance finding was.

Mason and Singh think-aloud (4 students, 'friction' vs vague 'force') confirmed; Hardiman's abstract supports novices using deep structure and surface hurting experts, but the 66% vs 26% figures could not be checked (paywalled).

Shi (72.4/6.0), Mirzadeh (65%, o1-preview -17.5), Rajeev (1.50 to 4.50%), Rodionov (up to 74%, IMOAnswerBench) and DAGGER (Qwen3-8B drop 14.2-19.9) all match full texts; 'smaller in absolute terms' is the note's comparison, not a claim in a single source.

Shi Table (CoT 6.0 to LTM 18.0 macro, LTM+SC 45.0, exemplars 76.8/14.0) and Mirzadeh 8-shot NoOp within one SD match; DAGGER 359 vs 3,128 tokens compares against a different (Qwen3-8B reasoning) system.
Zhou 99% vs 16%, Self-Discover 21/25 (PaLM 2 zero-shot), BoT distiller ablation and AoT-over-CoT all in the full texts; Self-Discover result is zero-shot on one model.
RE2 gains of 1.23-5.25 are category averages for davinci-003 (not per-dataset range); R&R says gains marginal on CSQA; 'not a deep-structure effect' is interpretive.

Webb OR 1.88/0.37 and ConceptARC GPT-4 below 30% on 15 of 16 concepts match full texts; Lewis and Mitchell found GPT models below humans even on the standard alphabet, and the ConceptARC result does not by itself show surface tie.

Sclar 76 points, Mizrahi Kendall W .71-.91 (labelled medium) match; Lampinen is the second author of the 'Language models show human-like content effects' paper (first author Dasgupta), and the listed 'synthesis' source is just GSM-Symbolic.
Chen (1,953%, over 92%) and Liu (94.0 vs 57.7) match; the Levy et al. source is unrelated to the claim, and the 'gate S2' conclusion is the note's own inference.

Nelson et al. abstract says the four theories fit existing human data equally well, supporting the 'cannot tell apart' point, but its own experience-based result favours probability gain over information gain, so 'EIG-like' is a broad label; Coenen review frames OED as successful across many tasks.
BED-LLM Table 1 numbers match (GPT-4o 93 vs 70, Mistral-Large 95 vs 53, Qwen 95 vs 61, Prompt-Only 45/33/45); 'code-side arithmetic is what matters' is the note's inference.
Kobalczyk Table 2 matches (GPT-3.5 t=10: 6.2 vs 4.1, a higher-is-better score); Chan et al. says probabilities are 'over- or under-confident', and the conformal result is on 20 Questions and MediQ.
Zhang et al. Table (GPT-4 0.31/0.50, 17.8/17.3 turns, open models Vicuna/Mistral at or below 0.22) and Mazzaccara zero-shot EIG 0.29-0.35 match; the 0.29-0.35 figures are for Llama-2-Chat 7B only.
Mazzaccara Table 1/2 numbers match (INLG 56.7 to 68.9, Things 51.1 to 61.1, Celebrities 71.1 to 72.2, FT 46.6, BigBench success 17.2 to 31.0 but EIG 0.31 to 0.28); 'out of scope' is a design remark.
Handa et al. text matches (OPEN beats LM-only, open-ended beat pairwise but overshadowed by OPEN prediction, 44 users in the OPEN arm, about 40 per setting); the Li et al. line only gives context.

Binz and Schulz abstract states no signatures of directed exploration, fails in causal reasoning, solves vignette tasks; the 'no re-test with 2025-26 models' is a search-negative the sources cannot confirm; Yiu et al. is tangential.

Laban: 39% average drop across six generation tasks and 200,000+ simulated conversations confirmed in the paper; Zhang and Choi supports only the 'decide when to ask' design idea, not the degradation.

Stechly et al. Table 1 gives sound external critique over self-critique gains of about 32-36 points (Game of 24 3 to 36/38, Graph Colouring 2 to 34-38, Blocksworld 55 to 87 with all-error feedback, only +5 with binary feedback), not 30 to 50; VisGym tested four models (GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Qwen3-VL, GLM-4.5V), not every frontier VLM. Zhang and Norman (no errors on external rules) and Fansher (more success, more moves with display) are confirmed.
fix: For humans, the same formal puzzle (Tower of Hanoi isomorph) is much harder when its rules must be held in memory than when the display enforces them, and external rules produced no rule errors. For LLMs the isolated test is still missing: in GPT-4, sound external critique beat self-critique by about 32 to 36 points in Game of 24, Graph Colouring and Blocksworld (best feedback type), and removing environment text feedback about invalid actions lowered all four VLMs tested in VisGym, but rules-in-prompt vs rules-in-checker on one puzzle was not found. A 2022 human study qualifies it: the external display raised success but cost more moves.

problem: Minor: VisGym 3-4x is 'often' (most tasks) not universal; claim wording covers it.
'Base external representation' is framing, not a measured finding; scale/training dependence supported by Wei (emergent at ~100B) and Nye (trained scratchpads).
Minor: Cramers V 0.032-0.073 compares baseline vs code-augmented interface per form; the five models include older ones (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama 3.3 70B).

The last clause is stated as settled fact but is a philosophical position (Starzak 2016, Heyes 2012 on Morgan's failure to justify the canon), not an established finding; a01 and b01/a13 duplicate sources (Mercado commentary listed twice).
fix: Morgan's canon is a rule of thumb for lowering over-interpretation, not Occam's razor (Mikhalevich et al. 2017; Heyes 2012): a simpler explanation does not mean a simpler mechanism, and Starzak (2016) and Heyes (2012) argue that nothing independently justifies preferring explanations lower on the scale.

problem: Minor: Pfungst reports 89% (about 50 of 56), so 50/56 is back-computed; Samhita and Gross confirm the method but give no percentages.

Kulke and Rakoczy found a mixed pattern (some conditions replicate, e.g. belief-congruent looking significant in some FB conditions; 7/12 is one condition, FB1, in adult Study 1), not first saccades at chance across the study; one failed replication plus a mixed-results study does not show poor replication in general.
fix: Implicit anticipatory-looking false-belief effects are inconsistent in humans: a two-lab preregistered replication of Southgate et al. (2007) found 49/90 infants (54%) anticipated at familiarisation and 22/49 at test (p=.57), and a three-experiment study (Kulke et al. 2019) found mixed results, with first saccades at chance in some conditions (e.g. 7/12 in FB1, BF10 0.64) and no unambiguous evidence for reliable spontaneous ToM.

problem: Minor: Zhang et al. frame GSM1k gaps as contamination/overfitting, and Wu et al. appears three times in the evidence (one paper).
Minor: b21, b22, d06, d07 are all the same SimpleToM paper (one source); reminder lifted Claude-3.5-Sonnet judgement 24.9 to 84.1 as stated.
Minor: Oren et al. say detection threshold is around 4 duplicates but abstract also says sometimes detected at only 2 copies.

Heyes names association-blindness and simple-mindedness as the two errors, not anthropomorphism; anthropomorphism as an error comes from Morgan's tradition and other sources, not from Heyes or Pang et al. Ghost control and nine-condition design are confirmed.
fix: Neither pole is a default: association-blindness and simple-mindedness (Heyes 2012) are both errors, and anthropomorphism is the error Morgan's canon guards against, so a simple and a rich rival should each be listed with a discriminating test (Heyes' ghost control, Penn and Povinelli's multi-condition competitive protocol) rather than one assumed.

problem: Minor: Kendall W upper value is .787 (about .79); 'no study gives a stopping number' is an absence claim not verifiable from sources.
Minor: ConStat attributes Phi GSM8k gap to reasoning-focused training as a suspicion; claim states 'can also come from training style' which is consistent.
Minor: the CSQA 75.8->38.1 and GSM8K 74.7 figures are rounds 1 and 2 respectively; Huang et al. attribute prior gains to oracle labels.
Minor: 'diagnosis not repair' is a broad framing; human-feedback result is from 16 participants and 40 programs.

Chen et al. show self-debug also helps without execution when the model explains its code (Spider +2-3%, MBPP Codex 61.4 -> 64.4 with explanation, 66.2 with trace); only simple yes/no feedback hurt (Codex MBPP 57.6), so execution feedback is not the sole driver.
fix: Self-debug gains are largest with unit-test execution feedback (up to +12 on TransCoder and MBPP), while without execution plain pass/fail feedback can hurt (Codex MBPP 61.4 -> 57.6) but code explanation or trace feedback still helps (Codex MBPP 64.4 and 66.2; Spider +2-3%).

problem: Only Aggarwal et al. compare stopping rules head to head (Beta, Dirichlet, CRP similar; Beta consistently beats entropy and majority; random worst); SPRT (ConSol), difficulty prior (DSC) and RASC are separate papers on different models and benchmarks with different savings (up to 84.8-86.2% tokens, 56-65% cost, ~70% samples), so 'similar savings' across all five rules is not shown.
fix: In a head-to-head comparison (Aggarwal et al. 2023) the Beta, Dirichlet and Chinese-restaurant-process stopping rules reach similar savings while Beta beats entropy and majority-only at equal cost and random stopping is worst; SPRT (ConSol), difficulty-prior (DSC) and quality-weighted (RASC) stopping each report 56-86% cost or token savings versus self-consistency, but on different models and benchmarks and not compared against one another.

problem: 40 to 85 percent mixes CISC's average 41-46% sample reduction (some cells over 67%) with DeepConf's best-case 84.7% token cut; DeepConf savings run 15-85% depending on setting and its aggressive variant can lose accuracy, so 'same accuracy with 40 to 85 percent fewer' is too uniform.
fix: Weighting votes by model confidence reaches the same accuracy with fewer samples or tokens: P(True)-weighted voting (CISC) cut samples by 41% at 5 and 46% at 10 samples on average (some settings over 67%), and trace-confidence filtering (DeepConf) cut tokens by 18-85% depending on variant, with the aggressive variant sometimes losing accuracy; between-question calibration (ECE, Brier) does not predict the gain, within-question discrimination does.

problem: Liu and Wang report models converge to their final answer after about 60% of reasoning steps on math, so about 40% (not 60%) of reasoning follows convergence.
fix: Reasoning models can stop their own chain early: exiting at a high-confidence trial answer (DEER) cuts chain length 19.1 to 80.1 percent with accuracy changes of +0.3 to +5.0 points, and on math tasks models typically converge to their final answer after about 60 percent of the reasoning steps, leaving about 40 percent of the chain after convergence.

problem: Minor: 'a verifier is needed to turn coverage into accuracy' is an interpretation; Brown et al. show majority voting and reward models plateau near 100 samples.
