Only Zhao et al. show a verifier (model self-verification) beating agreement at equal sample count; Brown et al. find reward models plateau like majority voting (40.50 to 41.41 range) and Setlur et al. compare verifier-based vs verifier-free fine-tuning, not selection at equal sample count, so 'tests, ... reward-based' beating agreement is not shown.
fix: At equal sample count, picking by repeated model self-verification beat picking by agreement (Gemini 1.5 Pro, 200 samples: AIME 8 vs 4 of 15, LiveBench Reasoning 97 vs 75 of 140), while agreement and off-the-shelf reward models both plateau near 100 samples (MATH Llama-3-8B majority 40.50 to 41.41 percent from 100 to 10,000 samples vs coverage 82.9 to 98.44). Equal-token comparison is not measured (verification used 50 calls per sample).

problem: Numbers check out, but Hanks et al. 2014 found the monkey LIP termination threshold did NOT differ between speed and accuracy regimes (speed pressure acted via an evidence-independent urgency signal), so 'in humans and monkeys the instruction moves the bound' is wrong for monkeys; Hawkins et al. speaks to fixed vs collapsing bounds, not the instruction effect.
fix: In humans a speed-accuracy instruction moves the diffusion boundary (boundary 0.109 vs 0.152, N=14; median RT 120-200 ms longer in the accuracy regime, accuracy changing 0-6%), and 72 of 85 humans are best fit by a fixed (non-collapsing) bound; in macaques the neural termination threshold was similar across regimes (RT 176 and 159 ms longer under accuracy emphasis), with speed pressure acting through an evidence-independent urgency signal. No LLM test of a careful-versus-fast instruction against a diffusion boundary was found; closest proxies are prompt-based token budgets.

problem: Minor: the -0.1 at 3.3x fewer samples is the maths category (73.2 to 73.1); the all-category average is -0.04, and the LLM comparison is a lowered adaptive bound vs fixed 40 samples.

Minor: the 62.5 and 42.4 are averages of 64 (Llama-2 7B accuracy 7.68 on MATH); 'hard items run to the cap' is an inference from averages, not per-item data. RASC (Abstract Algebra 8.54 vs 6.15 College Math samples) gives a second consistent data point.
Minor: the GPT-4o date CoD/CoT rows are mis-ordered in text extraction but consistent with 88.1 vs 90.2; TALE-EP's 67% token cut came with an accuracy drop (81.03 vs 83.75).

Minor: 'boundary a is a distance in accumulated-evidence units, not defined as logLR' is an inference; Ratcliff and McKoon define it as the evidence needed to decide, and state that diffusion analyses do not explain how criteria are set.

Hato et al. support bound dependence on model (R2 .99 to .77, boundary overestimated under misspecification), but the 114,803 to 37,537 WAIC figure (Sun et al.) is a model-fit improvement from adding trial-level predictors, not evidence that fitted bound values change.
fix: Fitted bound values depend on the model: boundary recovery R2 drops from .99 to .77 and boundary separation is overestimated when Levy-flight data are fit with a Wiener DDM (Hato et al. 2025). Separately, adding trial-level (systematic) drift predictors improved WAIC from 114,803 to 37,537 in a recognition-memory dataset (Sun et al. 2026), showing that the standard model is a poor fit, though that paper does not report resulting bound shifts.

problem: Minor: Chen et al. show non-monotone curves 'often' on the four datasets (Vote rises then falls on MMLU Physics; Filter-Vote does the reverse), not uniformly up-then-down on all four; the absence claim about error-rate numbers cannot be verified from sources.
Abstract says efficiency improved by more than 4x vs best-of-N; 14x and 40 percent cost confirmed; 'matched' wording is close.
Numbers match van de Ven Table (DGR 90.79, iCaRL 94.57, offline 97.94, EWC 20.01, SI 19.99); all numbers from one paper, DER supports regularisation failing in class-IL.
Chaudhry abstract gives 7-17% gain with one example per class; DER paper shows ER beating regularisation/other baselines; DER abstract itself is about logit-distillation variant.

12% and 6% oracle-retrieval figures verified in Fig 7 caption of Lampinen 2025 latent learning; near-zero/near-ceiling reversal result verified in the second Lampinen paper (same lab, so effectively one group).
All numbers verified in full texts (100->54 on 19-problem slice, 58.5->38.5, hold rate 0.88 vs 0.65, Mistral Large).

Stats verified (Ambrose z values; Liu 0.79 vs 0.37 p=0.020, 0.61 vs 0.54 p=0.16) but 'gain, not need' treats a non-significant need effect in one N=29 human study as evidence need does not matter; Liu's replay result is for combined utility (need x gain) and the theory predicts both.
fix: Reverse replay rose with reward size and fell with reward removal in rats (Ambrose 2016; forward replay did not change reliably); in humans (N=29) learning from non-local paths was faster for high-gain paths (alpha 0.79 vs 0.37, p=0.020) but the high-need difference was not significant (0.61 vs 0.54, p=0.16), so the data favour gain but do not show need is irrelevant.

problem: Ambrose z=3.57 vs 0.305 and Liu 160 ms backward replay tracking utility (p=0.003) with 30 ms forward replay p=0.74 all verified; note forward in rat removal experiment p=0.068 is n.s. only.

Remote (Karlsson and Frank) and unvisited-arm preplay (Olafsdottir) are supported, but none of the opened sources shows replay of 'rare' paths (Karlsson says nothing on rarity), and Olafsdottir preplay was weak in some animals.
fix: Replay is not limited to the animal's current location: awake rats replay a remote, previously run environment, and place-cell sequences preplayed a seen but not yet visited rewarded arm (cued arm only; Olafsdottir 2015, 4 rats).

problem: Davidson 263 events (40/26/33%) and 48 vs 25% for long events verified, Diba 841/887 and 395/464 verified in Mattar and Daw legend; Diba paper exists but the 36%/19% figures could not be re-opened (PMC blocked).
Schaul paper verified (median 48% to 106%, better than uniform DQN on 41 of 49); the evidence is essentially one paper listed twice plus Rainbow which does not carry these numbers.

ReLo (PER hurts SAC, Seaquest, SpaceInvaders), Fedus (limited benefit, n-step needed), Zhang and Sutton (large buffer slows learning), Panahi abstract (no prioritised variant consistently beats uniform) and Yoo (0.83 and 1.82 pp below at 4B) all verified.
Huang tables and Kamoi survey verified; note GPT-3.5 CSQA 75.8 to 38.1 is the first round, not second, and sources are one empirical paper plus a survey that cites it.
Huang oracle numbers (84.3, 89.7) verified; Kim RCI paper stops on ground-truth match; Kamoi flags RCI and Reflexion oracle use (Kamoi largely repeats Huang's point).
Tyen: GPT-4 52.87 best, oracle-location backtracking gains far exceed losses; ProcessBench is consistent.

Numbers verified (2 of 100 optimal colourings accepted, 1/100 self-critique, 84.45% false positives, 55 vs 88/100), but both papers are from the same lab (Stechly/Valmeekam/Kambhampati), so the two domains count as one source group.
fix: A model is a poor verifier of its own output on planning and constraint problems in one lab's studies: GPT-4 accepted 2 of 100 optimal colourings (Stechly et al.); 84% of invalid Blocksworld plans were accepted, and self-critique loops scored 1/100 (colouring) and 55/100 vs sound-verifier 88/100 (Blocksworld; Valmeekam et al.).

problem: Binary vs richer feedback results (colouring ~40% in all variants, Blocksworld 37/50 vs 43/50) verified, but both come from the same Kambhampati-lab papers, and colouring plain top-n sampling also reaches 40%.
fix: In two studies from one lab, with a sound external verifier the content of feedback mattered little (colouring about 40% for all variants, equal to plain resampling; Blocksworld binary 37/50 vs 43/50 with first error). The gain may be resampling plus a check, not critique.

problem: Figures verified (CRITIC +7.7 F1 and +7.0 math, Self-Debug up to +12, Reflexion HumanEval 91.0 vs 80.1) but 'reliable gains' is too strong: Self-Debug gains are +2-3 on Spider, Reflexion trails GPT-4 on MBPP (77.1 vs 80.1), and Olausson shows self-repair gains are modest and uneven per compute budget.
fix: Tool or execution feedback (code interpreter, unit tests, search) often gives gains in correction loops, though uneven: CRITIC adds about 7.7 F1 on QA and 7.0 points on math for ChatGPT; Self-Debug up to +12 with unit tests (+2-3 on Spider without them); Reflexion HumanEval 91.0 vs 80.1 but MBPP 77.1 vs 80.1.

problem: Olausson verified (1.05x, 0.97x, 33.3% to 52.6%); Self-Debug and Kamoi consistent but Olausson is the sole source of the numbers.
Huang table verified (44.0 to 67.0 Madaan; 81.8 to 75.1 improved prompt); Kamoi survey flags weak first prompt in Self-Refine but is derivative of Huang.
SCoRe (41.4 to 64.4, 15.8% to 1.4%) and RISE (+17.7, +23.9 GSM8K) verified in full texts; 'not available to scaffold-only agent' is an inference.

Verified: Huang 74.7%, Kumar 15.8% vs 4.6%, Zhang 81.3% >6 changes and are-you-sure on o1-mini/4o/V3/R1, Stav C2W at most 2.1% on SAT up to 13.25% and Gemini Pro HLE 10.56 vs 9.32; Zhang tasks are Yes/No and agent tasks, and 'main mechanism' is the authors' interpretation.
ReaLMistake abstract (low recall, prompt sensitivity) and ProcessBench (o1-mini 87.9 vs GPT-4o 61.9, 3,400 cases) verified; ProcessBench is step-level math errors, not the same task as ReaLMistake.
Reflexion table (HumanEval 0.80/0.91 FP 0.01; MBPP 0.80/0.77 FP 0.16 FN 0.59; 16.3% vs 1.4%), HotPotQA no-retry-gains baselines, and Stroebl K about 5 at ratio 4 all verified in full texts.

Snell verified: up to 4x less test-time compute than best-of-N, about 38% of correct answers flipped to wrong by the revision model, verifier or sequential majority vote needed; S2R/Kamoi support the training-dependence.
S2R verified (51.0 to 81.6 with 3.1k samples; equal-amount long-CoT SFT 80.2); Kamoi abstract supports no fair prompted success up to May 2024; the +1.4 is a single-run difference.

Stav SAT numbers, Self-Debug 61.4 to 69.4, 72.8 to 80.6, TransCoder 77.3 to 88.8 and Stroebl are right, but 'without execution the code gain vanishes' is too strong: without execution MBPP gains shrink (Codex simple 57.6 vs 61.4 but +Expl 64.4 and +Trace 66.2; GPT-4 76.0 to 76.4 vs 72.8; TransCoder Codex 83.4-83.9 vs 80.4).
fix: Where a cheap sound check exists, intrinsic revision pays: SAT revision at T=0: Mistral 34.62 to 64.96, Haiku 4.5 75.64 to 93.59, DeepSeek V3.1 78.63 to 92.74, with correct-to-wrong at most 2.1%. Code with real tests: Self-Debug MBPP Codex 61.4 to 69.4, GPT-4 72.8 to 80.6; TransCoder GPT-4 77.3 to 88.8. Without execution the code gain shrinks to about +3 to +5 points and for MBPP Codex simple feedback is below baseline (57.6 vs 61.4). No study compares check-and-fix with best-of-n at equal calls on a 2025 model.

problem: KOMBINE does report an abstraction bottleneck (blends coherent 97.1% given a valid generic space), but its tasks give the model both inputs, so it does not test retrieval of distant-domain sources; AnaloBench shows retrieval from a bank is hard but does not isolate abstraction from retrieval.
fix: In KOMBINE, finding the shared abstraction (generic space) is the bottleneck for LLM blending, not building the blend (coherent blend 97.1% given a valid generic space); separately, AnaloBench finds retrieving an analogous story from a large bank is near random for long stories. Whether the retrieval or the abstraction step is the harder one for distant-domain sources was not tested directly.

problem: AnaloBench confirmed (340 analogies, GPT-4 human gap 6.9 to 28.8 points, near-random on long stories/large bank); gap is for GPT-4 specifically and 2024 models; ARN (far analogies below random) is consistent.
Webb text verified (GPT-3 near analogy p=0.0039, far analogy p=0.065 not significant, human advantage OR=0.37); 'not above chance' means not statistically significant, and results are GPT-3 only.

KOMBINE 19.9% (412/2,070) share at least 2 near-identical properties and Hivemind pairwise similarity typically above 0.8 both verified; 'same ideas' means near-identical, and similarity metrics differ between studies.

71.4% is zero-shot accuracy on picking the accepted ICLR paper of an accepted/rejected pair, not idea-quality judging; the 56.1% is human inter-reviewer consistency on ideas, where the best LLM judge (Claude-3.5 pairwise ranker) got only 53.3%, so the pair of numbers is not comparable.
fix: LLM judges are unreliable for idea quality: the best LLM evaluator reached 53.3% agreement on idea ranking, below expert inter-reviewer consistency of 56.1% (Si et al. 2024; the 71.4% figure is for accepted-vs-rejected ICLR paper prediction), and LLM-human Pearson r on research-ideation contribution is only 0.159 (best 0.234) (arXiv 2508.05470).

problem: AlphaEvolve ablation is repeated feeding of the same initial program vs evolutionary database (figure-only); 'recombination' and 'equal compute' are slight paraphrases.
Su et al.'s 40% figure is for the deterministic-reuse subsequence analysis; 'held longest' is the Utsho et al. interpretation (deeper scaling), a mild paraphrase.

Donnarumma et al. 2016 report the 72% as empirical data cited from ref [74] (Solway et al. 2014), not as their own primary data, and the model reproduces it after four voting iterations; N=806 and 11,117 tasks for Correa et al. are right.
fix: Human planning uses subgoals and bottlenecks: with two shortest Hanoi paths people chose the one-bottleneck path in 72% of cases (empirical figure cited by Donnarumma et al. 2016 from earlier work, ref 74; their subgoaling model also reaches 72%); people decompose tasks trading off utility and cost (Correa et al. 2023, N=806). No LLM test of a bottleneck rule was found.

problem: The 98.2% result is in arXiv 2410.02162 (LRM paper), cost ratio 139.36/52.12 = 2.7x.
Gains are marginal (+2.9, +3.1, -3.3 risk differences) and Illusion of Thinking says non-thinking is more accurate/token-efficient at low complexity under equal budgets.

All numbers (1.58x, 32/80 vs 7/80, never uncertain, repair vs fresh samples) come from one paper (Olausson et al. 2024) listed three times; Self-Refine and Self-Debugging do not test these results. The figures themselves match the paper.
Fallacy-CBR result is a fine-tuned small-model CBR classifier, a looser fit to 'LLM-as-adapter'; 1.94% is the mean cosine gain.
The 0.452 vs 0.753 are pooled over all alphabets (including the default Roman one), not counterfactual-only; the drop appears per-condition in the figure.
Snell's 4x is a 'up to' figure for the compute-optimal sequential/parallel split; 'nearly outperform' in text.
Snell's 38% is stated in text 'around 38%' (cites Qu et al.); Llama 58.8% is on Yes/No questions under an 'Are you sure?' prompt.
AWM is abstracted workflow memory, not raw retrieved examples, so it is a separate example in the same sentence.

Numbers (.56/.53/.12/.09, 32 stories, 20 probes, one-week delay) match the MAC/FAC paper, but all four listed entries are versions of one paper by one lab reporting one study (Gentner/Rattermann/Forbus 1993 data); Gentner and Markman 1997 is same-lab review with no new data.

The 30% vs 80-90% figures are the MAC/FAC authors' summary of Gick and Holyoak; the 2025 paper's own citation of Gick and Holyoak 1983 Exp 2 gives 29% (8/28) unhinted vs only 50% (14/28) hinted, so 80-90% is not the classic hinted rate across studies.
fix: Hints turn analogy use on: Gick and Holyoak's classic radiation-problem studies are summarized as about 30% unhinted vs 80-90% hinted (Forbus, Gentner & Law 1995), though 1983 Exp 2 is cited as 29% vs 50%; a 2025 business replication (n=199) found lower rates (factory 6.3% unhinted vs 8.7% hinted; HR 20.3% vs 37%).

problem: 'Well recognised' for ~75% is generous (humans 97.9%); far-analogy average is 39.6%, 33.9-45.3 are the two far-involving cases.

Numbers are right (0.81 vs 0.26; 20.2 calls and $0.071; +12.2 'up to'; 17.4 vs 17.0), but 'recovers most of the lost structure' holds only for the 151-candidate CPR-eval shortlist; on BRIGHT the GPT-4 rerank adds just +3.1 over BM25 (14.3 to 17.4) and BRIGHT scores stay low.
fix: An LLM reranker over a 151-candidate shortlist lifts CPR-eval Recall@10 from 0.26 (best retriever) to 0.81 (20.2 calls and $0.071 per query), and LLM-written reasoning queries add up to +12.2 nDCG@10 on BRIGHT, but on BRIGHT GPT-4 reranking of the top-10 adds only +3.1 over BM25 (14.3 to 17.4) with no gain from widening to the top-100 (17.0).

problem: EPR gains over the best baseline are +5.9 (BREAK), +7.2 (MTOP) and +2.9 EM (SMCalFlow), not a uniform +6 to +7; the RA-RFT 47.4 vs GRPO 43.3 comparison is against GRPO without retrieval (similarity-retrieval GRPO scored 37.7), so it does not show usefulness-aimed retrieval beating pure similarity.
fix: Retrievers or selectors aimed at usefulness or structure coverage beat similarity or heuristic retrieval for in-context examples: EPR gains +2.9 to +7.2 EM over the best baseline (BM25 or CBR) on BREAK, MTOP and SMCalFlow, and structure-coverage selection gains up to +23 points (SMCalFlow-CS 50.3 to 73.5); RA-RFT (47.4) beats GRPO without retrieval (43.3) on Qwen3-1.7B, where naive similarity retrieval hurt GRPO (37.7).

problem: Sultan and Shahaf 2023 (100 random ProPara paragraph pairs, 3% analogies; SBERT top-100 100% mostly self-analogies, FMQ 79%, FMV 72%) is the only data source; StoryAnalogy merely cites it, and the sample is one crowdsourced science-process dataset, not 'ordinary text'.
Dynamic Cheatsheet curated memory beats raw retrieval in roughly 9 of 16 model-task columns (not clearly 'most' for GPT-4o); other numbers match.
Minor: Dynamic Cheatsheet text says GPT-4o FH 6.7 on AIME 2024 but its Table 2 lists 13.3; claim follows the text.

Mallen et al. say adaptive-retrieval gains are much smaller for models under 10B (not that it rarely helps); FLARE says performance plateaus above 60% on 2WikiMultihopQA and only drops above 50% on StrategyQA.
fix: Gate retrieval instead of always retrieving: FLARE finds triggering retrieval for 40-80 percent of sentences usually performs well, with a plateau above 60 percent on 2WikiMultihopQA and a drop above 50 percent on StrategyQA; PopQA adaptive retrieval retrieves for about 40 percent of questions with davinci-003, and its gain is much smaller for models under 10B (which almost always retrieve); Self-RAG reports a large drop on PopQA and ASQA when it always retrieves the top passage (41.8 PopQA in that ablation; full-model row not recovered); HippoSpark gains turn unstable after more than five retrievals and 10.67 percent of instances needed none. The threshold shifts with model strength.

problem: Johari et al. (Section 5.6.1) report under 5% power loss and at most 10% run-length cost for misspecification of about ONE order of magnitude; at two orders the cost is up to 20% power and 40% run-length.
fix: Anytime-valid methods (mixture SPRT, confidence sequences, e-values) keep error guarantees under optional stopping. Mixture variance can be misspecified by about one order of magnitude with under 5% average power loss and at most 10% run-length increase; missing by two orders can cost up to 20% power and 40% run-length (Johari et al., Section 5.6.1).

problem: Minor: headline 2x-8x range is loose since ESC MATH saving is 33.8 percent (about 1.5x) and Vicuna-13B 1.9x; component numbers all match.
Only the DSC paper supports the numbers (listed twice); third source is a cross-paper summary pointing at the Adaptive-Consistency arXiv page, not an independent source.
Sequence matches Nersessian 2007 (vortex model, friction, idle wheel, generic abstraction); two of three sources are Nersessian herself, Clement 2022 only summarizes her Maxwell study.
Sources are mostly Nersessian's own work; SEP presents model-based reasoning as one perspective with critics and one of several approaches, not as established how scientists generate new concepts.
fix: Model-based reasoning (analogical, visual, simulative) is argued, chiefly by Nersessian, to be a key way scientists generate new concepts; this rests on historical case studies and ethnography of labs, argued by a bootstrapping method rather than statistics.

problem: Minor: adult accuracy is 0.88/0.91/0.89 across alphabets (0.91 on Greek); the first-pass 'humans 0.753' is over 136 Prolific participants.
Table 2 of Sourati et al. averages 12 rows (SBERT plus 11 LLM variants), not 9 systems; recomputing the far-vs-near column over those 12 gives 33.9.
fix: Models fail ARN when a far analogy competes with a surface-similar distractor: 29.1% for GPT-4 and 33.9% on average over the 12 systems in Table 2 (random 50%, humans 91.4%). The 39.6% headline is the mean of the two far-analogy cells (45.3 and 33.9) across all 12 systems, not a single-model far-analogy score. GPT-4 on far-vs-far is 57.1.

problem: MOOSE does not describe BM25 inspirations as far, and its BM25 novelty (3.364) is close to ground-truth hypotheses (3.380) and above ground-truth inspirations (3.000), so 'only modestly' and 'fall short of real papers' are not supported by MOOSE; the 85% figure is SciMON only.
fix: Retrieving inspirations raises GPT-4-judged novelty in MOOSE (2.957 with random inspirations to 3.364 with BM25 inspirations, close to the 3.380 of ground-truth hypotheses), while in SciMON expert comparison the original paper's idea was judged higher in technical level and novelty in 85% of comparisons, so generated ideas still fall short of real papers in that study.

problem: Minor: Gemini-2.5-flash -9.7 is not slight; o3/Claude/Gemini ConceptARC numbers are from Beger et al. text-mode rows.

LLM-SRBench's 31.5 and 28.1 percent are for the best system evaluated there (GPT-4o-mini-era models), while NewtonBench on shifted laws reports 75.9 percent (GPT-5) and 65.4 percent (Gemini-2.5-pro), so 'best only 28-32 percent' is not general.
fix: Benchmarks built on known equations may largely measure memory: on LLM-SRBench's transformed and synthetic problems the best system evaluated (LLM-SR with GPT-4o-mini) reached only 31.5 percent (LSR-Transform) and 28.1 percent (LSR-Synth) symbolic accuracy, although on NewtonBench's shifted laws frontier reasoning models reach 75.9 percent (GPT-5) and 65.4 percent (Gemini-2.5-pro), while non-reasoning models stay under 10 percent.

problem: Minor: the 59.1 percent figure is for the AMIE system and 78.3 percent is for o1-preview; both are 'in differential' style metrics from different studies.
Minor: Brodeur's 78.3 percent is 'correct diagnosis in differential', not strictly top-10; McDuff's is top-10.
Minor: Hager autonomous-mode drops are 13.3, 12.9 and 11.2 points (so 11-13, not 12-13); the 16-25 point gap to hospitalists is from the 80-patient reader study, not specifically autonomous mode.

Bean et al. report 20/20 scenarios only for GPT-4o (Llama 3 19/20, Command R+ 17/20) and the comparison is MedQA accuracy vs users' accuracy with the model; the Bedi 519/5 percent figure is true (JAMA 2025) but is not among the listed evidence.
fix: Benchmark knowledge scores do not predict interactive or real-case performance: in Bean et al., MedQA accuracy exceeded the accuracy of users working with the model in 20/20 scenarios for GPT-4o (19/20 for Llama 3, 17/20 for Command R+), with benchmark scores above 80 percent matching human scores below 20 percent in several cases; only 5 percent of 519 LLM health care evaluation studies used real patient care data (Bedi et al., JAMA 2025).

problem: Non-significant before/after-cutoff difference (79.8 vs 73.5, P=.59) in 143 cases and McDuff's 56-case no-overlap subset (55.4 vs 59.1 top-10) are reassuring but cannot show that contamination plays no role.
fix: Training-data contamination is not evident in the CPC results: o1 scored 79.8% before vs 73.5% after its training cutoff (P=.59, not significant) and McDuff's 56-case no-overlap subset gave 55.4% top-10 versus 59.1% on the full set; these small checks cannot rule contamination out.

problem: Goh 2024 had 50 physicians completing 244 cases (6 vignettes each), each case graded by 2 scorers, with kappa 0.66 among 3 graders; 'very few cases and raters' fits Brodeur's 6 landmark cases (P=.055) but not Goh's participant count.
fix: Physician-vs-LLM comparisons can rest on few cases: Goh 2024 used 6 vignettes (50 physicians, 244 completed cases, each graded by 2 of 3 scorers, weighted kappa 0.66) and Brodeur's o1 vs physician landmark comparison on the same 6 cases gave a 20.2-point difference with P=.055, not significant.

problem: Minor: 'modestly' is a judgment; McDuff search arm gain is 8.4 to 10.9 points (44.5 vs 36.1 or 33.6).
Minor: Schoenegger and Park GPT-4 0.20 is on only 23 questions and not significantly different from 0.25 (p=0.23); crowd benchmarks differ (0.149 Halawi, 0.07 Schoenegger).
Compute CI 9.69e25-8.65e28 is rounded to 1e26-9e28 in the claim; the Lu 2025 source only gives a different projection, so the numbers rest on Karger alone.
Only the Turtel paper was checked in full (its text supports ReMax 0.190, o1 0.202, ECE 0.062 vs 0.093, market 0.151, plain GRPO overconfidence); Lee et al. not opened.

In Schoenegger et al.'s preregistered mixed-effects model the -0.014 (frequency-based) and -0.011 (base-rate-first) effects are not significant (adjusted p=0.774); they are only significant in the simpler t-test analysis (-0.019 and -0.016, adjusted p 0.022 and 0.036). The superforecaster-written prompt made forecasts significantly worse, not just no help.
fix: Prompt effects are small: in Schoenegger et al.'s preregistered mixed-effects model only Bayesian-reasoning (+0.030) and propose-evaluate-select (+0.033) prompts differed significantly from control (both worse); frequency-based reasoning (-0.014) and base-rate-first (-0.011) were in the helpful direction but not significant after correction (significant only in a simpler t-test analysis at -0.019 and -0.016); the superforecaster-written conditional odds-ratio prompt was significantly worse than control.

problem: Minor: the decline is not monotonic (Sonnet 4 thinking 0.1597 is above Sonnet 4 0.1560; Sonnet 3.7 0.1712 above 3.5 v2 0.1690), which the claim half-acknowledges; second source (Lu) does not contain these numbers.

Wisniewski and Gentner 30% property-type and relation/hybrid/construal routes check out, but 'similarity favours property mapping' is contested: Bock and Clifton (2000) found no correlation between assessed similarity and property mapping (r=-.06) when pairs were randomly paired within category.
fix: Novel noun-noun phrases are not read only as a relation: relation linking, property mapping and hybrid construals all occur (about 30% of descriptions were property-type in Wisniewski and Gentner 1991). Similarity between the nouns promoted property mapping in Wisniewski (1996; 72% vs 48%), but Bock and Clifton (2000) found no correlation between rated similarity and property mapping (r=-.06), so the similarity effect is not settled; salience and natural-kind category also matter.

problem: Minor: the 88 default figure is from the N=99 arm while 248 vs 197 is from the N=83 arms (default there is 83); the 0.428 hybrid arm pools 40 sessions but also picks and refines the best ideas.

Both sources are from the SME authors' own tradition (SME 1989 paper plus Forbus et al. 1997); Markman 1997 page was blocked (403/Anubis) so the Markman-based line was not checked, but the SME quotes (surmise, permuted-argument check) match.

Clement and Gentner 1991 numbers verified in the PDF (3 experiments); Markman 1997 full text was blocked (only a search summary of four studies seen), and Markman worked in the same structure-mapping tradition as Gentner, so 'two labs' overstates independence.
fix: People prefer to carry over facts that hang off a shared causal system (systematicity) over equally plausible isolated facts: Clement and Gentner 1991 (3 experiments) and Markman 1997 (four studies) both found it, though both come from the same structure-mapping research tradition (Markman worked with Gentner), so they are not fully independent replications.

problem: The grounding rule (consistent with substitutions and structurally grounded; coffee-diameter example excluded) is verified in the SME paper, but no source shows that ungrounded surface-similar facts are the main error source.
fix: SME's grounding rule: a base fact is carried over only if it is consistent with the mapping's substitutions and structurally grounded in the mapped relations; ungrounded facts, such as the coffee/ice-cube diameter comparison in the heat-flow example, are not projected as candidate inferences.

problem: Numbers match Lewis and Mitchell Fig. and Stevenson et al. Table 2; note Webb, Holyoak and Lu (2024) contest the counterfactual-task reading, and Lewis/Stevenson/Mitchell share an author.
Slip: Webb et al. report GPT-3 far-analogy p=0.065 as not significantly above chance (not 'not above chance'); ARN 75.0/39.6 are averages over models.

Numbers match. Scope slip: the 3-7% typo cost comes from InstructGPT analogy generation (Bhavya et al. 2022), not analogy judgement, and the 20-100% swing is GPT-4 completion accuracy in one condition (Only RHS).

ARN error analysis (right high-level message but wrong pick; keyword-driven) is confirmed, but neither Clement and Gentner nor ARN says human justifications are post hoc; C&G treat them as evidence of explicit awareness of causal structure.
fix: GPT-4's written rationales in ARN often name the right high-level message while the choice is wrong, follow keywords, or fail to map the message back to the query narrative; a written rationale is therefore not evidence of a checked mapping.

problem: Slip: 76.3 vs 75.5 is selective vs always-verify on MATH500 (Qwen3-4B); the GenRM '8x' is 'up to 8x' on Llama-3.1-8B/MATH.

Slip: the Claude/Gemini fall to ~12% is only on REL-A3 30x30 (GPT-5.2 drops about 40 points but not to chance), and the RDKit run used a different model (GPT-5.4) with no paired no-tool run, which the claim itself flags.

In Zhang and Zhu Table (avg over seed + 3 challenge sets) Claude 3.7 Sonnet flipped is 77.04 vs ARISE 88.48 (and zero-shot 75.36), so flipping cuts all six models and the paper says performance 'consistently degrades'; the 'Claude exception' came from reading the Unsafe-only row (85.33) as flipped.
fix: Source correctness gates transfer more than relevance does. Self-generated examples that are random but right can match or beat relevant ones on math (accuracy of the example is the key factor; GPT-3.5 and GPT-4o-mini), though on BBH relevant examples were best. Retrieving labelled analogous cases lifts F1 for all six models tested (GPT-4o 43.3 to 75.4), and flipping the labels of the retrieved cases cuts the result for all six (GPT-4o 59.2; Qwen3-8B 46.3, below its 50.5 zero-shot baseline; Claude 3.7 Sonnet 77.0 vs 88.5 standard). Similarity-only case retrieval plateaus; outcome-based utility re-ranking added 3.8 points on average over the strongest baseline (MemRL vs MemP).

problem: Ages and proportions verified in Gopnik et al. 2017; the 4-year-old and adult data there come from Lucas et al. 2014 (same lab), so the two papers are not independent samples. Values are the share calling object D a blicket under the conjunctive rule.

GX-Chen et al. and Samiei et al. support the adult-like disjunctive bias, AND harder than OR, and near-perfect disjunctive accuracy for gpt-5 and deepseek-reasoner, but Samiei Table 1 shows gpt-5 using 10.2 vs 7.7 tests (conj vs disj) against average adults 9.6 vs 6.4, i.e. about 6% and 20% more, not 30-45% (the 40-44 s figure is seconds per test).
fix: Frozen LLMs show the adult disjunctive bias, not the child flexible prior, on conjunctive blicket tasks; AND rules are harder than OR rules across the 8+ models tested (GX-Chen et al. 2025). In 2026 active-exploration data (Samiei et al.), gpt-5 and deepseek-reasoner reach near-perfect disjunctive accuracy and gpt-5 approaches adult conjunctive accuracy, but gpt-5 uses somewhat more tests than average adults (10.2 vs 9.6 conjunctive, 7.7 vs 6.4 disjunctive) and about 40 s per test versus about 30 s for adults.

problem: Spearman 0.76 is read from the figure panel (info gain vs accuracy) in the PDF; the 32-hypothesis pruning statement is in Samiei et al. text; the two papers share authors.
Original study had one player per skill level (3 players); the popular summary (93%/33%) is a different, partly unpublished data set; larger-N replication exists (Gobet and Simon 1998, N=26).
Slip: the 79.5% vs 1.11% figures are after a mouse-move-time correction to the latencies, and the computer-version between-glance latencies were slower than in 1973.
Slip: Gathercole et al. attribute the 7-to-79 result to Chase and Ericsson (1981); Wikipedia is a secondary source saying 'almost 80'.

Fingerprint numbers (d=1.76, 44+44) and bridge suit-grouping are verified, but bridge is itself a game and the music r=.69 is a random-material skill effect that Sala and Gobet call an empirical anomaly probably due to less random music stimuli.
fix: The expert memory advantage for domain material is not limited to chess: fingerprint examiners beat matched novices on visual short-term memory for prints (d=1.76, 44 vs 44), bridge experts' hand memory depends on grouping cards by suit, and the random-material skill effect also appears in programming (r=.36) and music (r=.69, though Sala and Gobet treat the music value as an anomaly probably due to less random stimuli).

problem: Xiong and SELM numbers verified; slip: SELM's ablation is of components (no validation gate 42.5 vs full 56.5, no graveyard 50.4), not an add-all vs small-verified library comparison, so 'pruning matters most' rests on utility score/graveyard being the next-largest drops.
Slip: ReasoningBank text gives 46.0 (not 46.5) for 2 items; claim's 49.7 and 44.4 are right (Gemini-2.5-flash, WebArena-Shopping only).
FRI describes Torchcast as a proprietary multi-agent architecture using Torchcast-trained models plus commercial LLMs; no mention of reinforcement learning.
fix: Equal-token comparison of the parity-reaching systems is impossible from public data: ForecastBench imposes and records no token, tool or retrieval limits; Cassi, xAI and DeepMind methods are unpublished beyond a one-paragraph FRI description; Torchcast describes only a proprietary multi-agent pipeline using its own trained models plus commercial LLMs.

problem: BLF per-question figure is a 5-trial total (25-50k per single run); 80-200k and 0.14-0.55 USD are in BTF-2 text, not in the d14 table.
'Most of the edge' is an interpretation; BLF +2.3 is nonsignificant per Murphy; numbers all check.
1.5% is of retained search results (21/1377); BTF-2 notes Opus 4.7 (Jan 2026 cutoff) appeared to show parametric leakage.

SBERT 77.9% is a good score on near analogies (not a failure); TF-IDF same-domain is one figure caption on a single seed; the human claim rests on Hope et al. citing earlier work; Lewis and Mitchell show GPT-4 accuracy drops with paraphrase, suggesting rather than proving a sentence-overlap shortcut.
fix: Surface similarity pulls both humans and tools: SBERT alone scores 77.9% on near analogies in ARN but far analogies defeat models; in Hope et al.'s example the TF-IDF baseline returned same-domain items; GPT generators retrieved birds as the analogy in over 50% of cases for a flying-car task; and GPT-4 accuracy on story analogies fell when the correct story was paraphrased to remove sentence-level overlap with the source, suggesting it partly relies on that overlap.

problem: GPT-3 p-values (near sig, far n.s.) are not a direct near-vs-far test, and StoryAnalogy's 37.7-point human gap (abstract says 37.7%) is not a near/far comparison; the quoted numbers are correct.
The '169 credited vs 10 real marginal helps' agent-memory audit is not supported by either listed source, and Si et al. measure human-reviewer ratings, not the model's own rating.
fix: LLM-generated ideas lose 1.0 to 1.9 points of reviewer rating after expert execution while human ideas stay flat (Si et al.), and intrinsic self-correction lowers GPT-4 GSM8K from 95.5 to 89.0 (Huang et al.); these are indirect evidence, and no direct test of LLM self-rating of analogue usefulness was found.

problem: Negative-search claim cannot be verified; all three cited items exist and match (survey gap statement is in its discussion, not the abstract).
Greiner et al. counterexample and correction verified (Artificial Intelligence, 1989).
Entropy gain figures are from Shchekotykhin/Rodler ontology-debugging work reproduced in the Rodler thesis; the two thesis listings (a20, d12) are one source.
DRAGO uses deterministic solver diagnosis (contract checks, probes), which the claim calls conflict-based; numbers 11.8% vs 1.3% and Huang table values match.
The 33.30% vs 52.60% figures are correct (Olausson et al. Table 1), but the second source (Kang et al. AutoFL) does not address repair-feedback quality, so the claim rests on one paper.
AutoSD 73% vs 63% plausible-patch runs is correct (Kang et al. 2023), but the only other listed source (AIOpsLab) concerns a different point, so the claim rests on one paper.
UoT 38.1% is reported as a success-rate improvement over direct prompting without stating relative vs absolute; all other numbers match.
Two of the three listed sources are the same paper (AIOpsLab), and all numbers (61.54%, 45.45%, saturation) come from it; the third (Roy et al.) does not report them.

The 450-candidate maximum is from Grastien et al.'s power-network automata benchmark, not shown to be a weak-fault effect; 'wrong or empty diagnosis' is the researcher's inference, not stated by Reiter; Oswald et al.'s 25% is of all domains (94% were valid), not of valid domains.
fix: The consistency-based theory needs a correct behavioural model and offers no likelihood ranking (parsimony picks subset-minimal sets); in Grastien et al.'s power-network benchmark the solved instances reached up to 450 minimal candidates. LLM-built models are error-prone: GPT-4 PDDL models had 2 to 53 errors per domain, and the best model in Oswald et al. produced valid PDDL in 94% of domains but only 25% of domains were heuristically equivalent to the reference.

problem: UoT 38.1% is stated without relative/absolute clarification; 42.5 to 67.8 FloDial and +37.4 points BED-LLM verified.
Guan et al.: 59 feedback messages for 56 factual errors, of which 2 introduced new errors and 1 was a repeat, not 3 new-error corrections; the 25% equivalence is of all domains.
CDA/HA 0-12% holds for weak-fault models on c880/c1908; stuck-at modes reached up to 62% on c880; Bylander not checked.
Final 'flat prior is the safe default' is a recommendation, not a measured result.
Oracle numbers are listed inconsistently in the evidence (b21/c14 give GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 95.5; the paper table shows 84.3), but the claim quotes only the intrinsic numbers, which match.
In Zhong et al. Table 2 the +2.4 is for GPT-4-generated seed programs debugged with a GPT-3.5 backbone, not LDB run with GPT-4.
Abstract gives Code Llama 34B at 50% input prediction, so 'best open models under 50%' is a rounding borderline (table values ~47/44 without CoT).
The 18.0% vs 11.0% and linting/summarised-search ablation numbers are correct, but both matching sources are the same SWE-agent paper; AutoCodeRover and RepairAgent do not test interface design.

Minor: StarCoder SD null/negative result is HumanEval only (SD helped on MBPP), and LDB's +0.6 to +9.1 is the HumanEval range (paper says up to +9.8 overall); 44.4/10.3 are model averages while 75.0/42.5 is GPT-4-Turbo.

Only a15 (a secondary report of Macquet 2020) gives the 60-81/13-28/3-24 figures; a16 is a single-goalkeeper case study (simple match 46%, simulation 34%, diagnosis 20%) that does not support them, and neither source mentions firefighting or circularity.
fix: In Macquet's (2020) review of the RPD model in sport, as reported by a 2022 Frontiers article, 60-81% of experts' decisions were coded as simple match, 13-28% as diagnosis and 3-24% as evaluating a course of action; these codes come from the RPD scheme itself, so the result is partly circular (inference, single secondary source).

problem: Numbers check out (N=63, r=0.664, 44% of variance in evaluation error; Burns 64-81% of variance, via secondary report), but 'skill is largely fast pattern knowledge' is stronger than the sources: 44% leaves most error variance unexplained and blitz-standard overlap is a correlation, not proof of pattern knowledge.
fix: In chess, quick judgement improves with skill: Elo accounted for 44% of the variance in position-evaluation error after 5 seconds (N=63, r=0.664; Chassy et al. 2023), and rank scores in 5-min blitz tournaments accounted for 64-81% of the variance in rank scores based on standard games (Burns 2004, as reported by Vidulich and Tsang 2026), which leaves 19-36% unexplained.

problem: Minor: Maia's lowest accuracy (46%, 1900-model on 1100 players) equals Stockfish's max, per-band accuracy is about 51-53%; the tree-search degradation is stated in Maia 1 (10 rollouts), not Maia-2, and the two papers are the same research line (overlapping authors).

System-1.x numbers confirmed (Maze Navigation, 70.4% at 13.6 states vs 48.7 and 37.2). Thinkless abstract says it cuts the USE of long-chain thinking by 50-90%, not reasoning cost; Table 1 shows tokens falling only about 40-70% and some accuracy loss (e.g. MATH-500 0.861 to 0.795, Minerva 0.958 to 0.925 for the efficient row).
fix: Learned switching between fast and slow reasoning can sharply cut slow reasoning: Thinkless reduces the use of long-chain thinking by 50-90% on Minerva Algebra, MATH-500 and GSM8K, with token savings smaller than that and a small accuracy drop on some benchmarks; and on Maze Navigation a tuned mix of fast and slow planning (System-1.x, x=0.5) gets 70.4% valid plans at 13.6 states vs 48.7% (System-1) and 37.2% (System-2).

problem: All figures match (Adaptive-Consistency 3.3x avg, <0.1% drop; ESC 33.8-84.2%; CISC over 40%; Huang GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0). The SwiftSage stuck-counter reference (K13) was not among the listed sources and was not checked.

All numbers verified (1,953%, over 92%, 48.6% MATH500 and 35-46% on GSM8K/GPQA/AIME with small accuracy changes), but b15, b16, c09 and c10 are the same paper (Chen et al. 2412.21187); the survey and Cuadron et al. (agentic overthinking) do not report these figures, so the claim rests on one paper.
fix: Chen et al. (2024, single paper) report that o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models on '2+3', that the first solution round was already correct in over 92% of cases, and that self-training cut tokens 35-49% at near-equal accuracy (e.g. 48.6% on MATH500).

problem: Minor: the Keystone intervention was a multi-part bundle (checklist plus other measures), and both were uncontrolled before-after designs, as the claim itself implies.

Minor: c17 and d10 are the same Adaptive-Consistency paper, so independent sources are Adaptive-Consistency and ESC; figures match (3.3x avg, 3.2x in Table 5, 0.07 mean accuracy drop, ESC 33.8-84.2%).

Minor: DEER's 19.1-42.9% shorter paired with +0.9 to +4.8 accuracy for the three main models; +0.3 to +5.0 is the all-model range, and 'no accuracy loss' holds on average for these methods rather than every setting. b24 and d05 are the same probing paper.

Beta 0.03 ms is real (but Entropy rule is also 0.03 ms; Dirichlet/CRP ~95-101 ms). DEER latency cut 27.9-40.1% was measured on MATH-500/AMC, while the 19.1-42.9% token cut spans all benchmarks; the ranges overlap, and the paper says latency speedup vs length savings is superlinear, so 'latency only' is not supported.
fix: Stopping-rule cost differs: the Beta rule in Adaptive-Consistency takes about 0.03 ms per decision (as does the entropy rule; the Dirichlet and CRP rules take about 95-101 ms), while DEER's trial-answer probing adds overhead that its branch-parallel variant reduces (latency cut 27.9-40.1% for original DEER vs 36.3-58.6% for branch-parallel, on MATH-500 and AMC), so probe overhead should be counted.

problem: Both snell entries (b19, c07) are the same paper (Snell et al. 2408.03314) and the sleep-time paper does not support the claim; figures match the abstract (more than 4x efficiency vs best-of-N, outperforms a 14x larger model in a FLOPs-matched test where the small model has non-trivial success).
fix: Snell et al. (2024, single paper): allocating test-time compute adaptively by prompt difficulty improves efficiency by more than 4x over a best-of-N baseline, and in a FLOPs-matched comparison a smaller model with extra test-time compute can outperform a 14x larger model on problems where it has non-trivial success.

problem: Minor: the 82.2 to 87.3 to 70.3 curve and the parallel-voting advantage (up to 20-22%) come from DeepSeek-R1-Distill-1.5B on GSM8K/MATH-500; Gema et al. confirm inverse scaling on specific task families only (the claim says 'some tasks').

Minor: 'Prompt-only budgets help only inside a band' is the author's synthesis of TALE token elasticity and the DEER AIME24 remark; the TALE -68% is for GPT-4o-mini averaged over datasets, with accuracy 83.75 to 81.03; Budget Tracker result is Gemini-2.5-Pro on BrowseComp.

Minor: Fan et al.'s position correlation is -0.34 overall and -0.17/-0.38/-0.48 for N=5/10/20, so the quoted -0.34 to -0.48 mixes overall and N=20 values; the ROI-Reasoning test is a different 3-problem setup than Fan's, so 'fixable' is an inference across studies.
Minor: 0.94 is GPT-4o with chain-of-thought (other settings lower, e.g. zero-shot 0.28), on risky-choice problems, not bandits; sources b25/c22 are the same paper.

Minor: all figures match (Ontario OR 0.91/0.97; Michigan Keystone Surgery null in registry and Medicare studies; Matching Michigan 1 of 17 units transformed); 'effects shrink with stronger design and larger scale' and 'enforcement decides' are the author's interpretation, and Matching Michigan was an English programme.

Minor: Huang et al. also shows small non-negative changes on HotpotQA, and the claim's 'often hurts' fits CommonSenseQA and GPT-4 GSM8K best; Kamoi et al. confirm that no prior work shows success from prompted self-feedback except in specially suited tasks.

Minor: the sampling-vs-critique numbers (Game of 24: critique+sound verifier 36-38%, sampling k=25 42%) come only from Stechly et al.; on Blocksworld critique (83-87%) beat sampling (72%), so 'strong baseline' is domain-dependent; CRITIC supports only the general point that external tools drive the gain.

Minor: the +7.8 LiveBench reasoning gain is for Command-R+ only (GPT-4o gained under 1 point overall); the CM2 gains (+8/+10/+12) are over an SFT baseline on tau-bench, BFCL-V4, ToolSandbox; RLCF gains are relative to Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct.

Minor: scratchpad 8.8% to 20.1% is polynomial evaluation (few-shot), and the +4.5 is a PAL ablation where Codex 'executes' code in text (23.2 vs direct 18.7), so the three numbers are from different tasks; the scratchpad is itself written by the model, so 'external trace' is loose.

The counts (24 of 26 and 20 of 20 on-turn re-executions with the step already marked DONE) and SOPBench's procedure-completeness rule are accurate, but they show agents ignoring their own marks and a benchmark rule requiring verification calls, not marks written without action; the ledger arm actually beat the accurate checklist (0.70/0.79 vs 0.55/0.59), so 'compliance without doing' is not shown.
fix: In an LLM-agent study with a self-written ledger, 24 of 26 and 20 of 20 on-turn re-executions fired with the step already marked DONE in the agent's own ledger, so re-reading its own record did not prevent redoing steps (though the ledger still beat an accurate checklist); and SOPBench requires the check calls to precede each service call, so a trajectory that skips them fails even if the final database state is correct.

problem: Song et al. (CCPT, GPT-4o, emergent property induction): Base 40.8, CoT 42.4, SA(LLM) 43.8, SA(ConceptNet) 45.8, SA(both) 45.2, oracle best-of-5 57.8, so spreading activation is +1.4 to +3.4 over CoT (+3.0 to +5.0 over base); the stated +2.4 to +5.0 over CoT matches neither. Other figures (IEI 2.40 to 1.98 and 0.26 to 0.35; MI 2.75/3.69/4.56 with N=100; PopBlends 0.87 to 2.03; PRISM 57.65%) check out.
fix: Scaffolds that improved LLM blending outputs add a named middle step plus a check: explanation/shared-attribute step (IEI, Midjourney mean rank 2.40 to 1.98; win rate vs experts 0.26 to 0.35); generic-space-invariant transfer with diagnostic retry (mean MI 2.75 plain, 3.69 strong one-shot prompt, 4.56 full loop; N=100 raters); bridge-then-expand (ideas per pair 0.87 to 2.03). A strong one-shot prompt closes much of the gap. Gains of added steps are small or model-dependent: spreading activation on GPT-4o gave +1.4 to +3.4 points over CoT (+3.0 to +5.0 over base) on emergent property induction, while an oracle best-of-5 gave +17 over base; a structure-score refinement loop (PRISM) won human forced choice 57.65%, with smaller gains with a stronger model.

problem: Minor: Matsuhira's BCD 0.621 / MCD 0.862 at ratio 0.5 and 0.389 / 0.471 averaged over ratios match Table; MCD counts any depiction of both concepts so 'mixed more common than fused' is by definition; Sato's paper is speculative and reports no counts.

Minor: UoT novelty 0.224 is at method level (n=27); Schapiro's 75% is on the 96 unanimous judgments (66% panel-majority overall); the Cho et al. 'GPT-4.1 rubric' detail was not located in the text read; 'good only for narrow checks' is the author's synthesis.

Minor: CREATE creative-utility r=0.55 is the average of 0.51 and 0.48 against two annotators; UoT novelty 0.224 is method level (n=27); 'no separate-family judge tested' is an absence claim that cannot be verified from the sources.

Minor: Semantic Scholar citer counts (6, 8, 2) and Cunha's 'no evidence of an implementation' were verified; the negative claim is only about the opened sources, and user-study sizes N=9, 14, 75 were not individually re-checked.

Minor: 'design target, not a runnable per-problem rule' is interpretation: Lieder and Griffiths say Eq. 3 is a problem solved by evolution and learning rather than by the person, while Gershman et al. (not re-opened, blocked) describe online metalevel stopping; a01, a02, a03 and b01 are the same paper, so independent sources are Lieder and Griffiths plus Russell and Subramanian.

The 3x threshold appears only in Lieder and Griffiths' review (a04 and b03 are the same text); the primary paper (Vul et al. 2014) says one sample is optimal for action/sample time ratios below 10 under a symmetric utility, and that no sampling pays off below a ratio of 2 with no penalty for errors, so the threshold depends on the utility function.
fix: The best number of mental samples per decision is very small: Vul et al. (2014) show one sample is optimal when execution takes less than about 10 times as long as sampling under a symmetric utility (Lieder and Griffiths' review reports a threshold of about 3x), and the effective number of samples rises with stakes (r(25)=.61 across probability-matching studies).

problem: Critic points are supported (commentators warn of added degrees of freedom in specifying resource costs; Lieder and Griffiths concede falsification is hard when constraints are uncertain and RRA is hard to apply when environment or constraints are unknown), but 'no count of independent replications exists' is an absence claim that none of the sources establish; the Vul et al. entry is unrelated.
fix: Critics in the BBS commentaries note that resource-rational models add degrees of freedom (resource costs), and Lieder and Griffiths acknowledge that falsification is hard in practice and the approach is hard to apply where constraints or the environment are unknown; no count of independent replications was found in the sources read.

problem: Numbers match for text-davinci-003, but the generalisation fails: for ChatGPT, CRITIC w/o Tool beats CoT by about 3 F1 on HotpotQA (46.1 vs 42.8) and AmbigNQ (67.3 vs 64.3), and on TabMWP (davinci) w/o Tool still adds +20.3 over PoT, so 'flat or negative' is not general; Kamoi's finding is about feedback from prompted LLMs and has an exception clause.
fix: Checks with an outside signal (interpreter, retrieval, tests) carry most of the gain in CRITIC: on text-davinci-003, CRITIC without the search tool equals plain CoT on QA F1 (HotpotQA 46.1 vs 46.1, AmbigNQ 58.3 vs 58.6, TriviaQA 74.7 vs 74.5) and loses 1.8 points on GSM8K program-of-thought (68.3 vs 70.1), though on ChatGPT and on TabMWP the tool-free variant still gains; Kamoi et al. find no prior work showing successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs, except in tasks exceptionally suited to it.

problem: Muldoon & Weisberg (a critique) and a blog summary of Kitcher both support it; blog is a secondary summary but independent of M&W.

Numbers match, but 'removes in-context exploration failure' generalises from one Qwen-7B two-armed setup (pA=0.6 vs 0.4, a single table) to exploration failure in general; the lock-in rate was 0.0% only for that setup.
fix: Supplying the allocation from code removed inferior-peer lock-in in one Qwen-7B two-armed delegation test: 50.0% prompt-only, 23.3% with the UCB formula in the prompt, 0.0% with an external UCB calculator, 0.0% with algorithmic UCB; separately, GPT-4 with a basic prompt showed suffix failure (best arm never chosen again) in more than 60% of replicates in a multi-armed bandit test, and only one GPT-4 configuration (with hint, chain-of-thought and externally summarised statistics) explored well.

problem: Minor: the 0.821 within-prompt average comes from a 42-model paraphrase-robustness test on 30 queries (not the full 26K/70+ model set); the 4000-idea figure is per topic.

NoveltyBench says in-context regeneration is the most successful approach, roughly matching human-writer diversity (3 models tested) and GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Pro even surpass humans in cumulative utility; so 'does not reach humans' is contradicted. Also 66.8% is the share of base-model diversity VS retains after the DPO stage in a creative-writing ablation (direct prompting retains 23.8%).
fix: Prompt and decoding tricks only partly restore diversity: verbalized sampling raises creative-writing diversity 1.6x to 2.1x over direct prompting and retains about 66.8% of the base model's diversity after DPO (direct prompting 23.8%); in NoveltyBench, in-context regeneration is the most effective prompting fix and brings three tested models roughly to human-writer diversity, but the authors note the diversity is not built into the output distribution; with min-p at T=2.0, 61.2% of response pairs in Artificial Hivemind still exceed 0.8 similarity.

problem: Only ShinkaEvolve ablates novelty rejection, weighted parent sampling and bandit ensembles (on circle packing); AlphaEvolve's ablations cover evolution, prompt context, meta-prompt, model size and full-file evolution, not these three, so there is one system, not several.
fix: ShinkaEvolve's circle-packing ablations report that weighted parent sampling beats hill climbing (which plateaus early) and random sampling, embedding-based novelty rejection (with an LLM novelty judge) beats no rejection, and a bandit LLM ensemble beats a fixed ensemble and a single model; AlphaEvolve's ablations test other components (evolution, prompt context, meta-prompt evolution, base-model size, full-file evolution).

problem: Minor: DGM Table 1 is a single 80-iteration run per variant (Polyglot on 50 tasks); ShinkaEvolve is not an LLM-agent search in the DGM sense but an evolutionary program search.

Numbers match FOBAR Tables 1-2 (CoT: 83.5 vs 81.4, 86.6 vs 85.5, 91.4 vs 91.1; GPT-4 ComplexCoT SC 91.6 vs FOBAR-CoT 91.4, though FOBAR-ComplexCoT is 91.9); 'within noise' is an interpretation, the paper reports no significance test; RevThink 13.53% matches abstract.

Numbers check out (GSM-NoOp Fig 8a: Phi-3-mini -65.7, o1-preview -17.5, o1-mini -29.1, GPT-4o-mini -40.0 accuracy points; R-GSM 94.1 to 85.0; GSM1k up to 8%), but 'brittleness, not method' is the researcher's interpretation, and the CatAttack update describes adversarially searched triggers (found on a DeepSeek V3 proxy, then transferred) with a relative >300% rise in error likelihood, not any ordinary irrelevant sentence.
fix: Models are brittle on maths: GSM-NoOp (one irrelevant clause) drops accuracy by up to 65.7 points for Phi-3-mini (o1-preview -17.5, o1-mini -29.1, GPT-4o-mini -40.0); changing names and numbers in GSM-Symbolic lowers and widens accuracy; premise reordering cuts R-GSM accuracy (GPT-4-turbo 94.1 to 85.0); GSM1k shows accuracy drops of up to 8% suggesting contamination in some families (Phi, Mistral, some Llama). Update: CatAttack triggers, searched adversarially on a proxy model, raised the likelihood of wrong answers by over 300% relative for DeepSeek R1 and R1-distill-Qwen-32B.

problem: Minor: 'richer prompts made no difference on GPT-4o' is a supplementary figure (S3, 100 samples/question) with a one-line statement of negligible effect; the 20-80% time figure is 10-20 seconds longer.
Sample sizes (60, 48, 128, 64) and the FOR effect match the 2011 abstract; the cited sources are Thompson's own tradition or secondary restatements, which the claim itself discloses.

74.8% and 87.6% are shares of final-correct trials on conflict problems and match Bago and De Neys; the Raoelison paper shares De Neys as author, so support is from one research network, with the Ackerman and Thompson review as a separate secondary source.

Minor: Mata Study 1 wrong CRT confidence is 6.82 of 9 (moderately high, comparable to correct general-knowledge answers 7.11); the 85% and 91.5% figures are second-hand citations in Mata, and wrong conflict answers were still less confident than correct no-conflict answers in later studies.

Numbers match Huang et al. Table 3, but 'LLM self-correction does not help' is stated for all LLMs and tasks while the evidence is GPT-3.5/GPT-4 on three reasoning benchmarks; Kamoi allows exceptions for tasks exceptionally suited to self-correction, and CRITIC without tools still gains 20.3 on TabMWP (text-davinci-003).
fix: For GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 on reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, CommonSenseQA, HotpotQA), prompted self-correction without external feedback or oracle labels does not help and often hurts (GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 -> 41.8; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0), and the apparent gains in earlier work came from using oracle labels to decide when to stop; Kamoi et al. find no prior work showing successful self-correction from prompted LLMs feedback except in tasks exceptionally suited to it.

problem: All three Xiong et al. entries are one paper; Kadavath et al. (2022) does not report these numbers and concerns logit-based P(True)/P(IK) confidence, not verbalised confidence, so the claim rests on a single study of 2023-era models (GPT-3, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Vicuna, LLaMA 2).
fix: In one benchmark of five LLMs on eight tasks (Xiong et al., ICLR 2024), verbalised confidence is mostly in the 80-100% range and overconfident (average ECE above 0.377 for GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and Vicuna), and a weak failure predictor (GPT-4 average AUROC 62.7%); white-box methods reach AUROC 0.605 vs 0.522 for black-box, a narrow gap. Kadavath et al. find large models better calibrated on multiple-choice and true/false formats using logit-based self-evaluation, a different setting.

problem: Numbers match, but 'no accuracy loss' is too strong: DeepConf itself reports notable accuracy drops in a few settings (Qwen3-32B BRUMO25 -0.9, GPT-OSS-120B HMMT25 drops), and Thought Calibration preserves performance only within a calibrated risk tolerance.
fix: Confidence-based early exit cuts reasoning length with accuracy usually kept or improved: DEER shortens chains 19.1-80.1% on average with +0.3 to +5.0 points; Thought Calibration uses up to 60% fewer thinking tokens in-distribution and up to 20% out-of-distribution while keeping performance within a calibrated tolerance; DeepConf saves up to 84.7% of tokens online (DeepConf-low 43-79%) but accuracy drops in a few settings (e.g. Qwen3-32B BRUMO25 -0.9).

problem: Minor: the 92% figure counts cases where a correct answer appears in the first round (conditional on an eventually correct response), not all questions; 48.6% token cut is for the authors' own self-training method on QwQ-32B-Preview.

Minor: the 225%, 418%, 70% and TIP figures all come from one paper (Wang et al.; the two listed entries are the same paper); Su et al. independently confirm that wrong answers are longer. TIP 38.3 to 44.1 is averaged pass@1 on AIME2024; the 43.7 to 51.4 figure is Pass@4 with self-consistency.
Minor: The Illusion of Thinking findings have been disputed in follow-up commentary; the claim reports the paper's own results.
Minor: Stechly et al. also find the sound-verifier gain on graph colouring comes largely from extra tries, since bare 'try again' feedback is nearly as effective as detailed feedback.

Minor: the under-0.1% average accuracy loss is reported for Adaptive-Consistency only (ESC says comparable performance); MATH length figures are from two 1.5B distilled models; 34.5% is a best-case gap.

Liu and Wang's 40% saving with no loss is on NaturalQuestions; on math (MATH-500, AIME24, GPQA) their Answer Consistency stop cuts tokens 58-87% but accuracy collapses (e.g. R1-Qwen-7B MATH-500 91.0 to 67.0), and the learned stop saves about 11-33% on math with small loss; the 60% figure is thought calibration's best in-distribution case.
fix: Thought calibration reaches up to 60% fewer thinking tokens in-distribution (s1K held-out split) and up to 20% out of distribution with performance preserved; answer-convergence stopping (Liu and Wang) cuts over 40% of tokens on NaturalQuestions with no accuracy loss, but on math benchmarks its simple answer-consistency stop can lose a lot of accuracy and the learned stop saves roughly 11-33% of tokens with small loss.

problem: ALFWorld and KATE numbers hold, but the Memp example misleads: on TravelPlanner hard-constraint, similarity-keyed retrieval (GPT-4o 8.95 and 8.25; Claude 28.56 and 29.61) also scores below no memory (12.88; 33.06), and Claude's query-keyed retrieval is below random (29.91), so it is not random cases specifically that fall below no memory, and 'TravelPlanner agrees in direction' holds only for commonsense score and Qwen.
fix: In LLM agents, retrieving similar past successful trajectories as in-context examples usually beats no memory and random examples: ALFWorld (gpt-3.5, ExpeL) ReAct 40.0, random 42.5, task-similarity 59.0; KATE shows the same for GPT-3 in-context examples. It is not uniform: on Memp TravelPlanner hard-constraint score GPT-4o drops from 12.88 (no memory) to 6.72 with random and 8.25-8.95 with similarity retrieval, Gan et al. report one random example can fall below zero-shot, and Dynamic Cheatsheet retrieval hurt GPT-4o on GPQA (57.1 to 55.1) and MMLU-Pro Eng (53.2 to 48.8).

problem: Numbers verified (ExpeL 59.0 vs 48.5; Skill-KNN 78.3 vs 74.6; EPR 31.9 vs 26.0 on BREAK), but EPR's gain over BM25 is 5.9 to 11.3 points across BREAK/MTOP/SMCalFlow (not 5 to 8), and 'the three agree the key should describe what a case is useful for, not how it looks' overreaches because ExpeL's winning key is plain task-text similarity (a surface key).
fix: Choice of retrieval key matters. In ExpeL, ranking by task similarity beat reasoning-step similarity (59.0 vs 48.5 on ALFWorld; the paper text calls the drop slight, the table gap is 10.5 points). Skill-KNN (LLM-written skill description as key) beat the best raw-text key on Spider (78.3 vs 74.6, text-chat-davinci-002) and was best among non-oracle methods across its tasks; EPR (retriever trained on measured usefulness) beat BM25 by about 6 to 11 points with GPT-Neo (BREAK 31.9 vs 26.0, MTOP 64.2 vs 52.9, SMCalFlow 54.3 vs 46.1). Skill-KNN and EPR suggest keys that capture usefulness beat raw surface similarity; ExpeL's best key is task-text similarity, and none tests subgoals.

problem: Minor: AgentPoison's about-80% attack success at under 0.1% poison rate is the abstract's headline (body also reports 63% end-to-end vs baselines); Xiong, MINJA and Evo-Memory numbers match.

Sarukkai Table 1 gives ALFWorld Fixed-DB 0.73 (not 0.72), blind accumulation (Traj-Bootstrap) 0.89 (the 0.91 is +DB-Curation), and 0.93 for both curations; curation gains are small and mixed (Wordcraft +DB+Exemplar 0.69 below Exemplar-only 0.72; SQL +DB 0.78 below bootstrap 0.79); Xiong's history-based deletion is mixed too (RegAgent combined deletion about 69.8 vs 70.95 without); Voyager commits only self-verified skills but the cited evidence is retrieval accuracy, not a gating ablation.
fix: Gating what is stored by verified outcome or measured downstream utility tends to beat blind accumulation: Xiong et al. find strict-evaluator addition beats add-all (e.g. RegAgent 70.95 vs 55.48, EHRAgent 38.50 vs 13.05) and history-based deletion can shrink memory and sometimes beat error-free memory; Sarukkai et al. on ALFWorld get 0.73 with a fixed database, 0.89 with blind self-collected trajectories, 0.91 with database curation and 0.93 with database plus exemplar curation (gains over blind accumulation are small and mixed across benchmarks); Voyager commits only self-verified skills to its library.

problem: Minor: in Memento the K=4 to K=32 drop is only 0.6 F1/0.4 PM, so 'more adds noise' is a mild effect; Gan and Sarukkai sub-claims were not independently checked.

Minor: numbers match ReasoningBank Fig 7 (WebArena-Shopping, Gemini-2.5-flash, no memory 39.0; AWM 44.4 to 42.2) and ExpeL Fig 6; 'only if' is stronger than the evidence (single-domain ablation by the method's authors), and the ExpeL example concerns lack of experience rather than failure format.
ReasoningBank does not lose its gain on the cross-website Multi subset (13.8 vs 10.3 no memory, Gemini-flash; paper reports +4.6 over strongest baseline); only AWM fails there (3.4, n=29).
fix: Memory gain depends on how much tasks share structure. Evo-Memory: gain vs within-dataset task similarity r=0.717 (Gemini 2.5 Flash), 0.563 (Claude 3.7 Sonnet), big on PDDL and ALFWorld, small on AIME-25 and GPQA. ALFWorld has templated tasks; AWM's gains vanish on the cross-website Multi subset of WebArena (29 tasks) although ReasoningBank keeps a gain there; the Game of 24 jump is reuse of one solution. Buffer of Thoughts' largest gains are Game of 24 (GPT-4 3.0 to 82.4, but program-writing PAL already 64.0) and Checkmate-in-One; Evo-Memory shows memory below no-memory success on BabyAI for Gemini 2.5 Flash (0.48 to 0.56 vs 0.61).

problem: ReasoningBank 'single run, no CI' is an absence inference: the paper reports pass@1 with no intervals or repeats stated.
'Neither matches tokens or compute' is the researcher's own observation; not checked against ReGAL/LEGO text beyond that no token matched controls were seen.

Bramley data show younger children chose single-switch first tests most often (62.5% sparse, 79.3% dense); 'do not spontaneously vary one thing at a time' is not what the 39-79% range shows, and Peteranderl only says some adults do not fully grasp CVS, not many.
fix: Children often do not vary one thing at a time when the problem is sparse, and some adults never fully grasp control of variables. At ages 7-13 the share of single-switch first tests ranged from 39% to 79% depending on age and sparsity (N=104): younger children chose single-switch tests most often (62.5% sparse, 79.3% dense), older children less often (39.3% sparse, 60.9% dense).

problem: The 1.90 (split-half, sparse) vs 1.25 (one-at-a-time, dense) figures come from different conditions so they do not show split-half beating one-at-a-time; Samiei reports the 1-to-2-object shift for human adults, while strong models rely on sparse one- or two-object interventions.
fix: Whether one change per test is the best test depends on causal sparsity. With few true causes among many candidates, testing about half at once (split-half) is the ideal strategy (expected return about 1.90 euro in the sparse switch-box condition), whereas in the dense condition testing one switch at a time is the only effective strategy (about 1.25 euro); so 'one change per test' is not universally optimal. Bramley et al. (N=104): first test used several switches in 60.7% of older children on sparse boxes vs 39.1% on dense. LLM agents show a related boundary: with AND (joint-cause) rules models struggle and improve when they sample and eliminate hypotheses (GX-Chen 2025); human adults in conjunctive worlds shift from 1-object to 2-object tests (Samiei 2026), and strong models rely mainly on one- or two-object interventions.

problem: Reading and maths predicting CVS (experimenting) gain scores is shown by Schlatter; Sobel shows theory of mind (and, as a related factor, executive function) relating to scientific reasoning in ages 4-7.5, not CVS gains specifically.
fix: Reading comprehension and maths skill predicted the pretest-posttest gain in experimenting (CVS) in fifth-graders (Schlatter 2020, N=138, gains uneven across components: hypothesis-evidence coordination and drawing conclusions did not gain significantly). Separately, theory of mind at age 4 predicted scientific reasoning at 5.5 and 7.5, controlling for executive function and language, which also related to scientific reasoning (Sobel 2026).

problem: Numbers (27% vs 66-82%, rho -0.937) come from FalsifyBench alone; Jhaveri only supports the qualitative direction (reasoning-trace models show lower bias).
ScienceWorld 0.17 is the best model overall (DRRN, an RL agent, not an LLM agent); ScienceAgentBench 32.4% excludes o1-preview which reached 42.2% at over 10x cost.
Absence claim cannot be proven; no CVS framing found in text of DiscoveryWorld, ScienceWorld, GX-Chen or Samiei, and one extra search found none.

Lorch 2010 abstract gives n=797 (WWC review 848), not strictly 800+; the N=618 study (J Educ Psychol 2023, ETH record) is not the cited ERIC EJ1039461 page (Lazonder and Egberink 2014, n=67), so that half was confirmed only through a search snippet.

Under MVT a richer environment lowers stay time (higher leaving threshold); sources show thresholds fall in poorer environments (longer travel, steeper depletion), so 'stay longer when the environment is richer' is reversed; richness only raises stays at the patch level.
fix: Humans, monkeys, rats and mice all follow the marginal value theorem qualitatively: they stay longer (leave at a lower reward threshold) when travel is longer or the environment is poorer, and leave at a higher threshold in richer environments; they also stay longer in richer patches.

problem: Overharvesting is not universal in the cited sources (no overharvesting on rich planets in Harhen, gerbils did not overstay in Guldener, early leaving in some Wolfe conditions); the 'almost every' hedge covers this; the human figure is an earnings loss of about 10 percent, not a stay-time measure.

Harhen and Bornstein explain overharvesting with their own model in one human task; Constantino and Daw still find a significant residual overharvesting bias in the MVT learning model, and Kane's rats overharvested in every condition.
fix: A learning-and-uncertainty account (rich-poor mix, uncertainty-adaptive discounting) explains much of human overharvesting in one task (Harhen and Bornstein 2023): it shrank with experience and was absent in rich environments; but a residual overharvesting bias remains in other human work (Constantino and Daw 2015) and rats overharvested in every condition (Kane 2019).

problem: Both indifference points come from Experiments 1 and 2 of one paper (Shenhav 2014); Kolling 2012 gives the bias qualitatively.
'Match discounted MVT' means not significantly different (p=0.74, n=12 agents); Fonseca is a preprint with three training runs per algorithm.
Gemma-2B did gain slightly with summarised history (7.6 to 10.5) but fell with algorithm guidance (4.9); Gemma-9B fell (10.5 to 5.3 and 4.1).
Chen et al. say 'in more than 92% of cases' the first round is correct; the 60% token share is 'generally less than 60%'; the 87.3 to 70.3 decline is one model/benchmark setting in Ghosal et al.
Peak result is from one model and setting in Ghosal et al. (which also says there is no reliable stopping criterion); the repeated-sampling figure is coverage with an oracle verifier, not accuracy.
Dynamic Cheatsheet's own DC-empty-memory arm (same structured prompt, no memory) already gets Claude AIME 2024 to 36.7, so about half of the 23 to 50 gain is not attributable to stored experience.
fix: Experience-memory systems without weight updates (Dynamic Cheatsheet, ExpeL, ReasoningBank) raise accuracy at test time, strongly where reusable code or strategy exists (GPT-4o Game of 24 10% to 99%; Claude 3.5 Sonnet AIME 2024 23% to 50%, though an empty-cheatsheet prompt arm alone reaches 36.7%) and little elsewhere (Claude Game of 24 12% to 14%).

problem: Generative replay reduces but does not prevent forgetting: Class-IL 90.79 vs 97.94 joint upper bound and 94.57 for exemplar-based iCaRL; the 98.5-98.8 figures in Shin et al. come from a chain of solvers trained from generated data on MNIST, not from learning new tasks.
fix: Generative replay greatly reduces forgetting in continual learning (split MNIST Class-IL 90.79 vs 19.90 with no replay and 20.01 for EWC, but below the 97.94 joint-training upper bound and the 94.57 of exemplar-based iCaRL; Shin et al. chain of five solvers on MNIST stays at 98.5-98.8%); regularisation fails when task identity is unknown.

problem: ReasoningBank result is one WebArena-Shopping setting (Gemini-2.5-flash) and Memento shows a plateau (63.9 at K=32, still above 59.9 at K=0) rather than a decline, so 'must stay small' is a mild generalisation.
Headline fifth-eigenoption finding rests on Machado 2017 alone; 2023 JMLR is same lab but supports the normalised-cut context; Momennejad does not address it.
Both papers share Machado but each supports a separate half of the claim; 'RND passed DCEO' is a caveat from DCEO authors, who did not run DCEO to 2B steps.
Minor: 53/78 binomial p=0.002 omitted but chi2 comparison to control (6.52, p=0.01) matches; Solway and Tomov are different labs (Solway overlaps Botvinick/Niv/Barto, Tomov/Gershman separate).

All numbers verified in Ribas-Fernandes 2011 (EEG 9; fMRI 30 analysed; accumbens 14 analysed, right NAcc only, p<0.05); the three evidence rows are one paper plus a review, but the claim itself says small samples and one task.

All numbers match (ARISE Table 9 object 71.7 vs 51.9; Liu et al. 73.6->27.4, 9.3->51.6, 73.9); the 'active entries' framing blends two different settings (induced agent subroutines vs. skill-routing at scale) and K only tested at 3/5/10.

Gemini-2.5-Pro in LLMThinkBench is best at its lowest budget (90% at 128 tokens, 88% at max, with a dip to 71% at one setting), so it is not a clean plateau; also Zhou reports a bootstrap CI [-1.4,-0.4] for the 12K-16K drop (so 'no paired test' is only partly right: no seeds, greedy only).
fix: Past a task- and model-specific length, extra sequential reasoning tokens lower accuracy (gain, plateau, mild decline). Seen in R1-32B/s1-32B on AIME and GPQA (budget forcing, temperature 0), R1-distill models on GSM8K with Wait forcing, Qwen2.5 on MATH Level 5 (CoT steps), and 9 models on constructed tasks. Gap search 2026-11: on basic maths in LLMThinkBench, GPT-5 and o3 plateau and Gemini-2.5-Flash is flat, while Gemini-2.5-Pro is best at its lowest budget (90% at 128 tokens, 88% at max, with a dip to 71% at one setting); Qwen3-235B improves smoothly to 32K on the vendor's plots. The drop is model- and task-specific. Zhou used greedy decoding, a single run with no seeds, though it reports a bootstrap CI for the 12K-16K drop.

problem: Zhou does report a bootstrap 95% CI [-1.4%,-0.4%] for the 0.9-point 12K-16K drop (though from one deterministic greedy run, so it is not seed-based or a paired test); numbers 55.8/54.9, Opus 4 100 to 85-90, R1 70 to 30, 87.3 to 70.3 are all correct.
fix: The decline is small in the best-measured natural-difficulty setting (R1-32B AIME: 55.8 at 12K to 54.9 at 16K, about 0.5 problem of 60) but large in constructed tasks (Opus 4 nearly 100 to 85-90, R1 70 to 30 with five distractors) and Wait-forcing on small R1-distill models (87.3 to 70.3 on the GSM8K panel). Magnitude depends on setup. Zhou ran one greedy (temperature 0) pass per model; it reports a bootstrap CI for the 0.9-point drop, but no seeds or paired test over repeated runs back it.

problem: Mixed units (Zhou in tokens by MATH level, Wu in CoT steps on MATH Level 5 for Qwen2.5 30 questions); Wu's difficulty trend is within the 1.5B model, numbers match.

Numbers match Hassid (GPQA-D LN-Super-49B 69.1 vs 57.6; up to 34.5; tercile table is the math-split Table 2); '40% fewer tokens' is specifically short-1@k in low-compute regimes; Zeng 2025 independently confirms correct solutions are shorter.

Ghosal 20% (abstract) vs 22% (intro) at 16K and GSM8K 1.5B +10.1/-11.8 relative to 385-token standard thinking match; Hassid short-3@k +2% at 80k and short-1@k loses to majority in 3 of 4 models match.
Numbers match; note the 57.7 vs 94.0 compares o1-preview (CoT-native) against GPT-4o zero-shot on a task subset, i.e. different models.

Hay et al. state the myopic policy 'often stops far too early' and the blinkered policy fixes it; Russell 1989/90 supports computation-as-action value of computation; Russell is a co-author of Hay, so sources are partly one lineage.

Lin et al. says metareasoning is a meta-MDP appreciably more expensive than solving the base MDP (stronger than 'at least as hard'); Callaway 2018 states metareasoning costs often outweigh gains and shows BMPS pays in a costly-simulation scenario; 'much costlier' threshold is an inference, not a stated rule.

Numbers (45.0%, 86.8%, 28.3%, 6.3%, 65.5%) match Callaway/Lieder CogSci 2018, but they come from one study in one planning task; the other listed sources (Lieder 2018 PMC5937797 opened) do not report stopping-early or these numbers, so the general 'humans systematically stop early' is single-study.
fix: In one planning experiment (Callaway, Lieder et al. 2018, CogSci), people's computations were close to VOC-optimal but biased toward stopping early: 45.0% of computations were suboptimal yet achieved 86.8% of the maximum VOC; of the deviations, 28.3% were stopping too early, 6.3% too late, and 65.5% were clicking the wrong node.

problem: Qualitative claim supported by Chen et al. (solutions after the first correct answer; overthinking more frequent on simple ASDIV) and Arora-Zanette (larger token reduction on GSM8K than AIME at same alpha).

Per-method numbers verified (RaM 23-45%, Arora-Zanette 16-65% by dataset with 1.7-3.3 pt loss, AdaptThink -53.0%/-40.1% with +2.4/+2.3 acc), but Thinkless reports a 50-90% cut in long-chain usage (not tokens), the lower bound is 16% on AIME not 23%, and AdaptThink/Thinkless are mode-selection RL rather than a plain length penalty.
fix: RL methods that cut reasoning cost keep accuracy within about 5 points: RaM (VOC-form reward, token cost in the reward) cuts tokens 23-45% at equal or better accuracy; Arora-Zanette's length penalty cuts tokens 16% (AIME) to 65% (GSM8K) with 1.7-3.3 point loss; AdaptThink cuts response length 40-53% with accuracy up about 2 points; Thinkless cuts long-chain usage 50-90%. Only RaM and the length-penalty form are literally VOC.
