problem: All numbers verified in Sprague et al. (110 papers; +14.2, +12.3, +6.9; 56.8 vs 56.1); the 'gate defaults to no chain' is a design inference; RaM paper opened but is tangential, so the evidence is one meta-analysis.

Adaptive-Consistency averages are 2.9x (commonsense) to 3.8x by category with 0.1-0.2% drop, with 7.9x only as a maximum, so '3.3-7.9x' is off; ESC 33.8-80.1% ok; Kim 2025 shows cross-model error correlation, but nothing opened tests within-model sample dependence (claimed only as 'probably').
fix: Statistical stopping rules for self-consistency cut samples about 3x on average (Adaptive-Consistency: 2.9-3.8x by task category, up to 7.9x, accuracy drop 0.1-0.2%) and 34-80% (ESC), accuracy kept; they treat samples as independent/exchangeable draws, while LLM errors are strongly correlated across models (about 60% agreement when both err); whether samples within one model are similarly correlated was not tested in these sources.

problem: Kim et al. numbers (about 60% agreement when both err, 1/3 chance) are for Helm multiple-choice; Chen et al. show Vote can first rise then fall with more calls due to hard queries; the final 'floor on risk, not a probability' sentence is an inference.
Gema numbers (Opus 4 nearly 100 to 85-90, R1 70 to 30 with five distractors in Natural Overthinking) and Ghosal rise-then-fall verified; R1 70-to-30 is one task variant.
NoThinking 51.3 vs 28.9 (AMC23, 700 tokens; paper writes ACM 23), NoWait 27-51%, DEER 19.1-80.1% (with accuracy +0.3 to +5.0) all verified; these are 'up to'/average ranges across model series.

FrugalGPT abstract matches (up to 98% cost reduction at GPT-4 performance, best case on HEADLINES); SwiftSage switches by hand-coded triggers and Damani routes by predicted difficulty, so the 'scorer unsure' cascade is supported mainly by FrugalGPT.

Chess paper (Russek et al., Cognitive Science 2025, 12M+ games) matches, but only the increase with Elo is called modest by the authors, not the overall move-time/benefit relationship; the other listed sources (Callaway 2021, Lieder 2018) are not about chess, so it is single-study.
fix: In over 12 million online chess games, players spent more time thinking in positions where extra computation was more beneficial (Russek et al. 2025); the relationship was stronger for higher-Elo players (the authors call the Elo difference significant but modest), and move time also rose with the expected benefit of computation when the true benefit was 0.

problem: TALE-EP GPT-4o-mini GSM8K-Zero 99.50 to 98.72, 252.96 to 22.67 tokens verified (it is the Vanilla CoT vs TALE-EP column); 4-8 point loss on MathBench-Middle/High/College verified; CoD coin flip 100% and 68%/86% fewer tokens verified (GPT-4o/Claude 3.5).

Qi et al. 2015 numbers (2 of 105 correct; 104 of 110 plausible patches equal one deletion) verified, but the 59% in Weimer 2009 is the per-trial search success rate on ten programs, not GenProg's 'claim'; the claim Qi tests is 55 of 105 bugs fixed (a later study), and Weimer 2009 is not the system Qi analysed.
fix: Test-based repair that passes the tests often overfits: of the 55 of 105 bugs GenProg was reported to fix, a re-examination (Qi et al. 2015) found a correct patch for only 2 of 105, and 104 of its 110 plausible patches were equivalent to a single functionality deletion. (Weimer et al. 2009's 59% is a per-trial search success rate on ten programs, a different measure.)

problem: LLMAO 22.3 vs Ochiai 4.8, ChatGPT-4 23.13 vs SmartFL 15.75, AgentFL 157/395 and FlexFL 164 verified, but only LLMAO and FlexFL are compared against Ochiai (ChatGPT-4 is vs SmartFL, AgentFL vs LLM baselines), FlexFL's 164 vs 122 is on AutoFL's 353-bug Defects4J v1.0 subset (not 'v1.2'), and FlexFL's own re-run of AgentFL gave 144 not 157.
fix: Independent LLM-localisation systems report Top-1 gains over non-LLM baselines on Defects4J: LLMAO 22.3% vs Ochiai 4.8% (395 bugs, v1.2.0); ChatGPT-4 with error log 23.13 vs SmartFL 15.75 (function-level mean Acc@1); AgentFL 157 of 395 (v1.2.0, beating ChatGPT/LLMAO baselines, but FlexFL's reproduction got 144); FlexFL 164 vs Ochiai 122 on the 353-bug v1.0 subset used by AutoFL.

problem: Wu 25.6% (error log removal), AgentFL Top-1 157 to 125 (-20.4%), FuseFL TestRes 187 vs SusScore 169 all verified; FuseFL set is 324 student programs (Refactory) with GPT-3.5, not Defects4J, and AgentFL 'test failure analysis' is an LLM analysis step rather than raw log; 'single most valuable' holds within each paper's ablation.
Agentless file 81.7% combined, skeleton 58.33% vs complete file 53.67% edit-location, LLM4FL -23.24%/-16.51% Top-1 all verified; LocAgent and LLM4FL are independent of Agentless.

Agentless (OpenCSG 90.0% file-level, 23.67% solved), RepairAgent (16 bugs, 25% drop, 81% cost) and Meng et al. (82.2% vs 69.6%) numbers verified; RepairAgent result is on a small Defects4J subset with no extra cycles.

Verified: 76% vs 53% (Liang), 12.47 to 3.97 and 32.67+31.08=63.75% (SWE-Bench+ sums solution leakage and weak tests, which is leakage/test weakness rather than memorisation per se), TheStack 80% membership (Ramos), Defects4J drops 4.1 to 15.98 (De Koning; table shows GPT-4o -4.01) and GitBug-Java p=0.819/0.667 for Claude-3.7/GPT-4o.

The 19 to 31 of 40 lift is ChatGPT's (Codex solved 21 without hints), not Codex's; and no cited source compares template/patch context against conversation/feedback, so the 'helps less' comparison is not supported.
fix: ChatRepair (ChatGPT conversation with failing-test feedback) fixes 162 of 337 Defects4J/QuixBugs-scale bugs at about $0.42 each, with no repair templates needed; separately, giving ChatGPT hints such as the expected output raised it from 19 to 31 of 40 QuixBugs bugs (Codex without hints: 21).

problem: Minor: the RepairAgent 40 vs 22 iteration figure comes from Bouzenia and Pradel, the RepairAgent authors' own follow-up, so only the OpenHands 54 vs 25 rounds (Liu et al.) is truly independent support.
Minor: the LLMAO 31.9% unseen-project figure is for CodeGen-16B, which is not a small model; UniXcoder is 125M.

Sources show leakage signals (80% TheStack membership, low NLL, 82% 5-gram for codegen-6B) and significant drops after transformation for all seven models (even Claude-3.7 -4.89 and GPT-4o -4.01), but neither proves Defects4J scores are 'inflated'; the 'localisation-only version has not been run' claim is a negative that neither source addresses.
fix: Defects4J shows signs of memorisation: 80% of its repositories are in TheStack and older or mid-size open models such as codegen-6B-multi reproduce it (82% 5-gram accuracy), and repair success on Defects4J falls significantly after meaning-preserving edits for all seven LLMs tested (from -4.0 points for GPT-4o to -16.0 for Llama-3.1), with larger drops for models that find the original bugs more familiar (low NLL); frontier models show smaller drops and less leakage signal, and these sources test full repair, not localisation alone.

problem: Minor: 'two opposite ways' and 'after finding a fault' are the notes' framing; sources list the anti-patterns (repeated identical actions, fixes without testing, termination without test validation) and the 54 vs 25 rounds and -7.894/-15.938 slopes, which all match.

Minor: Bilalic's search-time medians (7/9/10 s vs 9/8/8 s) are in the full text, which I could not open; the abstracts and the Sheridan and Reingold PMC full text (F(1,34)=43.45, n=9 optimal-move experts, no trend in Ba7 choosers) match.
Minor: Wiley's .15/.50 cell means are in the full text, which I could not open (abstract only); anagram RT/dwell costs (15.3 vs 13.4 s, accuracy n.s.) and DeCaro's children study (N=87) verified.

Fang et al. (N=30) is an association with a modest interaction (F=4.88, p=.035); high accessibility shows no significant cost, not 'none' (1.90 vs 2.07, p=.538), and the authors' own item-matched direct test of smaller cost under high accessibility was not significant (t(14) -0.133 and -0.951), so 'reduces' is too causal. Kurtz relational encoding is a separate finding and not accessibility evidence.
fix: In one small study (N=30), induced fixation hurt remote-associates performance when target accessibility was low (1.27 vs 0.70 correct, p=.009) but not significantly when it was high (1.90 vs 2.07, p=.538); the accessibility by induction interaction was modest (p=.035) and the authors' item-matched direct test of a smaller cost under high accessibility was not significant. Separately, a relational-encoding pre-task raised insight solving from 22% to 43% (p=.010 overall; significant for the two-string problem, p=.039, not for the peanut problem, p=.109).

problem: Minor: Opus 75.1% vs physicians 66% is not a significant difference per the paper, and Kim 2025 and Shidara 2026 share a research group (before/after comparison, not independent corroboration).

Minor: both papers come from the same group; Shidara reports a 'general trend' toward better calibration with residual overconfidence, and Kim's overconfidence is shown for top models (o1, Gemini-pro, Claude-opus, Llama-3.1-70B) and more so for smaller ones.

Only Tang (2026) supports all three parts; Meszaros et al. (2025) finds the opposite on brittleness (a 270M chess transformer shows compositional generalization on out-of-distribution positions and puzzles, losing to explicit search only on Chess960), so 'chess-trained LMs are brittle OOD' is mixed, and the verifier result is RedPajama-3B (a general LLM), not a chess-trained model.
fix: Tang (2026) argues chess-LLM puzzle scores are largely pattern-matching: a 25M-parameter KinGPT trained only on (position, best-move) pairs beats the 3B ChessGPT on a 600-puzzle mate-in-N suite and a 4B model on a 20-theme benchmark, and an external verifier (LLM-Modulo) raised general-purpose RedPajama-3B's move validity from 19.3% to 95.3% (best-move accuracy 1.2% to 21.2%); the evidence on out-of-distribution robustness is mixed, since Meszaros et al. (2025) find a 270M chess transformer generalizes compositionally OOD and falls behind explicit search mainly on Chess960.

problem: The ChatGPT code figures (75.76%/51.00%/47.56% of tasks with zero equal test output) are at the default temperature (1), not temperature 0, where non-determinism is lower but not zero; they also refer to equal test output, not equal text.
fix: LLMs configured to be deterministic (temperature 0) still vary: across 5 models, 8 tasks and 10 runs accuracy varies up to 15% across identical runs and the best-possible to worst-possible gap reaches up to 70% (Atil et al.). Separately, at ChatGPT's default temperature (1), 75.76%, 51.00% and 47.56% of CodeContests, APPS and HumanEval tasks had zero equal test output across five requests, and temperature 0 reduces but does not remove this (Ouyang et al.).

problem: Sclar figures verified (76 points LLaMA-2-13B, ~10 average, 50+ tasks), but Mizrahi et al. Table 4 shows Kendall's W spanning about 0.27 to 0.91 across tasks, with most below 0.85 (weak to moderate agreement), not 0.71-0.91.
fix: Meaning-preserving prompt format changes move accuracy by up to 76 points (LLaMA-2-13B) and about 10 points on average across 50+ tasks; scale, shots and instruction tuning do not remove it, and format performance correlates only weakly across models. Instruction paraphrase also reorders model rankings: Kendall's W across templates ranges from about 0.27 to 0.91 over tasks (most below 0.85, i.e. weak to moderate agreement; Mizrahi et al.).

problem: Numbers all verified, but the Krippendorff alpha values (SummaC 0.326-0.788, MT-Bench 0.265-0.563) were measured with sampling temperature 0.6 in Rating Roulette, so they do not show variation 'even when sampling is off'; only Lau (2026) tests temperature 0.
fix: Same-input LLM judging is unstable across repeated runs: with sampling temperature 0.6, Krippendorff alpha over 3 runs was 0.326-0.788 on SummaC and 0.265-0.563 on MT-Bench (no model reached 0.8 on MT-Bench; Rating Roulette), and Lau (2026) found none of five judges (including GPT-4o and Claude Haiku/Sonnet 4.5) fully deterministic even at temperature 0. GPT-4 inter-sample alpha (0.587) is below human inter-annotator alpha (0.659) on SummEval (Stureborg et al.).

problem: Minor: Chen's paper names the quantity beta (not delta); Ding's shared-error check on Claude models is a small exploratory test (not significant for Opus, p=.07) run on a student-cohort dataset.
Minor: the ensembling ablation (.1676 none vs .1651 median) is on the validation split where the human crowd scored 0.1600; the .179 vs .149 comparison is on the test set.

Minor: Chen's ceiling applies to policies that output one member's answer (route/vote/cascade), and the Self-MoA comparison is at matched quality; related work (Li et al.) reports Self-MoA often beats heterogeneous fusion in other settings.

The 98% order-swap flip is a single Gemini-2.0-Flash cell (Verdict-first XML, JudgeBench), not a GPT-5.2, Claude-Sonnet-4.6 or Gemini-2.5-Pro result (their flip rates are far lower, e.g. Claude up to about 50%); the 7-17% rerun change and the >0.95 retest with >0.10 position bias (Qwen3 8B, Gemini 2.5 Flash) are otherwise supported.
fix: In a six-judge audit (GPT-5.2, GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Gemini-2.0-Flash, Claude-Sonnet-4.6, Llama-3.3-70B), 7-17% of verdicts changed across identical reruns at temperature 0 and order swaps flipped up to 98% of pairwise verdicts in the worst case (Gemini-2.0-Flash on JudgeBench); in a separate 21-judge study, test-retest reliability above 0.95 coexisted with position bias above 0.10 for some judges (Qwen3 8B, Gemini 2.5 Flash).

problem: Minor: Bellibatlu et al. state the no-ordering finding only for their 6-model panel and 16 synthetic vignettes, so it should be scoped to that panel; the 9% GPU/batch variation is for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B in bf16 greedy decoding.
Minor: the human-difficulty part rests on Zhang & Norman's Tower of Hanoi isomorphs (qualitative discussion, e.g. II-E23 much easier than ZI23); IsoBench deltas (28.7/18.7/14.9) verified.

Numbers verified (VoT compliance 51.14/52.01, state accuracy 26.48/24.25, decision accuracy given correct drawing 65.16/77.20; MVoT 90.80%, CoT 0.9401 to 0.3911), but neither paper tests code verification of the written state, so 'code verification is the lever' is the notes' inference; the 0.94/0.39 CoT figures are a fine-tuned Anole-7B 'CoT with env layout' row.
fix: In Visualization-of-Thought the drawn state is often wrong (state accuracy 26.48% navigation / 24.25% tiling; constraint compliance 51.14% / 52.01%), while decisions given an accurate drawing were right 65.16% / 77.20% of the time, so drawing accuracy is the bottleneck; in MVoT, 90.80% of text-CoT errors on FrozenLake were wrong hole coordinates in the written state (fine-tuned Anole-7B CoT: 0.9401 at 3x3 down to 0.3911 at 6x6). Whether code verification of the written state would fix this is untested in these sources.

problem: Minor: Mind's Eye 1.3B-matches-175B is the zero-shot UTOPIA result (29.8% vs 29%); Sketchpad 11.2% is the paper's average gain for GPT-4o on math.
Minor: the 14,200 router training labels are machine-labelled (GPT-4o), and 'about 26% of CoT tokens' is the paper's 'over 74% average token reduction'.

The Gigerenzer and Hoffrage 'Bayesian algorithms 16% vs 46%/50%' figures are in none of the listed sources (the Cui et al. review gives 48% vs 22% correct for that study; I could not open the 1995 paper); the medical-student result (N=577, 36% vs 68% correct pretest, OR 11.55), visual aids, training, and the nested-sets rival account are supported.
fix: Natural-frequency wording raises Bayesian performance in people (Gigerenzer and Hoffrage 1995 reported roughly 22% correct with probabilities vs 48% with natural frequencies per Cui et al. 2023; 36% vs 68% correct in 577 medical students, OR 11.55), visual aids add, and training adds; a rival account attributes the effect to nested-set structure.

problem: Minor: Grossi and Pigozzi is a tutorial recounting Kornhauser and Sager / Pettit, and List (2005) builds on the same paradox, so the sources are independent authors but the example is a single well-known result; nested wording (premise-wise vs conclusion-wise verdicts differ on the same votes) is shown by the three-judge example.

Minor: List shows CBP can reach the correct decision faster than PBP when the premises are not both true, so 'tracks truth better' holds mainly when premises are true; the claim's PBP-to-1 statement is correct.

Condorcet theorem (Wikipedia, List 2008 for the >1/2 and independence conditions) is stated for equal-competence independent voters; 'only if' is too strong (heterogeneous competence, Berend-Paroush, and correlated cases are not covered), and List 2008 does not state the p<1/2 case.
fix: For independent voters of equal competence p, majority accuracy rises toward 1 with group size if p>1/2; if p<1/2 it falls toward 0 and a single voter is best (Condorcet jury theorem).

problem: Pearson/Kendall figures are from Chatbot Arena agreement, kappa from NQ; both match PoLL paper; deliberation abstract (2609.22497) confirms diversity needed, clones no benefit.
Minor: Halawi's aggregate is a weighted average (4x weight on crowd), not a plain average.

Adaptive-Consistency reports 3.3x average (up to 7.9x) with under 0.1% average accuracy drop, but ESC's -33.8% (MATH) is only about 1.5x and ESC reports only 'comparable' accuracy, so '2x to 8x with under 0.1 point loss' for both is wider than the sources.
fix: Agreement-based early stopping cuts samples roughly 1.5x to 8x (Adaptive-Consistency: 3.3x on math on average, up to 7.9x, GPT-3.5 4.4x, with under 0.1% average accuracy drop; ESC: -34% to -84% samples with comparable accuracy). It measures lead stability, not correctness.

problem: Minor: Weaver's 87.7 average includes MATH500, so 'outside code and math' strictly applies to the GPQA/MMLU entries; Stroebl's K about 5 is for code with a false-positive cost ratio of 4, and Weaver's majority baseline varies 71.6-72.2 across tables.

Ferreira et al. and Wang et al. support the numbers (+3.3/+6.6/+5.7, 1.6x, 3.4x), but Mansuri et al. show discussion's gain shrinks as dissent withholding rises and can overturn a wrong majority only below a critical withholding rate, not that discussion helps 'only if' dissent is voiced.
fix: Debate versus vote at matched budget: debate is a mild gain over one answer (+3 to +7 points) but ties or loses to independent-sample majority vote and costs 1.6x wall-clock and 3.4x tokens; discussion's gain shrinks as agents withhold dissent, and it can overturn a wrong majority only when withholding is below a critical rate.

problem: Minority Sentinel's 22.3% is the recovery rate of minority-correct 2:1 cases (39 of 175), not 22% of the oracle margin (net +1.71 of a 10.0-point margin is about 17%); other numbers (-19.16, +1.5/+2.24, 366 vs 185) match.
fix: Flipping to the minority is risky: always trusting the minority costs 19 points, a trained flip rule in a 3-vendor debate recovers 22% of the minority-correct cases (39 of 175) for a net gain of only +1.71 points (about 17% of the 10-point oracle margin), and on one small model a label-free delegation rule adds 1.5 to 2.2 points (366 wins vs 185 losses). An LLM reconciler recovers minority-correct answers on math but with unreported harm counts.

problem: All numbers match Table 1 of Xiong et al. (2025), but every supporting evidence line is the same paper (arXiv 2505.16067) or a synthesis of it, so the claim rests on a single study.

Ordering strict > C3 > coarse and noisy gates below fixed (C1 RegAgent 63.18, C2 CIC-IoT 68.80 vs fixed 71.50) match Xiong Table 1; the add-all-vs-selective part is independently supported by ReMe, but the gate-quality ordering rests on Xiong alone.
Minor: MemRL r=0.861 is Q-value vs success rate (predictive, not a deletion result) and Sarukkai gains vary by condition (some -0.01).

Minor: ExpeL's success-only store not opened; numbers (48.33, 63.76, 66.68) and the NP-CBR ablation match CASCADE; the 'retention never ablated' point holds only in the sense that no retain-vs-not ablation appears.

Minor: Dynamic Cheatsheet text says GPT-4o full-history 6.7 on AIME 2024 but its Table 2 shows 13.3 (both below the 20.0 baseline); Claude 23.3/26.7/50.0 match. Claim rests mainly on one paper plus Sarukkai/ReMe for the general curated-beats-append direction.

Memento's -18.0/-2.1 DeepResearcher drop is the step from offline to online executor without planning (attributed to data contamination), not case memory; case-based reasoning actually added +6.7 F1/+8.2 PM on DeepResearcher. CASCADE 4-of-12, Evo-Memory r 0.717/0.563 and SEDM 73/32 all match.
fix: Retention is not always beneficial: always retaining ground-truth cases hurt 4 of 12 tasks in CASCADE (retriever could not cope with larger bank); memory gains correlate with task similarity (r 0.717 / 0.563); SEDM shows a relevant memory turned 73 failures into successes and 32 successes into failures; Sarukkai notes verified-success trajectories that fail when retrieved. (Memento's case-based reasoning helped on all three benchmarks including DeepResearcher.)

problem: Memento K sweep matches (K=4 best at 64.5/78.5, K=8+ flat), but CASCADE says performance steadily improves with more retrieved cases and only that REINFORCE+LoRA's single-case lead on 3 of 12 tasks is closed at 4 cases, not that CASCADE beats it on all 12; 'more adds nothing' does not carry to CASCADE.
fix: In Memento's 7-dataset QA sweep, K=4 retrieved cases gave the best average (F1 64.5 / PM 78.5) with K=8 to 32 flat or slightly lower; in CASCADE, 4 retrieved cases closed the gap on the 3 of 12 tasks where REINFORCE+LoRA led with a single case, though CASCADE kept improving with more cases.

problem: Minor: ExpeL table labels are jumbled in extraction but the ordering 40.0/48.5/42.5/59.0 matches the text (task-similarity best, random sampling drops sharply); the ablation tests example selection, with insights likely kept.

Zilberstein (1996) states exactly this (monotonicity guaranteed by returning best result so far when quality is recognizable); the two Zilberstein entries are the same paper and the other listed papers do not address the guarantee, so it rests on one source, though the claim is close to definitional.

Zilberstein's Theorem 5 states myopic value-of-computation monitoring is optimal when the profile is increasing and concave-down and time cost is increasing and concave-up (a sufficient condition), not 'only' then; the LLM non-concavity evidence is a synthesis, not a measured concavity test.
fix: Zilberstein's Theorem 5 shows myopic value-of-computation stopping is optimal when the performance profile is increasing and concave-down and the cost of time is increasing and concave-up; LLM quality-vs-thinking curves are often non-concave (rise then fall), so a single marginal-gain stop rule is not guaranteed safe.

problem: Minor: Gema reports Opus 4 falling to about 85-90% (an evidence line also says about 80%); all figures match.

Numbers match (DEER 19.1-80.1% shorter chains with +0.3 to +5.0% accuracy, ESC -34% to -84% samples, probe -24% tokens), but the hidden-state probe is a trained probe, so it is not training-free, and ESC saves samples rather than chain tokens.
fix: Early exit and early stopping save compute at little or no accuracy cost: training-free DEER cuts chains by an average 19.1-80.1% with +0.3 to +5.0% accuracy; training-free ESC cuts 34-84% of samples with comparable accuracy; a trained hidden-state probe used as an exit rule cuts 24% of tokens with no performance loss.

problem: Wu et al. (2502.07266) states the inverted U and 14 steps at 1.5B to 4 at 72B (Qwen2.5 series), but the second line is the same paper and Su et al. only corroborates overthinking easy problems, so the specific claim rests on one study.

s1 shows token-conditional prompting gave only 40% control for its own fine-tuned model (hard truncation/budget forcing gave 100%), so '40 percent' is the failure of prompting, not of truncation, and 'current models' overgeneralises one model; L1's 20-25 point absolute gain over s1 at 512-1024 tokens is correct, and TALE reports prompt budgets do shrink CoT.
fix: In s1's fine-tuned model, a prompt-stated token limit controlled length only 40% of the time (token-conditional control, Table 3) while hard truncation via budget forcing gave 100% control; but hard truncation loses accuracy at small budgets (L1, a length-trained model, is 20-25 points absolute better than s1 at 512-1024 tokens).

problem: Minor: E1 separates thinking and solution budgets and Wu et al. report up to 10x longer answers after hard interrupts; 'cheap' is the researcher's judgment (E1's robustness comes with a light GRPO training stage) and the leakage was shown on Qwen3, GPT-OSS and Magistral.

ESC on MBPP (max 30 samples) used 6.79 samples, a reduction of 23.21 samples (about 77%), not -23%; other figures (AC 2.4-3.8x, ESC -34% to -84%, DeepConf consensus stop -52.8% at K=512 with no accuracy change) match.
fix: Stopping when independent trial answers agree saves 15-84 percent of samples or tokens at no or tiny accuracy cost: Adaptive-Consistency 2.4-3.8x fewer samples, ESC -34% to -84%, DeepConf consensus stop -52.8% tokens at K=512 with identical accuracy. Outside math the evidence is thin: MBPP 23.21 fewer samples out of 30 (about -77%, ESC), code +0.4% accuracy at 2.4x (Adaptive-Consistency), GPQA-D only multiple choice.

problem: Minor: S* attributes the no-gain result to generated tests in selection/debugging ablations (Table 3, Section 5); R2E-Gym plateaus 43.7% and 42.8% then hybrid 51.0% match.

Minor: S* QwQ plateau beyond N=32 and MRT 41-45 episodes (later episodes do not improve, maj@p better) and R2E-Gym 43.7/42.8 to 51.0 match; the 'no study fitted a concavity test' part is an absence claim that cannot be verified.

Zeng et al. find failed revisions exceed successful ones only for QwQ and R1-Distill-1.5B; for R1-Distill-32B/14B and LIMO successful revision was higher (though plateauing after about 10 steps), so 'net harmful for QwQ, R1-Distill and LIMO' is too broad.
fix: Extending one trace with Wait or Alternatively on untrained reasoning models gives weak, model-dependent sequential gains: revision flipped correct answers to wrong more often than the reverse for QwQ and R1-Distill-1.5B (successful revisions were under 10% everywhere), while R1-Distill-32B/14B and LIMO had higher successful than failed revision rates that plateaued after about 10 steps; correct solutions are shorter than wrong ones. The s1 result (sequential extension helps) holds for a model fine-tuned on 1k traces, so the Ghosal vs s1 conflict may be partly explained by training for continuation and critic quality.

problem: Kocsis-Szepesvari proves consistency and shows B^(D/2) iteration growth only empirically on random P-game trees, and says UCT may be faster at higher failure rates; the Browne survey does not support it; "no free lunch on small trees" is the researcher inference.
fix: UCT is provably consistent (failure probability goes to zero); on random P-game trees (B=2,D=20 and B=8,D=8) it reached near-zero failure in a similar number of leaf nodes as alpha-beta, with iterations growing roughly as B^(D/2) like alpha-beta, and was faster if a small failure rate was accepted.

problem: Liu et al. say DVTS wins easy and medium problems and beam search wins hard ones for 7B-32B policies; the claim wrongly says diverse tree search wins on hard items.
fix: On math with process reward models, the best test-time method depends on policy size and difficulty: best-of-N wins on easy items for policies under 7B and at every difficulty for 72B, while for 7B-32B policies diverse tree search (DVTS) wins easy and medium items and beam search wins hard ones.

problem: Wu et al. report unfinished solutions with weighted voting and the 7B-vs-34B result as competitive accuracy at about 2x fewer FLOPs; fine.
Go-vs-chess explanation is the researcher synthesis, but the survey (trap states common in chess, Go branching/evaluation difficulty), AlphaZero and R1 appendix support it.

Coverage figures are MATH with Llama-3-8B; the 77.0 (Claude 3.5 Sonnet PlanSearch) vs 60.6 (GPT-4o repeated sampling) comparison is cross-model as in the paper, and same-model repeated sampling for Claude is 55.6, so direction holds.

Numbers match, but ReAct vs Act-only compares reasoning-plus-acting against acting without thoughts (not grounded feedback vs reasoning alone), and InterCode Try Again stops when reward=1, which uses an oracle signal.
fix: Grounded feedback from executing code or tools improves LLM agents: CRITIC with an external tool beats the same loop without the tool (HotpotQA F1 50.5 vs 46.1 for text-davinci-003, 52.9 vs 46.1 for ChatGPT); InterCode-SQL GPT-4 rises from 9.1 to 73.7 over up to 10 interactive turns with execution feedback (the loop stops when reward=1, an oracle); and in ALFWorld interleaving reasoning with actions (ReAct, best trial 71%) beats acting without reasoning (Act, 45%).

problem: Supported by Olausson et al. (APPS grid cells 1.05 and 0.97, 33.30% vs 52.60%); the other listed papers do not bear on it, and Self-Debugging reports gains over larger sample budgets, so the equal-compute conclusion rests on one paper and these two cells.
The $0.70 is Agentless total cost per issue (reproduction tests add about $0.25), not the cost of the tests alone.
EIG-uniform best rank in Kobalczyk et al. is against implicit question-choice strategies rather than prompting alone; UoT 38.1% is a success-rate gain over direct prompting.
The 39% drop is real (Laban et al.), but the +73% clarification F1 in Matsnev is the proposed method versus the ReAct+UE baseline, not asking versus not asking; Wu (2023) reports no results.
fix: Missing information is costly: spreading information over multiple turns (underspecified sharded input) drops performance by 39% on average across six generation tasks, and a prompt-only uncertainty-decomposition method for deciding when to ask raised clarification F1 on ALFWorld-Clarification by 73% over a ReAct+UE baseline and 36% over UAM.

problem: Numbers match; the 70.9 to 77.6 gain comes from Kim et al.s rollout-summary selection method (PDR+RTV) and the 15.9 to 56 coverage rise is DeepSeek-Coder-V2 on SWE-bench Lite with an automatic verifier, so the pairing is loose.

Position paper (no experiments), Kumar (cites Kirsh and Maglio, experiments) and Annese (ASK actions, o3-mini) check out, but the Tetris serving benchmark (2603.02348) never mentions epistemic action, Kirsh or Maglio, so it is not a named-term item; the universal negative is only a search record.
fix: In searches on 2026-11-01 no study was found that tests Kirsh and Maglio's epistemic-action hypothesis by name as a probe-before-attempt test on an LLM. Items using the term: a position paper with no data, a belief-query study that cites Kirsh and Maglio (results in figures only), and an ASK-action study with o3-mini; a Tetris serving benchmark was found by the search but does not use the term.

problem: Ceka et al. measure the 17-26% overfitting (18-30% in the reproducer figure) only for SWE-agent and 4-5% for Agentless, not for open-process agents in general; the 41-57% trigger rate and the Sun et al. 47% figure check out; Huang et al. is only loosely related.
fix: A probe the model writes itself can mislead: in Ceka et al.s trace study, patches passing the agent's own reproducer failed the real tests in about 17-30% of cases for SWE-agent versus 4-5% for Agentless, agent-written reproducers trigger the bug only 41-57% of the time, and models copy a silently wrong tool output (accuracy up to 47% below the best no-tool setting, Sun et al.).

problem: The ASK figure comes from a very small o3-mini study (5 trials per scenario); the under-1%, 15%, 5% and 30% figures match.

Lindenbauer et al. say masking does not significantly reduce solve rate (higher than Raw Agent in three of five setups), so no loss means no significant loss; the Tetris source adds nothing for this claim.

Margins quoted as about 0.6 to 3 points omit MemRL +3.6 over MemP (listed in the same evidence) and Sarukkai +8 on Wordcraft; CASCADE uses Qwen3-32B and Sarukkai gpt-4o-mini, so none is a frozen frontier-class test, and "every direct head-to-head" is a claim about the researcher's own search.
fix: In the head-to-head comparisons found, choosing cases by learned value beat similarity-based retrieval, with small margins online (Memento parametric vs non-parametric retriever +0.6 to +1.0 F1/accuracy points; CASCADE +2.92 over non-learned retrieval with Qwen3-32B; MemRL +3.6 over MemP); Sarukkai (5 seeds, gpt-4o-mini) finds learned exemplar curation adds about +1 (ALFWorld), +2 (SQL) and +7 to +8 (Wordcraft) over naive accumulation; no paired test with a frozen frontier-class model was found.

problem: MemRL, Active Example Selection (65.4 vs 63.5) and Evo-Memory numbers check out; the EPR and LLM-R in-domain dependence is not supported by any source listed for this claim (it is plausible from those papers), and 65.4 is 1.9 above the reordering baseline.
The 57.0 and 51.4 starting points for MTOP and SMCalFlow are the earlier learned retriever CBR (BM25 gets 52.9 and 46.1), so those are gains over the strongest prior retriever, not over BM25.

Wang et al. say the LLM-R gains are substantially smaller on knowledge-intensive tasks (commonsense, reasoning, memorised facts; NQ excepted) and say it helps on Sentiment140; the claim re-labels this as small gains on reading comprehension and sentiment, which the paper does not state (sentiment is +41 over random in its table). SQuAD below random, Min et al. 1.7/2.6, and Levy 2.5 to 6.9 check out.
fix: Learned retrieval has failure cases: LLM-R falls below random on SQuAD (many questions share a passage, so it retrieves near duplicates with low diversity) and its gains on knowledge-intensive tasks (commonsense, reasoning, memorised facts; NQ excepted) are much smaller than the 30-task average; random labels in demonstrations cost only 1.7 points on average for multi-choice and 2.6 for classification (Min et al.), so demonstrations mostly convey format, input distribution and label space. Gap pass: set-level coverage selection (Levy 2023) beats top-k similarity by 2.5 to 6.9 points on GeoQuery with Codex (smallest on the i.i.d. split).

problem: Numbers check out (>97%, >99% no search, 72% over 50 games at 10M visits, defences failed), but both papers are by the same FAR.AI group (Wang, Gleave, Tseng, Pelrine), so they count as one source; the 72% result also shows more search lowers the win rate from 95.7% at 4,096 visits.

Karvonen numbers (99.6% probe, 99.8% legal moves) match; ChessGPT-Base (RedPajama-3B fine-tuned on chess data) scores 92.8-99.5 vs LLaMA-7B 29.5-53.0 (its own base RedPajama scores 23-52), so "from about 30-53%" uses LLaMA-7B as baseline.

Numbers are right (Game of 24 10 to 6, MMLU-Pro Eng 53.2 to 48.8 under DR; Memp 74.59 vs 73.38), but curated memory did not gain on MMLU-Pro Eng for GPT-4o (DC-Cu 44.0, DC-RS 51.2, both below baseline 53.2); it gained only on Game of 24 (93 and 99).
fix: Naive verbatim retrieval can hurt: Dynamic Cheatsheet retrieval-only (DR) dropped GPT-4o on Game of 24 (10 to 6) and MMLU-Pro Eng (53.2 to 48.8); curated memory gained on Game of 24 (93 to 99) but not on MMLU-Pro Eng, where GPT-4o fell under every variant. Memp: random sampling beat query-keyed retrieval for GPT-4o on TravelPlanner (74.59 vs 73.38).

problem: Fig 8 values are read from a plot (about 52 to 47.6); cross-benchmark comparison is loose but hedged.
Memento says the case bank saturates with about 3k training data (not 3k items strictly); minor.
Cross-benchmark comparison (AgentDriver vs WebArena) is loose; numbers match.

Chapelle and Li is not context-free: it includes contextual bandit experiments (display-ad CTR with features, LinUCB, news recommendation), so "All are stationary and context-free" is wrong; also the 10% to 100% figure is Boltzmann versus its closest competitor, not versus UCB1, and Chapelle and Li call Thompson sampling highly competitive rather than strongest.
fix: Classic bandit sources do not support a UCB bonus as the default: tuned epsilon-greedy almost always did best in Auer 2002; softmax and epsilon-greedy beat UCB1 in most of 12 instances in Kuleshov and Precup 2014 (softmax beat its closest competitor by 10% to 100% in regret); Chapelle and Li 2011 found Thompson sampling beat UCB and epsilon-greedy in simulation and in contextual ad and news experiments. Auer 2002 and Kuleshov and Precup use stationary context-free bandits.

problem: The no-tests-of-drift-extent part is an absence claim not checkable from the sources; Evo-Memory not needed for the wording.
Last sentence (no study ablates failures under a learned selector) is an absence claim, not checkable.
The two Brown et al. figures come from different tasks (SWE-bench Lite vs MATH with Llama-3-8B); wording does not say so but numbers are right.
Listed a25 url (1603.06560) is Hyperband, not a synthesis; claim does not depend on it.

Numbers match EVOLvE Table 1 (contextual RH Flash 0.0, Pro 7.1; AG 46.4, 64.3), but external statistics helped only the larger Gemini models: for Gemma-2B and Gemma-9B summarised or algorithm-guided win rates were lower than raw history (SH 10.5/5.3 and AG 4.9/4.1 vs RH 7.6/10.5; AG below RH for Gemma-9B). Metric is pairwise win rate.
fix: For Gemini-1.5 Flash and Pro, giving externally computed per-arm statistics (summarised history or UCB statistics in the prompt) raises bandit performance (MAB win rate Flash 27.7 to 32.2-34.8, Pro 45.5 to 59.6-60.0); raw history is poor, and in contextual bandits raw history is near useless (Flash 0.0, Pro 7.1 vs 46.4, 64.3 with algorithm-guided support). The small Gemma models did not benefit.

problem: 87% and 64% figures are from Gemma2 models (largest), not LLMs in general.
Zuo and Zhu 11.10% is a coverage gain at average budget 8 on Llama-3.1-8B (accuracy gains are 1.4 to 2.5 points); nothing-helps-at-level-5 is Snell saying no method makes meaningful progress.
Gains are average relative improvements over baselines in the paper.
Older adults showed similar directed exploration but lower random exploration and less information seeking; the 26% is from the abstract while the results section gives 11 of 51 (21.6%).
Damani predictor is a hidden-state probe, not the LLM stated estimate; the 1% vs 0% pathology is real but concerns a learned predictor, so the framing is a synthesis.
Zhang gives decrements of 14% from a 79% peak (read as points, giving 65%); ST-BoN 70-80% savings holds at certain N values; the no-rank-correlation sentence is an absence claim.

The final-third shift is in Bilalic 2019 real data, but the change point near the 90% bin comes from Graf 2023 data that the paper states are simulated to represent a sudden shift; the original 2019 data show a gradual group-level shift (27% of solvers sudden-looking, 54% incremental). Also Graf 2023 re-analyses the same data from the same lab, so the two sources are not independent.
fix: Solvers who later succeed shift attention from the values to the critical element (the plus sign/operators) only in the final third of the solving period, while non-solvers stay on the obvious parts (values); on the original eye-tracking data the group-level shift looks gradual (individually 27% of solvers sudden-looking, 54% incremental), so whether the shift is abrupt is unresolved.

problem: a09 and b03 are the same Danek and Wiley 2017 paper (PMC and Frontiers copies); the later-work claim rests on Wiley and Miller 2026, which is independent.

Effect sizes match (Salvi d 0.39 to 1.85), but Webb non-insight Aha-accuracy r was 0.02 only in Exp 1 (0.24, p=.04 in Exp 1a; 0.19 with BF10 about 40 in Exp 2), so near 0 is too strong; Salvi says analytic solutions had relatively more commission errors than timeouts compared with insight, not that insight errors are mostly omissions.
fix: On average, self-labelled insight solutions are more accurate than analytic ones (d about 0.4 to 1.85 across four experiments), and analytic-labelled responses include relatively more errors of commission (wrong guesses) and insight responses relatively more omissions (timeouts). Aha and accuracy correlate r about 0.4 to 0.5 for classic insight problems and CRAs, and only weakly (r 0.02 to 0.24) for non-insight problems.

problem: Nine-dot point is the authors expectation plus a citation to Ollinger 2014, not a new test here.

Salmon-Mordekovich and Leikin found verbal insight problems differed from verbal non-insight (resembling only spatial non-insight), found impasse reports 37 to 41% on insight vs 1.7% on verbal non-insight, and conclude with mixed evidence for both business-as-usual and special-process; Wiley and Miller study 4 puzzles of one type, so solver state vs problem type is not shown as the claim states.
fix: Insight is not a clean property of problem type: insight ratings vary within a problem type, Aha-accuracy links differ by task (strong for insight problems and CRAs, weak for non-insight), and insight and spatial non-insight problems resemble each other on dual-task and individual-difference tests (both unaffected by secondary tasks), though verbal insight problems differed from verbal non-insight problems and the authors find some evidence for a rarer special-process mode.

problem: Loewe networks need L1-regularised gating plus update noise, so plain gradient-trained is shorthand; numbers 46/99 vs 49/99 and none at zero noise match.
Creative-vs-factual drops are stated as percentages (-6.08% to -17.21%) and may be relative rather than points; Only Connect table columns are garbled in text extraction but 6/59/471 of 494 match.

Numbers match, but for NazoNazo GPT-5 falls inside the human 95% CI (46.6 to 59.2), so the gap is closed for the best model; the averages (7.6/17.6 vs 52.9) do not close it. Rebus GPT-5 60.42 vs gpt-4o 18.75 and CresOWLve doubling are correct.
fix: More reasoning effort or a reasoning model helps on insight-type riddles and usually does not close the gap to humans: NazoNazo non-reasoning 7.6% vs reasoning 17.6% vs human mean 52.9% (120-item subset), though GPT-5 alone falls within the human 95% CI; rebus puzzles GPT-5 60.42% vs gpt-4o 18.75%; CresOWLve GPT-5.4 nearly doubles from no thinking to medium effort while non-thinking models stay under 30%.

problem: BRAINTEASER (45% fail, SemEval 80% drop) numbers are right, but BRAINTEASER only suggests memorisation, CresOWLve reports some contamination evidence and a risk, and Mizumoto argue memorisation does not explain NazoNazo scores; contaminated or memorised as established fact is too strong.
fix: Riddle and lateral benchmarks carry contamination or memorisation risk: ChatGPT fails 45% of original or semantic puzzles whose context-reconstructed twin it solves (BRAINTEASER authors suggest memorisation), CresOWLve reports some contamination evidence for its public quiz sources, and in SemEval-2024 Task 9 over 80% of leaderboard models lost accuracy on grouped original+semantic puzzles even with 80% training data; the NazoNazo authors argue memorisation does not explain their low scores.

problem: The abandoned qualifier for the 70% figure is the authors interpretation (the figure counts wrong responses containing at least one correct thought).

Numbers match (GLM-4-9B in d14, GPT-3.5-turbo in d15), but RM-PoT also adds program-of-thought execution and 5 retrieved examples, and PoT alone (78.9/65.6/87.1) already beats SC, so the gain is not due to re-encoding alone.
fix: RM-PoT (reformulation K=4 plus retrieved examples plus program-of-thought code, GLM-4-9B, N=16 paths) scored 80.4 / 69.1 / 88.0 vs self-consistency 77.3 / 64.9 / 87.6 on GSM8K / AQuA / SVAMP, but PoT alone scored 78.9 / 65.6 / 87.1, so part of the gain is not from reformulation (d14); question-reformulation plus sampling (QuestionC-SC) averaged 83.0 vs 79.5 for plain self-consistency on GPT-3.5-turbo across ten tasks (d15). This is rewording, not constraint relaxation, and token counts are not matched.

problem: ROC-AUC above 0.9 is reported only for R1-Distill-Qwen-32B on AIME (in-distribution generally above 0.7); the 24% saving at 88.2% is for R1-Distill-Llama-8B on MATH.
fix: A latent-progress probe predicts later success in LLMs when you have access to the model or can truncate its trace: hidden-state probes give ROC-AUC above 0.7 in-distribution and above 0.9 for R1-Distill-Qwen-32B on AIME (d04), early exit at threshold 0.85 on R1-Distill-Llama-8B (MATH) saves about 24% tokens at 88.2% accuracy, equal to no early exit (d04), and truncated-trace answer distributions track final accuracy (d01). It does not yet show that a flat probe reliably precedes a restructure that works.

problem: d12 wrong-prefix numbers only in a figure (text confirms accuracy falls with longer wrong prefix); d16 is a tiny 5-puzzle pilot, as the claim says.

Balanced accuracies .86/.83/.83/.83 verified (SVM crashed on two sets); note Gigerenzer & Brighton's cross-validated city task shows take-the-best ahead across all sizes, so 'flexible models catch up' is the general bias-variance argument, not that figure.

54% vs 89% (Pohl 2006) and about 30% (Oppenheimer) check out, but the contradicting-cue figure is 95% to 82% mean (Richter & Spaeth; median stayed 97%); 98% belongs to Newell & Fernandez, where it fell to 64%.
fix: People use the recognition heuristic selectively: adherence drops when recognition is not tied to the criterion (54% for distance vs 89% for population in Pohl 2006; about 30% choosing the recognized object for Chernobyl vs a fictitious city) and when a contradicting cue exists (Richter & Spaeth: mean adherence 95% to 82%, median unchanged at 97%; Newell & Fernandez: 98% to 64%).

problem: Sprague et al. give average CoT gains of 14.2 for symbolic, 12.3 for math, 6.9 for logical; the claim swaps the labels. The 95% MMLU equals-sign figure is confirmed.
fix: CoT helps mainly on math and symbolic tasks (average gains 12.3 points for math and 14.2 for symbolic); elsewhere direct answering is near equal, and as much as 95 percent of the MMLU gain is on questions containing an equals sign. This supports a gate that skips deliberation on non-symbolic items.

problem: RouteLLM's 95% of GPT-4 is the MT Bench figure (8.8 vs 9.3); GSM8K at the same point is 87%, so the evidence note saying GSM8K 95% is wrong, but the claim does not rely on it.
Numbers verified (RF 90.2, Sonnet 4.6 rules 80.3, GPT-4o rules 70.5; 12 of 12 pairs below zero-shot); the studies test LLM rules and trees generally, not fast-and-frugal trees as such.

Itzhak et al. find decoy effects mixed (and the T5 to Flan-T5 certainty rise not significant) and cannot separate RLHF from instruction tuning; Ansari's 15 of 15 is for distributions becoming less uniform, while endpoint avoidance is reported as medians (base already avoids endpoints at 0.30-0.60 of interior rate, tuned near 0).
fix: Tuning-installed heuristics in LLMs are measurable: instruction-tuned or RLHF models show higher certainty-effect and belief-bias scores than their pretrained counterparts (decoy-effect results are mixed, and RLHF cannot be isolated from instruction tuning), and across 15 base/tuned pairs instruction tuning made number choice less uniform in all 15, with tuned models almost never returning the endpoints (median ratio to interior rate near 0 vs 0.30-0.60 for base). Scale changes human-like heuristic errors non-monotonically (CRT: davinci-003 5 percent, ChatGPT-3.5 59, ChatGPT-4 96).

problem: Schulz et al. (2016) test only the 81-city data (plus simulated data) and compare TTB, ABC-TTB and CART, not logistic regression; the four datasets (homeless, profsalary, city, mileage) and the logistic-regression comparison are Peltola et al. (2019), where regression wins on mileage.
fix: Learned take-the-best variants recover cue order from data: ABC-TTB (Schulz et al. 2016) outperforms classic TTB and CART on the 81-city data set (read from a figure) and recovers simulated TTB structure, and probabilistic TTB (Peltola et al. 2019) performs comparably or better than classic TTB and ABC-TTB and better than logistic regression on three of four small benchmarks (homeless, profsalary, city; logistic regression wins on mileage, the largest). These are model papers on few benchmark data sets, with Peltola's reusing Schulz's data.

problem: AbstentionBench's budget sweep (s1.1 32B, R1 Distill 'same trend') shows abstention not improving on GSM8k-Abstain and worsening on UMWP while accuracy rises, and o1 reasoning effort was mixed, so 'generally worsen' is too strong.
fix: More reasoning is not safe on unanswerable or ill-posed items: reasoning models write much longer answers on missing-premise questions (Fan et al.), reasoning fine-tuning lowers abstention by 24% on average across 20 LLMs (Kirichenko et al.), and bigger reasoning budgets in a sweep on two models did not improve abstention (no gain on GSM8k-Abstain, a decline on UMWP) while accuracy rose. Two independent groups, same direction, different designs.

problem: Numbers verified in v3 of the metacognition paper (rho -0.80 TriviaQA, +0.00 NQ over four models, 1.98-fold); the 'mirrors human 54% vs 89%' link is the researcher's analogy, not a source finding.
Per-benchmark Thinkless accuracy checked only on GSM8K (0.8418 vs 0.8347 for the R1-1.5B baseline); 1,953% and over-92% figures verified in Chen et al.

Schwartz & Metcalfe (1992) verified via Europe PMC abstract (four experiments; cue priming raised judgments, target generation did not; in Exp 3 target priming also raised them); Reder & Ritter (1992) confirmed to exist only through a citing record, abstract not read.

Minor slip: Kimball & Metcalfe's delayed cue-only .72 (Exp 2) is compared with delayed cue-target .43, not immediate .36 (that comparison is Exp 3, .76 vs .36); Rhodes & Tauber's cue-only g=0.03 and Dunlosky & Nelson '45 of 45 subjects' verified. Kimball & Metcalfe attribute the retrieval-attempt advantage to a memory boost rather than better monitoring.

Kimball & Metcalfe verified (reexposure erased the effect: Exp 3 delayed .53 vs immediate .43 n.s.; Exp 2 .39 vs .46); 'selection of recall outcomes' is their memory hypothesis (retrieved items get a spaced-study boost).
Rhodes & Tauber abstract numbers verified; the 0.70 and 0.03 values are in Tekin & Roediger's introduction (not the R&T abstract), as the claim says.

Undorf & Broder report that scene JOLs rest on cues most of which also predicted actual recognition (not cues that fail to help memory); in the font-size study (first author Fan, not Tian) word frequency moderates the contribution of beliefs, not the font-size effect itself; only Kornell et al. show a cue (type size) that moves predicted but not actual memory.
fix: Judgments of learning are influenced by superficial cues that need not help memory: type size raises predicted but not actual memory (Kornell et al. 2011), and the role of metamemory beliefs in the font-size effect depends on word frequency (beliefs mediate it for low-frequency words, not high-frequency ones; Fan et al. 2021). For naturalistic scene pictures, JOLs use several intrinsic and extrinsic cues, most of which also predict recognition (Undorf & Broder 2021).

problem: Xiong et al. Table 3 verified (GPT-3.5 only: CoT top-K M=1 54.8 to 5-sample consistency 92.7 AUROC on GSM8K); Kadavath et al. section 4.2 confirms showing many own samples improves self-evaluation.
ECE above 0.377 (GPT-3, GPT-3.5, Vicuna) and GPT-4 average AUROC 62.7% verified in Xiong et al. text; Yona et al. abstract-level only (one lab's paper counted once for the numbers).

Kapoor et al. Table 3 verified (AUROC 80.0/85.1/70.2 vs 56.9/66.2/47.1; ECE worse for LLaMA-2-7B and Mistral-7B-Instruct); all specifics come from one paper, with Lin et al. (2022) supporting finetuned verbalized uncertainty only generally.

Orgad abstract confirms concentration in specific tokens and failure to generalize across datasets (exact-answer-token detail is from the paper body, not the abstract); Azaria 71-83% and Ferrando refusal steering verified.

In Zhang et al. Table 2 (R1-Distill-Llama-8B) math-to-math transfer AUC runs 0.69-0.83 (GSM8K to AIME is 0.69), not .76-.83; the other figures (math to logic .56-.63, logic to math .74-.77 with ECE .17-.19, AIME ECE .25-.31, early exit 88.2% vs 88.6% at 24% savings) check out.
fix: Hidden-state probes trained on at most 1,000 examples predict correctness well in-distribution (AUC above .7; above .9 for one model on AIME) and give 24% token savings in early exit at 88.2% vs 88.6% accuracy, but transfer across task classes is partial: math to math AUC .69-.83, math to logic .56-.63, logic to math .74-.77 but with ECE .17-.19, and ECE degrades on AIME (.25-.31).

problem: Abstract-level verification only; the 'does not track knowledge' framing is the authors' hypothesis that models mimic observed language use.

Zendo and experiment-selection numbers verified in arXiv 2402.06025 v6-v8 (NeurIPS version); UoT +38.1% is vs direct prompting (unstated in claim). Two sources are different papers for different sub-claims.

Numbers match Table 1 of PMC5880367 (the only source printing them; Griffiths 2011 and Sobel and Munro 2006 do not, and the original 2004 paper was not reachable). Screening-off 100% holds for 3y and 4y Exp1 only (4y Exp2 was 94%).
Kuhberger 2023 review confirms d=.31/.52/.60 and h=.612 (49 countries, >100,000); Druckman confirms the 72/28 vs 22/78 founding shift. 'Medium-sized' is a mild label for d .3-.6.

Roberts 2022 (d=1.32 gain, 0.003 loss, first-fixation shift) and Gong 2026 (N=26, F=309.5, etap2=.93) verified; 'even larger' compares different effect-size metrics (etap2 vs etaG2) though means and F support it.
FrameBench-HPS (32.41%, 63.33% GPT-4o-mini, 0.63%, 98.1% uncertain-class) and PsyAgentBench Table 5 (.020 blind vs .619 named, gpt-oss-120B, single scenario pair) verified.

CogBias Table 13 (clean text extraction) gives Framing Effect 17.7% -> 24.3% (+6.6); 35.6% -> 41.4% (+5.8) is Risk Compensation; Hyperbolic Discounting is -21.0 and -13.4 is Halo Effect (the researcher read a garbled table). Echterhoff self-help 0/1.4/2.7% and few-shot failure verified.
fix: Naive debiasing instructions are unreliable: a be-careful prompt helps framing only a little (CogBias, averaged over 3 models: framing-effect accuracy 17.7% to 24.3%, +6.6 points) and backfires on other biases (hyperbolic discounting -21.0 points, disposition effect -19.6, halo effect -13.4); few-shot debiasing can push models to admit-all or reject-all; self-help rewriting leaves 0-2.7% framing-biased prompts (Echterhoff et al.).

problem: Hwang numbers (5.69% GPT-5-mini, 66.29% LLaMA 3.2 1B, 14 judges) verified; but Germani and Spitale find the agreement drop for attribution to Chinese authors specifically, not 'a nationality' in general.
fix: Wording and source cues shift LLM judgments beyond the content: 14 LLM judges vary from 5.69% (GPT-5-mini) to 66.29% (LLaMA 3.2 1B) inconsistency across logically equivalent framings of the same query, and attributing statements to Chinese authors lowered agreement across four LLMs (most for Deepseek Reasoner).

problem: Sharma (98% Claude 1.3), Kawada and Kellis (93-100%, up to 99.4%, 12 LLMs, over ten million trials) and Pander Score (instructional prompts +17 to +70, Claude Fable 5 about 0 to +19) all verified.

Kawada and Kellis (helps weaker, harms stronger; receiver-congruent errors; 93-100%) and Zhao 2025 (tools flip already-correct answers when beliefs are strong) verified; c19 and d26 are the same paper, so only two independent papers support it.

Hesselmann (N=117/89, 825 vs 821 ms, BF01=5.07, 60% vs 47% hard accuracy, Camerer 104+130) verified; Camerer 2018 page confirms Sparrow 2011 among the 21 replications (13 of 21 replicated) but its page does not show the Sparrow-specific numbers; original N=46 is from the supplement (Hesselmann notes main text fits N=69).

Gilbert et al. 2020 JEP:General and Sachdeva and Gilbert 2020 (Conscious Cogn, registered report) abstracts match; both from the same lab (Gilbert), so independence is limited, and 'driven by' is the authors' account (underconfidence not full explanation).

Grinschgl et al. 2021 verified (N=172 per experiment; Exp 1 identity t(170)=-2.76 p=.006; faster, no accuracy difference); the claim rests on this single paper (Storm and Stone is a different, tangential effect), and p=.006 is Exp 1 only.

Soares and Storm 2022 (Exp 1 N=60 d=0.35 [0.09,0.61]; Exps 2-3 between-subjects with 5-photo impairment) and Lurie et al. 2025 (photos/screenshots impair memory in three experiments) verified. 'Items' are paintings/artworks.

LongMemEval table (GPT-4o 0.870 to 0.606, 30.3%; Llama 3.1 70B 0.710 to 0.454, 36.1%; text says 30-60%) and LoCoMo (32.4 vs 87.9; RAG 56% below human) verified; table rows for other settings reach 66.3% drop, so '30 to 60%' is the authors' summary.

Nye et al. numbers match Table 2 (11% vs 26.5%, 20% vs 41.5%), but the 26.5% few-shot scratchpad figure uses a loosened accuracy criterion (checks v0 instead of output); under naive scoring few-shot tracing accuracy is roughly zero, so the few-shot gain is not like-for-like. The SEP entry is a conceptual source without numbers.
fix: Writing intermediate steps to a scratchpad improves multi-step computation: on 200 synthetic Python test programs, fine-tuned accuracy rose from 20% (direct) to 41.5% (scratchpad); few-shot rose from 11% to 26.5%, but the few-shot scratchpad figure uses a loosened accuracy criterion (naive scoring gives roughly zero), so only the fine-tuned comparison is like-for-like.

problem: Smart, Clowes and Clark name two problems (redundancy, agency); use-versus-ignore is the condition under which they say the redundancy problem is resolved, not a third named problem. ClashEval (over 1200 questions, 6 domains, 6 LLMs, context bias vs prior bias) does measure when models follow retrieved text over their prior. 'Redundancy and agency have not been measured' is an absence claim the sources cannot show.
fix: In an LLM+retrieval system the extended-mind analogy faces a redundancy problem and an agency problem (Smart, Clowes and Clark 2025); whether the redundancy problem is resolved depends on whether the model actually uses retrieved text rather than ignoring it, and that use-versus-ignore question has been measured for facts by ClashEval (context bias 0.157-0.313 across six models). The authors themselves tested it only qualitatively on 20 queries.

problem: Mallen et al. (46.5% PopQA, '5.3% higher than any non-adaptive method', API cost cut by half in abstract) and Adaptive-RAG (misclassifications about 22%, 23%, 31%, 47%) verified; the paper writes 5.3% without saying points, and the cost halving is stated for adaptive retrieval generally.

Huang et al. Tables 2-3 (HotpotQA 26.0 to 49.0 oracle vs 26.0 to 25.0 without; CSQA 75.8 to 38.1) and ExpeL (insights-only 36% vs retrieval-only 31% HotpotQA; 50% vs 55% ALFWorld; WebShop tie) verified. 'Only' is the authors' reading of intrinsic self-correction on reasoning tasks, not a universal law for reflection.

Lorenz et al. state the identity (collective error + diversity = average individual error) and Farrell argues shrinkage helps individuals, but Farrell also disputes the bracketing measure and asks whether estimates shrank too much, so the two sides do not differ 'only' in level judged; the Rauhut reply could not be opened (captcha).
fix: The diversity prediction identity (collective error + group diversity = average individual error) means that shrinking spread lowers average individual error even when the crowd mean does not move; this reconciles much of Farrell's 'individuals benefit' (rewards rise) with Lorenz's 'crowd does not improve', though Farrell also disputes the bracketing metric and raises over-shrinkage as an open question.

problem: Lorenz et al. verified (arithmetic mean closer than individuals in 21.3% of cases, 77.1% in log space; geometric mean and median recommended for their data), but Kao et al. 2018 find the median tends to underestimate and the geometric mean can be the worst choice for small samples at large numerosities, so 'use median or geometric mean' is not a general rule.
fix: For right-skewed (lognormal-like) estimates the arithmetic mean is a poor aggregate (closer to the truth than individuals in only 21.3% of cases in Lorenz et al., 77.1% in log space); Lorenz et al. found the geometric mean and median work well for their data, but Kao et al. (2018) show the median underestimates and the geometric mean is not uniformly best, motivating bias-corrected aggregators.

problem: All three claim parts (median S=0.34, linear rise with distance up to ~2.5 orders, confident people follow less and are more accurate) are verified in Jayles et al. 2017, but a11 and b06 are the same paper; Mavrodiev et al. 2013 only corroborates the linear distance dependence (slopes 0.27-0.97) and does not test own-vs-group weighting.
fix: In Jayles et al. (2017), a single estimation study with hard questions in France and Japan, people weighted their own opinion more than the group on average (median sensitivity S=0.34); sensitivity rose linearly with the distance to the group up to about 2.5 orders of magnitude (Mavrodiev et al. 2013 also find guess change linear in distance to the group mean); confident people followed the group less and were more accurate.

problem: Bertalanic and Fortuna (2.1-3.4x tokens, vulnerability up to 70.0%), Huang (voting 88.2 vs debate 83.0 at 9 responses), Choi (0.7691/0.7377, 0.7242/0.6929), Zhang (about 15% of 36 cells) and Wynn (Llama MMLU 61.6 to 57.8, Mistral 33.6 to 24.4, GPT-4o-mini flat) all verified. The 2.1-3.4x token cost is versus isolated self-correction.

Asch study (22 to 49 points, under 3 points n=5 to 10), Herd Behavior (0.48 flip rate; strong/weak prompts same 0.55 as baseline; format effects) and Kraidia et al. (10-40% accuracy drop from a persuasive adversary) verified; 'persona prompts' refers to the be-stubborn/be-agreeable system prompts.

Kong et al. (semantic collapse over 200-1000 rounds, thirteen interventions 'did not reliably restore' diversity; a custom diversity-targeted RL gave some positive effect) and Pokharel and Dantu (hidden anchors, 3 open models, 90 runs) verified; but Yazici et al. show consensus departs from the DeGroot centrality-weighted forecast (binary accuracy 60% vs 50% chance, 3-class 32%), which is weaker than 'ignores starting opinions'.
fix: Interaction among LLM agents drives semantic collapse (Kong et al.); thirteen interventions did not reliably restore semantic diversity (only a custom diversity-targeted RL gave a partial positive effect); in three open models each carries a hidden anchor belief that pulls opinions (Pokharel and Dantu), and networked-LLM consensus departs from the DeGroot prediction from initial opinions and network centrality (Yazici et al.), though initial opinions retain weak predictive value (binary 60% vs 50% chance).

problem: Schoenegger et al. (12 LLMs vs 925 humans, Brier 0.20 vs 0.19; 17-28% gain; simple average beat updated forecasts) and Douven (15 LLMs, learned aggregators below all individual models; weight vs error-decorrelation rho=+0.482, vs individual rank rho=-0.075) verified. Douven reports contamination effects, so the learned-aggregator result is on prediction-market items with a clean subset of only 94 items.

Jayles et al. (sensitivity rises with distance to group up to ~2.5 orders) and Becker et al. (revision size vs initial error rho=0.41, 4,340 estimates, 1,040 subjects; falls to 0.25 after controlling distance from neighbourhood average) verified; the two sources measure different quantities (distance to group vs distance to truth).

Huang Table 3 (GPT-3.5 CSQA 75.8 to 38.1; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0), Snell (about 38% of correct answers converted to incorrect by naive revision; selection needed) and Xu (six LLMs show self-bias) verified.

Numbers verified (Li: Self-MoA +6.6 AlpacaEval 2.0 and +3.8 average, reported as % improvements; Zhang Table 3/4: GPT-4o-mini CoT mean of 9 datasets = 77.01 vs Heter-SoM 76.7; Barrera-Lemarchand: best single model deliberating with its own copies beat the heterogeneous consensus, d=0.88). But the headline 'does not beat' is wider than the sources: Li say Self-MoA wins in 'a large number of scenarios', and Barrera-Lemarchand also find mixed groups beat size-matched clone groups (d=0.48).
fix: Mixing model families usually does not beat sampling the best single model many times once the best model is the baseline: Self-MoA beat mixed MoA by 6.6% on AlpacaEval 2.0 and 3.8% on average over MMLU, CRUX and MATH (Li et al.), in a large number of but not all scenarios; Heter-MAD's gain is measured against the two-model average, and from Zhang et al.'s tables GPT-4o-mini CoT alone averages 77.0 vs Heter-SoM 76.7; Barrera-Lemarchand found the best single model deliberating with copies of itself beat the heterogeneous consensus (d=0.88), although mixed groups beat size-matched clone groups of weaker models (d=0.48).

problem: Renze and Guven (GPT-3.5 CoT 1,000 questions H(10)=10.439 p=0.403; nine models, 100-question exam; collapse above 1.0), Wang et al. (robust across T=0.3-0.7 and top-k) and Li et al. (temperatures 0.5-1.2 varied jointly with mixtures) verified; but 'no study measured' temperature effects on peer exposure is an absence claim the sources cannot show, and the confound statement is the researcher's inference.
fix: Single-attempt accuracy is flat in sampling temperature from 0.0 to 1.0 (GPT-3.5 CoT, 1,000 questions, Kruskal-Wallis p=0.403; nine models on a 100-question exam) and drops quickly above 1.0; self-consistency gains hold across T=0.3-0.7 and top-k settings (LaMDA-137B, GSM8K); this search found no study measuring how temperature changes the benefit or harm of peer exposure, and the Self-MoA regression over temperatures 0.5-1.2 varies temperature together with the model mix.

problem: Taylor 2020 (pull vs push, string vs metatool, breeze weight; 'prudent to be cautious', 'too early'), Jelbert 2019 (35/48 vs 23/48) and Martin-Ordas 2008 (tube 8/20 vs platform 12/20, no transfer, raking preferred to pushing) verified; the example 'single tool vs rake' is not a stated contrast in these sources (closest is trap-tube vs trap-platform and raking vs pushing), a minor labelling slip.
Numbers verified in 5 papers; minor: massed practice did not beat spaced during practice in Rohrer Exp1 (83 vs 82), and restudy won on a 5-min test rather than during learning.
In Kornell and Bjork 78% said massing was as good as OR better (not preferred massing); Karpicke's flat predictions show insensitivity to condition, not a preference for the easier condition.
fix: Learners misjudge this: in Kornell and Bjork 78% said massing was as good as or better than spacing even though 78% did better with spacing, in the replication 71% said massing produced most learning, and in Karpicke and Roediger predicted recall was flat at about 50% across conditions whose actual one-week recall ranged from about 33% to 80%.

problem: Cepeda 2008 and Rogers 2025 verified; Rogers mostly found no lag effect (ANCOVA exception), so 'mixed' is a fair summary; two listed evidence lines (Kang, Rogers) merely repeat the claim text.

Kornell et al. 2009 numbers verified; second source is a Bjork review (shares coauthors) that reports the independent Huelser and Metcalfe 2012 wrong-guess result, so independence is thin but acceptable.

All Brunmair and Richter numbers verified in full text (the three d-lines are the same paper); other listed sources (Kornell and Bjork, Rohrer and Taylor) support direction only; temporal-spacing g 0.22 is non-significant (CI -0.13 to 0.45).
Bastani and Fan numbers verified; Kosmyna not opened.
Kang and Janik verified; both are small synthetic/preprint LLM studies as the claim notes.
SkillsBench and Wang et al. numbers verified including the caveat; the d08/d09 lines merely repeat the claim text.
Moran/Whiting, Huff/Ulakci and Beyond Confidence verified; the 'prompt-quality predictors do not transfer' clause and the no-direct-study negative were not checked.

Allen-Zhu and Li and Lin et al. verified; note 'depends on ... not verbatim repetition' is an interpretation, and Lin's 7.42 is the base model while +313% is relative to vanilla fine-tuning, as the claim states.
Noise numbers verified, but the '3 seeds floor, 5 or more for strong claims' is not in either source; Bjarnason et al. say detecting a 2 pp gain needs about 9 runs and a 1 pp gain about 36.
fix: Run-to-run noise is large enough to hide small schema effects: single-run pass@1 spreads 2.2-6.0 pp (SD above 1.5 pp at temperature 0, 60,000 SWE-Bench-Verified trajectories); the best reasoning strategy wins only 77% of head-to-head runs against its nearest competitor over 30 trials. Trajectories diverge within the first few percent of tokens. Bjarnason et al. estimate about 9 runs per agent to detect a 2 pp gain and about 36 for 1 pp, so a few seeds are not enough for small effects.

problem: Poirier 2012 and Goh and Lu 2012 numbers verified in full text; Nairne 2002 abstract matches; Goh and Lu show extra match did help under low cue overload, consistent with 'not reliably'.
Goh and Lu Exp3 numbers verified (intralist .32 vs strong extralist .25 vs weak .09); empirical support is one experiment from one lab, Poirier supplies only the choice-rule framing.
Higham 2002 and Postman 1975 verified; claim rests mainly on one study (Higham), and the Joren et al. line is irrelevant.
Guo et al., Wang and Sun, Cuconasu et al. verified; Guo et al. human comparison data not independently checked.

Sciavolino 2021 macro averages (49.7 vs 72.0) verified and Dense X 25% Recall@5 gain on EntityQuestions with weak retrievers verified; the two are different groups. Claim generalises from entity questions only.

HippoRAG Table 5 numbers verified (72.9 vs 67.8 R@5); the ablation tests only node specificity, and the gain comes mostly from 2Wiki (89.1 vs 77.5) with MuSiQue unchanged, so 'IDF' is supported only indirectly via BEIR's BM25 baseline.

Weller et al. verified (BM25 drops more than 89% on synonym LIMIT-small, only on that synthetic test); the dense-weakness half is supported by Sciavolino. Both halves of the claim lean on single papers.
Liu et al. and Chroma verified; caveats: Chroma found no notable needle-position effect in its NIAH task, and the contrast benefit held for PG-essay haystack but was minimal in the arXiv haystack.

Goh and Lu, Badham et al. Exp 2 (df 59 matches 61 participants) and Poirier 2012 verified; Badham shares authors with Poirier as the claim says; the negative 'no failed or preregistered replication found' cannot be verified from the sources.
Tulving and Wiseman, Gardiner 1988 and Gardiner 1990 numbers verified.

Numbers match Duan et al., but 'is an aggregate artefact' states one paper's conclusion (Exp 1 of 48 pairs plus a database meta-analysis) as settled; the .59 vs -.03 is the P(RN)-P(RC) correlation in subject-wise vs item-wise tabulation, offered as an explanation for differing results rather than proof of inflation.
fix: Duan, Glass and Raanaas (1998) argue the clean Tulving-Wiseman function (c=.50, r=.95) results from collapsing across items: in their data recognition failure concentrated in items whose cue and target are related outside the study episode, and the P(RN)-P(RC) correlation differed between subject-wise (r=.59) and item-wise (r=-.03) tabulations; this rests on one paper (a database meta-analysis and two experiments) and has not been independently replicated in the sources reviewed.

problem: Fisher 1979 and Ley 1977 verified; Fisher's second statistic is F 53.0 vs 1.3 for recognition.
Wells and Hryciw 1984 and Stein 1977 numbers verified.
Epstein et al. 1979 numbers (small N=22) and Postman 1975 verified.
Isarida et al., Shin et al. and Choi et al. numbers verified; the 'item-bound / no better cue' framing is an interpretation across three small studies.

Gospodinov et al. say p=0.3 keeps only the top 30 percent of generated queries (drops 70 percent), not drops 30; unfiltered Doc2Query beat BM25 (.277 vs .185), so it hurt only relative to filtered; the index shrank 24 percent at n=40 (1.17 to 0.89 GB) and 33 percent only at n=80.
fix: Generated index keys must be supported by the item: Doc2Query's hallucinated queries limit it, and keeping only the 30 percent of generated queries that an ELECTRA relevance filter scores highest raised MS MARCO dev RR@10 from .277 to .316 (n=40; unfiltered Doc2Query still beat plain BM25 at .185) while shrinking the index by 24 percent at n=40 and about a third at n=80.

problem: In Forster and Lavie 2008 the 36 ms vs -4 ms (N=16) comes from Exp 1, where the display stayed on until response; the brief 100 ms displays (Exp 2a/2b, N=16 each) are a separate experiment with different values (about 25 vs -7 ms in Exp 2a per the researcher notes, not re-read from the table).
fix: High perceptual load cuts or eliminates distractor (flanker) interference in Lavie-lab studies: in Forster and Lavie (2008) the congruency effect was 36 ms at low load vs -4 ms at high load with displays shown until response (Exp 1, N=16), and the elimination also held with 100 ms displays (Exp 2a/2b, N=16 each).

problem: Numbers and sensitivity finding verified (Macdonald & Lavie 2008 d' drop with no criterion change; 2011 21/28 vs 7/28), but none of the listed sources is a meta-analysis, so 'meta-analyses agree on the direction' is unsupported (also the notes swap beta: source has 9.0 high vs 5.5 low).
fix: High perceptual load increases inattentional blindness and deafness for unexpected stimuli (e.g. 21/28 vs 7/28 aware of a tone), and in a detection task it lowers sensitivity (d') rather than shifting criterion; results come from multiple experiments across Lavie-lab papers and a review (Lavie, Beck & Konstantinou 2014).

problem: Entries a27, b09, b10 are the same de Fockert 2013 review (one source); numbers verified there (26 studies/49 experiments, r=.202, 35 up vs 14 down) and direction independently confirmed by Lavie, Beck & Konstantinou 2014.

Shi et al. abstract says 'no more than 18%' and Table 3 gives code-davinci-002 COT micro 72.4 / macro 6.0; the three Shi entries are one paper, so the specific figures rest on a single source (Yoran 2023 only loosely supports the general point).

Verified in Shi et al. (COT micro in-topic 63.1 vs off-topic 80.7; role overlap 68.3 vs 76.6) and Cuconasu et al. (peak -0.24, -25% with one distracting document; random documents up to +35%); independent authors.

Yang 2025 (0.11 to 0.49 for Grok-3-Beta, 43% to 19% at 5 steps), CogniLoad (U-shape more pronounced as d increases), CatAttack (5.33x easy vs 1.80x hard for R1, authors attribute to low baseline) all verified; minor: claim omits that the 43%->19% figure is Grok-3-Beta at depth 5.

All figures verified (Liu 56.1/88.3 and >20 point drop; FLenQA 0.92 to 0.68; NoLiMa GPT-4o 99.3 to 69.7 at 32K; Bianchi Gemini 48% to 73%; Du 13.9%-85% incl. whitespace/masked; Martin & Roger 99.7% vs 69%, 2x-30x); Du's 'perfect retrieval' effect is per paper, not all items.

S2A (62.8->80.3, 51.7->61.3, keep-original 74.5), ThoT (best on PopQA), ATF (COT 50.2->74.9 on GPT-3.5-Turbo), Focused CoT (2-3x fewer tokens, extraction counted), Xia 2026 (context management as test-time scaling) and Arjmandi 2026 all verified; minor: the oracle filter gains are significant only for Haiku/Sonnet, Opus and GPT-5.5 sit at ceiling (+0.008, +0.017), and 'free' is the notes' reading, not a measured cost.

CogniLoad (U-shape deepens with difficulty), Yang 2025 and CatAttack floor effect check out, but Zhang et al. vary the injected distractor's complexity (not the main task's difficulty), MedDistractQA never varies task hardness (it only shows baseline accuracy predicts robustness), and 'no 2025-26 study finds' is an unprovable universal negative.
fix: In the studies reviewed, none found that a harder main task makes a planted off-topic distractor intrude less at equal length. Harm stays or grows with intrinsic difficulty in synthetic text tasks (CogniLoad, Yang 2025), is not strongly tied to the complexity of the injected task (distractor injection attacks, which vary distractor not main-task difficulty), and in MedDistractQA is smaller for stronger models (baseline accuracy predicts robustness; task hardness was not varied). The only counter-pattern is a floor effect in relative error (CatAttack). Lavie's shield is therefore not a safe default for S1, though none of these studies test perceptual load.

problem: Logan says the colour-cue explanation is 'likely' (authors' inference), claim states it flatly; Hennefield numbers all match.
o1 drops are read from GSM-Symbolic Fig 8a (-17.5, -29.1); Ullman and Shapira details not re-opened.
Schulze Buschoff reports Claude-3 Opus above chance in some domains, but still below humans; wording 'near chance or below humans' holds.

The interface/floor-effect interpretation rests only on one paper (Mecattaf et al., listed three times) whose authors overlap with the Voudouris platform paper (same Animal-AI lab); the authors themselves only say control 'might' dominate.
fix: Poor scores in the embodied Animal-AI LLM test may partly reflect the coarse action-script control scheme and floor effects (the authors' own caveat in a single paper, Mecattaf et al. 2024); RL agents (PPO at chance, Dreamer-v3 modest) were also significantly more likely to fail the Causal Reasoning level in the Animal-AI platform paper. Per-level LLM scores are only in figures (12 trials per level); no tool-API rerun was found.

problem: Max accuracy (78.3%, BERT) and max verifiability (10.6%, RoBERTa) come from different models; this matches the paper's abstract framing.
The chi2=1.775 is a GLMM full-null comparison; first-touch counts match the crow paper (35/48 vs 23/48).

Voudouris et al. and Milliere & Rathkopf are position papers rather than checklists; only Ivanova gives an explicit list; 'strip cues' rests on Rane's case study (GPT-4o numbers not seen on the proceedings page).
Self-Debug 'Simple' feedback on TransCoder still uses unit-test pass/fail; table layout in the PDF is garbled but values 80.4/89.3/91.6 match.
SWE-Bench Pro notes the problem-only setting suffers false negatives from unit-test verifiers, so part of the 8.4-to-25.9 jump is under-specification; numbers match.

Beller et al. found no correlation between experience and use of an IDE debugger or tests, but Ko and Uttl found comprehension strategies WERE related to programming experience (and not to success), so the two do not agree on experience; the b28 synthesis is the same Beller PDF listed twice.
fix: Beller et al. (176 developers surveyed, 723 IDE sessions) found no correlation between developer experience and use of an IDE debugger or unit tests for debugging, with printf debugging common; Ko and Uttl (2003, lab study) found that three comprehension strategies were related to programming experience but no strategy gave better debugging performance (domain knowledge of the bug and computer attitudes predicted success). Both suggest strategy choice is not the main driver of debugging success, but they differ on whether strategy tracks experience. Neither manipulated strategy experimentally.

problem: 21 steps is a mean for unresolved vs 12 a median for resolved; 'rather than strategy' is the notes' interpretation, not tested in the papers.
