Mizell et al. shares senior author Wilson with the original Horizon paper; Gershman uses a different task, so independence for the Horizon-specific claim is limited but Gershman supports the bonus separately.
Both horizon and within-game noise effects match Wilson et al. (F=65.97; 28/30); Gershman supports the noise-scales-with-uncertainty idea in a different task.

Gershman (listed three times) is the only independent test; Fan, Gershman and Phelps (2023, N=984) is a follow-up co-authored by Gershman, and the Wilson reanalysis is inside Gershman's paper; the 984-participant total was not visible in the preprint text I could access.
fix: Gershman (2018, two online experiments, N=44 and 45) found a hybrid of an additive bonus (relative uncertainty) and noise scaled by total uncertainty, favored over pure UCB or pure Thompson sampling and in a re-analysis of Wilson et al. (2014); a co-authored follow-up (Fan, Gershman and Phelps, 2023, about 984 participants) also reports directed, random and value-based exploration together.

problem: Numbers match (GPT-3 b=-0.15, p=.58; the -0.31 to -0.08 values are a 4-model example in CogBench), but GPT-3 (Binz & Schulz, listed 4 times) and CogBench (Coda-Forno, Binz, Wang, Schulz) and the meta-learning paper are all from the Schulz lab.
fix: In the Schulz lab's studies, GPT-3 showed no directed exploration on the Horizon task (horizon effect b=-0.15, p=.58) and favoured the more-seen option; CogBench (same lab, 35 LLMs) reports that models lack human-like exploration (directed exploration near or below zero in its example models), apart from random exploration in LLaMA-2-70-chat. No independent lab replication is in the evidence list.

problem: All exploration-parameter findings (bonus up, randomness down with CoT/thinking; negative bonus in the 4-armed task) come from one paper (Zhang et al., listed 4 times); Loya et al. only report regret under CoT prompts, not a bonus; I confirmed them against v3 text.
fix: In one study (Zhang et al. 2025), chain of thought and larger thinking budgets raised the fitted uncertainty bonus and lowered randomness in a stationary two-armed bandit (o3-mini at high thinking went past humans; Gemini-2.5-flash moved only part way), while in a nonstationary four-armed task the bonus stayed negative, with early over-commitment, and ChatGPT gained nothing from thinking. Loya et al. separately find CoT prompts lower regret in a different bandit setup. No study crossing thinking budget with an external bonus was found.

problem: Gains are indeed on different tasks and baselines; Voyager/OMNI not re-opened.
78/89/44% figures are for a trained 7B SFT agent in one environment, and the 'out of scope for scaffold-only agent' clause is interpretation; EVOLvE numbers match.

Sayfulina et al. is confirmed as a Russian review with no Horizon task and no Wilson citation, but calling Chakroun 2020 and Wiehler 2021 'the true 2020-onward primary data' is too strong: they are one lab (Peters) and the notes themselves cite other 2020s primary studies (Mizell 2024, Fan 2023).
fix: Sayfulina et al. 2020 (Modern Foreign Psychology 9(2):93-106) is a Russian-language narrative review with no new data and no Horizon-task content (Wilson 2014 is not cited), so it should not be cited as evidence for directed exploration. Examples of primary human data since 2020 include Chakroun et al. 2020 (L-dopa lowered directed exploration, N=31, restless 4-armed bandit) and Wiehler et al. 2021 (23 gamblers vs 23 controls, same lab), plus other work such as Mizell et al. 2024 on the Horizon task.

problem: Wamsley analysed about 75 (maze) and 94 (motor) participants out of 100 recruited, so 'N about 100' is loose; Wilhelm exclusions (suspecting unexpected-group subjects) confirmed.

Main-effect numbers match (Wamsley F=7.35 p=.008; Barner F=8.78 p=.005), but 'regardless of sleep' is too strong: Barner found a sleep advantage only for relevant items on planned contrasts at 1 week, and Wilhelm and van Dongen (in the evidence list) found sleep-dependent relevance effects.
fix: Telling people which items matter improves memory for those items, and in several studies (Wamsley 2016, F(1,71)=7.35 p=.008; Barner 2023 relevance effect F(1,54)=8.78 p=.005, sleep x relevance interaction p=.12; Kurdziel 2025, where a remember instruction beat emotion and sleep did not change behavioural memory) the benefit did not depend on sleep, though Wilhelm 2011 and van Dongen 2012 reported sleep-dependent effects.

problem: Lipinska reports 31 studies, 36 datasets, 2,832 participants; moderators match.

Both sets of numbers match (9 of 15, up to -93.7%; 74% and 0.319 vs 0.333), but they are separate single-team preprints, and in ZenBrain the NoDecay ablation itself cost almost nothing (P@5 0.002), so the 'forgetting can hurt' framing rests mainly on ConsolidationBench.

Wamsley F(1,71)=7.35 and the null sleep x expectation interaction match, but Wamsley's authors told participants after encoding and argue the effect arises in consolidation, not encoding or attention (attention and rehearsal were not supported).
fix: In human tests a test-expectancy instruction given after learning raises retention after both wake and sleep (Wamsley 2016: maze F(1,71)=7.35, p=.008; sleep x expectation p=.38), and two online replications of Wilhelm 2011 (Ashton and Cairney 2021) found no sleep x expectancy interaction, so the instruction effect is not specific to sleep; the mechanism is unresolved (Wamsley's authors suggest an early consolidation process initiated by the instruction).

problem: 'Under 10 points at 100 updates' and negative for gpt-4.1-mini confirmed in Wang and Sun; SleepGate (Xie) only says interference resists prompt engineering and is not independent evidence of the numbers; mock-QA 'declining benefit' not checked.
Example 8.1 text matches (n=0 about 25 episodes, n=5 about 5, n=50 about 3); the 'prioritised ordering cuts it further' part rests on Moore and Atkeson's different mazes, not on the same tiny maze.
Moore and Atkeson Table 2 values match (94,000 / 155,000 / 240,000; small-maze exceptions 600 vs 400); Mattar and Daw not opened.
Numbers match, but Karlsson and Frank 2009 (3 rats) and Gillespie et al. 2021 (4 rats) are both from the Loren Frank lab, so the two rat-replay sources are one lab's work.
fix: In work from one lab (Karlsson and Frank 2009; Gillespie et al. 2021, 4 rats), rat hippocampal replay reflected past experience and remote locations, and in Gillespie et al. it did not predict the next choice, which those authors argue favours a memory-maintenance role for replay over planning; no independent lab is represented in the evidence.

problem: Holland et al. is limited to Atari and recommends fewer, longer rollouts while Janner et al. favour short branched rollouts; the hallucinated-value idea is a hypothesis; Aminmansour and Holland share authors Talvitie and Bowling.
WebDreamer 17.6 to 23.6 (+34.1%) and tree search 26.2 confirmed in the paper; 'a little' understates Dyna-Mind gains such as GPT-4o ALFWorld 51.3 to 64.8; Dyna-Mind and WebDreamer are different labs.
Dyna-Mind reports Spearman r (claim says just r); layout otherwise matches Table 2.

Damani et al. report 25-50% savings for Math at budgets B>=8 only; for Code they report up to 50% (and gains mainly at low budgets, online variant below best-of-k at high budgets); Snell's 4x is 'up to' and holds for predicted as well as oracle bins.
fix: Optimal compute allocation depends on difficulty: easy items gain from sequential revision, hard ones from parallel sampling or search; difficulty-adaptive allocation matches best-of-N with up to about 4x less compute (PaLM 2-S*, MATH; both oracle and predicted difficulty bins). With a learned difficulty predictor, a second group saw up to 50% savings on math and code (25-50% on math at budgets B>=8), 0-10% on chat (25-40% on a high-variance subset), and 25-40% fewer calls for model routing; the oracle curve stays above the predictor.

problem: Evidence line b15 misattributes 2506.04210 to Wu et al.; it is Ghosal et al. (no effect on the claim).

Only Yue et al. supports the pass@k finding and it is scoped to the tested models/RLVR setups; the DeepSeek-R1 paper reports pass@1 and length growth, not base-vs-RL pass@k, so it is not independent support, and Brown 2024 is not a listed evidence line.
fix: Yue et al. (2025) find that in the RLVR setups they tested (math, code, visual reasoning), RL-trained models beat their base models at small k (e.g. k=1) but base models reach higher pass@k at large k, suggesting RLVR mostly reuses reasoning paths already present in the base model; this rests on one study, and DeepSeek-R1 only shows RL raising pass@1 (R1-Zero AIME 2024 15.6% to 77.9%) with longer outputs.

problem: Two papers share authors (Wei, Wang) but support different halves of the claim; the 17.9 in 'CoT 17.9 to 56.9' is the standard-prompting baseline, not CoT.
Snell's PRM was trained on Lightman's PRM800K, so the second source is partly derivative; headline numbers are from Lightman.
The 19% low end comes from DEER's average CoT-length cut (not DeepConf); the 85% top end is a single DeepConf aggressive-setting cell (84.7%).
Critique does not collapse accuracy in every domain (Blocksworld rose 40% to 55%), but the claim only cites Game of 24 as an example.

OPPO Table 1 shows step-level BoN-wise 58.79 and beam search 56.97 above the 55.76 baseline (paper calls both significant gains); only DVTS equals baseline (55.76), so 'no gain or lose' is wrong for beam and BoN-wise.
fix: Test-time scaling transfers to tool-using agents but modestly: on GAIA (n=165) whole-trajectory best-of-N with list-wise selection lifts GPT-4.1 from 55.76 to 63.03; step-level methods gain less (BoN-wise 58.79, beam search 56.97) or nothing (DVTS 55.76); reflecting at every step slightly lowers the score (55.15) and reflect-only-when-low-score (threshold <2) helps slightly (56.36). SWE agents (R2E-Gym) gain from 34.4% pass@1 to 51.0% Best@26 with hybrid verifiers.

problem: AoT 52% vs ToT 46.5% is the AoT authors' reproduction; original ToT reported 60%, so 'similar' is loose but acceptable.

Numbers are right, but 'small and noisy' is not what the sources say: ToT human preference 41 vs 21 (38 ties) and CBS 45% vs 29% are called a clear/significant margin by the authors; only QDAIF (0.772 vs 0.767) is a near-tie, and no noise estimate is given for any of them.
fix: When only an LLM judge or human taste is the oracle, gains from search are smaller and less clear-cut than with a programmatic oracle: ToT writing coherence 6.19 (IO) / 6.93 (CoT) to 7.56 (GPT-4 judge), humans preferring ToT over CoT in 41 vs 21 of 100 pairs with 38 ties; Creative Beam Search preferred 45% vs 29% for standard decoding, with 26% of pairs too alike to tell; QDAIF human QD score 0.772 vs 0.767 for fixed few-shot (small human study).

problem: Prior best 496 for cap set n=8 not located in page text I fetched, but 512 and the other numbers verified; 496 is the known prior record.
'ELM Radial seed used physics quirks' paraphrases the paper's 'chaotic dynamics overfit to flat terrain'; DGM node 114 deleted the special tokens the detector looks for (described as logging).

Minor: paper text says EvoRePE 0.174 to 0.192 while Table 3 gives 0.193; Qwen vanilla 0.168 to 0.193 is the table value. Reasoning, scaling and pass-rate numbers match; NoveltyBench corroborates size-diversity drop independently.

Game of 24 (+66 points, ToT 74 vs IO 7.3), ToT creative-writing and QDAIF numbers match, but none of the opened sources contain cap sets or bin packing (FunSearch results not in the evidence), so those oracle examples are unsupported here.
fix: Search benefit depends on task structure: large when an exact checker exists (Tree of Thoughts on Game of 24: 74% vs 7.3% for IO, about +66 points), small or mixed when only an LLM judge exists (ToT creative writing GPT-4 coherence 6.19 to 7.56; QDAIF human QD 0.772 vs 0.767 for a fixed few-shot prompt, which had the higher human quality rating, 4.133 vs 3.9). Cap-set and bin-packing examples need their own FunSearch citation.

problem: NoThinking (51.3 vs 28.9 at 700 tokens, comparable at up to 9x latency) and Zeng (correct answers shorter, parallel coverage better) match, but Inoue shows repeated sampling beat tree variants on ARC-AGI only at the 128-call budget; AB-MCTS beat repeated sampling on LiveCodeBench and CodeContest (which have test checkers) and passed it on ARC with DeepSeek-V3 at budgets 200-512, so the general 'beat a deep tree' wording is too wide.
fix: On tasks with a cheap checker, many parallel tries plus the checker are a strong baseline against one long thought: NoThinking best-of-N is comparable to full thinking at up to 9x lower latency (AMC23 51.3 vs 28.9 at 700 tokens); for o1-like models correct answers are shorter than wrong ones and parallel scaling gave better coverage than sequential revision; at a 128-call budget repeated sampling beat all tree variants on ARC-AGI, but adaptive-branching tree search (AB-MCTS) beat repeated sampling on LiveCodeBench and CodeContest and on ARC with larger budgets.

problem: Minor: the 'So a decomposer needs hard depth and node budgets' clause is a design inference, not a source finding; the complexity facts match Erol 1994 and Alford 2015 (no recursion, total order, no variables is PSPACE).

Sources support that hand-written SHOP domains had mistakes in two AIPS-2000 domains and that ChatHTN found LLM decompositions interacting unexpectedly with hand methods, but 'often wrong' generalizes one team's two-domain anecdote.
fix: Hand-written methods can be wrong (the SHOP team made mistakes in two AIPS-2000 domains and SHOP was disqualified from them for incorrect plans), and in ChatHTN LLM decompositions interacted unexpectedly with well-crafted hand methods, so the authors added effect-checking verifier tasks to every decomposition.

problem: Numbers match (SCAN length 16.2 to 99.7; GSM8K 60.97 to 62.39 in text, table shows 60.87; TextCraft depth 3 1.8 to 38.7), but ADaPT's depth-2 gain (26.9 to 78.2, +51.3) is larger in points than depth-3 (+36.9), so 'largest when the task is harder' is not shown by the TextCraft depth comparison.
fix: Decomposition gain is large when the executor is weak or the task is harder than the examples (ALFWorld weak executor with atomic skills only: 3.3 to 41.7; SCAN length split with least-to-most: CoT 16.2 to 99.7; TextCraft depth 3: ReAct 1.8 to ADaPT 38.7, though the depth-2 gain, 26.9 to 78.2, is larger in points) and small where the model already copes (GSM8K overall 60.97 to 62.39, with 39.07 to 45.23 on problems needing 5 or more steps).

problem: Web-agent (60.6/67.7% subgoal match, 36.4% success), DecomP single-hop errors and the 89% illegal-step figure (Blocksworld/Gripper/Logistics, solvable tasks) check out, but Least-to-most says GSM8K misses are fixed by a manual decomposition, i.e. the model's own decomposition is the failure point there, which contradicts the claim's direction.
fix: Decomposition quality is not always the failure point; in several settings leaf execution is: web agents match human subgoals 60.6-67.7% but finish only 36.4% of tasks, DecomP errors sit in single-hop sub-answers, and in classical planning domains (Blocksworld, Gripper, Logistics) plans with an inapplicable step make up 89% of failed plans. Counter-evidence: least-to-most prompting on GSM8K fails mainly because its own decomposition is wrong (almost all misses are solved with a manual decomposition).

problem: Minor: Agent Planning Benchmark table also lists Qwen3VL-235B at 11% on missing information, below the quoted 19-65% range (range is for the named frontier models).

Minor: TDAG Table 3 values are each method's share of all errors of that type across methods (4.35 vs 32.61 confirmed), and fixed-plan P&S scores 8.70, below ADaPT 19.57, so the pattern is not uniform; Plan-and-Act dynamic replanning adds only 53.94 to 57.58 on top of fine-tuning and synthetic data, consistent with 'mostly from fine-tuning'.

Numbers match (GPT-4 206/600=34.3%, deceptive mystery 26/600=4.3%, about 12% average, 82% with back-prompting, about 10% on Mystery BW), but all listed sources are one lab (Valmeekam, Kambhampati et al., ASU): PlanBench, the Critical Investigation and the LLM-Modulo position paper (which re-reports the same results).

Minor: the 19-65 vs 65-80 ranges hold for the five frontier models (GPT-5, Gemini 3 Pro, Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Pro/Flash); across all 12 models in the Agent Planning Benchmark missing-information refusal ranges 6-65.
Minor: REFUTE abstract says up to 48% while Table gives 48.7% for o3-mini (high), so 'about 49' is fine; the TestCase-Eval comparison is a different task so 'points the same way' is loose.

REFUTE says randomized-search prompting gives only marginal gains for chat models and that reasoning models' performance deteriorates (o3-mini is the exception, doubling to 8.3 with mostly disjoint successes), not that it 'helps weaker chat models' while reasoning models 'gain little'; 35% invalid runs (86% wrong brute force) and SymCE 0.27 to 0.00 match.
fix: Prompting an explicit randomized search plus brute-force checker gives only marginal gains for chat models and lowers success for most reasoning models (REFUTE: DeepSeek-V3 4.0, R1 4.0, Flash Thinking 3.7, o3-mini 8.3 percent, where o3-mini doubled its rate and solved cases other strategies missed); about 35 percent of runs end in an invalid counterexample, 86 percent of those from wrong brute-force code. SymCE adds that a model fine-tuned only on counterexamples fabricates a witness for true theorems (true-theorem Pass@1 0.27 to 0.00) because it learns the counterexample output form without the negated-conclusion constraint.

problem: Minor: WILT best is 14/50 = 28% (Jhaveri et al. cite it as 26%); the two papers are independent.

PatternBoost numbers check out (81 edges vs conjectured 82, a 30-year-old Graham conjecture), but Wagner (2021) is a co-author of PatternBoost (not independent) and his refuted conjectures (e.g. Aouchiche-Hansen, about 2010) were not decades old, so 'conjectures that stood for decades' over-reads the pair.
fix: PatternBoost (local search plus transformer) found a 6-cube spanning subgraph with 81 edges and diameter 6, below the 82 edges conjectured minimal by Graham, refuting a conjecture open for about 30 years. Earlier work by one of its authors (Wagner 2021, cross-entropy reinforcement learning) refuted several younger open conjectures in graph theory, so learned search can disprove published conjectures.

problem: Minor: 'weaker open-source results' is vague; the second paper (Ellenberg et al.) shows its open-source FunSearch reimplementation falling short of the known cap-set score 512 (best 448) and of PatternBoost on no-isosceles (96 vs 110), not a head-to-head with AlphaEvolve.

CriticGPT (63%, more bugs than contractors, hallucinations) and ARBITER 40.61 to 62.67 match, but the audit reports P(counterexample succeeds | diagnosis correct)=71.6% vs 10.3% for incorrect diagnoses, not that the failing input predicts a right diagnosis; the direction is reversed.
fix: LLM critics (CriticGPT) catch more bugs than paid contractors but hallucinate bugs; critiques were preferred in 63 percent of naturally occurring bug cases. Executed-counterexample training (ARBITER) raises hack success on wrong programs from 40.61 to 62.67 percent, and counterexamples track diagnosis quality: among compilable candidates a counterexample succeeds for 71.6 percent of correct diagnoses versus 10.3 percent of incorrect or vacuous ones.

problem: Minor: 97.7% is 173/177 decision accuracy of the verifier (accept and reject decisions), which supports 'not perfect' rather than a rate of remaining invalid counterexamples.

Minor: the Mace4/Paradox/FM-Darwin figures (802, 1083, 1074 of 1251, 328 problems Mace4 cannot solve, partial overlap) are from Baumgartner et al. alone; Reynolds et al. is on TPTP 5.4.0 and does not include Mace4, so the portfolio inference rests on one comparison.

Minor: UDR was not among the listed sources; EPR random 1.7/7.3/8.9 (BREAK/MTOP/SMCalFlow) and CEIL random 30.68 vs BM25 45.84 match; 'no exact replication found' is a negative search claim that cannot be checked from the sources.
Minor: the comparison numbers MTOP 57.0 and SMCalFlow 51.4 are CBR, a supervised retriever, not surface similarity (BM25 is 52.9 and 46.1); BREAK 31.9 vs BM25-oracle 32.3 is a near tie.

SST-2 94.13 vs 92.75 and SQuAD 73.28 to 77.71 match Xiao et al.; Kapuriya et al. report MMR outperforms or matches the similarity baseline in 17 of 24 settings, so 'helps in about 70%' counts ties as help, and 'mostly by small amounts' is not stated (COLA gains reach +9.7%). On GSM8K TopK-Div (82.98) is slightly above TopK (81.74).
fix: Diversity is not free: on easy or high-zero-shot tasks pure similarity wins or ties (Llama-3.1-8B SST-2 TopK 94.13 vs TopK-Div 92.75; GSM8K TopK 81.74 vs TopK-Div 82.98, a gap of about 1 point); it helps harder tasks (SQuAD 73.28 to 77.71). MMR reranking matches or beats the similarity baseline in 17 of 24 settings (about 70%), with gains from 0 to over 9 percent depending on dataset.

problem: Minor: EPR 'copied' means an abstract (structure) match with a retrieved prompt; Xiong et al. show output similarity rising with input similarity on several agents and backbones (GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3 in the appendix), which supports but is not identical to copying.

Minor: 'differences within noise' beyond K=1 for Memento (63.6 to 64.5 F1) is an interpretation, since no confidence intervals are reported; Memento's best is K=4, not K=1, and two systems are a thin base for 'agent settings' generally.
BRIGHT's 59.0 is the MTEB retrieval subset score, not overall MTEB.
FLARE figures are percent of sentences triggering retrieval, 'plateaus above 60%'; claim wording 'plateaued at 60% or fewer retrieval steps' is loose.
Both are Northwestern structure-mapping sources (thesis by Falkenhainer, review by Gentner and Markman) but different authors and papers; thesis alone supplies the false-inference example.

All three experiments are one paper (Clement and Gentner 1991) and the review (Gentner and Markman 1997) only cites it; numbers (.53 vs .12, N=32; Exp 3 N=48) match, but this is a single study from one lab.
fix: Analogy-group participants predicted the shared-system base fact in .53 of responses versus .12 for the target-only group (Clement and Gentner 1991, Exp 2, N=32), with the same pattern in Exp 3 (N=48); this is one lab's single paper, not independent replication.

problem: The 90% contract rate is the guided-analogy condition; the plain comparison condition formed 70% vs 55% for separate cases (Exp 3, N=158); 48% vs 19% (Exp 2, N=128) is correct.
fix: Comparing two cases beats studying them separately for transfer (48% vs 19%, N=128); in live negotiations contingent contracts formed in 70% of comparison dyads vs 55% for separate cases (guided analogy 90%, baseline 37%; N=158). A meta-analytic effect of about d=0.5 to 0.6 (Alfieri et al.; SREE report d=.60) is not checked here.

problem: 39.6% is the all-model average on ARN far analogies, not GPT-4; GPT-4 scored 57.1 and 29.1 on the two far partitions (about 43), and ARN used 2023 models.
fix: Models in 2023 to 2024 tests find near story analogies but fail on far ones: on ARN the all-model average on far analogies is 39.6% (below the 50% chance level; GPT-4 about 43%) vs humans 94.1%; ChatGPT scored about 30% on StoryAnalogy multiple choice (humans over 85%); GPT-3 was above chance on near story analogies but not on far ones (p=0.065).

problem: Single study (Puranam et al. 2025, 60 GPT-4 runs, two source stories supplied); 'recall' there means using the relevant story when given, not retrieval from a bank; other listed sources do not separate recall from matching.
fix: In one small study (Puranam et al. 2025; 60 GPT-4 runs, 199 students, two supplied source stories) GPT-4 almost never missed the relevant analogy but often applied the wrong one (high recall, low precision), while humans showed the reverse; this suggests matching may be a weak step but is untested at scale.

problem: Hu et al. say GPT-3 at 77.2% on Center is only 'nearing' human performance; beating humans holds for the 2x2Grid and 3x3Grid sub-tasks (93.2% with decomposition), and for Webb et al.'s digit matrices.
fix: Re-encoding Raven-style matrices as text lets GPT-3 reach 77.2% on the Center sub-task (nearing human performance) and exceed human performance on the 2x2Grid and 3x3Grid sub-tasks (3x3Grid 93.2% with attribute naming and decomposition); GPT-3 also beat the human average on Webb et al.'s text digit-matrix task, so explicit structure aids inference.

problem: Numbers and p<.004 verified, but every supporting source is the same paper (Li et al. 2024/2025); the ARC Prize report adds nothing on induction vs transduction.
fix: Li et al. (2025, single paper) report that induction and transduction solve different ARC tasks, stable across seeds (p<.004); a fallback ensemble beat both in a small-compute setting (26.50% vs 18.78% and 15.25%), but with test-time training the ensemble (38.00%) was below transduction alone (43.25%) on ARC-Heavy; no independent replication is cited.

problem: Voita and Titov say variational and online codes agree and are both more stable than accuracy; 'more stable than variational codes' is not supported (Blier and Ollivier show variational codes compress poorly, not that they are unstable).
fix: Description length is a more stable probe of model complexity than accuracy: Voita and Titov find code lengths separate real from control tasks and ignore seed noise, with variational and online codes agreeing; Blier and Ollivier show prequential coding gives far shorter codes than variational or two-part codes for deep nets; Elmoznino et al. show prequential ICL prefers simpler functions.

problem: Both papers come from Ard Louis's Oxford group (Valle-Perez is a coauthor of the 2025 paper), so they are one lab's line of work; content matches.
fix: Work from one group (Valle-Perez, Camargo and Louis 2019; Mingard et al. 2025) shows random-parameter nets favour simple Boolean functions exponentially and that a Bayesian posterior built from a function prior matches SGD-trained nets; the bias varies with architecture (ordered vs chaotic regimes), so it is not universal; not yet replicated by an independent lab.

problem: EvalPlus pass@1 drops are up to 19.3% (individual models 12.6-18.5%); wording '12-19%' is a fair summary.
Baumann also found people searched too long at positions 7 and later, so 'usually' stop early is fair but not universal.

Both the face-task reversal (Furl, Averbeck, McKay 2019) and the paid-by-value and horizon results (van de Wouw, McKay, Furl 2024) come from the same Furl/McKay group; Goldstein et al. does not address the claim.
fix: From one group (Furl and McKay), the undersampling bias reversed to oversampling with attractive faces (2019), and shrank or became inconsistent when every choice was paid by its value or with fewer options (2024); this is not yet shown by independent labs.

problem: Lee et al. 2004 page could not be opened; claim rests on Baumann et al. and Goldstein et al.

The sqrt(n)-1 skip is Bearden's result for iid uniform[0,1] values where the decision maker learns only whether each is best so far, not cardinal payoffs in general; the value-dependent rule is a separate full-information case.
fix: The 1/e rule (win probability 1/e, skip n/e) is optimal for the classic rank-only, win-on-best payoff with known n; in Bearden's variant (iid uniform[0,1] values, payoff equal to the chosen value, told only whether each is best so far) the optimal skip is sqrt(n)-1; goals like low expected rank have staged cutoffs (Chow et al.; Ferguson ch. 2).

problem: Three of four sources are one textbook (Ferguson) and Goldstein et al. only gives the known-distribution threshold table; 'most costed search problems' is a loose generalisation of the textbook cases.
Minor: PETS figures are 'up to 75% offline, 55% online' on GPQA, written as a 55-75% range; ESC accuracy is 'comparable' rather than a stated 0.2% bound.

The oracle-stop gain of up to 21% was measured starting from multimodal benchmarks (language-only results only 'generalize' qualitatively), and the AIME -6.9% is one model (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B) at the best-AES point.
fix: Stopping chain-of-thought via answer convergence or learned stop modules saves about 16-60% of tokens with little accuracy loss on easy and medium tasks, but saves little on hard tasks (AIME -6.9% for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B with OS-Pruner), and answer-level signals such as confidence and trial-answer consistency fire too early on hard items. An oracle stop at the first correct prefix improved accuracy by up to 21% (measured mainly on multimodal reasoning benchmarks), while practical early stopping mostly cuts verbose overthinking and does not fix harmful overthinking; hidden-state probes lose false-stop control under calibration-to-test shift (about 31-41% false stops vs a 5% target on MiP and MMLU in Xie et al.).

problem: Direct flip evidence comes from one study (Zhou et al., two 32B models on AIME, 12K-token turn); Liu and Wang and PUMA only corroborate indirectly (overthinking after correct answer).

StreamStop's gain (40.3% vs 35.0% success on WebShop) comes with more tokens per episode (2675 vs 1519), so it is not an equal-compute comparison; other numbers (Kalayci 15-35%, CLEAR +11.6 and +1.2, Blend-ASC 4.8x vs 3.75x) check out.
fix: Adaptive stopping or allocation beats a flat fixed N or fixed token cap at equal total compute in several independent labs, but the gain is large only under tight budgets and small against a well-tuned fixed setting: Kalayci et al. 15-35% fewer generations at the same quality; CLEAR +11.6 points at 256 tokens per query but +1.2 at 2048 (Balanced stream); Blend-ASC 4.8x fewer samples vs 3.75x for oracle fixed allocation. StreamStop gains a few points of success over validation-selected fixed token budgets on WebShop (40.3% vs 35.0%) but at more reasoning tokens per episode, so that comparison is not at equal compute, and the best stopping signal is model-dependent.

problem: Minor: Qian's paper is about LLM-written exercise policies for Bermudan options (not a formal controller), and the 'stop rules alone at most 4 points' comes from Di Gioia's simulated worlds.

All the specific numbers (97-100% useless, +0.026 to +0.097, budget and rule effects) come from one paper (Zhang et al. 2026, listed as d02 and d03); the only other source (Context Gathering Decision Process) tests a different setting and only loosely corroborates that LLM self-judged stopping is unreliable.
fix: Single-study finding (Zhang et al. 2026, 7-8B open models and Claude Haiku 4.5): agents label a failing source's results useless 97-100% of the time but rarely stop on that judgment; a stated budget or rule shifts when they stop; a harness-enforced rule (answer after 5 useless results in a row) raises success by +0.026 to +0.097. Independent work (Context Gathering Decision Process) agrees that LLM self-judged stagnation stopping is unreliable, in a different setting.

problem: Minor: the time-pressure result (Kira et al.) rests on four participants; the PNAS result gives a linear threshold in proportion of nights remaining, which is consistent with 'thresholds fall with fewer trials left'.
Jacobs (Prop 4.3/5.3) and Dziurosz-Serafinowicz (citing Field and Wagner) are two different papers; b01 and b03 are the same paper listed twice.

Jacobs and Stein show the repeated-Pearl-conditioning program (prog1) going to 100% as the number of tests grows, while the Jeffrey-style programs stay put; no source shows Jeffrey sequences reaching confident false beliefs.
fix: Counting repeated noisy checks as independent evidence can pile up confidence: with 5% prevalence, 90% sensitivity, 95% specificity and results pos, pos, neg, three ways to model the repeats give 64% (condition on each test, a repeated Pearl update), 9% and 33% (Jeffrey-style update on the empirical test distribution), and the repeated-conditioning program goes to about 100% with 3000 tests in the same 2:1 ratio while the others stay put. Repeated samples and checks from one source share errors, so extra independent-looking checks can add little real information (majority vote and reward-model selection gain only 40.50% to 41.41% from 100 to 10,000 samples).

problem: Filbry et al. find the failure for non-reasoning models; with reasoning (and code) updates become close to the oracle (e.g. Gemma-4-31B-it matches it on ProteinWorld-simple), so 'without code' is too wide, and Qiu et al.'s null results for CoT prompting, numeric encodings, 30 rounds and base models are on a flight-recommendation task.
fix: Without reasoning or code execution, LLMs update badly on evidence in context: Filbry et al. find non-reasoning updates cut final success by at least 30% versus an oracle, and in a five-round flight-recommendation task Qiu et al. found chain-of-thought prompting, numeric encodings, 30 rounds and base models did not fix the weak updating. Fine-tuning on a Bayesian assistant's predictions does improve it, whereas reasoning plus code execution brings updates close to the oracle; a scaffold cannot train, but it can supply reasoning and code.

problem: Belief-R numbers all come from one paper (Wilie et al.); Huang et al. corroborates stickiness only indirectly.
Minor: Falck et al. conclude ICL is not Bayesian while Gupta et al. and Zhang et al. attribute most deviation to priors and discounting; the claim's 'roughly Bayesian' wording reconciles them.
Minor: 'flip at turn 4.85-4.90 of 5' is the SYCON Turn-of-Flip average (essentially rarely flipping); the 'opposite to human conservatism' remark is interpretation, not sourced.

Minor: 'not independent and gains are task-dependent' is the claim writer's reading of Xiong et al. (gains vary by task: AUROC 60-79 elsewhere); one-number vs several-option comparison is from Tian et al.'s abstract.

Minor: Halawi et al.'s own system score is not quoted (the 0.149 and 0.208 are crowd and zero-shot GPT-4 baselines on the 914-question test set); BLInD's 'holds up better' rests on mapping approaches versus direct prompting.
Minor: Yu's calibration gain is 'upwards of 20% in some cases' (benchmarked against an argmax noisy-label baseline); the two halves of the claim come from different papers and different settings.

The false-negative and false-positive rates come from one paper (Stechly et al. 2024; Graph Coloring FNR 95.8% and Mystery Blocksworld FNR 97.09%, FPR 0.5-18.55% over the four domains, GPT-4); the other listed sources are the same group's earlier paper and Huang et al., which support only the direction (self-verification without an external signal does not help).
fix: In one study (Stechly et al. 2024, GPT-4 verifying its own answers), the self-check rejected 95.8% of correct graph-coloring answers and 97.09% of correct Mystery Blocksworld answers (false negative rate), while its false positive rate was 0.5-18.55% across the four domains, so a 'fail' can be nearly uninformative while a 'pass' is informative; this is one study, with Huang et al. agreeing only that self-review without an outside signal does not help.

problem: Brown et al. show that majority voting and reward-model selection plateau at about 100 samples while coverage keeps rising to 98%, so repeated sampling does not stop helping, only these selection checks do; the correlation numbers (42.3% and 60% agreement, 0.97 for one Llama pair, +11.2 points) check out.
fix: Errors are shared across models, so more checks do not mean more independence: when both models are wrong they pick the same wrong answer on average 42.3% (HuggingFace) and 60% (HELM) of the time (0.97 for one same-provider Llama pair), weighted verifier ensembles beat naive averaging by up to 11.2 points, and gains from adding verifiers shrink because of correlated biases. Majority voting and reward-model selection from repeated samples of one model plateau at about 100 samples even though coverage keeps rising.

problem: Minor: 'frontier' and 'still' describe 2025 models (o3-mini, DeepSeek R1, Claude 3.7 Sonnet); the 'not measured' sentence is a negative statement no source can confirm.
Minor: the researcher note attributing a 17.1% correction rate to Sure Rebuttal is garbled (17.1% sits on the Detailed Rebuttal row), but the claim's +24.6% for neutral judging checks out.
Minor: Mitchell et al. show the 50%-satisfiable point at 4.55 for 20 variables, 4.3 for 50 and 140; the first-order claim rests on Monasson et al.'s statistical-physics analysis.
Minor: SatNoSolver 26.6 is above standard 21.0, so 'no gain' applies to LINC's Scratchpad (which does not beat the most-common-label baseline for StarCoder+), not to SatLM's no-solver variant.
Minor: the 13-38% syntax-error range spans StarCoder+, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 in LINC; 63.8 is the FOLIO paper's inference-engine execution accuracy for GPT-4.

The 'about 6 and 3' gains are Logic-LM++ execution accuracy (not final accuracy; final GPT-4 gains are +5.9 FOLIO, +3.3 AR-LSAT, 0 ProofWriter), and Logic-LM's FOLIO '+0.5' is the change in accuracy of executable samples for GPT-4, which is 80.4 to 79.9 by the table values (a slight drop), not an accuracy gain.
fix: Solver-error self-refinement mainly raises the share of formulas that execute, not correctness: Logic-LM's average executable-rate gain is 5.01 points, while GPT-4 FOLIO accuracy on executable samples is essentially unchanged (80.4 to 79.9); Logic-LM++ pairwise-comparison backtracking raises execution accuracy by about 6% (GPT-4) and 3% (GPT-3.5) per its authors, with final-accuracy changes of +5.9 on FOLIO and +3.3 on AR-LSAT and 0 on ProofWriter for GPT-4, and for GPT-3.5 a slight drop on FOLIO (62.80 to 62.25).

problem: Minor: the Hao 78.6% and 81.6% are the Table 4 repair rates on 12 modified TravelPlanner queries; the abstract's 81.6% and 91.7% refers to a different average over two datasets.

Minor: the SATBench 66.7% and 39.3% are means over all tested models including reasoning models (o4-mini hard UNSAT 65.0, R1 83.6), so 'text-only LLMs' is an average, not a per-model rule; ZebraLogic x-large accuracy is 0.0-1.0% for the non-reasoning models in Table 1.

The 39.2% FOLIO figure is real but concerns a factuality-and-bias screen of the natural-language stories (identity-marker bias, factual accuracy), not loss of unstated facts in formalisation, so it does not support the translation-incompleteness point.
fix: A sound solver is only sound for the formula, not for the problem: when translation drops unstated facts the pipeline is precise but incomplete (LINC GPT-4 predicts Uncertain 57% vs CoT 41% on FOLIO); separately, FOLIO's authors found 39.2% of its stories had factuality or bias issues and needed rewriting.

problem: Minor slip: GPT-5.5 gap is 12.2 pp in the source table (79.0 vs 66.9 as rounded gives 12.1); the 12-to-54 range covers only the three named models (all 12 models span 8.2 to 54.4).

Numbers check out (He and Wang Table: GPT-4o CoT 8.9 vs Python declarative one-shot 62.1; EntailmentBank CoT 81.8 vs Prolog zero-shot 27.4; PoT 82.4% compiled, 58.22% precision), but 'No measured gate classifier exists' is a universal negative that no opened source supports, and the grid comparison pairs CoT with a declarative one-shot Python prompt.
fix: Wrong routing is costly in both directions: on hard ZebraLogic grids GPT-4o with CoT scores 8.9 vs 62.1 with declarative one-shot Python (+53 points), and on EntailmentBank Prolog zero-shot scores 27.4 vs 81.8 for CoT (-54 points). Compile success is not a gate: Proof of Thought compiled 82.4% of StrategyQA programs with 58.22% precision. No measured gate classifier was found in the sources reviewed.

problem: Lu et al. say whole-result hallucination happens 'rarely' (early prompt version); the 'often' rests on Beel et al.'s re-run.
All figures come from one study (Si et al. 2024) and the second listed source (Lu et al.) only supports the repeated-ideas point qualitatively.
Hedged absence claim; blog also includes a Codex follow-up beyond the single ChatGPT Pro run, and the one arXiv query returned zero hits as stated.
All figures come from a single survey (Morgan 2021); Rodman 2023 reuses its data; the 2026 Diagnosis replication could not be opened.
The 4% vs 24% pooled figure was seen as quoted by Weber 2018 and the McDowell abstract page lists only 35 articles / 226 estimates.

Li and Rui find dual modes that depend on the description: even with base rates supplied, representative descriptions give posterior odds ratios near 1 for all LLMs (non-normative), and only uncharacteristic descriptions give near-normative ratios (about 9) for 4 of 6 models; Talboy and Fuller (one mammography problem) show Bayes use with numbers and an incidence-rate answer without numbers, not a similarity judgment.
fix: LLMs show two modes of posterior judgment (Li and Rui 2024): near-Bayesian on uncharacteristic descriptions (odds ratio about 9 for 4 of 6 models) but similarity-based and base-rate-insensitive on representative descriptions (ratio near 1), and they struggle to recall base rates from memory; on one mammography problem GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 used Bayes when numbers were given and returned the 10% incidence rate when numbers were removed (Talboy and Fuller 2023).

problem: Numbers match (GPT-4 69 vs reference 2-11; o1-preview 10.9), but the two papers share authors (Rodman, Manrai, Morgan) and GPT-4 was also worse than clinicians on UTI after a positive culture (87.8 vs 62.2 MAE) and o1-preview still failed that case.

Lijmer (RDOR 3.0, CI 2.0-4.5) and Leeflang (0-40 points, significant in 8 of 23) check out, but the 10.8-19.1% figure is a modelled prediction for two swab-based TB tests from a single unreviewed medRxiv preprint, stated in the claim as if it were a general result.
fix: Published test accuracy is inflated by weak design and is not portable: diseased-plus-separate-control (case-control) designs give diagnostic odds ratios about 3.0 times higher (RDOR 3.0, 95% CI 2.0-4.5; Lijmer 1999); sensitivity or specificity shifts 0-40 points across prevalence within a review (significant in 8 of 23 meta-analyses; Leeflang 2013); and in one modelling preprint on two swab-based TB tests, a single pooled value predicted 10.8% and 19.1% more positives than a bacterial-load-stratified model in community settings.

problem: Both figures come from MacGregor and Armstrong 1994 (68.3 is a reanalysis of two earlier studies, 19.78 is its new 280-subject experiment); the Armstrong 1975 repository page could not be opened (403).

The 458% rise applies to four problems the authors call 'not extreme' (true value of four digits or fewer) in their new experiment, and they note their test overstates significance; the earlier studies' non-extreme set showed about 50% worse error or little overall effect; 'familiar quantities' is not what the authors say.
fix: Decomposition does not help and can hurt on problems that are not extreme and uncertain: in MacGregor and Armstrong (1994), four not-extreme problems (true value of four digits or fewer) had median error raised by 458% (p<0.05, a test the authors say overstates significance), while six such problems from earlier studies showed little overall effect (error about 50% higher in the low-disagreement subset).

problem: The 'shared wrong anchor' point rests on MacGregor and Armstrong's US-population example (error factor 1.97); Kalyan et al. only illustrates failed decompositions.
Rests on one study (Epstein et al.) using Science Olympiad questions and three small models (GPT-4o-mini, Claude-3.5-Haiku, Grok-3-mini); the two arXiv/HTML listings are the same paper.
The two scores use different datasets/settings (T5 fine-tuned, question-only task vs zero-shot GPT-4); fp_score 0.5 is about 1.5 orders of magnitude off, consistent with the claim.
On Bamboogle the Vicuna-13B decomposer (48.8) is slightly below single-stage GPT (49.6), so 'small loss' holds on GSM8K/DROP but the two-stage advantage is not uniform.
Averages confirmed in Table 4 (CoT 86.0, CoT-decomposition 85.6, factored 81.8); the other listed sources are the same paper or a related Anthropic paper (Lanham).

Chang 2016 never mentions decomposition (scenario training did include 'identify key causal drivers'); Hauenstein et al.'s re-analysis is disputed by Mellers and colleagues, which the claim omits, and was verified only via search abstract (publisher page 403).
Single-paper result (Deng, Brucks and Toubia); the Meincke et al. listing only adds that CoT prompting raised GPT-4 diversity.
Deng et al. report garbled text only at temperature 2.0; at 1.5 diversity rose only marginally (22 to 23 categories, 88 to 99 combinations), so '1.5 to 2.0 gave garbled text' is wrong.
fix: Same-model repetition is severe: average pairwise similarity exceeds 0.8 in 79% of cases; min-p at temperature 2.0 still has 61.2% of response pairs above 0.8; cross-model similarity ranges 71 to 82%. Temperature is a weak lever (Deng: temperature 1.5 gave only marginally more diversity, and 2.0 gave largely garbled text).

problem: Evidence labels attribute NoveltyBench to Jiang et al. in some lines and Zhang et al. in others; the claim itself names no author.
Anderson et al. is a small within-subject study (N=36); Padmakumar and He used 38 writers; the group-level effect is not shown for the base model in Anderson.

Gick & Holyoak themselves note that the one-analogue baseline (21% / 53%) was unusually low versus the usual ~30% / ~75%, so total 80% vs 53% overstates the two-analogue advantage; Catrambone & Holyoak show the two-analogue total advantage appears even without comparison (74%), with comparison mainly lifting pre-hint rate (47% vs 16%).
fix: Studying two analogues and describing their similarities raised pre-hint transfer (45% vs 21% in Gick & Holyoak Exp 4; 47% vs 16% in Catrambone & Holyoak Exp 1); total transfer was 80% vs 53% in Exp 4, but that one-analogue baseline was lower than the usual ~75%, so the total-solution advantage is smaller than it looks. Schema quality strongly predicts transfer (91% of good-schema writers solved pre-hint), but this is correlational.

problem: Wording is wrong as written: principle-only group (no story) reached 28% before hint, above the 10% base rate; null results are for ADDING a principle or diagrams to a single analogue.
fix: Adding a verbal statement of the principle (32% vs 29% before hint) or a pair of diagrams (23% vs 40%, n.s.) to a single analogue did not raise transfer in Gick & Holyoak (1983); the principle statement alone without a story still gave about 28% convergence solutions. Adding the principle to two analogues helped (62% vs 40% before hint), and diagrams added to two analogues helped (57% vs 37% before hint; 92% vs 79% total).

problem: ACME and ARCS are models from one lab (Holyoak/Thagard) fitted to a few human data sets, not independent evidence; they simulate rather than show that a weighted sum predicts retrieval; the authors only say the unmapped constraint is 'likely' a major reason for impaired human transfer.
fix: MAC/FAC (Gentner & Forbus 1991) models retrieval as a cheap content-vector filter followed by a structural match; ACME and ARCS (Holyoak, Thagard and colleagues) are constraint-satisfaction models combining semantic, structural and pragmatic constraints that reproduce the ordering of human mapping and retrieval results from a small set of studies, and in ACME the key radiation constraint has no counterpart in the poor-constraint lightbulb versions, which the authors suggest is likely part of why human transfer was impaired.

problem: Numbers match, but 'succeed after a hint' is too strong: GPT-4 with a hint claimed the correct source every time but also claimed the wrong story about half the time (precision .50-.52, accuracy .50-.53); generalising to 'LLMs' rests on one GPT-3 single-run anecdote and one GPT-4 study with 15 runs per condition and only one distractor source.
fix: In one GPT-3 single-run anecdote, adding two distractor stories removed the analogical solution until it was prompted to consider the earlier stories; in one GPT-4 matching study (15 runs per condition, two source stories) GPT-4 never claimed the correct source without a hint (0/15), and with a hint it always claimed it (recall 1.00) but also the wrong story about half the time (precision about .50).

problem: Minor: 96.0 is the human mean (humans were 91.4 on far-vs-near); 37.1% is text-davinci-003/GPT-3.5, not GPT-4; AnaloBench length drop reflects length not surface preference.

GPT-3 was below 10% on the synthetic alphabet only for 4 of 6 problem types (not remove-redundant or sort); the counting explanation is the interpretation of Webb et al., whose own reply is one lab's view and the code-tool result is a single GPT-4 variant.
fix: Letter-string analogy results do not hold up on counterfactual alphabets: humans 0.753 vs GPT-3 .488, GPT-3.5 .350, GPT-4 .452 (Lewis & Mitchell); GPT-3 was below 10% on a shuffled alphabet for four of six problem types (Hodel & West); children and adults transfer to Greek/symbol alphabets while LLMs lose up to about 0.5 accuracy (Stevenson et al.). Webb et al. report that GPT-4 with code execution reaches human level on the shuffled alphabet and argue the failure is partly a counting difficulty.

problem: Minor: Lewis & Mitchell say with only 18 stories the paraphrase effect may not be statistically significant; order effect is based on 18 items per position.

Minor: Aczel et al. found analogical vs awareness difference non-significant for the statistical composite, and call the interpretation tentative; the two studies measure different things, so 'limited by bias type' is the authors' tentative reading.

Minor: n=281 was Experiment 1 (no cognitive-forcing arm); CF interventions were tested only in Experiment 2 (n=373); 'often fail' rests on two studies, one of them a small underpowered RCT (CI -0.94 to 0.45).

Minor: Lyu et al. say CoT gives partial protection (e.g. 0.348 vs vanilla 0.4765 on FOMC gpt-3.5), so 'little or worse' for CoT holds in Sovrano and Lou & Sun but not uniformly; the Electronics paper (d18) could not be opened.
Minor: 'can backfire' rests on Echterhoff's GPT-4 framing delta (-0.470 vs baseline -0.405) and He & Liu's colour table; SoPro (not awareness) was the clearly harmful prompt in Sumita et al.
Minor: the Anti-DP gain is Llama-3.1-8B only (Qwen2.5-7B went 40.0% to 40.8%); reasoning models are lowest but still anchored (22-61% of questions across models). The SSRN source was not opened.
Malberg et al. report evidence of all 30 biases only in at least some of the 20 LLMs, not that LLMs generally show all 30; 'human-like' is not tested there; sources are abstract-level.
fix: Instruction tuning and RLHF can add or strengthen decoy, certainty and belief biases (Itzhak et al.); across 20 LLMs, evidence was found for each of 30 cognitive biases in at least some models (Malberg et al.); small changes to vignettes sent GPT-3 far astray (Binz and Schulz).

problem: Minor: authority transfer is small (68.5% to 72.9%) versus distraction (40.6% to 79.7%); the final sentence (in-context transfer in judgment families untested) is an absence-of-evidence statement not checkable from the sources.

Flavell's four failure modes are confirmed, but the claim cites c18 and b21 for wrong self-knowledge and these are not among this claim's evidence; the opened LLM sources only support 'known but not acted on' (MIRROR, Cao et al.) plus MIRROR's overconfidence gap; mapping LLM findings onto Flavell's four modes is the researcher's analogy.
fix: Flavell (1979) warned that metacognitive knowledge can be inaccurate, fail to be activated when needed, fail to influence behaviour when activated, and fail to help when influential; in LLMs, MIRROR (Wang 2026) finds above-chance but imperfect self-knowledge that is not acted on (giving models their own calibration scores did not reduce confident failures, 0.600 to 0.605, while external control cut them to 0.143), and Cao et al. (2026) report that a harness that uses the model's own confidence signals to control retries raises pooled accuracy from 48.3 to 56.9.

problem: Numbers match, but the model with CFI .84 / RMSEA .11 is the eight-first-order-factor model nested under two second-order factors, not a higher-order three-type model; the first-order 8-factor CFA fit acceptably (CFI .93, RMSEA .06) while the abstract says the eight-factor solution did not fit, so 'three-way split not recovered' is only partly supported.
fix: In MAI factor analyses, a two-factor structure (knowledge and regulation of cognition) is recovered rather than separate declarative/procedural/conditional factors: in Colombian undergraduates (N=528) the two-factor model fit excellently (CFI .96, RMSEA .05) while the higher-order model with eight first-order factors (including declarative, procedural, conditional knowledge) under two second-order factors fit poorly (CFI .84, RMSEA .11); in Finnish students (N=462) only two dimensions emerged from 18 items.

problem: Select-then-Solve self-routing numbers are wrong: the paper says self-routing averaged 48.4 (slightly above Direct 47.6), and GPT-5 reached 67.1 vs 60.3 Direct (not tied); only Qwen3-Max (42.4 vs 49.8) is clearly worse in the figure; Phi-4 and MRP numbers are correct.
fix: LLMs follow a named strategy but do not choose better than a fixed strategy when left free: Phi-4 on TruthQuest free 47.2 percent vs forced 45.1 to 49.0; GPT-3.5 MRP 0.433 vs best fixed SPP 0.469. In Select-then-Solve, zero-shot self-routing averaged 48.4 vs Direct 47.6 across 4 models, helping only GPT-5 (67.1 vs 60.3) while Qwen3-Max fell to 42.4 vs 49.8.

problem: Minor: oracle gaps are upper bounds (max over noisy runs/strategies); the ZebraLogic 10-point gap is only 'small' relative to TruthQuest.

Numbers are accurate but the 'gains shrink as baseline accuracy rises' pattern is the researcher's inference from confounded comparisons (different models, datasets and methods); none of the sources reports a baseline-dependence analysis. MC2 on GSM8K was +5.5 (91.38 to 96.92 vs CoT), small only relative to its +12 on MATH-500 and +81 on Game-of-24.
fix: Skill or strategy selection gave smaller gains where the baseline was already strong in these studies, though across different models and methods: GPT-4 on GSM8K 93.00 to 94.31 with skill selection, SMART single-pass gains of +15.2 (Gemma 7B), +11.0 (Mistral 7B) and +3.5 (Qwen2 7B), and MC2 (GPT-4o-mini) +5.5 on GSM8K versus +12.5 on MATH-500.

problem: Minor: the 69.55 vs 80.71 GSM8K result is a single model (Llama-3-8B) and the overthinking share (68.3%) is of MP's errors on the datasets inspected; gains of MP over CoT are 2.8-6.4 points average.

Minor: a normative instruction (C3) did significantly reduce confident failure (0.514, p=.0004), so 'do not act on it when told' applies to being given their own calibration scores; MIRROR is a single-author preprint.
Minor: 87.0 vs 84.0 is the Meta-R1 Pro variant (base Meta-R1 is 85.7 at 3831 tokens); AdaptThink numbers are for the 1.5B model.

The 'from' numbers (78.93 MATH-500, 41.33 Game-of-24) are the strongest baselines (CoT-SC; Meta Prompt), not a no-knowledge version of MC2 (CoT is 72.67 and 7.67); the up-to-46% token cut belongs to a different method (Didolkar behaviors), while MC2 uses more tokens than plain CoT (1631 vs 625 on MATH-500).
fix: Reusable procedural knowledge distilled from the model's own traces can cut reasoning tokens by up to 46% at matched or better accuracy (Didolkar et al., behavior handbook), and a different system, MC2, with GPT-4o-mini beat the strongest baselines on MATH-500 (85.13 vs 78.93 for CoT-SC) and Game-of-24 (88.67 vs 41.33 for Meta Prompt) at fewer tokens than CoT-SC but more than plain CoT.

problem: Numbers match, but RTR's 82.5 vs 80.0 at 1091 vs 2745 tokens compares a model-and-strategy router with the single strongest model (QwQ-32B), not a best fixed strategy; and Select-then-Solve shows no cost saving over Direct (router about 7.0k vs 3.5k tokens for GPT-5), only versus always-ReAct.
fix: A learned per-task router gave a modest accuracy gain over the best fixed option: Select-then-Solve 53.1 vs 50.3 for the best fixed paradigm (4 models, 229 test tasks, recovering about 26 percent of the oracle gap); Route to Reason (jointly choosing model and strategy) reached 82.5 vs 80.0 for the strongest single model at 1091 vs 2745 tokens; PRISM improved on the best fixed strategy by 3.8 to 9.1 points on math (per its tables).

problem: The 85% and 'three times' figures are confirmed only in one secondary review (VanLehn, Jones & Chi 1992, which reports Chi 1989 and Fergusson-Hessler & de Jong 1990, small-sample protocol studies); Chi et al. 1994 shares authors with it and shows only that more self-explaining goes with more learning (87 vs 29 explanations; gain 38% vs 27%), not that bare 'I understand' monitoring fails or that explaining exposes gaps.
fix: In protocol studies reported by VanLehn, Jones and Chi (1992), poor solvers said they understood 85% of the time when their problem-solving showed they did not, and 'Everything is clear' occurred three times more often in poor solvers' protocols; in Chi et al. (1994), students who produced more self-explanations learned more (gain 38% vs 27% for top vs bottom four explainers, p<.07).

problem: Spider is not a case of gains shrinking for stronger models: in Self-Debug GPT-4 (73.2 baseline) scored below Codex (81.3), the paper suggests GPT-4 is not tuned for SQL, and the feedback there is explanation plus execution; Ye and Durrett found the strongest GPT-3-era model (text-davinci-002) gained most. SYNTH 52.4 to 74.8 is a reject-and-retry procedure over top-5 answers, other numbers check out.
fix: LLM explanation gains depend on model and explanation reliability: Lampinen et al. found smaller models do not benefit, Turpin and Lanham found explanations can be unfaithful, and in Self-Debug the Spider gain from explanation feedback was +2.8 for Codex but only +0.4 for GPT-4 (despite GPT-4's lower baseline, 73.2 vs 81.3). In Ye and Durrett, checking explanation factuality and rejecting nonfactual answer-explanation pairs lifted SYNTH accuracy from 52.4% to 74.8%.

problem: d=.26 vs .51 comes only from Lucas (2000), which is listed twice (a11 and b01 are the same paper); Hutchison (2003) is a critique of Lucas that reports no d values, so the numeric claim rests on a single meta-analysis (numbers themselves match).
Hutchison is author of both sources (Heyman paper is KU Leuven-led), so independence is partial; both do support the claim and the 'no universal SOA' point is explicit in Hutchison 2003.

First half (convergence to near query-independent state) rests on a secondhand literature review in SA-RAG citing earlier work; the gating numbers come from a single paper (Glybovets and Makarov) listed twice.

Minor slip: decay sweep changes F1 by 2.8 (2Wiki) and 4.0 (MuSiQue), not strictly under 4, and the paper says it lies within the CI; depth gain from the Glybovets paper only (n=500), 'beyond 3' backed by SA-RAG.
Numbers match the SA-RAG paper (phi4 reader; listed three times, one paper); Han et al. only qualitatively agrees that iterative retrieval helps graph methods on multi-hop.
Minor: effect sizes 0.859/0.869 omit Claude Haiku (0.866, in range) and rho -0.61 omits Haiku at -0.662 (stronger than human -0.626); only 50 prime-target pairs.

Neither source says social-priming replication failures 'do not apply'; Wikipedia only reports that the 2012 failures concerned behavioural priming and cites Meyer 2014 (a short letter) saying semantic priming is well established, and the Semantic Priming Project (Hutchison et al. 2013) only shows a large dataset exists, not that it is immune or independently replicated.
fix: The 2012 replication failures concerned behavioural (social) priming; semantic priming is described as well established (Meyer 2014, via Wikipedia) and has a large dataset in the Semantic Priming Project (1,661 targets, 768 subjects, 4 universities), so those failures are not known to extend to word-level semantic priming.

problem: Numbers match Soto and Humphreys 2008 (58-86 ms), but the three contrasts are not all one held item with a short gap: Exp 1 spanned gaps of 188-1008 ms with no shrinkage, Exp 2 used articulatory suppression, and Exp 3 (1,101 vs 1,015) held two items; all three are one paper.
fix: Held visual contents bias attention toward matching items: in Soto and Humphreys 2008 a distractor matching the held item slowed search by about 60-85 ms against neutral (Exp 1, one item, gaps 188-1008 ms: 1,209 vs 1,146 ms; Exp 2, with articulatory suppression: 1,049 vs 991 ms; Exp 3, two held items: 1,101 vs 1,015 ms), and Hollingworth and Beck 2016 found a 68 ms capture effect with one held colour.

problem: Holds only for the gap-location task: there capture was 124 ms (two matches) vs 44 ms (one match) at memory load 2 and 68 ms for one item; in the singleton task of the same paper, Match-2 (51 ms) was no larger than load-1 Match-1 (58 ms), and the large-sample replication (Fratescu et al. 2019) found no capture at load 2 in its other paradigm.
fix: In the gap-location task, capture was larger with two matching distractors than one when two colours were held (Match-2 124 ms vs Match-1 44 ms at load 2; Match-1 at load 1 was 68 ms; Hollingworth and Beck 2016, N=24), replicated in the Match-2 > Match-1 pattern by Fratescu et al. 2019 (BF10 = 158); the singleton task showed no such scaling (51 vs 58 ms).

problem: Numbers and N verified in Woodman and Luck (delay 500 ms, described by authors as longer than Soto et al.); the Hollingworth (2022) chapter page only lists a citation so the 'later work' conclusion was checked only via Fratescu et al. 2019, whose conclusion allows templates that do not always become active.

Fratescu et al. numbers verified (56 analysed, BF10 0.163 and 0.117 at load 2; its Exp 2 replicated two-item capture); the replication list was not readable on the Hollingworth publications page, but Chen and Du 2017, King and Macnamara 2020 and Zhou 2020 were confirmed to exist via Crossref with multiple-item guidance titles.

The CDA part is supported by Carlisle et al. 2011 (-0.80 uV at repetition 1, binned -0.66/-0.50/-0.30 uV; the -0.8 to -0.30 pairing mixes a single trial value with a 5-7 bin), but the opened sources do not show that deprioritised held items do not capture (Hollingworth and Hwang 2013; Olivers 2011): Van der Stigchel and Olivers 2019 does not mention those studies, and the Hollingworth chapter page lists only a citation.
fix: When the same target is searched repeatedly, the contralateral delay activity declines (-0.66 uV on repetitions 1-2 to -0.30 uV on 5-7, not different from zero from repetition 5; Carlisle et al. 2011), taken to mean that long-term memory takes over from working memory as the template; with a constant target across the experiment there was no CDA. Memory-driven bias also drops within one or two repeated memorisations (Van der Stigchel and Olivers 2019).

problem: The one-or-two-trial drop is quoted in Van der Stigchel and Olivers 2019 from earlier work (van Moorselaar 2016; Gayet 2019) that I did not open; Carlisle et al. 2011 shows the analogous CDA decline over repeated same-target searches.

Sasin and Nieuwenstein 2016 numbers verified (75.2 vs 81.9, d=0.42, N=58, 80.0 vs 80.1); the ISI effect (150 to 250 ms) is attributed to Niu and Hollingworth 2026, whose article existence/authors were confirmed via Crossref but whose text I could not open (paywalled), so that sentence is unchecked.

Minor: the Shi et al. self-consistency gain is stated as more than 11 micro points overall (88.1 vs 72.4 for COT+SC); 'ignore' instruction numbers and LTM+SC 93.4/45.0 match; Wang et al. mitigations within about 0.03 match Table 5 (-0.013 to +0.026).
Wang et al. numbers match (average 0.843 to 0.323, Claude-3.5-Sonnet 0.879 to 0.495, static GSM-IC 1.8% average drop); 52.0% is an absolute point drop (about 62% relative).
Yoran 77% vs 37% is for NQ errors only; 'matching feature-match capture' is the researcher's analogy, not a finding of the papers.

Niu et al. numbers all verified (+4.01, +4.92, +4.08, 3.2-10.7% of heads, 36 heads = 3.5%, gap 7.69 to 13.20), but Liu and Chu (sentence-level, different models and intervention, 2-4% shared heads) and Zheng and Shi (head-recovery metric 1.464) extend and are consistent with the finding rather than replicate the Llama-3.1-8B logit results.
fix: Llama-3.1-8B raises the logit of any token already in context, even random (+4.01) or irrelevant (+4.92) vs related (+4.08); a small set of heads (3.2-10.7%; 36 heads = 3.5% for country-capital) mediates it, and ablating them widens the counterfactual logit gap 7.69 to 13.20 (Niu et al. 2025). Two 2026 papers extend this: Liu and Chu find a shared set of 2-4% of heads controlling sentence-level entrainment, and Zheng and Shi find a shared global head core across relations (average recovery 1.464).

problem: Kukreja numbers verified (b=-0.330, +0.217, 4x, 2x), but Liu and Chu do not confirm the counterfactual trend: they report counterfactual entrainment rising slightly with model size, i.e. resistance more pronounced in smaller models, which contradicts Kukreja; only the overall decline with size (Qwen3 3.91 to 3.35) agrees.
fix: Kukreja et al. (Cerebras-GPT, Pythia) find larger models resist counterfactual context more (b=-0.330; largest about 4x more resistant) but copy arbitrary tokens more (+0.217; about 2x). Liu and Chu 2026 (26 LLMs) agree that overall entrainment falls with size (Qwen3 3.91 at 0.6B to 3.35 at 32B) but find counterfactual entrainment rising slightly with size, contradicting Kukreja on that point.

problem: Below-closed-book result applies to GPT-3.5-Turbo in the middle position at 20-30 documents (Claude-1.3 only has closed-book/oracle figures quoted); 0.92 to 0.68 is an average across models.
Minor: 'even when the model knows better' is interpretive; Qwen3-235B thinking is 22.0% and Qwen2.5-0.5B 60.5% as stated.

Minor scope slip: the 95% snowballing figure is for failures under 'Let's think step by step' prompting on Zhang et al.'s QA datasets; length-bias A=13.18 holds for oracle consolidation on older models (3 seeds), and authority A=0.00 over 15 runs, as stated.

SEP supports the Lakatos/Zahar parts, but Beel et al. only show one system (Sakana AI Scientist) using keyword-search novelty checks mislabelled known ideas as novel; this does not show a model's own novelty claim is invalid in general.
fix: Novelty is comparative and contested: a prediction counts only if rivals and conventional wisdom did not predict it (Lakatos), and Zahar lets known facts count if the core was not built to explain them. Judging novelty needs a reference set; in one evaluation (Beel et al. 2025) the AI Scientist's keyword-search novelty check labelled well-known ideas such as micro-batching for SGD as novel.

problem: SCoRe model attribution swapped: the 15.6-point MATH gain is on Gemini 1.5 Flash and the 9.1-point HumanEval gain is on Gemini 1.0 Pro (coding runs fine-tune 1.0 Pro, MATH runs 1.5 Flash).
fix: Kamoi et al. survey: no major work shows successful self-correction from self-prompted feedback under fair settings in general tasks; it works with reliable external feedback (tools, code execution) and after large-scale fine-tuning (SCoRe: +15.6 points MATH on Gemini 1.5 Flash, +9.1 HumanEval on Gemini 1.0 Pro). The bottleneck is generating feedback, not applying it. 2025 update: o1-preview and o1-mini also lose accuracy under intrinsic self-correction (Zhang et al.), so the result is not limited to older models.

problem: Minor: the 14 models are open-source non-reasoning models, claim says 14 open models.
Only Reflexion (one paper) supplies the numbers; Kamoi supports the general point.
Source says the first round gives the correct answer in over 92% of cases; Wang et al. is listed as extra but is a different claim.

All numbers (225%, 38.3->44.1, 73.8->74.8, 72.4) check out against Wang et al. 2025, but every supporting evidence line is that single paper; s1 and Mirage papers listed with it do not test underthinking.

Numbers match HypoGeniC (Zhou et al. 2024), but all supporting lines for them are that one paper (Wang et al. Hypothesis Search is a different method and gives no corroboration); the paper also notes the Tweet gain is inflated by safety-mode refusals in baselines.
Numbers come from one paper (Stroebl et al.); the negative statement about no single break-even rate is the researcher's gap check.
Minor: SEP credits the finite-bet restriction to Kemeny/Lehman; de Finetti 1937 is credited with coherence/Dutch Book theorem framing.
Minor scope: 95% identical is for GPT-OSS-120B only and the under-20% figure is from the paraphrasing experiment on GPT-3.5/4; averaging does modestly improve coherence.

Numbers match, but Imran et al. conclude BCC rises significantly with scale (r=0.906 vs log parameters), so 'improves only weakly' is the researcher's own spin on small absolute gaps; batch>BP is supported by the Apple paper (Chen et al., not Williamson).
fix: Bayes-consistency of in-context belief updates rises with model size but from modest levels (Llama 3 1.24B 0.658 to 8B 0.739; BCC vs log parameters r=0.906), and batch updating usually beats sequential belief propagation.

problem: Minor: the 30.0-point figure is a best-case gain over the uncalibrated baseline (argmax is unchanged by renormalisation, so it is consistent with the claim).

Sources show proofs are checked by the proof assistant, but not that this verifier is 'exact' for every result or that every result is reportable only because of it: it checks validity against the formal statement only (Seed-Prover IMO statements were human-formalised; lean-gym wrongly rejected 21.1% of correct proofs; miniF2F statements have been found flawed).
fix: A proof assistant kernel (Lean, Isabelle) gives an exact check that a proof is valid for the formal statement as written, which is why recent prover results can be reported with confidence; it does not check that the statement matches the intended problem, and benchmark tooling can still misjudge proofs.

problem: Minor: gains are log-like with budget (steady but costly), and numbers span different systems.

Thor numbers (57.0 vs 39.0 vs 25.7, 8.2% neither) are correct, but Magnushammer is a learned premise selector that replaces Sledgehammer's selection (59.5 vs 38.3, a different Sledgehammer baseline from Thor's 25.7), not a generator paired with a symbolic tool beating both.
fix: Pairing a language model with a symbolic tool beats either alone: Thor 57.0% vs LM 39.0% vs Sledgehammer 25.7% on PISA, with 8.2% solved by neither alone. Separately, a learned premise selector (Magnushammer) beats Sledgehammer's own premise selection, 59.5% vs 38.3% on PISA.

problem: All numbers check out, but 'helps mostly in-distribution' is not supported by LeanDojo: retrieval adds +3.6 points on the random split and +3.1 on novel_premises (a larger relative gain on the harder split), so the gain is not concentrated in-distribution.
fix: Retrieval of relevant facts helps in and out of distribution but absolute accuracy is much lower on new premises: LeanDojo ReProver 51.2% random split vs 47.6% without retrieval, and novel_premises 26.3% vs 23.2%; GPT-4 zero-shot 29.0% and 7.4%. Gap check: in-project step-wise retrieval (Rango) keeps unseen-project accuracy at 32.0% vs 36.8% file-wise; LeanAgent continual updating proved 155 sorry theorems; neural clause guidance in Vampire falls below default off-distribution.

problem: Minor: the 9.8-point 'no automated prover' drop is on miniF2F-valid (9.0 on test); the DSP/Minerva/Hilbert numbers match.
Minor: the prover-only baseline is Goedel-V2-32B pass@4, about 75%; the depth-2 figure is 98.36%.

Numbers are right (Thor 29.9, Seed 99.6, GPT-4 1/640, Seed 331/657, Hilbert 462/660), but only miniF2F is saturated; PutnamBench at 50-70% solved is not, and problem counts differ by version (640, 657, 660).
fix: miniF2F-test went from 29.9% (Thor, 2022) to 99.6% (Seed-Prover, 2025) and is now saturated; PutnamBench rose from 1/640 (GPT-4, 2024) to 331/657 (Seed-Prover) and 462/660 (Hilbert) in 2025, so it is far from saturated yet. Numbers from different eras and benchmark versions should not be compared directly.

problem: Feyerabend (anything-goes, waiting objection), 'never showed scientists switched' (Wikipedia) and Laudan's alternative are supported, but SEP presents Musgrave as a defender attempting a Lakatosian reply, not a critic, and Kuhn is cited only as saying no historical process matches falsification (and as seeing the MSRP as vindicating his view).
fix: Critics hold Lakatos's rule unusable or empty: Feyerabend (any development can claim intermittent progress; waiting objection) and Kuhn-style historical objections; Lakatos never showed scientists switched when the criterion fired (he admitted he did not compare reconstructions with actual history); Laudan's problem-solving count is an alternative. Musgrave is a Lakatosian who tried to answer Feyerabend's dilemma.

problem: Seed-Prover passage calls the AMC problems straightforward in natural language but hard in Lean; 'easy' is a fair paraphrase.
The Llama-13B attack F1 of 12 is on Nixon-Kennedy (CDCP has only support labels, so its attack F1 is undefined '-'); other numbers match Stab and Gurevych .413, Gorur et al., and Baba and Chudziak.
fix: Attack relations are systematically harder than support for both pre-LLM and LLM systems (attack stance F1 .413 in ILP; attack F1 below support in nearly all LLM datasets; Nixon-Kennedy Llama-13B attack F1 12). Gap search: on UKP essays a confidence-gated second pass raised attack F1 from .383 to .427 (14% of pairs debated; 42 attack test items; not significance-tested); debating all pairs gave .378 (d06).

problem: In Gorur et al. Table 1 (checked by cell coordinates) 96/95/96 for Llama-70B belongs to Debatepedia/Procon (RoBERTa 90/89/90); on Microtexts Llama-70B is 81/52/73 vs RoBERTa 73/53/67.
fix: Relation classification (support/attack between two texts) is dataset-sensitive: Llama-70B 96 vs RoBERTa 90 on Debatepedia/Procon but 64-68 vs 56-62 on Nixon-Kennedy (and 73 vs 67 macro on Microtexts); on essays Llama-70B attack F1 is only 52.

problem: 'Far exceed' is too strong against the stronger neural baselines: zero-shot LLM 79.28 beats RoBERTa 75.64 by only 3.6 points and LSTM 70.5 by 8.8; only the original 2018 systems (.556-.560) were near chance.
fix: A zero-shot single LLM (79.28%) beats a fine-tuned RoBERTa (75.64%) and an LSTM (70.5%) on the ARCT test set (baselines reproduced by Ku et al.), whereas the original 2018 systems were near chance (.556-.560).

problem: Minor: the .836 vs .821 comparison in the table is for different ensemble rows but the paper text does state structural features were counter-productive in ICL; Potash .849 and Kuribayashi .856 are above GPT-4, so 'near or above' is apt; fine-tuned GPT-3.5 reached 0.863.
Minor: SEP says charity can favour the logically minimum premise rather than mandating it; Davies et al. is a practitioner method (rabbit rule) not the SEP recipe itself.
Minor: Dewey 1910 itself states fusion of steps one and two and 'no cast-iron rules'; 'phases not steps', no invariant sequence, spiral and redefinition come from SEP (Hitchcock), not Dewey 1910.
Negative claim; SEP entry reports no stage-order test, and the Wang et al. and Chen et al. numbers match.
Evidence line c04 misattributes oracle-table numbers but the claim's own numbers (CSQA 75.8 to 41.8, GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0) match Huang Table 3.
Minor: CRITIC +7.7 F1 and +7.0 are for ChatGPT; oracle-label numbers match Huang Table 2 (oracle labels are an unrealistic signal per Huang).

Minor: the +2.33% self-verification figure is Weng et al.'s backward-verification average gain on Instruct-GPT, a real small gain rather than plain self-critique; it coincides numerically with CRITIC's +2.33 F1.
Atomic Reasoner (2503.15944) names Dewey, cites How We Think and has an appendix mapping its actions onto Dewey's five steps, so Dewey is named in an opened LLM paper (Hitchcock is not).
fix: Dewey is named in only one of the opened LLM prompting papers (Atomic Reasoner, which maps its actions onto Dewey's five steps) and Hitchcock in none; the other stage-prompting papers (Self-Discover, Plan-and-Solve, Cognitive Prompting) reach a Dewey-like cycle by convergence (Polya, Toulmin), so LLM evidence supports staged prompting loosely, not Dewey specifically.

problem: Both listed evidence lines are the same paper (Kramer and Baumann, 2410.02953), so only one distinct source; its text supports every stated point (95% is the hybrid H-CP on LLaMA 70B, GC-DC-PR most frequent SA-CP sequence, proportional gain larger for mid-size).
Minor: the mixed-approach advantage (0.38 vs 0.23-0.29) is not statistically significant per SEP, which the claim omits; TUM summary calls 341 'studies' while SEP says 341 effect sizes.

Kappa 0.74 was reached only on the third transcript after three training sessions (earlier kappas .35 and .49); 42% exploration is the largest share, not 'most'; the '1 to 18% across reviews' resolution range is not in the opened sources (Akyol et al. cite 20% at the highest phases).
fix: Coders applying the four-phase practical-inquiry model (trigger, exploration, integration, resolution) reached kappa 0.74 only on the third transcript after three training sessions (earlier kappas .35 and .49); in that study exploration was the most frequent phase (42%), integration 13% and resolution 4%, and most coding disagreement was between exploration and integration; a later study cited by the CoI authors reported 20% of contributions at the highest phases.

problem: Minor: Liu and Wang report unsupervised stop rules become unstable on MATH-500 and GPQA, so 'work' is conditional; the 92% figure is read from a figure of QwQ/R1 on easy sets.
Minor: nonlinear probe error 1.7% is the best layer of the synthetic model; interventions 0.12 vs 2.68 are natural-position averages.
Minor: 'coding artefact' is the researchers' framing of Nanda et al.'s relative-to-player finding; numbers match (99.6 peak, ~75, 0.10 vs 0.12, null 2.723).

SEP (Pitt) does not present exactly four families or say that no theory is accepted: it lists causal-informational, teleological, functional-role and phenomenal-intentionality accounts, treats resemblance only as an older view, and says there is widespread agreement that causal-informational relations alone are insufficient; Swampman and disjunction are in the separate SEP content entries, not Pitt.
fix: Philosophical theories of content include causal-informational, teleological, conceptual (functional) role and phenomenal-intentionality accounts (resemblance being an older view held insufficient alone); the SEP entries record persistent named problems for them (disjunction, Swampman, indeterminacy), with widespread agreement only that causal information alone is not sufficient for content.

problem: SEP says carrying information (tree trunks, smoke, thermostats) is not sufficient for representation and teleosemantics adds a function, but the consumer requirement is Millikan's version only; Neander's account does not rely on consumers.
