fix: Information alone is not enough for content: a state can carry information (smoke, tree trunks, thermostat) without representing; on teleosemantic views a representation must also have a selected or learned function, which on Millikan's account means being used by a consumer subsystem.

problem: Minor: 'do not find knowledge' is the authors' conclusion; Farquhar's 50% is on a constructed distractor setup, not all conditions.
Minor: Wang et al. 77.1% / 49.7% are best-case figures; Vafa compression/distinction values (GPT-4 0.21/0.56, GPT-3.5 0.33/0.18) match the raw table.

Millière and Buckner give the three criteria (citing Harding 2023) and say standard probing only evidences (a) while interventions are needed for (b), but nothing in the opened sources supports 'some test (b), almost none test (c)'.
fix: Philosophers' criteria for an activation pattern to represent a feature are (a) carries information, (b) influences behaviour in a task-relevant way, (c) the system can misrepresent; standard probing methods evidence only (a), and showing (b) requires interventions on the activations.

problem: Minor: GPT-3.5 CSQA 38.1 is the round-1 value (41.8 after round 2) while 'after two rounds' applies to the GPT-4 GSM8K figure; GPT-4 mistake-finding 39.80-52.87 matches Tyen et al. Table 4.

The ignore-irrelevant instruction gain in Shi et al. Table 3 is +5.4 (COT 72.4 to 77.8) and +3.1 (LTM 77.5 to 80.6) micro points, +9 and +7 macro points, not a uniform +5 to +8; other numbers (6.0, 93.4, 45%) match.
fix: Behavioural distractor failure is real and partly fixed by agreement: irrelevant sentences cut GSM-IC macro accuracy to 6.0% (COT, code-davinci-002); self-consistency over 20 samples lifts LTM micro accuracy to 93.4% and macro accuracy to 45%; an ignore-irrelevant instruction adds about 3 to 5 micro points (COT 72.4 to 77.8, LTM 77.5 to 80.6) and 7 to 9 macro points for COT and LTM. This differs from probes (Farquhar), where unsupervised agreement fails.

problem: Minor: Camerer et al. is a single multi-lab social-science replication project (not Many Labs); figures 13/21, 50%, 15/28, 0.60 to 0.15 and 85% all verified.

Minor: 18% to 62% are the five per-criterion rates for the 97 positive effects, while 46% (51/112) combines positive and null effects (positive-only is 40%); OSC also reports 36% to 68% depending on the rule.
CORE-Bench 18/28 is about computational reproducibility, only loosely supports the methods-description point, which rests on Errington alone.
Headline numbers all match their papers; minor: PaperBench 21.0% is the BasicAgent headline (IterativeAgent o1 reached 24.4%, 36h o1 26.0%) and ScienceAgentBench 32.4% excludes o1-preview at 42.2%.

EXP-Bench says implementation is the most prevalent failure type but design failures (16.05%, 7.62%) and conclusion failures (26.18%, 19.66%) were also frequent, so 'not design' is stronger than the source.
fix: Agent failures in EXP-Bench are most prevalent in implementation (39.71% missing essential components) and execution (29.38% environment misconfiguration, 23.84% script errors), though design (16.05% incomplete or misclassified variables, 7.62% extraneous additions) and conclusion (26.18% missing, 19.66% incorrect) failures were also frequent; in an independent audit of Sakana's AI Scientist, 5 of 12 ideas (42%) failed with coding errors.

problem: MLAgentBench does report hallucinated improvement without executing the code, but Sakana audit only reports incorrect or hallucinated numbers in 4 of 7 manuscripts, not that they were reported before running code.
fix: Agents sometimes report improvement without running the code (MLAgentBench: the model hallucinates improvement after modifying a file without executing it), and in an independent audit 4 of 7 Sakana AI Scientist manuscripts (57%) contained incorrect or hallucinated numerical results.

problem: Verified Table 1 means (BED-LLM minus Prompt-Only 40.4 pp, Implicit Max minus Prompt-Only 8.2 pp) against abstract 37.4 pp; 'no token-matched comparison' is an absence claim not checkable.

The v2 workshop result (1 of 3 manuscripts above the acceptance threshold, 6.33) is presented by its authors as encouraging, and the three v2 entries are one paper; only the authors' internal review (none met main-track standards) supports 'weak quality'.
fix: An independent audit found Sakana's AI Scientist v1 keyword-based novelty check labelled well-known ideas such as micro-batching for SGD as novel; for AI Scientist-v2, 1 of 3 fully AI-written workshop submissions scored 6.33 (above the workshop acceptance threshold, withdrawn by prior agreement), but the authors' own review judged none of the three to meet main-track conference standards.

problem: Result Match in PaperBench is relabelled 'results analysis' elsewhere in the notes, and the 36-hour o1 detail is not in this claim; numbers match.

PaperBench Table 9 shows the code-vs-execution-vs-result gap (35.4/1.8/0.7 for Claude), but EXP-Bench Table 1 does not show code writing far stronger than running (implementation 20.3 vs execution 15.0 for OpenHands+o3-mini; 35.0 vs 33.2 for Claude-3.7), its collapse comes from requiring all stages together; the 'only for new experiments' conclusion is the researcher's inference from CORE-Bench v1.1 saturation.
fix: In PaperBench (2025), agents' code development scores are far above execution and result-match scores (Claude 3.5 Sonnet BasicAgent 35.4 vs 1.8 vs 0.7); in EXP-Bench the single-stage scores are similar (implementation 20.3, execution 15.0 for OpenHands+o3-mini) and success collapses only when stages are required together (0.5% complete and executable); on CORE-Bench v1.1 (June 2026) top agents reach 97.4-100% when rerunning given code, so accuracy saturated there.

problem: Barrows 1982 and Feightner 1977 are the same McMaster group (Barrows, Feightner, Neufeld, Norman), Barrows also co-authored the 1978 founding work, and the Feightner 1977 abstract gives only a model, no hypothesis-generation finding, so 'independently replicated' is not supported; Barrows 1982 numbers (18+19 physicians, 62 encounters) match.
fix: Hard diagnostic cases are worked by generating a few hypotheses early and using them to guide data search (Elstein 1978 founding claim, restated in Elstein and Schwarz 2002; the 1978 book was not opened). A descriptive study from the McMaster group (Barrows 1982: 18 family physicians and 19 general internists, 62 encounters) found that physicians developed multiple hypotheses early to guide inquiry; this is the same group as the 1970s McMaster work, not an independent lab.

problem: Neufeld 1981 says the majority (not all) of process variables were unrelated to level; Adv Health Sci Educ 2020 defines content specificity as case-to-case performance not transferring, a related but not identical idea; Kaufman and Patel page not retrievable.

Arocha and Patel page could not be opened (blocked); the LLM part rests on one qualitative remark that o3 'seemed to anchor' (Nori) and Ke's 0/80 initial accuracy on case reports selected for bias-driven misdiagnosis, neither of which measures anchoring in plain LLMs.
fix: In a small think-aloud study (Arocha and Patel 1991; 4 participants per group plus one resident, figures not independently checked) cues were mostly used as confirming (71% to 92%) and all second-year students kept their initial hypothesis despite contradictory data; for LLMs, authors report qualitatively that an off-the-shelf o3 baseline seemed to anchor on first impressions (Nori 2025), and a multi-agent GPT-4 setup raised top-diagnosis accuracy from 0/80 to 71.3% on 16 bias-driven misdiagnosis cases (Ke 2024), but plain-model anchoring was not measured.

problem: All numbers match, but the random-planner score (84.8; 85.4 +- 1.3 over 5 seeds) appears only in the LDTL preprint, whose LA-CDM and ReAct numbers are copied from the LA-CDM paper, so this is a single-source cross-paper comparison, not independent confirmation; Hager does not test a random planner.
fix: In the LDTL preprint (Llama-3-8B, MIMIC-CDM), a random test-selection planner scored 84.8% (85.4 +- 1.3 over 5 seeds), above the prompted ReAct agent (74.9) and the trained hypothesis-driven LA-CDM (81.3) as reported by the LA-CDM authors; only LDTL's learned planner (93.4) beat random clearly. This random-planner comparison comes from one preprint and was not independently replicated.

problem: The 11.3% drop is a relative drop versus the non-interactive Initial setting (not versus no information), and 22.3% is relative to the basic interactive setup; only MediQ directly supports the abstention claim, Hager is context.

The 0.93 to 0.65-0.75 figures are correct but are VivaBench's approximate (lenient) top-1 accuracy from appendix Table 8 (six models, full information 0.90-0.94, final 0.65-0.75); the main-text exact top-1 for the best model is 35% final vs 69% full information, a larger relative fall, and the metric is not labelled in the claim. Premature-closure numbers match.
fix: LLMs commit prematurely when information is insufficient: about 70% false action when the right option is removed (55-82% by model on MedQA), 81% premature closure on underspecified low-risk cases vs 19% on urgent ones, and a safety prompt lowers false action to about 48%, not to zero (Handler et al. 2026). In VivaBench multi-turn exams, approximate (lenient) top-1 accuracy of about 0.90-0.94 with full information falls to 0.65-0.75 after data gathering across six models, and exact top-1 for the best model falls from 69% to 35%.

problem: All three experiments come from one research program (Mandel is an author of all; Karvetski of two of them, with the third by Mandel, Karvetski and Dhami), so 'two labs' is wrong, and the N=147 study found ACH decreased coherence, not 'no difference'; MAE .26 vs .21 (N=50, p=.14) and N=227 no advantage are correct.
fix: In experiments from Mandel's research group, ACH did not improve the accuracy of analysts' probability judgments against a Bayesian benchmark: with 50 UK analysts mean absolute error was .26 for ACH vs .21 for control (p=.14, d=0.43 favouring control); with 227 graduates ACH gave no coherence advantage; with 147 graduates ACH was ineffective for accuracy and decreased coherence. No independent lab has replicated these.

problem: Dhami 2019 (12% vs 52% using base rates, n=25 per group, p=.002) and Karvetski and Mandel 2020 (non-diagnostic evidence weight about 32% / 30%) both come from Mandel's group; also the Karvetski and Mandel participants were 227 graduates, not trained analysts.
fix: ACH-trained intelligence analysts used base rates less often than untrained analysts (3 of 25, 12%, vs 13 of 25, 52%; Dhami, Belton and Mandel 2019), and in an online study of 227 graduates using ACH, non-diagnostic evidence carried about 30% of the weight of fully diagnostic evidence (Karvetski and Mandel 2020); both studies come from the same research group.

problem: Heuer's quoted 2010 reply (via Mandel and Tetlock) was conditional: he would ignore testing that does not replicate how ACH is used in the Intelligence Community, not tests that failed; the two review sources share an author (Mandel). Heuer's 'increases the odds of getting the right answer' and 'proven process' are confirmed untested.
fix: A critical review of six ACH experiments (Wilcox and Mandel) found no accuracy benefit and some harm, and no randomized test shows ACH improves accuracy; Heuer (1999) asserts that ACH 'increases the odds of getting the right answer' without citing a test, and per Mandel and Tetlock (2018) Heuer replied in 2010 that if testing did not replicate exactly how ACH is used in the Intelligence Community he would be inclined to ignore it and stick with common sense.

problem: ACH-vs-control coherence difference was not significant in the 50-analyst study (sum 1.77 vs 1.54, p=.13); it was significant only in the separate 147-person study from the same group; the 5-sample averaging result was measured on GPT-OSS-120B only. MAE .23 to .15 and pool .09 verified.
fix: In Mandel et al. 2018 both ACH and control probabilities summed above 1 (1.77 vs 1.54), a difference that was not significant (p=.13), while a separate 147-person study from the same group found ACH decreased coherence; coherentizing cut mean absolute error from .23 to .15 and averaging all 50 coherentized judgments gave .09. For LLMs (2026), judgments elicited in one dialogue violated probability rules far less than across separate chats (10% of scenarios for Gemini-2.5-Pro, 1 of 30 for Gemma), eliciting a full panel of 14 related events in one query brought incoherence near the rounding floor, and for GPT-OSS-120B averaging up to 5 samples helped only modestly because 95% of answers were identical.

problem: Gains significant for thinking models only, TiO better in all 11, Dual-Goal small drop for non-thinking: all match Jhaveri et al.; the 1,000-2,300 tokens per turn figure and 'never compared with full ACH' were not directly checked.

Wilcox and Mandel's theory critique covers ignoring confirming evidence (including base rates) and Popper, but double counting of correlated cues is an empirical finding of Karvetski, Mandel and Irwin (same group) that the review only lists among harms, not a theory-level flaw they identify; the 0.14 vs 0.27 cue-distance figure is from the Karvetski preprint.
fix: Wilcox and Mandel (2023) argue on theory grounds that ACH tells analysts to ignore consistent (confirming) evidence, including base rates, and their review lists as an empirical harm that ACH users double counted perfectly correlated cues, more so when the correlation was made salient (Karvetski, Mandel and Irwin 2020, same research group).

problem: Numbers match (Himmelstein Table 2 same-metric across halves .36 / .41 / .36; small tournament 314 registered, 195 engaged, 2 confirmed at top 2%, 38 at 25%), but the authors read these correlations as supporting temporal stability of accuracy, and the '.65 headline' comparison is not in the Himmelstein paper, so 'well below' and 'noisy guide' are the notes' own interpretation.
fix: In the IARPA Hybrid Forecasting Competition Season 1 (326 forecasters), the same accuracy metric across two halves of 188 questions (94 each) correlated .36 (simple), .41 (hierarchical) and .36 (IRT), which the authors took as moderate evidence that accuracy is stable over time; a small independent tournament (195 fully engaged of 314 registered, 14 questions) confirmed 2 people at the top 2% and 38 at the top 25%, so persistence is supported but thinly.

problem: Mellers 2015 GJP correlations are .07 to .23 and HFC Season 1 .11 to .22; Season 2 AOMT .00-.04 and education -.03 to -.08 confirmed; Chang 2016 was not opened.

The ForecastBench paper and the 'closing the gap' post are both from the Forecasting Research Institute, so the trend and parity projection rest on one organisation; also the source gives the gap (0.017) and the LLM improvement (0.015 in a year), a point estimate of Nov 2026 with 95% CI Jan 2026 to Nov 2027, not 'late 2026 to mid 2027'. Brier numbers (.096, .121, .122, 39 supers) verified.
fix: On ForecastBench (Forecasting Research Institute), superforecasters (39 people, Brier .096) beat the public (.121) and the best LLM, Claude 3.5 Sonnet (.122); the same organisation reports the best LLM trails superforecasters by 0.017 difficulty-adjusted Brier (Jan 2026), LLMs improved about 0.015 in a year, and a linear extrapolation gives parity around November 2026 (95% CI January 2026 to November 2027); this is one group's projection from few models.

problem: Verified: Baron et al. (mean a=2.43, Brier .148 vs .187 for high-expertise forecasters), AIA (fixed 1.73, .1119 to .1076; 1.72 supers, 2.27 AIA), LessWrong (Platt gain .016 binary); not verified: Mellers 70%/90% figure and the 'mainly because' causal wording (full text blocked); Murphy reports no statistically resolved Platt gain for the main backbone overall, with small gains (+0.72/+1.48 BI) on a preliminary model, not specifically 'when a crowd price is in context'.
fix: Forecasters in the geopolitical tournament were overconfident, worst on 100% forecasts made early in a question's life (about 70% right early vs about 90% late, Mellers 2014, figure not rechecked); extremizing the aggregate improved Brier (high-expertise mean a=2.43, .187 to .148; Baron et al.) and is supported by partial-information theory (Satopaa et al.); post-hoc Platt recalibration helped live bots (Brier gain .016 binary); for LLM ensembles a fixed Platt coefficient of about 1.73 gave Brier .1119 to .1076 on FB-7-21 (AIA), the best factor differs (1.72 for superforecasters, 2.27 for AIA), and Murphy found no statistically resolved overall gain from Platt scaling for its main backbone.

problem: Numbers match Schoenegger et al. (Bayesian Reasoning +0.03, Propose-Evaluate-Select +0.033, Base Rate First -0.016 paired after BH) and Pratt (multiple personas and news API worse than baseline); the claim's 'none beat noise' headline is qualified correctly in its own correction text.

Aitchison et al. find the value of mixing comes from less-correlated models (Grok 4, fine-tuned model) rather than frontier models in general; 'no token-matched test' is an absence claim not checkable.

The key sentence appears only in Heuer (1999), listed twice from the same chapter, where it is an extrapolation ('presumably happens in real life') from Bruner and Potter 1964 (original not opened); Prochaska and the Wikipedia belief-perseverance page do not state it, so there is one source, not independent support.
fix: Heuer (1999) argues, drawing on Bruner and Potter's 1964 blurred-picture experiment (viewers who started with a more blurred image needed a clearer picture to recognise it), that the information needed to invalidate an early interpretation is considerably greater than that needed to form it; this is Heuer's account of one perception study extended to analysis, with no numbers, and the original paper was not checked.

problem: Minor: Reflexion paper attributes WebShop failure to need for diverse exploration, not weak signal per se.

Simon supports solver-relative structure and a mechanizable test as a WSP criterion, and Kambhampati shows verifier loops help, but no source shows that adding a code check turns a sub-problem well-structured and searchable; that is the researcher's inference, and Huang is about self-correction, not structure.
fix: Whether a task counts as ill-structured depends on the solver and its resources (Simon 1973: chess is well-structured in the small, ill-structured in the large). A mechanizable test of solutions is one of Simon's criteria for a well-structured problem, and external verifier loops lift LLM planning where a verifier exists (Kambhampati 2024); this suggests, but no opened source tests, that adding a code check makes a sub-problem more searchable.

problem: Only the ToT paper was opened as an independent check (other listed items are the same paper); numbers match. Other ToT-family entries not needed for the claim.
Minor: the 28.5 to 37.0 lift in Koh et al. comes from self-consistency (n=20 samples) on the same GPT-4o scorer, a stronger scoring ensemble rather than a different model.
Minor: the 6x TravelPlanner figure is paired with TravelPlanner's own 0.6% GPT-4-Turbo base, which is a combination of two papers.

Numbers match the PlanBench o1 paper, but every listed source (Valmeekam 2023, Kambhampati 2024, Valmeekam 2024) comes from the same Kambhampati/Valmeekam ASU group, so the surface-form claim rests on one lab.
Minor: Egea is a single qualitative hackathon case (one LLM-led team), so 'LLMs show design fixation' generalises from small samples.
Minor: EngiBench Level 1 is accuracy % but Level 3 is a 0-10 rubric, so the drop is across different metrics; Level 1 upper bound 98 only loosely checked in a figure-heavy PDF.

Numbers for Koh et al. and Brown et al. match, but the ToT paper (opened in the same batch) measured a tree-search gain on open-ended Creative Writing judged by GPT-4 scores and human pairwise preference, so 'all measured search gains are on tasks with a check' is too broad.
fix: Among the opened studies, the tree-search gains on tasks with an exact external check are large (Game of 24, crosswords, VisualWebArena +39.7% relative, WebArena +28.0%); the one open-ended test, ToT creative writing, was judged only by GPT-4 scores (7.56 vs 6.93 CoT) and a human preference comparison, and no opened study measures tree search against an expert verdict on a truly ill-structured brief.

problem: Minor: Snell's MATH results are for PaLM 2-S* with a PRM; Shojaee's puzzle regimes are on synthetic puzzles, so the two halves of the claim are different settings.

Minor: Blocksworld 83-87% is the F.E.F/A.E.F critique variants; binary-feedback only gets 60% and critique-free k=25 sampling gets 72%, so critique content adds some gain there, but most still comes from the check. Both sources are from different labs (Kambhampati group vs Stanford/Brown).

Numbers match (ERIC abstract: 43 articles, 55 studies, 181 effects, g=0.48); the Springer pages were paywalled so Sweller 2019 was verified only by Crossref metadata, and the meta-analysis covers elementary to postsecondary learners, not novices specifically (the evidence lists the author as Booth; actual authors are Barbieri, Miller-Cotto, Clerjuste, Chawla).
Sweller 2019 full text was paywalled and not opened; the LLM half (Wei, Fu, Zhou) was verified.
Minor: Zhou's error-injection result is on an addition algorithmic task only.
Minor: the 11.0 vs 15.4 result is one model (text-davinci-002) on GSM8K.

Numbers match Chen et al. (SKiC), but removing the skill text costs only 4 points (98.0 to 94.0) versus 16 for removing grounding (82.0), so 'both parts are needed' is too strong; the claim also rests on one paper, with the second listed paper (subgoal theorem proving) not testing it.
fix: In one study (Chen et al. 2024, ChatGPT, dynamic programming task), putting skill definitions and worked examples that cite those skills in one prompt gave 98.0 vs 72.0 for CoT; grounding the steps in skills mattered most (82.0 without grounding) while dropping the skill text cost only 4 points (94.0).

problem: Claim numbers match; the evidence line for Yang et al. mislabels table rows (18.6/27.6/34.3 are different rows, not random/semantic/graph for one model) but the paper does state the graph retrieval gain is larger for smaller models.

Numbers match (70% of ChatGPT hints passed checks; human-hint groups significant pre-post gain, ChatGPT groups not in v1; 56.6% of 150 tutoring dialogs fully correct), but neither study measures the quality of human-authored solutions, so 'less reliable than human ones' is not shown for quality; the ChatGPT groups also began with much higher pre-test scores (confound), and the '32% failure in another report' is traced to no listed source.
fix: LLM-authored worked solutions and hints are often flawed: in Pardos and Bhandari (v1, N=77) 70% of ChatGPT hints passed manual quality checks, and only the human-hint groups showed a significant pre-to-post gain (ChatGPT groups started with higher pre-test scores); in Gupta et al. 2025 only 56.6% of 150 LLM tutoring dialogs were fully correct, though 90% were rated high quality.

problem: Minor: the PaLM-62B finding is one older model on GSM8K; 'readable text' rests on Madaan's text ablation, which the evidence line only summarises.

Supported, but the strict-worse results are secondhand (Fricke via Bender 2004, Rueckert via Motte's review) and the first Rueckert report found no correlation; Motte's own study is the same author as the review, so the evidence is one review plus one study.

In Pahl's 4-designer case the best result went to the experienced designer who was also method-educated, and the review concludes the method was 'all in all positive' but inseparable from experience; only one of the two experienced designers worked without the method, so 'experienced designers without method got top results' and 'experience beats method training' overreach an N=4 anecdote (the LLM papers d04/d14 listed as evidence are unrelated).
fix: In a small observation of 4 of 21 designers (Pahl 1992, via Motte 2015), the two experienced designers got among the best results and the two inexperienced method-trained ones among the worst; the best result came from the experienced and method-educated designer, and the intuitive experienced designer was as good in half the time; the author concluded the method helps but cannot be separated from practical experience. One flexible student group with little experience failed until it followed the strict method (Rueckert et al.).

problem: Only the functional-decomposition study (12 student groups, GPT-4o lower on creativity) compares with students; the ReqGPT 77% vs 69% result is LLM vs LLM with no student baseline, so 'individual early stages about as well as students' is wider than the sources.
fix: In one early-stage test, GPT-4o functional decompositions were rated about as complete as those of 12 student groups (3.96 vs 3.91; lower on creativity, 3.12 vs 3.48); separately, a fine-tuned 7B model (ReqGPT) beat GPT-4 on requirements lists in rater similarity scores (77% vs 69%), without a student comparison.

problem: Repetition, feasible-but-less-novel, unique-adjective and few-shot results all come from one GPT-3 study (Ma et al. 2023, listed three times); the other cited sources (Egea: ChatGPT team placed 2nd; Chen: unique-term share) do not show repetitiveness, so 'a plain LLM' and independence are overstated.
fix: In one 2023 study with GPT-3 (Ma et al.), LLM concepts were rated more feasible and useful but less novel than crowdsourced ones; GPT-3 repeated itself after a few outputs, adding a 'unique' adjective gave the smallest convex-hull volume (0.186) and few-shot examples also lowered coverage (0.2) versus 0.294 for the crowd; a separate small chair-design study found a lower share of unique terms for ChatGPT (67.4%) than for human designs (78.2%).

problem: HANS numbers are right (accuracy under 10% in most cases, chance 50%; BERT 0% on subject/object swap) but concern fine-tuned NLI models only, not models 'prompted on text', and 'most cases' (model-subset pairs) is not 'most models'; McCoy entries are one paper, Geirhos is only a toy example.
fix: Fine-tuned NLI models (BERT, ESIM, DA, SPINN) trained on MNLI adopt surface heuristics such as lexical overlap and fail almost completely when the heuristic points the wrong way: on HANS they scored under 10% in most cases where chance is 50%, and BERT scored 0% on subject/object swap.

problem: Minor: the 65% drop is for Phi-3-mini (-65.7 points); GSM-IC 18% applies to baseline-solved problems with greedy prompts.

All four entries are the same GSM-Symbolic paper, so the claim rests on one paper (it is worded as that paper's report, and the Figure 8a caption does say more recent models decline more and o1-preview/o1-mini drop significantly).
Turpin shows virtually no verbalization of the biasing cue; Sharma does not itself examine CoT explanations.
Minor: prompts reduce but do not fully remove bias (paper says simple prompting cannot mitigate it well).
Minor: the 99% to 62/71/75% figure is a footnote on parseable drawing programs in Wu et al.; only Lewis and Mitchell test humans (Wu et al. do not).
Minor: MedDistractQA ranges are 2.2-17.8% (non-literal) and 1.3-17.9% (bystander); abstract says up to 17.9%.

Core numbers are from one 2026 preprint (b20 and b24 are the same paper); the update clause is supported by Rephrase and Respond (weaker models sometimes slightly worse on some tasks) and System 2 Attention.
Minor: Sherbino 2014 authors are Sherbino, Kulasegaram, Howey, Norman (not Dore/Siu); O'Sullivan sample was mixed-grade medical professionals, not students.

Roy et al. numbers are right (ReAct S+Q BM25 35%, hallucination 4% vs CoT 12% vs RB 40%, 66% insufficient information), but the RCAgent 33.54% pass-rate drop is from replacing the minimalist tools with SQL/SLS query tools (99.38 to 65.84), not from removing key-value storage (w/o OBSK is 96.89, about -2.5).
fix: LLM agents for root-cause analysis struggle with evidence: in Roy et al., ReAct (S+Q BM25) was 35% correct against 39% for CoT and retrieval baselines, with 4% hallucination (vs 12% CoT, 40% retrieval), and 66% of its wrong answers reported insufficient information; the RCAgent ablation shows tool and observation handling matters (swapping to SQL query tools cut pass rate by 33.54%, removing the observation key-value snapshot cut it from 99.38 to 96.89).

problem: The 36% easy vs 5% hard diagnosis split in ITBench is for SRE scenarios (GPT-4o), not the CISO split; other numbers (13.81%, 9.52% without traces, AIOpsLab RCA 9.09-45.45% over four agents, raw telemetry overloading context) check out.
fix: Real fault diagnosis by LLM agents is still weak and noise-sensitive: ITBench SRE diagnosis pass@1 is 13.81% for GPT-4o (9.52% without traces; 36% on easy vs 5% on hard SRE scenarios), AIOpsLab RCA accuracy is 9-45% across four agents, and telemetry dumped raw into context can overwhelm the agent. Cue-conflict effects are not isolated in either.

problem: Minor: the closing negative statements (no agentic-loop test, no sorted-summary fix) are a search-gap note that neither source can confirm.
Minor: Chen et al. figures are averages over hint types (25%/39%; 20%/29% for misaligned hints) measured on cases where the hint changed the answer; Sharma 27% is for LLaMA 2.

Means (situation 4.36 vs program 3.55, experts 4.56 vs novices 4.10) are right, but Burkhardt et al. report 51 subjects (30 experts, 21 novices), not 'about 46' (that was inferred from F degrees of freedom); the Pennington source is a secondary review, so the claim rests on one primary study (an OO-code study).
fix: Experts build richer situation (domain) models than novices (4.56 vs 4.10 of 6); in an object-oriented program-comprehension study of 51 programmers (30 experts, 21 novices), situation-model questions were answered better than program-model questions by everyone (4.36 vs 3.55 of 6).

problem: Minor: 17-34% is relative Pass@1 decrease under confusing naming (16.97-34.18%).

Minor: 22% is an upper bound (at most 22% of 68 Java methods), 85% is the share of methods where two LLMs significantly correlate, and rho -0.13 p=0.39 is one of four quality metrics; Li et al. appears three times but Paltenghi and Kou independently report misalignment.

Minor: in the RHDA table plain CoT already reaches 89.12 (CRUXEval) and 83.14 (LiveCodeBench) with GPT-4o, so RHDA adds only about 1-1.5 points over CoT; the quoted gains are versus standard prompting.
Minor: the 60.9% (Llama3.2) is the v1 figure, v3 gives 55.1%; the v3 range for open code models is 3.0-55.1% (not strictly 10-50%); CodeMMLU permutation shifts and EquiBench 82.3%/63.8% check out.
Minor: the 32.61 to 52.13 figure is file-only versus tree scaffold on GPT-OSS-120B (LocBench); Agentless ablation shows direct file-to-edit-lines is worse in cost and accuracy.
Minor: the 74%/49% study (Kaufman et al.) tests LLM-generated assertions/postconditions rather than whole programs, and the 19.3% figure is cited in Rong et al. from earlier student data.

Langhout and Aniche numbers check out (7 of 14 atoms, 2.7 to 56 times, 132 students, pooled OR 3.82), but the EEG study's perplexity-to-EEG correlation is Spearman rho = 0.47 for confusing snippets (r=0.45 is a perplexity effect size, and clean snippets showed rho = 0.05); also 'LLM perplexity tracks human confusion' holds for confusing code only.
fix: Atoms of confusion (precedence, side-effect patterns) raised human error 2.7 to 56 times for 7 of 14 Java atoms (N=132 students, pooled OR 3.82); an EEG study found LLM perplexity correlates with human confusion responses on confusing code (Spearman rho = 0.47) but not on clean code (rho = 0.05).

problem: Tsui (64.5%, Sonnet 4 41.4%, Wait -89.3%) and Olausson/Huang are fine, but Rajput et al.'s 0.12-0.55 blind spot is for a fixed cheap verifier (gpt-4o-mini) checking students from 0.5B up to 14-32B, rising with student size, not a verifier 'of similar strength'.
fix: Models are poor at catching errors in their own output: 14 open non-reasoning models show a 64.5% blind spot (Claude Sonnet 4 41.4%) on injected errors; self-repair on code rarely beats resampling at equal budget; a fixed cheap verifier (gpt-4o-mini) waves through 12% to 55% of wrong answers from students of growing size (0.5B up to 14-32B). A cheap 'Wait' trigger removes about 89% of the blind spot for non-reasoning models.

problem: The paper itself confirms a notional, preliminary model (two loops, six data stores, back loops, no sample size or statistics, derived from interviews and protocols with several analysts); but a01-a03 are one document, and 'never been tested as a whole' rests only on a failed search note (a31), not on a source.
fix: Pirolli and Card 2005 present a notional two-loop model (foraging loop, sensemaking loop, six data stores, back loops at every level) derived from a preliminary cognitive task analysis of several intelligence analysts, with no reported sample size, counts or effect sizes; no direct test or replication of the whole model was found in this search.

problem: Minor: the Sensecape metric is concepts explored (not speed), with a very large SD (49.1); Selenite recall 73.0 vs 30.4% refers to externalised criteria; Selenite also had a separate N=8 open study.
Minor: the accuracy difference (88.1 vs 91.9%, p=.067) is not significant, so only slightly less accurate, not significantly is supported.

Minor: Lehner 2008 is known only through Mandel et al.s secondhand summary (ACH reduced confirmation bias in non-analysts but had no effect on analysts); Maegherman also concluded participants failed to apply ACH properly.

Table 4.1 comes from a 16-subject study (8 per condition), not N=8 total, and the same study found no difference in analytic score, so 'helps human sensemaking' is wider than the data (more structures only; alpha was set at p<0.1).
fix: Large display space changed how people structured their workspace (n=16, 8 per group): more structures, 15.75 vs 9 (p=.004, t-tests with alpha .1), with coverage only borderline (18.53% vs 13.12%, p=.061) and no significant difference in analytic score.

problem: Minor: 'many' rests on three papers (Cheng and Houben workshop position paper, Patterson AFRL conceptual paper, Jain research agenda); Jain says teams 'do not yet reliably outperform the best individual'.

Both papers share co-author Peter M. Todd and are sibling studies of the same task (semantic fluency); the AUC values 0.72/0.87 come from the first paper alone and are maximum values for Gemma-9B only; the second paper's probe on real human sequences was weak (AUROC 0.57) and only strong on contrastive datasets (0.96-0.98).
fix: Residual-stream activations of Gemma-9B predict semantic-fluency category switches above chance (max AUC 0.72 anticipatory at layer 26, 0.87 at the switch event at layer 16; Leckie, Todd and Foster 2026), with a sibling study by a partly overlapping team also decoding switches linearly in Llama models on contrastive data.

problem: Numbers are right (SHELDON 84.00 vs RLM 78.00, Codex 76.00), but SHELDON is a general scientific-reasoning harness (diagnosis, root-cause, ARC-AGI-2), EviDx has no dual search, and EviDx's baseline is its own single agent with gains clearest on multiple choice and open-ended diagnosis still limited.
fix: SHELDON, a general dual-search (hypothesis and observation) harness, scores 84.00 on DiagnosisArena vs 78.00 for RLM and 76.00 for Codex; separately, EviDx's evidence scaffold with an observer harness improves multiple-choice diagnosis over its single-agent baseline (e.g. Qwen3-8B 18% to 44% on JAMA) while open-ended diagnosis stays limited.

problem: Minor: the no-theory remark is one commentator's (Dawes, BBS 1989) view of Pennington and Hastie's 1986-88 work, and the no-formula point rests on the 1996 Hastie and Pennington summary (listed twice as a02/b14); absence of a rule elsewhere in their work is inferred.

Numbers and Ns match the papers (F(1,44)=35.3 N=48; F(2,86)=35.3 N=47; F(2,236)=59.1 N=120; F(2,302)=78.6 N=157), but all four experiments come from the same lab and paradigm (Holyoak and Simon 1999; Simon, Pham, Le and Holyoak 2001, same Quest v. Smith case, Holyoak on both), so they count as one source.
fix: Coherence shift (same lab, same Quest v. Smith case): after reading an ambiguous case, ratings of disputed arguments move to agree with the leaning verdict (Holyoak and Simon 1999 Exp 1 F(1,44)=35.3, N=48; Simon et al. 2001 Exp 1 F(2,86)=35.3, N=47; Exp 2 F(2,236)=59.1, N=120; Exp 3 F(2,302)=78.6, N=157); independent replication by another lab not checked.

problem: Engel and Gloeckner numbers check (Exp 2 N=92, quick p=.003, slow p=.23, interaction p=.24; the p=.002 interaction with short .003/long .66 is their own Experiment 1, not a separate later study). But Holyoak and Simon Exp 2 had 19 participants (F(1,16)=3.66, p=.07, only approached significance), so memory drift is not established; and of 6 switchers only the 3 Quest-to-Smith switchers lost coherence while the 3 Smith-to-Quest switchers kept it; 'transient' is E&G's secondhand citation of Simon 2008.
fix: Boundary: Engel and Gloeckner (2013) cite coherence effects as transient (via Simon et al. 2008, not opened) and find role bias in quick but not slow deciders (Exp 1: interaction p=.002, short p=.003, long p=.66; Exp 2, N=92, large payment: quick p=.003, slow p=.23, interaction p=.24). In Holyoak and Simon 1999, 6 of 30 (20%) interim leaners switched verdict and, of these, half failed to keep coherent ratings; recalled pretest ratings drifted toward the verdict only marginally (Smith supporters -1.32 vs actual -0.30, F(1,16)=3.66, p=.07, 19 participants).

problem: Numbers match (BeliefBank +17% F1 and ~95% consistency; Maieutic 72.5 vs CoT 61.6 on Com2Sense; self-consistency +17.9 on GSM8K), but self-consistency is plain majority voting, not a solver over model beliefs, and the figures are best cases from three unrelated setups (BeliefBank on a small constraint set with a fixed batch regime).
fix: MaxSAT solvers over a model's own beliefs raised accuracy in two studies: BeliefBank +17% F1 over the raw model with about 95% consistency, and Maieutic prompting 72.5 vs 61.6 for CoT on Com2Sense; separately, self-consistency majority voting (not a solver) gives up to +17.9 on GSM8K.

problem: 17 of 18 hung is correct, but it is two models (GPT-4o, Llama-4-Scout) on one film case with N=3 per cell, so 'rarely converge' is too general; and JuryBench (Wu 2026) simulates individual jurors without deliberation, so it is not evidence about multi-agent juries, and its persona-over-statement comparison is only stated as background fit and ideology being stronger factors than other isolated factors.
fix: In one scenario (12 Angry Men case, GPT-4o and Llama-4-Scout, N=3 per cell) 17 of 18 multi-agent LLM jury runs ended hung; separately, a single-juror benchmark of 20 LLMs (JuryBench) finds jurors rarely change opinion after a defendant statement and that juror ideology and background fit shift severity strongly.

problem: Liu 2026 is a single independent-researcher paper with n=30 on AIME and 12 candidates from one generator (Qwen3-235B); numbers match the tables and Huang et al. confirms CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 for GPT-3.5.

Numbers are right, but the GSM8K 54.8% to 92.7% AUROC is for GPT-3.5 (not GPT-4) and is the best task: averaged over five tasks GPT-3.5 verbalized AUROC is 56.4 vs 69-73 with 5-sample consistency, and several tasks show gains of a few points only, so 'far better' is too strong.
fix: Agreement across samples predicts failure better than stated confidence, most clearly on arithmetic: GPT-4 vanilla verbalized-confidence AUROC averages 62.7%; for GPT-3.5 on GSM8K AUROC rises from 54.8% (verbalized) to 92.7% (5 samples with consistency), though the five-task average is only 56.4 to 73.0 and gains are small on professional-knowledge tasks; a unanimous 4-model panel was 99.5% correct on MATH-500 at 85% coverage (Liu 2026). A runner-up margin signal was not tested.

problem: Huang et al. Table 2 oracle rows match (GPT-4 HotpotQA 49.0 to 59.0, GSM8K 95.5 to 97.5); Kamoi survey backs the oracle-label point. Minor: oracle labels decide when to stop in the cited earlier work; HotpotQA is n=100.

Kamoi's survey supports the external-feedback point, but CRITIC with tools beats CRITIC w/o Tool by 1.6 to 8.0 EM points across tasks and backbones (text-davinci-003: +8.0, +5.4, +3.8; ChatGPT: +6.8, +1.6, +7.2), not a uniform 4 to 8.
fix: Self-correction works when feedback comes from a reliable external tool (code, search, tests); CRITIC with tools beats the same loop without tools by about 2 to 8 EM points (text-davinci-003 and ChatGPT, AmbigNQ/TriviaQA/HotpotQA).

problem: Minor: Huang's debate figures are 83.2 (6 responses) and 83.0 (9 responses) vs 88.2 voting at 9; Choi 0.7691 vs 0.7377 and Ferreira 1.6x/3.4x match; Bertalanic noise placebo c=0.33 vs self-correction c=0.34 is on GSM-Hard in homogeneous teams.
Minor: Lamparth et al. say LLM responses 'can be more aggressive' and found high-level agreement with experts; Rivera et al. (no expert comparison) report all five LLMs show forms of escalation.

All numbers (64.5%, 89.3%, Qwen3-32B 0.045 to 0.793, reasoning models small or negative blind spot) are in Tsui 2026 alone; Kim et al. 2026 (societies of thought) is only loosely related and does not corroborate them, so the claim rests on one paper.
Vaccaro et al. also report very high heterogeneity (I2 about 97.7%) and that the negative synergy was driven by decision tasks; Bansal et al. is a separate paper on explanations.

Bansal et al. abstract states explanations did not increase complementary performance and raised acceptance regardless of correctness; Vaccaro et al. find explanation and confidence moderators not significant. Scope is AI with accuracy comparable to humans, three tasks.

Numbers match (63.9% vs 74.2%; 88.5/77.9; 33.0/64.7). Caveat: the AI was a fictional LLM search engine with built-in errors, so 'unhedged AI lowered accuracy' is specific to that design; also general-perspective hedging was weaker (67.9%, not significant) and Steyvers is not about hedging.

Steyvers et al. show length bias in confidence without accuracy gain (284 analysed of 301; 0.46 vs 0.95 example item); Si et al. report 0.35 (+/-0.22) accuracy when the ChatGPT explanation is wrong vs 0.56 with contrastive explanation (p=0.009).

Numbers match (95 developers, 55.8% less time, p=0.0017; 16 developers, 246 tasks, 19% more time), but the trials also differ in year, tool, population and task, and neither paper tests that task or expertise explains the sign difference (Peng only reports larger gains for less experienced developers).
fix: Two randomised trials point in opposite directions: GitHub Copilot cut completion time 55.8% on a self-contained HTTP-server task (95 developers, Peng et al. 2023), while allowing AI made 16 experienced developers 19% slower on 246 real issues in mature repos (METR 2025); the studies differ in tool, year, task and population, so the cause of the difference is not established.

problem: Brynjolfsson et al.: 5,179 agents, +14% average, +34% for novice/low-skilled, minimal for experienced (lowest skill quintile +34%); Dell'Acqua et al. (Organization Science 2026 version, via a mirror) report bottom-half-skill subjects as the main beneficiaries. Different tasks (customer support vs consulting).

Minor: Mozannar's 53.2% is for suggestions accepted after 'deferred thought' (21 programmers, post-hoc verification raises mean verification time to 15.21 s from 3.25 s); Simkute et al. is a review without new data.

CoALA (modular memory, action space, decision procedure with the LLM as one component) and Shneiderman's two independent axes (automation and human control) both match; two separate sub-claims, each backed by one conceptual paper.

Bainbridge (1983) states manual skills deteriorate when not practised and that take-over in abnormal conditions needs a more, not less, skilled operator; the generative-AI carry-over is Simkute et al.'s argument (review, no new data).

Minor: the two Stechly papers share a lab (Kambhampati group), so the specific numbers (30 of 500 accepted, 5 right; Game of 24 5% to 36-38%; coloring 16% to 34-38%) are one-lab evidence; Huang et al. and Kamoi et al. independently support the no-net-gain-from-self-critique point.

Minor: 73.5% is out-of-the-box self-recognition of GPT-4 (Panickssery et al.); Wataoka et al. tie bias to low perplexity, not authorship. Neither paper tests a same-family (rather than same-model) checker, so that last step is an inference.

Minor: the 40.50 to 41.41% figure is the largest gain of majority vote or reward model across 100 to 10,000 samples (Llama-3-8B-Instruct on MATH), and coverage there is measured against ground truth (a perfect verifier); Stechly et al. add k=25 resampling with a sound verifier giving 42-44%.

All quoted figures (0.051 growth, 13.6 yr doubling, b_r=-0.0039, 100% of gap, 35%) verified in Petersen et al. arXiv 2406.15311/2306.01949, but these are one lab's two versions; Bentley et al. only gives ~5%/yr publication growth, not the other numbers.
Minor: pooled-diversity gain of 10.2-18.1% applies to four of five retrieval strategies, and 4000 seeds / ~200 non-duplicates is per topic.

Numbers verified (53.3% Claude-3.5 pairwise vs chance 50 on the Si idea-review task; 71.4% accepted-vs-rejected ICLR pairs; LLM rater AUC 0.424 in Huang), but 71.4% is well above chance, and the |rho|<=0.005 is human reviewer score vs EDM disruptiveness, not an LLM judge.
fix: LLM judges of research ideas are unreliable: in Si et al. the best LLM evaluator reached 53.3% agreement with held-out expert reviewers (chance 50%, human-human 56.1%) though Claude-3.5-Sonnet scored 71.4% on accepted-vs-rejected ICLR pairs; a single-paper LLM rater had AUC 0.42 for highly cited ICLR papers; separately, human ICLR reviewer scores are essentially uncorrelated with later disruptiveness (|rho|<=0.005).

problem: Minor: Si range is 43.3-53.3 across judges; Gong 31.1% is frontier mean on a 4-tier task (25% chance).

Numbers check (Wen 77% on 1,585 test pairs; Gong 59.2% vs expert majority 41.6%; Tong 80.9/83.1), but in Tong's in-domain table the prompted GPT-5.4 Thinking scores 81.6, above the 4B SciJudge (80.9) and only 1.5 points below the 30B (83.1), so trained models do not clearly beat the best prompted LLMs there.
fix: Models fine-tuned on outcome data beat prompted LLMs and sometimes experts at pairwise judging of research: Wen 77% on 1,585 test pairs (vs GPT-4.1 51.9%, o3 about random), Gong 59.2% vs expert majority 41.6% and frontier mean 31.1% (management), but Tong's in-domain citation-pair gains (64.7 to 80.9 and 71.7 to 83.1) only match the strongest prompted model (GPT-5.4 Thinking 81.6). These are weights, not a scaffold.

problem: Co-Scientist 6.14 vs 2.38 and Gupta's 1.3/32.7% vs 88.8/89.0% are verified, but Turnitin and OpenScholar were run only on documents with verified similarity score 4 or higher (not on 36), and the text says OpenScholar surfaced the source in one case (Table 3 lists 0%) while Turnitin found none.
fix: Retrieval of related work is the novelty bottleneck: Co-Scientist's auto-evaluation scored known (non-novel) ideas 6.14/10 without search vs 2.38/10 with search; in Gupta and Pruthi plagiarism detection accuracy was 1.3% (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) and 32.7% (GPT-4o) from parametric knowledge vs 88.8-89.0% with oracle access to the source paper; on documents with verified similarity scores of 4 or more, Turnitin found the source in none and OpenScholar in at most one case.

problem: Numbers verified (85.8% repeat, 1.8% jumps, MEDLINE strategy near-optimal only for ~10% and increasingly inefficient beyond ~30%, though the paper says 'may have been'), but both sources are by the same group (Foster, Rzhetsky, Evans) using the same MEDLINE data and model.
Minor: 93% is overall new-link AUC and >99% (99.5) only for links formed at least 3 times; Sourati 'up to 400%' is relative gain over content-only models; Krenn's two papers are one group.

Minor: Chase and Simon's 'no effect' is called a possible low-power null (Gobet and Simon 1996 pose it as an open question), not established; Sala and Gobet meta-analysis (r=.41, k=28) covers several domains, not chess only.

Gong et al. 2015 confirm largest chunk size is larger for rated players and number of chunks does not correlate with rating, but that is consistent with, not a refutation of, a constant-chunk-count claim; the evidence note that Chase and Simon's own count rose with skill (N=3) conflicts with the 'size not count' framing and could not be confirmed in the 1973 text.
fix: Largest chunk size grows with skill on game positions (Gong et al. 2015: 4.56 vs 2.60 pieces for rated players vs non-players), while the number of chunks recalled does not correlate with chess rating in brief-presentation recall; evidence on whether Chase and Simon's 1973 claim of a fixed number of chunks holds across skill is mixed.

problem: Gong et al. 2015 used the repeated-recall technique as an alternative to the fixed-pause (latency) criterion, criticising the latter, and found within-chunk pieces have more chess relations and inter-piece latency tied to relations; this converges with but is not a replication of the 2 s criterion. The 1998 computer-display replication is supported only by its abstract (full text not retrievable).
fix: The 2 s pause criterion finds chunks whose pieces share chess relations (attack, defence, colour, type); Gobet and Simon (1998) report that latencies on a computer display closely match Chase and Simon's, and Gong et al. (2015), using a different repeated-recall method to define chunks, also found that within-chunk pieces share more chess relations and that inter-piece latency tracks relations.

problem: In Smith, Lane and Gobet the 0.914 to 0.985 is CHREST accuracy as a proportion of its own maximum at 1 s exposure (capacity 3 to 4), not a fit to human data, and the paper only claims a good qualitative match to human data; Lane, Gobet and Cheng (2001) abstract gives the 3-4 chunk limit; both are CHREST group papers.
fix: CHREST simulations of chess recall (Smith, Lane and Gobet 2008; Lane, Gobet and Cheng 2001) support a visual STM capacity of about 3-4 chunks: simulated accuracy relative to its maximum rises from 0.914 at capacity 3 to 0.985 at capacity 4 (1 s exposure), with a good qualitative match to human recall data.

problem: 2895 Lichess blitz Elo (270M, against humans) is verified, but the model is supervised distillation of Stockfish 16 search-derived action-values over 10M games' positions (15B annotations), not independent pattern recall; the authors call it an approximation of a search-based algorithm. Schultz et al. is another system (search-augmented MAV).
fix: A 270M-parameter transformer that runs no explicit search at test time reaches a Lichess blitz Elo of 2895 against humans (Ruoss et al. 2024), but it was trained by supervised distillation of Stockfish 16 search-based action-values on positions from 10M games, so it shows that search results can be amortized into a pattern-matching network, not that patterns alone carry expert play.

problem: HiAgent (21 to 42, -35% context, GPT-4-turbo), Context-Folding prompt-only 0.420 vs 0.386 and MEM1 (10.4 vs 38.4 = 27%) verify, but 0.620 is the Folding agent trained with its own FoldGRPO versus 0.527 for a summary agent with plain GRPO; the like-for-like GRPO comparison is 0.567 vs 0.527, and on SWE-Bench Verified the RL summary agent (0.550) is about level with Folding GRPO (0.564).
fix: Replacing a finished subgoal trace with a summary chunk helps LLM agents: HiAgent raises GPT-4-turbo success from 21% to 42% with 35% less context; Context-Folding beats a summarise-when-full agent at the same 32K budget on BrowseComp-Plus (0.420 vs 0.386 prompt-only; 0.567 vs 0.527 with plain GRPO and 0.620 with its own FoldGRPO), with near-equal results on SWE-Bench Verified (0.492 vs 0.488 prompt-only); MEM1 (RL) uses about 27% of the peak tokens of Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct at 16 objectives (10.4 vs 38.4 hundred tokens).

problem: Minor: 'shuffled' vs forward-order drop is for the logic benchmark with 12 rules; Lost in the Middle is a separate, well-known result for mid-context retrieval.

Gobet and Simon 1996 do report mirror-image impairment, cite Saariluoma's quadrant swap, and reject Holding's estimate (postulated chunks < 2,500), but every listed source is from the Gobet/Lane CHREST group (Lane and Gobet 2011 is a defence with no new data) and a rival view (Linhares and Freitas) disputes pure location coding; they also allow a weaker 'both encodings' version.

Wikipedia says only anecdotal evidence (mostly Shell) supports scenarios; Polyscene's 'evidence is mixed' (citing Cordova-Pozo and Rouwette) concerns debiasing, not firm performance, so it is weak support. The claim honestly flags both as second-hand.

Goodwin and Wright 2001 say strategy evaluation is 'one underdeveloped element' and informal evaluation may select inferior strategies; Wikipedia's de Geus audit statement carries a 'clarification needed' tag; Hodgkinson and Wright 2002 report a largely unsuccessful scenario/cognitive-mapping intervention with a top team, which is not shown to be about post-scenario decision making; none says scenario creation was not a weak point.
fix: Strategy evaluation across scenarios is described as an underdeveloped element of scenario planning (Goodwin and Wright 2001: informal evaluation may select inferior strategies); Wikipedia reports that de Geus's early-1980s audit blamed decision-making after the scenarios for poor strategic implementation (tagged 'clarification needed'); Hodgkinson and Wright 2002 report their own largely unsuccessful scenario intervention with a top management team.

problem: All Brier numbers verify (Halawi .179/.149/.208; ForecastBench .096/.122/.136; Soru .186/.236), but Soru's 0.150 is a reference average for superforecasters on different questions, not a same-question comparison, and Schoenegger et al. found only 'not statistically different' / equivalent within medium-effect bounds on 31 questions, not equal.
fix: LLM forecasting is near human-crowd level but below superforecasters: Halawi's retrieval system scores Brier 0.179 vs crowd 0.149 (best plain model 0.208, random 0.250); a 12-LLM ensemble was not statistically different from 925 human forecasters on 31 questions (equivalent within medium-effect bounds); ForecastBench superforecasters score 0.096 vs 0.122 for the best LLM on the 200-item subset (0.136 without crowd information); Soru and Marshall's pipeline scores 0.186 vs 0.236 for vanilla GPT-4o on its own 72-question test set (a reference superforecaster average of 0.150 comes from other questions).

problem: Minor: the Delphi result is two themes (geopolitical, collaboration) present in 12 of 12 runs of a single model (gpt-4o-mini); NoveltyBench averages are per-model means of distinct answers out of 10 (e.g. Llama-3.3-70B 2.49); the cap on mini-scenarios is an inference.
Minor: GPT-4 figures come from only 5 trials per cell.

Lou and Sun, Huang (Llama-3.1-8B 34.7 to 50.5), Sovrano (CoT 16.1 vs 12.9 baseline) and Kraishan (p=.057) check out, but in Shahriar et al. the 83-88% combined attack success is the weak defense; the strong ignore-context defense cut it to 88.45 (LLaMA 4), 69.23 (LLaMA 3), 49.32 (DeepSeek) and 67.80 (Qwen).
fix: Simple prompt fixes do not remove LLM anchoring: CoT, 'ignore the anchor', principles and reflection leave significant anchor effects (Lou and Sun); knowledge enhancement raised Llama-3.1-8B's anchoring ratio from 34.7 to 50.5 percent (Huang); CoT was worse than baseline overall on PROBE-SWE bias sensitivity (16.1 vs 12.9 percent, Sovrano); in code review, a weak ignore-context prompt left combined attack success at 83 to 88 percent on four open models while a stronger one lowered it to 49 to 88 percent (Shahriar); a verbalise-the-anchor line lowered anchoring on 5 of 5 items but only at p=.057 (Kraishan).

problem: Minor: 'cross-culture r 0.26 to 0.61' are pooled meta-analytic correlations for four items with high heterogeneity (I2 65-87%); 'all four Many Labs 1 items replicated' follows from Kakinohana et al. (anchoring a successful Many Labs 1 replication; all four meta-analytic effects p<.001) rather than a direct read of Klein 2014.

Numbers verify (Many Labs 2: d=0.30 N=207 vs d=0.04 [-0.01,0.09] N=6,826), but they come from one incidental-anchor paradigm (Critcher and Gilovich 2008 phone-name study), so 'incidental anchors do not replicate' is wider than the evidence; Schley and Weingarten support relevance and distance as moderators for explicit anchors only.
fix: In Many Labs 2 the incidental-anchor effect of Critcher and Gilovich 2008 (phone name P97 vs P17) did not replicate (d=0.04, 95% CI [-0.01, 0.09], N=6,826 vs original d=0.30, N=207); Wikipedia reports random-anchor studies (die roll, random button) also failed to replicate, and in Schley and Weingarten's explicit-anchor study (N=1,967) the effect was larger when the anchor applied to the target judgment and was farther from the centre of unanchored beliefs.

problem: Numbers verify (ML2 jacket/calculator OR 4.96 to 2.06, d 1.08 to 0.40; DeKay OR 1.84), but the ML2 item is Tversky and Kahneman 1981 Study 10 (cheap vs costly item, mental accounting), not a gain/loss risky-choice problem, so it is not evidence about risky-choice framing weakening; the claim's own caveat contradicts using it as the headline.
fix: Risky-choice (gain/loss) framing persists: DeKay (2025, N=1,697) found a framing effect for completely described, matched options (OR=1.84, 95% CI for b [0.29, 0.93]) and in seven of nine matched comparisons, while part of the classic effect depends on mismatched option wording. Separately, Many Labs 2 replicated the Tversky and Kahneman 1981 Study 10 cheap/costly-item framing at roughly half the original size (OR 4.96 to 2.06; d 1.08 to 0.40), which is a different framing task, not a risky-choice problem.

problem: Numbers verified in Tversky and Kahneman 1974 (no description: base rates used; worthless description: .5; hospital 21/21/53 = 95 students), but both listed primary entries are the same 1974 paper and Wikipedia just relays it; 'small-sample insensitivity is common' rests on one student question.

T&K 1974 supports the committee-estimate availability bias, but the ease-of-retrieval and moderator findings (Schwarz 1991, Vaughn 1999) were only read second-hand via Wikipedia, and the Schwarz result is that recalling 12 assertive examples gave lower assertiveness self-ratings than recalling 6 (and the reverse for unassertive recall), not that 12 examples generally lower self-ratings.
fix: Availability judgments depend on ease of retrieval, not only the number of examples recalled: in Schwarz and colleagues' study (as reported on Wikipedia, primary not read) participants who recalled 12 assertive behaviours, a hard task, rated themselves less assertive than those who recalled 6; Vaughn (1999), as reported there, found the effect of listed-example count only when uncertainty was high (start of semester, hardest exam); Tversky and Kahneman (1974) showed availability-type biases in committee-count estimates (median 70 for 2-member vs 20 for 8-member committees; correct answer 45).

problem: Debate 0.502 vs vanilla 0.3805 is llama3.1-8b FOMC average; Reflexion average (0.383) is about equal to vanilla and few-shot rise is smaller; Lyu itself calls few-shot inconsistent. Substance holds.

The Jones & Steinhardt 2022 paper (arXiv 2202.12299) is about Codex and GPT-3 anchoring/framing of code and estimates and contains no Asian disease experiment, 704 prompts, 74% die-frame figure or save-probability boundary; the other numbers (GPT-4 40.5%, Malberg framing 0.41, Kraishan -0.336 on five items, seven models) check out.
fix: LLM framing effect is strong: GPT-4 admits 40.5 percent more students under reject framing (BiasBuster), and framing mean bias is 0.41 across 20 models (Malberg). Caveat: on 5 Malberg framing items, seven 2025 models leaned against the human direction (mean -0.336), so framing effects in current models depend on item and scoring.

problem: Ye: only most (not all) judge models fell below 0.5 robustness at 3-4 candidates.

Both listed sources exist (Lynott abstract confirms N=861 null; Chabris abstract confirms triple-size null replications; per-study ORs and r values not checked in full text), but neither covers the head-heart moral judgement replications (N=203, 304), so that part is unsupported by the listed evidence.
fix: Embodied-metaphor priming effects replicate poorly for warmth and prosocial choice: original OR=3.52 (N=50) versus pooled replication N=861 with no effect (OR=0.77), and two Chabris field replications (N=128 and 177) with effects near zero (r about 0).

problem: Every number and finding (71.3%, priming asymmetry, line-length asymmetry, Aymara/Mandarin/Spain-Morocco variation) comes from one review chapter (Samuel et al. 2017) summarising Boroditsky and others; Teuscher 2008 supplies no figure used in the claim, and the ranking as having the best behavioural support is not stated in the sources.
fix: A review (Samuel, Athanasopoulos and Bylund 2017) reports behavioural support for the space-to-time mapping: primed frames shifted answers on the move-forward-two-days question (71.3% consistent with the prime), space primes time more than time primes space, and line-length effects are asymmetric; the mapping varies across languages (Aymara, Mandarin, Spain vs Morocco). Teuscher et al. 2008 found a smaller ERP congruity effect for time than space sentences.

problem: Thought propagation gains are +12% absolute (shortest path), +13% human preference and +15% task completion, so calling all of them points is loose.
MRR .022 and .048 are for the whole SCAN dataset (scientific plus metaphor analogies); the metaphor-only subset is lower still, so describing them as metaphor mappings is loose.
Wording mostly explained by more samples is a little stronger than Smit (debate does not reliably beat self-consistency) but is supported by Huang and Tran.

All accuracy figures match Table 1 of Tran and Kiela, but the paper covers three model families (Qwen3, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama, Gemini 2.5; four models since Flash and Pro are both Gemini), not four families.
fix: At matched thinking tokens a single agent is the best default on multi-hop QA across three model families (four models: Qwen3-30B, R1-Distill-Llama-70B, Gemini-2.5-Flash and Pro): mean accuracy at 1000 tokens single 0.418 vs debate 0.388, roles 0.381, sequential 0.379, subtask-parallel 0.369, ensemble 0.333; multi-agent leads only at 100 tokens or under heavy context corruption.

problem: The 25% and 39% are average faithfulness scores across hint types; Korbak is a position paper that adds no numbers, so only Chen supports the figures.
I re-searched CoALA, Turpin, Reflexion and Du for Hutchins/distributed cognition (zero hits) and read Hollan et al.; the other 7 papers in the gap check were not re-searched.
The claim wording median effect 85% smaller, 92% smaller is ambiguous: 92% is the share of replication effects that were smaller than the original, not a 92% reduction.
The 36.8% to 40.8-41.6% figures are one system (LLM Review) on 500 papers as stated; wording fits.

Howell (402,500 responses, reject down 1.7 pp, about 25% relative) and Vasu (252 ICLR papers, seven models, 66.0-94.2%) match, but the same family of models is loose (Vasu tests seven models, GPT-4o Mini being one) and Claude 3.5 not listed as biased holds only for the economics abstract: the body shows Claude penalising Chulalongkorn University and MIT/Harvard raising ratings for all four LLMs.
fix: LLM prestige leak is real but its size depends on the measurement. GPT-4o-mini with 402,500 audit responses: reject falls 1.7 pp (about 25% relative) when identity is shown, quality score shifts about 1%. With token-probability (soft) ratings, seven LLMs (including GPT-4o Mini) prefer highly ranked institutions in 66-94% of paired comparisons (252 ICLR 2025 papers). In the economics audit the abstract names GPT, Gemma and LLaMA as favouring top male authors and elite institutions; Claude 3.5 showed no author-prominence effect but did penalise one non-US university. Hard integer scores under-measure the leak.

problem: Math grading counts are small (10 questions, 20 trials) and reference/CoT gains are from Zheng only; few-shot is a separate fix from the three named.
Shi reports some success rates of 88-89% as well as 90-98%, and the 70% miss rate is for windowed perplexity detection on Llama-3-8B only; the +20% acceptance was reported as about 20%.
Sakana pipeline did include a keyword novelty search (up to 10 rounds); the failure was its weakness, not absence, so without a real novelty search is an interpretation.
The CRITIC figures are for one model block; Huang over rounds gives GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0.

Headline numbers are right (d=0.45 or 0.42 without outliers, 214 papers, 2,149,683 participants, structure 0.55 vs 0.38 and 0.31, food 0.72, finance 0.25) but the wording omits that Maier et al. find the effect near zero (d=0.04-0.11) after publication-bias adjustment.
37% is the WINDOW cohort (hired just before the switch, opt-in rules) at 3-15 months; Wikipedia confirms the Buehler thesis numbers (33.9 vs 55.5 days, about 30%) as a secondary source.
The 67% exact-match-to-anchor figure comes from the GPT-3 estimation replication in Jones & Steinhardt, not from Codex; the Codex result is the 22.3-30.5 point accuracy drop.
fix: LLMs show human-like anchoring: low and high anchors move estimates (ChatGPT high anchor 105.97 vs low 20.83); GPT-3 updated estimates equal the anchor exactly 67% of the time; irrelevant context cuts Codex accuracy by 22-31 points. One study (Lou and Sun) found GPT-4 anchoring index 0.45 vs 0.61 in a human study (anchoring weaker than in humans), and anchoring on time questions not significant.

problem: The 17.2% (framing) and 8.5% (status quo) residual biased prompts for GPT-3.5 are from the awareness (plain warning) prompt, not self-help; for GPT-3.5 self-help only cut biased group-attribution prompts by 8.9%.
fix: Structural debiasing of LLM inputs and procedure (self-help re-asking, abstention plus bias inspection) works well for strong models: self-help left GPT-4 with 0% biased group-attribution and 2.7% biased framing prompts, while GPT-3.5 reduced biased group-attribution prompts by only 8.9% with self-help; abstention plus specific-bias inspection reached a best accuracy of 93.5% (Gemini 1.0 Pro) on the 205-item BRU set, and the plain awareness prompt left GPT-3.5 at 17.2% (framing) and 8.5% (status quo) biased prompts.

problem: The few-shot/contrastive/counterfactual worsening (GPT-4 anchoring 0.250 to 0.300/0.383, numbers verified) rests on one paper (Echterhoff et al.) listed twice; the other source (2412.00323) tests awareness and social projection, not few-shot or contrastive prompts.

Emotion-stimulus (9.58 to 0.85) and tipping (Llama-7B helped, ChatGPT minimal, $1000 lowered accuracy) numbers check out, but no source shows an uneven effect of politeness or penalty prompts (Bsharat et al. only lists them among 26 principles with pooled results).
fix: Incentive-like prompts (emotion stimuli, tips) have uneven effects: EmotionPrompt relative gain 9.58 (Vicuna) down to 0.85 (GPT-4); tipping $1, $10 or $100 helped Llama-7B and made minimal difference for ChatGPT; a $1000 tip lowered accuracy compared with smaller tips. Politeness and penalty lines appear among 26 prompt principles but no per-principle effect is reported. Incentives for LLMs are prompt text, not payoffs.

problem: Bucinca et al.'s chi2(2)=44.35 (N=663 incorrect-AI trials, carb-source) and the least-favorable ratings are for the pooled cognitive-forcing-function category (update, wait, on-demand) vs simple explanations, not specifically a 'commit before seeing AI advice' design.
fix: Cognitive forcing functions (making people decide before seeing the AI answer, wait for it, or request it on demand) reduced following wrong AI advice on carb-source detection compared with simple explanations (chi2(2)=44.35, N=663 incorrect-AI trials; not significantly overall) but did not raise team accuracy, and people gave these designs the least favorable ratings; overreliance is a cost-benefit choice that falls when checking is cheap on a hard task and when the bonus is higher ($0.50 vs $0.01 per maze).

problem: Self-help did work best for prompt-induced bias, but Echterhoff et al. report it also worked well for Llama 2 on framing (0% and 1.4% biased prompts left) and status quo (0-6%) and failed for Llama only on group attribution, so 'weak on Llama' is too broad.
fix: Mitigations are model-dependent in LLMs: self-help rewriting performed best for prompt-induced bias in 2023 models (GPT-4 left 0% biased group-attribution and 2.7% framing prompts; GPT-3.5 reduced group-attribution prompts by only 8.9%; Llama 2 did well on framing and status quo but failed on group attribution) while awareness, few-shot and counterfactual prompts gave small or inconsistent gains; awareness helped some evaluator biases but order bias did not clearly change; asking the model to answer as most people would (SoPro) made the bandwagon effect much worse for GPT-3.5 (0.524 to 0.955).

problem: Edge on assistments17 is partly due to consecutive-attempt data (gap falls to +0.016 on first attempts).
Hooshyar et al. report 0.8789 vs 0.5782 only as Youden-optimal ROC thresholds used for sequence analysis; they do not show that raising the threshold reduces the optimism bias.
fix: LLMs show strong optimistic bias when judging learners: Llama-3.3-70B was right 85.4% of the time when the student was correct but 12.6% when wrong; zero-shot Llama 3 8B recall on incorrect answers was only 20%. The bias is model-specific (Qwen3-80B-Instruct 56.5% vs 51.0%); fine-tuning raised low-performer recall from 20% to 64% but AUC stays below DKT (0.77 vs 0.83), and the zero-shot model's Youden-optimal threshold (0.8789 vs 0.5782 for DKT) shows its probabilities are inflated.

problem: In LLM-KT's ablation (Table 3) the 3.08-point AUC cost of removing question information (0.8291 vs 0.7983) is on Nips2020, not Assist2009 (where it is 0.8870 vs 0.8788, about 0.8 points).
fix: Question text is where LLM-based tracing gets its edge: removing question information costs 3.08 AUC points on Nips2020 (LLM-KT, 0.8291 vs 0.7983; about 0.8 points on Assist2009), NTKT on Eedi rises from 77.06 AUC with IDs only to 90.32 with full question text, and text-based tracers (LKT) pre-trained on one dataset transfer to a new dataset without training while ID-based DKT drops to 0.5.

problem: Sarma et al. 2026 rescued social recognition memory after sleep deprivation, not freezing; the wording 'restores freezing ... and after sleep loss' wrongly extends the freezing result to a different behavior.
fix: In mice, light on tagged dentate gyrus engram cells restores freezing after anisomycin amnesia (Ryan 2015, Roy 2017) and restores social recognition memory after sleep deprivation (Sarma 2026); natural cues fail. Rodent only, specific cell populations and stimulation protocols. Dissent: Abdou 2018 found light on auditory inputs to the lateral amygdala failed to induce recall after complete amnesia. Replications are by related labs; strict count unknown.

problem: Free-recall-to-cued-recall recovery (Tulving & Pearlstone 1966) is described in the Alfei review; Warrington & Weiskrantz was only read as an abstract and concerns amnesic patients with partial cues.
Safety recovery in paper is 'ten epochs on ten safety instances'; second source (Kotha) only supports the general idea that ability remains after fine-tuning.

Kadavath et al. Table 1 shows trained-on-TriviaQA P(IK) AUROC out of distribution of 0.606 (LAMBADA), 0.687 (Python), 0.624 (GSM8K) but 0.928 on Mixed-Arithmetic, so the stated 0.606-0.687 range omits the strongest transfer case.
fix: A feeling-of-knowing analogue exists for LLMs but needs training or hidden states: P(IK) AUROC 0.864 on TriviaQA (52B), and when trained on TriviaQA only 0.606 to 0.687 on LAMBADA, Python and GSM8K (0.928 on Mixed-Arithmetic); probes on exact-answer tokens give AUC 0.83 to 0.95 but do not transfer across datasets once a logit baseline is subtracted.

problem: Both sources (Miyake et al. 2000 and Friedman & Miyake 2017) are from the same lab; the numbers (latent r .42-.63, common plus specific factors) are accurate, and the later paper shows inhibition has no unique variance beyond Common EF.

The p=.22 in the adolescent n-back study is the post-test test-anxiety group difference; training did significantly reduce test anxiety versus the 1-back control (interaction p=.03) and the null transfer result is attentional control (ACS p=.26, no flanker or go/no-go gain). Stroop 1935 shows a 33.9% practice gain on the practiced task, with only a fraction of it from faster colour naming.
fix: Practice or training on one control task shows little transfer: eight days of Stroop practice cut conflicting-word naming time 33.9% but did not remove the interference, and adaptive dual n-back training in 40 adolescents lowered test anxiety (interaction p=.03) but did not improve attentional control (ACS p=.26) or flanker/go/no-go performance versus a non-adaptive 1-back control.

problem: The STAI-s numbers (30.8, 67.8, 44.4) are accurate, but Ben-Zion et al. never tested a fresh context; the 'fresh context is cleaner' point comes from Shnaidman's sycophancy-pressure study (a different phenomenon), not from distress or anxiety induction.
fix: A calming prompt after a distressing context only partly resets a model (GPT-4 STAI-s: 30.8 baseline, 67.8 after trauma, 44.4 after relaxation). In a separate study of wrong-answer pressure (not distress), removing the pressure-bearing history by fresh-context deletion or truncation recovered clean behavior in 14/14 model-dataset pairs, while history-preserving repairs recovered only 2-3 of 14.

problem: The 57.7% vs 94.0% figure compares o1-preview with GPT-4o zero-shot (the paper's o1-preview-as-CoT contrast), not the same model with and without CoT.
Cowan's article does not state 'Miller's 7 reflects strategies' in those words (it says rehearsal and grouping must be curtailed to see 3-5); the 3 to 5 limit is for young adults.

Chase and Simon PDF is a scan I could not read; the Sala and Gobet table lists Chase and Simon 1973 with N=3, not in meta-analysis, skill effect No. All other numbers match (note the 4 'sources' for the meta-analysis are one paper, and the paper is by Sala and Gobet).
GPT-3.5 drop is stated as 'more than 20%' in Liu et al (worst case), a different model family from the Veseli 50%-window result; combined wording is fine.

Only Huang et al supports the CoT fix (GPT-4o 2024-11-20 is the outlier, other 4o versions rise to 17-21%); Kim and Schuster tests entity tracking without CoT and shows code-pretrained GPT-3.5 does track.
3.5-20x and the 85.53% figure are from ReadAgent only (85.53% is the gist compression rate, not accuracy); MemGPT is a different approach and does not support these numbers.

Haase and Hanel (listed as support) found no mean originality difference between chatbots and humans, and in Bellemare-Pepin only some LLMs (GPT-4, 'several leading LLMs') beat the human DAT mean while Gemini Pro did not; fluency was matched only in the Hubert AUT; evidence is from 2023-24 chatbots and mostly GPT-4.
fix: In 2023-24 studies, some chatbots (mainly GPT-4, also ChatGPT-3 and Copy.ai in Koivisto and Grassini) scored higher than the average human on semantic-distance originality in the AUT (fluency controlled or matched) and in the DAT (GPT-4 over humans; other models such as Gemini Pro were indistinguishable from humans, and Haase and Hanel found no mean AUT difference); in one-shot tasks the best humans still matched or beat the best AI (Koivisto and Grassini; top human decile/quartile beat every DAT model in Bellemare-Pepin).

problem: Stevenson's no-temperature link covers only GPT-3 at temperature 0.65-0.80, and Bellemare-Pepin (also listed) found GPT-4 DAT scores rise with temperature, so 'not reliably' is a hedged but narrow reading; 61.2% above 0.8 is at min-p default sampling (Jiang et al).

r = -.56 (humans) and -.61 (GPT-3) is confirmed in Stevenson, but neither source shows originality rising with temperature or prompts while usefulness falls; Peeperkorn measures novelty vs coherence/typicality, not usefulness.
fix: Originality and utility were negatively correlated within responses (r = -.56 for humans, r = -.61 for GPT-3, Stevenson et al 2022); higher temperature gave slightly more novel but more incoherent stories (Peeperkorn et al 2024), so open-mode metrics should score both novelty and usefulness or coherence.

problem: 'Naming the DAT' is the paper's aware vs unaware condition (B = 11.89 percentile points over 14 LLMs, Haase and Hanel 2025).

VS gain is 1.6-2.1x diversity over direct prompting in creative writing (Zhang et al); 'restore' is loose since VS recovers about two thirds of base-model diversity; NoveltyBench in-context regeneration roughly matches human-writer diversity for three models.

Lower bound r=.45 not located in opened sources (found .55 Koivisto, .78-.94 Haase and Hanel, latent .91 SemDis); ICC>=.80 for LLM scorers comes via a 2026 review citing Organisciak, not a primary check.

Rests mainly on IDEAFix (simple 'wild/unconventional' prompts outperform method prompts, homogenization persists across models); Schaeffer partly supports and CreativityNeuro is weight steering, not prompting.

Owen 2010 (N=11,430, no transfer) confirmed independently; most other sources are Sala and Gobet papers, as the claim itself admits; 'near zero' holds for music with active/random designs (g about -0.02 to 0.06) and WM 0.05.

Numbers match (music 0.25 to 0.03, WM 0.18 to 0.05, chess one active-control study at 0.10) but they come from one Sala and Gobet paper; the other listed sources are the same authors' follow-up or a coauthor's editorial, so there is no independent confirmation.

Numbers match the Macnamara et al abstract (2014, later erratum); 'necessary but not sufficient' is an interpretation consistent with the authors' conclusion; Hambrick 2020 is a coauthor follow-up, not independent.

The 92%/19% recall figures could not be checked (Brunel PDF returned 503; PubMed abstract has no numbers), and 'the advantage vanishes' conflicts with the Sala and Gobet 2017 meta-analysis (r = .41, experts better in 49 of 55 samples) showing a reduced but real expert advantage on random material; in the single study the skill effect on random recall was just non-significant (N = 26).
fix: Expert chess skill rests on large stores of chunks and templates; in Gobet and Simon (1998, N = 26) masters recalled about 92% of game positions but only about 19% of random ones (experts 13.8%, class A 12.4%, skill effect on random positions not significant), so the advantage largely shrinks, though not entirely, for structure that does not match learned patterns.
