problem: Sheridan and Reingold 2014 (experts distinguish relevant from irrelevant regions earlier, 'early part of the trial') is supported, but the only other source is the same authors' 2017 review of that and related work, so one lab; 'first fixations' is a loose paraphrase of 'early part of the trial'.
Numbers match Huan et al (base 45.7, RL 53.2, SFT no-think 29.0, TI -104.1); the 'SFT' figure is the no-think variant.

19.8% is on the selected free-form questions (about 6% on the preregistered set); +8.2% is the best-variant relative NL reasoning gain when code is added in pre-training, a different regime from narrow finetuning.
Training labels come from Stockfish search (supervised distillation), so 'without search' means at test time only; the Elo 2895 vs humans and 2299 vs bots, 270M size match.

R2 0.96 (toy) and 0.71 (LLM) are in Shenfeld et al; Chu et al does not measure KL shift so only one source supports the numbers; 'prompt scaffolds change no weights' is a logical statement, not a sourced one.

SEP says the causal and no-essential-difference conditions are 'on the right track' but too restrictive, whereas for the material-analogy (observable similarity) requirement it says there are good reasons not to accept it in Hesse's narrow sense (formal analogies drive maths and physics).
fix: Hesse (1966) gave three requirements for a good scientific analogy: material analogy (observable similarities), a causal condition on the source's vertical relations, and no essential difference in the negative analogy; she sharpened Aristotle's earlier account. SEP judges the causal and no-essential-difference conditions on the right track but too restrictive (they exclude correlational cases such as Franklin's lightning list and good analogies like rectangle/box), and rejects the narrow material-analogy requirement because formal analogies drive inference in mathematics and physics.

problem: 'Liberal Bayesianism' is not a label used verbatim in the SEP text I read; the rest (Carnapian rules, Bayesian conditionalization difficulty, Achinstein swan example, Norton warranting local fact) is present.

In Lewis and Mitchell (TMLR 2025) Table 1 the 0.078 at three generalisations belongs to GPT-3.5 (GPT-4 is 0.195, humans fall to 0.260 too, so humans also degrade with more generalisations but stay above the GPT models); all other numbers check out.
fix: Counterfactual letter-string analogies (permuted, symbol or longer-interval alphabets) break GPT models far more than humans. Lewis and Mitchell: mean accuracy over all alphabets, humans 0.753, GPT-3 0.488, GPT-3.5 0.350, GPT-4 0.452 (136 humans); extended study with 263 humans shows accuracy falling with more generalisations for all (at three generalisations humans 0.260, GPT-4 0.195, GPT-3.5 0.078). Hodel and West (121 humans) find the same for GPT-3; Stevenson et al. find children (7-9) and adults transfer to Greek and symbol alphabets while GPT-4o falls from 0.85 to 0.48 and Llama-3.1 405B to 0.27. Boundary: Webb et al. reply that GPT-4 with code execution matches humans (P=0.496).

problem: ARCANA is a grid-transformation analogy benchmark, not narrative, and compares model pass@3 with human pass@1; numbers all match the ARN, AnaloBench and ARCANA papers.
Yoran concerns irrelevant context copying rather than memory similarity, but both support the gist.
Chelazzi 1993 and 1998 are the same lab; Downing is independent; claim parts are each single-sourced and match the abstracts.

Paper's per-questionnaire pooled alphas run from .73-.74 (Klepsch GCL .734, Eysink ECL .740) to .91 (Leppink 2013 GCL), not .77-.91; the paper calls reliability 'satisfactory' and Eysink gives only an ECL alpha.
fix: Self-rating questionnaires have satisfactory internal reliability (pooled alpha .77 to .86 overall for ECL/ICL/GCL, about .73 to .91 across scales of the four instruments; 53 articles, 67 experiments, N=7413).

problem: Last sentence about mis-aimed reward is the note's inference.

All numbers come from Padmakumar et al. alone (listed twice); Lu et al. only introduced denial prompting and reports no matching result. Numbers do match (OLMo-Instruct, asking-for-novelty and denial prompting pooled).
The story study is a preprint (not peer reviewed) and the authors call it initial support.
Models tested are 2023-24 vintage (GPT-4-0314), so 'current' is dated.
Temperature finding is from a design-solution study (Ma et al.), not general; min-p figure is from Hivemind.
RT figures are for correct trials; 67% is share of analysed water-jar participants who found the alternative (31 of 46).

Numbers match Pope-Caldwell & Washburn 2022 (89.6% = 100 minus 10.45%; 70.6% = 24 of 34; 29.4% of informed still did not adopt), but the claim rests on that one study (listed twice); Ninomiya et al. is a different water-jar study with no shortcut-viewing data.

Numbers match Gigerenzer & Goldstein 1996 Table 2 (.658 Take The Best vs .657 regression, 83 German cities simulation), but that is the only source for them (listed twice); Fenwick et al. is a Bayesian-reasoning paper that does not report them.

Percentages match Macnamara, Hambrick & Oswald 2014 (confirmed via Crossref abstract), but Burgoyne et al. 2019 is a follow-up by the same authors (Macnamara, Hambrick) that only cites those figures, so there is one lab and one source.
57% is from Luchins 1942 thesis data reanalysed by Binz & Schulz (87/153 used the Einstellung solution on C1/C2 vs 83% plain).

Hummel & Holyoak 1997 call current models 'arguably' overpowerful and say the evidence is 'only suggestive' that people tend to re-represent; 'only via re-representation' is too strong; the sources are one lab (Holyoak) and the 6/8 and Keane figures are cited second-hand in Hummel & Holyoak 1997 (the 6/8 is not found in the Holyoak & Thagard 1989 text).
fix: Hummel and Holyoak (1997) argue that ACME and SME can map analogies of any size with equal ease and so are arguably overpowerful; on the unnatural boys-dogs mapping people tend to re-represent the analogs (6 of 8 students solved it in 3 min per Holyoak and Thagard; about 3 to 6 min with error feedback in Keane et al. 1994), though the evidence is only suggestive.

problem: Numbers (43% vs 35%, 29% vs 65%) match Hummel & Holyoak 1997, quoting Spellman & Holyoak 1996, but both listed sources are the Holyoak lab and the human data come from a single experiment; Holyoak & Thagard 1997 is a same-lab review with no new numbers.
The synthetic-domain-only remark is Musker et al.'s literature characterisation, not a systematic check.
Table row labels are not ambiguous in the raw PDF text (Humans .753, GPT-3 .488, GPT-3.5 .350, GPT-4 .452). Webb et al. later disputed the interpretation.

Numbers match Lewis & Mitchell 2024 (GPT-4 .86 to .72 on 36 trials from 6 problems; humans .78 to .70; answer-order effect), but the only other source (Inani et al.) merely cites that work, so there is one source, and the paraphrase sample is small.
The 25% zero-shot figure is at temperature 0.5 (19% at temperature 0); per-group GPT-4 range 3-33% is zero-shot from the ConceptARC paper.

The 95%-or-better with as few as 2 entities result is ESBN's alone (Webb, Sinha, Cohen 2021); Abstractors are reported as sample-efficiency gains, not that figure; all listed sources share authors (Webb, Cohen), so one research group.
fix: Key/value binding in external memory (ESBN, Webb, Sinha and Cohen 2021) let networks generalise learned rules to novel entities at 95% or better on all four tasks, with as few as 2 entities on same/different; relational-bottleneck models such as Abstractors (same group) show better sample efficiency on relational tasks; this resembles LISA-style role binding by analogy (the note's gloss).

problem: All numbers match, but I-RAVEN-X raises rule length, value range and perceptual noise (not 'binding load'), the 3.4x token figure is o3-mini only (5445 to 18482), and the Llama-3.1 70B letter-string result is a non-reasoning model that says nothing about long chain of thought.
fix: Reasoning models do not stay robust on analogy as task size and perceptual uncertainty grow: o3-mini falls 86.6% to 17.0% and R1 80.6% to 23.2% on I-RAVEN-X, o3-mini despite about 3.4x more reasoning tokens (and only 31.0% at high effort); separately, non-reasoning Llama-3.1 70B letter-string accuracy falls 0.35 to 0.00 as the alphabet is permuted.

problem: Ormerod 2020 shows loose-chunk easier than tight-chunk and standard tautology hard (12% low value), not the full five-class order; Nasvytis numbers match exactly.

Naeini et al. supports red-herring fixation and few-shot gains that stay far below humans; Haq et al. (six problems per condition, three models) reports that zero-shot CoT improves exact match for all models while raising step counts, with no finding that CoT 'helps only partly'.
fix: LLMs are fixated by red herrings and few-shot examples bring only gradual gains that stay far below human scores (Naeini et al. 2023); a small study of mathematical equivalence problems (Haq et al. 2025, six problems per condition) suggests mental set, with in-context examples not reducing step counts and zero-shot chain of thought raising accuracy while taking more steps than the human one-step shortcut.

problem: Paper exists (Cognitive Psychology 2008; Europe PMC abstract confirms the set effect in experts and an effect equal to about 3 SD lower skill), but the full-text PDF host was down or blocked on every attempt, so the 100/50/18/0% figures could not be checked; a search snippet only corroborated that Grand Masters all found it and Candidate Masters 0%.
Both sources are Wikipedia pages (secondary only), but the claim says so and the figures match.
Only Wikipedia; the 23/55 vs 25/50 discrepancy is real and disclosed in the claim.

Wikipedia attributes the 70/98/58/97 figures to a stress-vs-non-stress speed test of 98 students (Luchins and Luchins), not to Luchins 1942 (483 children); chess N=34, anagrams N=60, chunk N=32/28 are correct.
fix: Einstellung (mechanised set) is real in humans: in a Luchins and Luchins water-jar speed test (98 students, as reported on Wikipedia) rigidity was 70% without stress and 98% under anxiety, extinction-problem failure 58% and 97%; also seen with experts in chess (Sheridan and Reingold 2013, N=34), anagrams (N=60) and chunk decomposition (N=32 and 28). Luchins figures come from Wikipedia only; primary Luchins 1942 and 1959 unopened.

problem: Strick g=0.224 is for 92 decision-making studies (immediate incubation); meta-analytic numbers seen only via a 2016 review; the 4 vs 12 minute result is Segal 2004.
MAD gain is +11 points, not strictly small; 8.41pp appears to be pooled over checkpoints/temperatures on a Qwen2.5-1.5B run; 'single run' not checked.

The 67.4% vs 78.2% novel-term figures compare ChatGPT output vocabulary with Red Dot award designs (AI-output fixation), not designers' fixation after exposure; originality effect is -0.03 (negligible), fluency -0.21 has only 76% probability negative.
fix: A 60-person sketching study found that seeing AI-generated example images was linked to more fixation on the example and fewer, less varied ideas (GenAI fluency about -0.21, 89% interval about -0.66 to 0.26, 76% probability negative; originality -0.03, 97% probability negative but negligible). Separately, a 10-designer ChatGPT case study found ChatGPT's own chair descriptions had a lower novel-term share (67.4%) than Red Dot award designs (78.2%), which shows fixation in the AI output, not in the designers. Effects are small with wide intervals.

problem: Ackerman is given as r=.48 (CI .44-.52) in the opened source, not .479; Kane 2005 median .72 over 14 datasets and >3,100 subjects confirmed on PubMed abstract.

Sources say the .80-.90 may be partly due to arithmetic content overlap and an arbitrary battery (K and C conceded arbitrariness); they do not show it was inflated, nor that .58-.72 come from overlap-free designs.
fix: The strongest headline (.80-.90) may be partly inflated by content overlap (an arithmetic reasoning test in all four samples) and an arbitrary, impure WM battery; later latent-variable studies with other designs report lower values (.58-.72), though the sources do not establish those designs were free of overlap.

problem: Only Conway et al. (one Sternberg-variant study) supports the overlap-specific slope result; the second source (Little et al. 2014) is about item difficulty, not interference, and the general rule is extrapolated from one example.
fix: In one Sternberg-scan variant reviewed by Conway, Kane and Engle (2003), low-WMC people had steeper RT slopes than high-WMC people only when letters overlapped across sets; with no overlap slopes did not differ. This is one example, and it suggests (not shows) that capacity matters most under interference.

problem: In Kane et al. 2016 [.46,.74] is the 95% confidence interval around one correlation (attention restraint with attention constraint), not a range of correlations, and it is not 'of mind wandering'; Draheim 2021 full mediation (N=396) held only with accuracy-based tasks and needs replication.
fix: Attention control (antisaccade, visual arrays) may carry much of the WM-Gf link (Draheim 2021, N=396: full latent mediation only with reliable accuracy-based tasks, not yet replicated); attention restraint and attention constraint are correlated but separable (Kane 2016, 95% CI around the correlation .46 to .74, which excludes 1.0).

problem: Melby-Lervag numbers, Q(1)=6.09, five n-back studies and Lawlor-Savage BF 39.97 all match; the 'baseline correction' part of the explanation is not shown in opened sources (control type is); Lawlor-Savage ages 30-60 and 57 analysed.
The n=3 decline is for GPT-3.5; GPT-4 was only tested to n=3 and far exceeds it, so 'chat LLMs' is slightly wide; Zhang et al. abstract was opened but gave no n-back specifics.

Numbers match (most larger models above 95%, not all), but 'limit is architectural' overreaches: Gong 2026 locates it in readout under interference, and the 2-layer perfect solution shows capacity depends on model size/training, not a fixed architectural ceiling; all but Xiong are one author (Gong).
fix: In small transformers trained from scratch, a 1-layer 1-head model shows a logarithmic accuracy decline up to N=6 while most models with more layers or heads stay above 95%; in 15 pretrained LLMs (70M to 14B) errors cluster on lures (models say match to 79% of N-1 lures at N=2), which Gong 2026 attributes to readout under interference rather than finding the item; Xiong et al. report a 2-layer transformer solves the task perfectly. This points to interference and attention dispersion, not a fixed architectural limit.

problem: The 3.1% is a probing classifier's accuracy on non-trivial Alchemy cases (from earlier work, as analysed by Kim and Schuster), not a direct LLM measure; 'resembling WM limits' is interpretation.

Camposampiero abstract and table say R1 fell to 23.2% (text elsewhere says 22.8%); the 'LLMs approach humans on simple forms' lead sentence is vague but Webb et al. (GPT-3 above 40 students, OR 1.88) supports it; 73.6 is the 3x3 value with per-attribute queries.

Schulz 2019 and Giron 2023 share authors (Schulz, Wu, Meder, Ruggeri); Blanco/Sloutsky and Nussenbaum are separate labs, so independence holds; Nussenbaum/Blanco abstracts support direction only (numbers not re-read).

Friedman and Miyake's bifactor model also has an Updating-Specific factor, which the claim omits; the abstract was seen in full, and the absence of an inhibition-specific factor is confirmed in the text.
Both EVOLvE entries are one paper; Harris and Slivkins supports only in-context summaries helping medium tasks, not the UCB-statistics or fine-tuning parts.

Hao et al. confirm CoT text reaches human-level and direct is near random; but in NeuroCognition the drift/returning-to-rejected-rule error pattern is shown only for weaker models on the image WCST, not LLMs generally.
fix: Wisconsin Card Sorting Test: with chain of thought and text input, GPT-4o, Gemini-1.5 Pro and Claude-3.5 Sonnet reach human-level set-shifting while direct answers are near random (Hao et al. 2025); in NeuroCognition's image WCST, most errors of weaker models come after the right rule was found, as drift away from it or a return to a rule already shown wrong.

problem: Go-Explore and Intelligent Go-Explore are one lab (Clune is on both); Voyager is a skill-library LLM agent compared to ReAct/Reflexion/AutoGPT, not an archive-and-return exploration method compared to flat exploration.
fix: Archive-and-return exploration beats intrinsic-motivation baselines on hard-exploration Atari games (Go-Explore: Montezuma above 43,000, about 4x prior state of the art) and beats LLM-agent baselines on text tasks (Intelligent Go-Explore, same lab); Voyager's skill library, a related but different mechanism, helped an LLM Minecraft agent (diamond tool reached 1/3 runs with it, 0/3 without).

problem: Gopnik 2020 states the tools boundary; Liquin and Gopnik Study 3 shows stickers earned rose with age (fewer rewards in children); 'goal-directed tasks' is a broad paraphrase of this one task and Gopnik's reasoning.

In Jamrozik and Gentner, label position mattered only for labels at test (after the passage n.s., p=.188); at encoding before vs after did not differ (3.19 vs 3.40 relational matches), and the 1600 ms decay comes from a perceptual 'five' search task (Lupyan and Spivey), not relational labelling.
fix: In Jamrozik and Gentner (2020), test labels helped only when placed before the test passage (labels after the passage did not, p=.188), while at encoding the position (before or after) made no clear difference. In a separate perceptual search task (Lupyan and Spivey 2010), a spoken label's benefit disappeared when it preceded the display by more than about 1600 ms.

problem: The claim glues the Lu et al. 2012 meta-analysis figures (65 studies, 3,189 groups, eight times) onto the Faulmueller sentence; Lu et al. numbers are correct per PubMed, Wikipedia supports the shared-information bias, but the Faulmueller 1-of-15 vs 100% figures could not be checked (paywalled, abstract does not give them).
fix: Hidden-profile tasks: groups discuss shared information more than unique information and rarely find the best option. Lu et al. (2012) meta-analysis (65 studies, 101 effects, 3,189 groups): hidden-profile groups were about eight times less likely to find the solution than groups with full information. Faulmueller et al. (2010, Experiment 2, figures taken from a researcher note and not re-checked): 1 of 15 hidden-profile groups solved it versus all groups with full information.

problem: The authors call 33% (N=202) a replication of Asch's 36.8% (no significant difference, p=.57), so it is not 'smaller'; only Bond and Smith's 44-replication average (about 25%) is lower, and the paper does not test against it.
fix: Human conformity is real: a modern Asch replication (Franzen and Mader 2023, N=202) found a 33% error rate, statistically indistinguishable from Asch's 36.8% (p=.57); a small monetary incentive (1 CHF per correct answer) lowered it to 25%; Bond and Smith's 44 strict replications average about 25%, so rates vary across samples and eras.

problem: Choi et al. numbers are correct (0.7205/0.7691/0.7377/0.7050), but they and Zhang et al. do not match compute (debate uses more); Smit only says Medprompt performs best/most consistently; and Wunderlich et al. 2026 (in the same note) found debate slightly beat self-consistency at comparable budgets on MMLU-Pro.
fix: Debate usually does not beat simple baselines even while using more compute: Qwen2.5-7B, average over 7 benchmarks, single 0.7205, majority vote 0.7691, debate T=2 0.7377, T=5 0.7050 (Choi et al.); Zhang et al. found four MAD methods beat CoT in only about 15% of 36 configurations; Smit et al. found no debate protocol reliably better and Medprompt best overall. Under comparable inference budgets on MMLU-Pro, however, Wunderlich et al. report debate (70.0%) slightly ahead of self-consistency (68.7%), so the result depends on how compute is matched.

problem: The 30-34% / 3.6% / 97% figures are from Knight-Knave-Spy puzzles (where debate overall raised accuracy), and Wynn et al. show C-to-I flips exceed I-to-C but do not quantify 'largely'; the wording is slightly broad.

Smit reports the gain as 15% (not clearly points) and says disagreement helped on the counter-intuitive dataset, so 'moderate is best' comes mainly from Liang; HiddenBench dissent figures (v4, May 2026) match.

Numbers match Yao et al. Table (CSQA, 2 agents), but DCR is defined differently with a judge (judge agrees with a wrong answer), the judged accuracy is only 1.15 points above the single agent (85.50), and in the 3-agent Qwen-Qwen-Llama case DCR is higher with a judge (59.09 vs 43.32); 'works better than prompt fixes' is not directly tested.
fix: In Yao et al. (CommonsenseQA, two Qwen agents) adding a centralized judge raised accuracy from 83.62 to 86.65 (single agent 85.50) and lowered the disagreement-collapse rate from 81.71 to 41.27, although DCR is measured differently with a judge and in a three-agent Qwen-Qwen-Llama setup it was higher with a judge (59.09 vs 43.32); judge-free debate showed high collapse. This is suggestive, not a direct test against prompt-based fixes.

problem: DCI results are one model (Gemini 2.5 Flash, 45 tasks, no cross-lab check); Wunderlich abstract gives +1.3 and +2.7 while the intro says +1.4 for debate; the 'no study tests... (gap 1)' negative claim cannot be verified from the sources.

ARN, AnaloBench, Stevenson and the function-vector paper match; 'most' for far analogies is a mild reading of the function-vector results (near analogies were flat or slightly lower), and the function-vector paper is a small-model (GPT-J, LLaMA) study.
Minor: the above-chance inconsistent-trial figures (68.5/70.2) are for one baboon (DAN) only, not all; claim does not use them.

Minor: the 10,000 rhesus trials (Thompson 2016, above/below RMTS variant) and 260,000 trials (Smith and Church review) are different studies; the capuchin 'sessions 14 and 15' detail in the notes is from earlier work, but 'only without Clever Hans controls' is in the abstract.

Minor: Lewis and Mitchell listed twice (one source); Hodel and West is the independent second. Table column order in the PDF is garbled but the evidence values match (GPT-3 0.488, GPT-3.5 0.350, GPT-4 0.452).

The ACRE numbers are right (Gendron: GPT-4 0.272 text vs 0.512 symbolic), but in KiVA the rotation/colour exception applies only to the verbal classification stage (GPT-o1, GPT-4V, MANTIS beat children there); models trail children on specification and extrapolation generally.
fix: Text format hurts relational reasoning for LLMs: on ACRE GPT-4 scores 0.272 with text input vs 0.512 with symbolic input; and on KiVA large multimodal models identify what changed (even beating children at classifying rotation and colour changes) but trail children and adults at specifying and extrapolating the rule.

problem: Yasunaga Table 1 matches (GPT-3.5 77.8 vs 75.8 CoT), but 14.8 for text-davinci-003 is the 0-shot baseline; against 0-shot CoT it is 50.3 and 5-shot CoT 54.0, so the gain over CoT is about 7-11 points. PaLM2 also rises 60.8 (0-shot) to 81.7; 'only for weak models' is an interpretation.
fix: Prompting for analogy helps modestly: self-generated analogical exemplars gave GSM8K GPT-3.5-turbo 77.8 vs 75.8 for 0-shot CoT; the larger gains are for weaker models (text-davinci-003 61.0 vs 50.3 with 0-shot CoT and 14.8 with plain 0-shot).

problem: Webb et al. 2021 Table 9 (same/different: ESBN+TCN 100.0 vs Transformer 73.7 at m=95, 56.1 at m=98) is right, but 99.7 vs 28.0 at m=95 is Table 11 (distribution-of-three), not RMTS; in the RMTS Table 10 it is 95.0 vs 49.9. The listed supporting sources (Webb 2021, Altabaa/Webb/Cohen 2024, Webb et al. 2024 review) are largely one research group.
fix: Architectures with explicit relational bottlenecks generalise out of distribution where standard nets fail (Webb et al. 2021: same/different, ESBN+TCN 100.0 vs Transformer 73.7 at m=95 and 56.1 at m=98; distribution-of-three at m=95, 99.7 vs 28.0; relational match-to-sample at m=95, 95.0 vs 49.9), evidence mainly from one research group.

problem: Wu et al. is right (arithmetic 'sometimes dropping from near-perfect to near-zero'), but Qiu et al. 2024 describes the MiniSCAN drop (>80% to almost zero) as the gap between hypotheses applied by an LM interpreter vs a symbolic interpreter, not a counterfactual variant; Qiu also shares authors (Qiu, Wang, Kim) with Wu, so it is not an independent lab.

Penn, Holyoak and Povinelli (2008) supports every element (baboons fell to chance on different trials with 2 icons; Bovet and Vauclair baboons needed 14,576 additional trials for the conceptual S/D task; Sarah's analogy performance unreplicated). Minor: the second source (Dymond and Stewart 2016) does not discuss Penn and is a critique of a crow RMTS procedure, so effectively only Penn supports the claim.

Numbers verified (Atari: r=-.70, 94,278 people, 65 nations; Tao et al.: GPT-4o 2.42 to 1.57), but Tao et al. call cultural prompting 'effective' (not a panacea: no improvement for 19-29% of countries); 'weak lever' is the claim's own interpretation, and a 35% distance cut is not weak.
fix: LLM value alignment tracks distance from US/WEIRD populations (r=-.70, WVS 94,278 people, 65 nations); cultural prompting narrows the distance for most countries (GPT-4o 2.42 to 1.57) but is not a panacea (no improvement for 19-29% of countries) and leaves substantial distance.

problem: Minor: the GSM-Symbolic +3.8% to +8.6% figures are relative gains over the best baseline and include GPT-4o (a strong model), and 'mean +18 to +35' is thesis-to-synthesis in the same pipeline (Candussio), not versus a baseline; the 'no equal-token test on strong models exists' gap is a negative claim not checkable from the sources.

Minor: CommonSenseQA 89.7 to 85.5 is Huang's intrinsic (no-oracle) result, which the claim marks with 'but'; all other figures verified (Huang Table; CRITIC Table 10: 72.5/78.2/83.9/77.0, davinci 68.3 (-1.8); TabMWP LLaMA-2-70B +16 vs +32.3).

Minor: Kamoi et al. is a survey whose conclusion is conditional (self-correction works with reliable external feedback or in tasks well suited to it), wording 'no robust self-correction without reliable external feedback' is a fair paraphrase.

Kim and Khashabi: the 93.9% is Llama-4-Maverick's Sure Rebuttal (SR) value, not 'Are You Sure'; the paper says Are-You-Sure is about as persuasive as the full rebuttal (56.1% avg) and the casual Sure Rebuttal averages 84.5%. Minor: SYCON Llama-3.1-8B holds 2.44 turns (Qwen-7B 0.83), so '1-2 turns' is loose. SycEval and SYCON (4.97, 4.90) and Silicon Mirror (9.6 to 1.4) figures verified.
fix: LLMs yield too easily to challenge, which makes a keep-both-alive rule fragile: sycophancy in 58.19% of cases (43.52% to correct, 14.66% to wrong, persistence 78.5%); a casual Sure-Rebuttal assertion persuaded far more (average F 84.5%, up to 93.9% for one model) than a full rebuttal (56.1%), while Are-You-Sure was about as persuasive as the full rebuttal. Gap search: on SYCON-Bench strong models hold a debate stance for about 4.9 of 5 turns (o3-mini 4.97, Qwen2.5-72B 4.90) while 7-8B models flip within about 1-2.5 turns; a third-person prompt cut sycophancy by up to 63.8%; a gating approach cut Claude Sonnet 4 sycophancy from 9.6% to 1.4%.

problem: Minor: Qiu et al. Table 1 numbers verified (ACRE task accuracy IO 28.0, SC 29.0, hypothesis refinement 59.0, GPT-4); 'no study found' is a negative search result that cannot be confirmed from the sources, and the search-log source is a PubMed query URL not a paper.

Minor: the +5.8 to +8.2% range mixes different baselines (Heter-SoM vs CoT-average +5.8, Heter-EoT vs EoT-average +8.2, Heter-SoM vs SoM-average +6.4) from Zhang et al.; Zhu et al. shows same-model debate is below majority vote (e.g. Qwen-2.5-7B GSM8K 0.847 vs 0.908), i.e. worse than 'little added'.

Mixed top-down/bottom-up switching is supported (von Mayrhauser and Vans 1997/1999, N=4). But 'as-needed reading is the common pattern in large programs' rests on Koenemann and Robertson (12 programmers, a 636-line program), a single-engineer case study (Singer and Lethbridge, who also report a full-coverage strategy for development work), and a statement in von Mayrhauser and Vans; strategy depends on the goal.
fix: Human code reading is mixed, goal-driven switching between top-down hypotheses and bottom-up chunking, not one fixed strategy; as-needed reading of only the relevant code is typical of maintenance work in larger programs (small lab studies and one longitudinal single-engineer case), while development tasks can call for fuller coverage.

problem: Minor: the 11-29 point class-summary drop is on ClassEval (LiveCodeBench method summaries barely change); the 10-14 point execution drop is Pass@1 9.6 (ClassEval) and 14.2 (LiveCodeBench) in Le et al. Table 1; Haroon's mutations are semantic-preserving code edits, not identifier removal. Fault-localisation 78% figure verified.

Chen et al. (15 models, average accuracy 44.4%, IC 10.3) and Liu et al. (81.42% coherent, 46.92% of those correct output) verified, but 'best model fully traced 47% of tasks' appears in none of the opened sources (Chen, Liu, Abdollahi); GPT-4-Turbo, the best in Chen, has average 75.0 and IC 42.5.
fix: LLM mental simulation of execution is unreliable: across 15 models the average accuracy is 44.4% with Incremental Consistency 10.3 (Chen et al.), and of the 81.42% of HumanEval simulations that are coherent only 46.92% give the right output (Liu et al., 16 LLMs).

problem: Agentless numbers verified (32.00%, 96/300, $0.70; skeleton 58.33% vs full file 53.67%). Minor: only Agentless supports the claim; LocAgent (also opened) shows graph agents localise better than Agentless (Loc-Bench file Acc@5 83.39 vs 67.50), and Agentless is the best open-source result, not the best overall, so 'matches' is fair but not 'beats'.

Majgaonkar et al. report the file-level match numbers (success 92-97%, failure 59-81%) but conclude that on SWE-bench Lite failures usually find the right file, whereas on Verified 35-40% of failed trajectories miss the file and file localisation is 'a bottleneck for a successful outcome'; so 'not file finding' holds only for Lite. SWE-Explore line recall (AutoCodeRover 0.233, Codex 0.194, Claude Code 0.154, Mini-SWE-Agent 0.151 vs oracle 0.953) verified; CoSIL scores 0.788.
fix: Agent failure on SWE-bench Lite is mostly fine-grained localisation and long trajectories rather than file finding (file-level match 92-97% for successes vs 59-81% for failures, with failures matching the file 79.8-81.4% on Lite), but on SWE-bench Verified file-level localisation is itself a bottleneck (failures match the gold file only 59-63% of the time); in SWE-Explore, agent line recall is 0.15-0.23 against an oracle 0.95.

problem: Li et al. (at most 22% of 68 methods significant; 85% between two models; negative results on summary quality) verified. But Paltenghi et al. report 47% vs 42.3% as a positive result (follow-up attention has the highest model-human agreement and beats the baseline), not as evidence that alignment is weak.
fix: Human-model attention alignment on code is weak in code summarization: at most 22% of methods show a significant human-model rank correlation (vs 85% between two models), and alignment does not predict summary quality; attention-derived follow-up predictions of a developer's next line reach 47% accuracy vs 42.3% for a history baseline, a modest but positive result.

problem: Minor: the AUROC 0.63 vs 0.86 (Beyond Accuracy) and the weak human-side result (Lavazza et al.: models built on structural measures have about 30% prediction error, Cognitive Complexity no better; 3 students) verified; the human-side evidence is one small study (Lavazza et al. 2023 and the 2022 preprint share authors).

Minor: all figures verified in Wyrich et al. (95 experiments, median 34, 53.7% students only, 6 of 25 between-subject designs balanced on skill, one qualifying replication); the second source (Munoz Baron et al.) shares Wyrich as an author, so effectively one research group, and 'methodologically thin' is the claim's interpretation.

Minor: pooled OR 3.82 (all atoms grouped), 7 of 14 atoms significant, 132 students (Langhout and Aniche) and rho 0.37 (CI 0.19-0.53; 24 participants x 72 trials, Abdelsalam et al.) verified; the 'C (professionals)' part is only reported second-hand via the Gopstein et al. replication context, and each half of the claim rests on one source.

Minor: Lin et al. (+2.2pp Func@5, -1.6 rounds, variance roughly halved; preliminary n=274 LocAgent 0.595 vs Codex grep 0.832) and DualView (355 to 375 +20, 316 to 351 +35, 342 to 388 +46 of 731) verified; the graph-vs-grep comparison is labelled preliminary.

von Mayrhauser and Vans (1995) verified: hypotheses fail for three reasons and the key is to keep open hypotheses manageable. But in Tiemens (1989) the why/how/data-description classes are the question types answered by Letovsky's CPU program, not Letovsky's general question taxonomy (which also has other types), and Tiemens is a secondary technical report.
fix: Von Mayrhauser and Vans name three reasons a hypothesis fails (no verifying code found; one code satisfies several hypotheses; code cannot be explained) and say to keep open hypotheses manageable; Tiemens' summary of Letovsky's CPU program lists three question classes it answers: why, how, and data description.

problem: Sio and Ormerod verified (117 studies, 3,606 participants, weighted mean d 0.29 CI 0.21-0.39, unweighted 0.41; Gilhooly 2016 confirms), but the pooled effect spans insight and divergent-thinking tasks, with divergent thinking benefiting MORE than linguistic and visual insight; the low-demand-beats-rest result holds specifically for linguistic insight problems.
fix: Incubation breaks give a small, reliable benefit on problem solving overall (weighted d about 0.29; unweighted 0.41), larger for divergent-thinking than for insight tasks; the effect depends on the break task: high-demand fillers reduce it, and undemanding interpolated tasks beat rest for linguistic insight problems.

problem: Minor: Knoblich et al. Ns (20, 38, 78) and Spiridonov et al. Ns (105, 88, 73; interference with relaxing higher-level constraints) verified; in Knoblich the transfer was significant for Type B and C problems but not A or D, so 'transfers to later problems of the same type' is not uniform.

Minor: Danek and Wiley 2017 figures verified (66.50 vs 52.34, t(69)=10.21, 417 of 1,124 = 37%); the study had 37 tricks (35 analysed), and 'not a verification signal' is the claim's interpretation of the paper's statement that Aha is not exclusive to correct solutions.

Danek and Wiley 2020 give 57.7% vs 35.4% recalled after one week, but for correct vs incorrect solutions, and conclude that the advantage comes from correctness, certainty and pleasure and did not seem to rely on sudden restructuring; the 'partly via surprise and restructuring' part is not supported by that paper (only the Becker et al. 2025 fMRI study links representational change to later memory).
fix: Correct solutions are remembered better one week later than incorrect ones (57.7% vs 35.4% recalled), mainly through correctness, certainty and pleasure rather than sudden restructuring (Danek and Wiley 2020); an fMRI study (Becker et al. 2025) links representational change and hippocampal activity to later memory.

problem: All numbers match the d'Aliberti paper (the evidence lines a21/b01/b02 are one paper; trace count is 11M+ in the paper vs 1M+ on abs page); Wu et al. corroborates qualitatively.

Huang et al. Table: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8->38.1 is round 1 (round 2 is 41.8), while GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5->89.0 is round 2; 'by round 2' misattributes 38.1. Also oracle gain is real (GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9->84.3, CSQA 89.7).
fix: Intrinsic self-correction without external feedback does not help and often hurts (GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 after round 1 and 41.8 after round 2; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0 by round 2); oracle labels help, so the gain comes from the external signal.

problem: Matches Huang et al. Tables (GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9->74.7, CSQA 75.8->41.8, GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5->89.0, all round 2); Kamoi abstract corroborates.
Huang et al. report GPT-3.5 GSM8K oracle 75.9->84.3; 95.5 is GPT-4's standard-prompt score, not a GPT-3.5 oracle result.
fix: Reported self-correction gains in earlier papers came largely from oracle stopping (gold label), weak first prompts, or unequal compute; with oracle stop GSM8K GPT-3.5 goes 75.9->84.3 (Huang et al. 2024).

problem: Verified from papers: Nazonazo 17.6/52.9/7.6; BRAINTEASER ChatGPT 53/63 vs human 92 (3 experts, 102 items); OCW GPT-3.5/4 solve 0-7 of 494 walls until red herrings removed. Mizumoto listed 3x and Jiang 2x (same papers).
OCW: 0-7 of 494 walls solved vs 279-471 on OCW-WordNet; Haq et al. CoT raises shortcut exact match (e.g. GPT-4o 0.33->0.66) but on only 6 problems per condition; Haq listed 3 extra times (one paper).

Lu et al. abstract and body match (37 models, 9 benchmarks, 96%/73% self-verify); the Tan et al. second source only motivates external verifiers and does not test the claim, so support rests on one paper.
Fleming & Lau (listed 3x, one paper) says sensitivity scales with task performance and favours meta-d'/d'; Rahnev & Fleming is a shared-author follow-up; Steyvers link not opened.
Mazancieux et al. (N=181, 5 of 6 cross-task correlations, via 95% HDI) and Rahnev & Fleming (type 2 AUC difference 0.034, d=0.57) match.

Wang (17.9 abs, LaMDA 17.1->27.7, flawed prompts 17.1->14.9 then 23.4 with 40 paths), Huang Table 7 (82.5/85.3/88.2 at 3/6/9 responses) and Xiong (M=1..13 saturates) all match; Wang is listed 3x as one paper and the 82.5/85.3/88.2 figures come from Huang, not Wang.

DeepConf 99.9% (offline, tail confidence, 10% retention) and the 84.7% token cut (online DeepConf-low, 97.9% accuracy) are different settings, so the sentence implies both gains come together; CISC, P(True) and Adaptive-Consistency numbers match.
fix: Confidence-weighted voting cuts cost: CISC needs over 40% fewer paths; P(True) SC needs 18.6 samples to match CISC at 10 (46% saving); Adaptive-Consistency cuts samples up to 7.9x with under 0.1% accuracy loss; DeepConf reaches 99.9% on AIME 2025 (GPT-OSS-120B, offline) vs 97.0% majority, and separately its online mode cuts tokens up to 84.7% (at 97.9% accuracy).

problem: Lin et al. Multi-answer MSE: finetuned verbalized numbers 22.0, constant baseline 34.1; 37.4 is the zero-shot answer-logit baseline. The 1,000-example claim is Kapoor et al., not Lin et al.
fix: Models trained to express uncertainty can generalise: finetuned verbalized numbers beat a constant baseline out of distribution (Multi-answer MSE 22.0 vs 34.1; zero-shot answer logit 37.4); a thousand graded examples suffice for finetuned calibration (Kapoor et al. 2024), and prompting alone is insufficient.

problem: Steyvers et al. (AUC humans 0.589-0.602 vs model 0.746-0.781, length effect, tone matching) and Zhou et al. (humans biased against uncertainty in alignment data; 47% error among confident responses when prompted) match; Steyvers listed 3x as one paper; Yona et al. gives no number.

Fleming & Daw 2017 treat confidence as Bayesian probability correct and own action as evidence; Kiani & Shadlen 2009 figure caption cites 70 LIP neurons (from PubMed record); the 'own action' idea belongs to Fleming & Daw only.

Both statements verified (EFE 'not simply free energy in the future' and natural version discourages exploration; AIF vs CAI value in prior vs likelihood, AIF keeps epistemic info gain CAI lacks), but all sources are one lab (Millidge, Tschantz, Buckley, Seth), so it is a single-group theoretical position.

Krishnamurthy et al. (one configuration works; >60% suffix failures with basic prompt, T=500, N=20) and EVOLvE Table 1 (MAB 45.5->60.0/59.6, CB 7.1->64.3) match; 'small Gemma models gain nothing' is slightly loose (Gemma-2B got a small gain from summarized history, none from algorithm-guided support).

CDE Table 1 (Qwen3-4B-Base GRPO vs PPL bonus: 20.8->23.3, 21.0->23.5, avg 48.2->50.6) matches; the curiosity-reward dialogue paper rewards user-model accuracy (never says 'information gain' explicitly) and reports no numbers checked here.

PUMA numbers (Qwen3-8B 1.62 vs 1.07, 75.9% vs 52.0%, DynPatient simulator), Prakki (no baseline) and Wen (conceptual) verified; but Dutta et al. Section 7 does include a no-question 'baseline' policy, so 'no plain-prompt baseline' is too strong; BED-LLM/K24 update not checked against any listed source.
fix: LLM-agent uses of active inference are weakly validated: Prakki 2025 reports no baseline comparison, Wen 2025 papers report no experiments; only PUMA (2026) reports measured gains in a simulator (Stage Lift 1.62 vs 1.07, Prep 75.9% vs 52.0%, Qwen3-8B vs DIIR). Dutta 2026 (2608.19202) is a framework paper with a dynamic-programming oracle comparison and a no-question baseline in its clarification experiment, but no direct with/without active-inference prompt comparison on the main question-asking task. (BED-LLM update not verified here.)

problem: Ambrose 2016 (only reverse replay rate follows reward change), Mattar & Daw 2018 (explains it via gain term), Pfeiffer & Foster 2013 (forward sequences to HOME well) and Sagiv et al. (value model is special case when a single goal dominates) all consistent; Sagiv quote is about the model reducing to Mattar and Daw, not an empirical 'wins' test.

Sagiv et al. says prioritized replay matters in data/compute-limited regimes and reduces to the value model when one goal predominates, but does not say goal-general replay pays off 'only' then; the HSL numbers (WebShop 63.81->66.97, ALFWorld unseen 78.36->97.76) are right, but the single-goal explanation is that paper's hedged 'likely', and the 'same boundary' analogy is the notes' own inference from one preprint.
fix: Goal-general replay is most useful when experience or replay is limited and goals recur or switch (Sagiv et al.). A hindsight-relabeling LLM paper (HSL) is loosely consistent: its WebShop gain is smaller (63.81 to 66.97), which the authors say is 'likely' because WebShop allows only one achievable goal per trajectory, vs ALFWorld unseen 78.36 to 97.76.

problem: Numbers verified (HSL 78.36->97.76 Llama-3.2-1B; AgentHER current abstract +7.6-11.4, v1 +7.1-11.7; ECHO up to 80% over ReAct in XMiniGrid avg reward, 34/40=85%), but 'All are training-time' contradicts the next sentence: ECHO is prompt-only with no weight updates.
fix: Hindsight relabeling for LLM agents (HSL, AgentHER, ECHO, SAC-GLAM) reuses a trajectory as a demonstration for other achieved goals: HSL ALFWorld unseen 78.36 to 97.76 (SFT vs SFT+HSL, 1B agent), AgentHER +7.6 to +11.4 pp over SFT-Success (current version; v1 said 7.1-11.7), ECHO up to 80% over a ReAct baseline in average reward. HSL, AgentHER and SAC-GLAM are training-time; ECHO is in-context (prompt-only, no weight updates) and 34 of 40 imputed workflows (85%) reached their goal. All are self-reported; no independent replication of HSL or AgentHER was found.

problem: Neighbours verified (sleep-time compute gain depends on query predictability; TraceRetain is value-scored eviction in frozen-agent memory); the absence claim itself cannot be verified and is already hedged as weak evidence.

Preplay numbers (62.39%, CI 53.99-69.53, p=0.0049; 62.80%) and Lampinen oracle-retrieval match; but the sleep-time ~5x saving is for a single query per context, and only the extra amortised 2.5x (t=10, cost-weighted) needs several queries sharing the context.
fix: Preplay of unpursued but accessible tasks is reflected in human behaviour (partial path reuse 62.39%, CI 53.99-69.53, vs 50% chance, p=0.0049; 62.80% in the shortcut experiment) and beats baselines in deep RL; latent learning fails in parametric systems without episodic retrieval (oracle retrieval helps). Sleep-time compute: about 5x less test-time compute at equal accuracy for a single query per context, a further average cost cut up to 2.5x when about 10 queries share the context, and the gain is larger when the query is more predictable from the context.

problem: ExpeL HotpotQA->FEVER transfer is ReAct 63 -> ExpeL Transfer 70 (Act 58); the 59.0 -> 64.2 figures are ExpeL+Reflexion on ALFWorld (R0 vs R3). AWM +51.1% relative and HippoRAG +11 R@2 on 2Wiki (59.2->70.7) are right; the 'none weights by future goal likelihood' part is an unverifiable absence claim.
fix: Goal-agnostic stored routes and workflows help LLM agents (Agent Workflow Memory +51.1% relative on WebArena; ExpeL transfer HotpotQA to FEVER 63 to 70% over ReAct; HippoRAG +11 R@2 on 2Wiki) but none found weights memories by likelihood of future goals.

problem: Russek et al.: SR-Dyna solves the detour task only with enough offline replay (else it degrades to SR-TD); Momennejad et al. bioRxiv Exp 1 N=58 and reward > transition revaluation (t(57)=2.89), but the means 0.52 and 0.45 appear nowhere in the text/legends (possibly only in Fig 4A), so they could not be confirmed; Piray & Daw not opened.
fix: Replay-based updating can repair transition (detour) changes that plain successor representations miss, provided enough offline replay (Russek et al. 2017); humans revalue more after a reward change than after a transition change (Momennejad et al. 2017, N=58, t(57)=2.89, p<0.01).

problem: PER beats uniform replay on 41 of 49 Atari games (abstract); HER paper text says 'future' with k=4 or 8 performs best among strategies.

Jiang et al. (54 of 56 experiments' p-values above 0.05; Table 2 caption has a typo) and Stechly et al. (graph colouring: 1 of 100 with self-critique vs nearly 40% with sound verifier) match; Stechly 2024 abstract also reports self-critique collapse.

All numbers match (SCoRe MATH +4.4, 5.8%/1.4%, base right-to-wrong 15.8%; HumanEval +12.2; Xiong 78.6 vs 76.8), but 'gain comes mostly from not breaking correct answers' holds only for MATH; on HumanEval the gain is mostly more wrong-to-right fixes (7.9%->15.2%), and Xiong's gain also comes from fixes (6.0 vs 0.2).
fix: Trained (not prompted) refinement can give a positive net gain: SCoRe MATH (Gemini 1.5 Flash) delta +4.4, wrong-to-right 5.8%, right-to-wrong 1.4% vs base 15.8%; HumanEval (Gemini 1.0 Pro) +12.2. On MATH the gain comes mostly from not breaking correct answers; on HumanEval it comes mostly from more wrong-to-right fixes. Xiong et al. (Qwen2.5-Math-7B) give a second group with a similar small gain (MATH500 78.6 vs 76.8 single-turn DPO, single greedy runs).

problem: Kumar et al. Table 1 (MATH) deltas are -14.2 to +1.8 (STaR -14.2, Pair-SFT +1.8), not -11 to +2 (-11.2 is the base model); failure modes (distribution shift, collapse to minor/no edits) match, but the paper argues on-policy data fixes shift while collapse needs SCoRe's two-stage design, and RISE (iterative on-policy fine-tuning, not RL) also reports gains, so 'on-policy multi-turn RL is needed' is too strong.
fix: Offline SFT or STaR on correction traces fails to give a gain on MATH (deltas -14.2 to +1.8 vs base -11.2) because of distribution shift and collapse to minor or no edits; Kumar et al. argue self-generated on-policy data is required and add a two-stage multi-turn RL design to avoid collapse (RISE reports gains with iterative on-policy fine-tuning).

problem: Zhang et al. Table 2 (GSM8K, LLaMA-2-13b-chat, SCORE refiner): self verifier contribution 10.8 vs GPT-4 verifier 15.6 match; 'self-trained verifier' is loose wording (the verifier is the model itself), and the other source (SelfCheck) does not address small models, so support is one paper.
Minor: Reflexion's tests are model-written, and 80% is a prior-reported GPT-4 baseline; 'external signal is the driver' is the authors' framing but matches the Rust ablation.
38% is measured for one model (PaLM 2-S revision model) in Snell et al.; SCoRe shows a different figure (15.8% right-to-wrong) for a different setup.

Three of four evidence lines are the one Self-Refine paper; the fourth (listed as 2404.17140) is a different paper (Zhang et al. small LMs need strong verifiers) that has no Self-Refine sentiment numbers. The sentiment (GPT-4) and math (GPT-3.5) figures also come from different models, so 'task type is the moderator' is one paper's cross-model comparison.

Lovett and Anderson set the Gaussian noise variance to 0.05 squared (0.0025, SD 0.05), not 0.052; the .99 and .66 R2 values, 68 subjects with 1 removed, and 90 problems check out (page says eight conditions, not four).
fix: People shift strategy by experience. Lovett and Anderson 1995 (N=67 analysed, 90 problems) found most chose the more successful strategy and overmatched, and a Bayesian-posterior ACT-R model with Gaussian noise variance 0.05^2 (SD 0.05) fit R2=.99 in aggregate but only .66 for individuals' last-45-problem selections. Xie and Moss 2025 (N=100) replicated the related Lovett and Schunn 1999 result. The 1996 journal paper was still not opened; the 'over 80% chose overshoot on problem 5' detail comes from a 2006 chapter.

problem: Sources confirm 0.5 convention (Taatgen), 0.491 fitted (Gray 2006) and alpha 0.759 / noise 0.440 for one participant (Stocco), but noise 0.440 is close to 0.5 and 0.491, so 'very different procedural model' is not supported for the noise; only alpha and the single-participant fit differ.
fix: Utility noise is a free parameter, not a constant: about 0.5 by convention in ACT-R, 0.491 fitted in Gray et al. 2006, and 0.440 (with learning rate alpha 0.759) in a single-participant likelihood fit in Stocco et al. 2024.

problem: Gall and Fruehwirth confirm ACT-R's difference-rule utility update with time-discounted shared reward; but 'neural work favours TD with eligibility traces' rests on one human ERP study (Walsh & Anderson 2011, from the ACT-R lab; its BIC comparison could not be re-opened because PMC blocked the full text), and Fu & Anderson 2004 shows ACT-R already has a TD extension.
fix: The ACT-R utility rule is a Rescorla-Wagner-style reinforcement learning update with credit for multi-step sequences handled by time-discounted shared reward; Fu and Anderson (2004) extended it with temporal-difference learning, and one human ERP study (Walsh and Anderson 2011) found TD models with eligibility traces fit best.

problem: Numbers check out (Claude v1.3 0.87 vs 0.10, GPT-3 horizon/descriptions results), but no source tests scaffold-kept success counts; the optimism bias is also reported only when the model chose the option itself (it reverses for foregone outcomes and vanishes when another agent chooses).
fix: LLMs learn with an optimism bias when they choose the option themselves: positive learning rate 0.87 vs negative 0.10 (Claude v1.3, 50 runs); the bias reverses for foregone outcomes and disappears when someone else chooses. GPT-3 was human-like on the short-horizon bandit but below human on decisions from descriptions. Whether success counts kept by a scaffold would avoid the bias is an untested hypothesis.

problem: Kaddour's 77% / 22% is a post-execution estimate (Gemini pre-execution mean 99%); Barkan shows predicted success stays above 0.5 but does fall with in-context failures, so 'do not recover' means 'stay overconfident'.

The 75% constant-confidence example is not literally in Fleming and Lau (they distinguish calibration/bias from discrimination/sensitivity and efficiency); it is a mathematically correct illustration.

Xiong et al. do report GSM8K AUROC 54.8 to 92.7 (5 samples with consistency vs Top-K verbalized), but that is the arithmetic best case (five-dataset average 56.4 to 73.0), and Kapoor et al. find sampling methods give good calibration but very weak discrimination on open-ended MMLU.
fix: Sampling consistency can be a strong confidence signal on arithmetic: in Xiong et al., 5 samples with consistency aggregation lifted GSM8K AUROC from 54.8% to 92.7% (five-dataset average about 56.4% to 73.0%), while Kapoor et al. find sampling-based methods discriminate weakly on open-ended MMLU. It costs extra samples, so it must be compared at equal tokens.

problem: Kapoor et al. say prompted-method ECE does not improve with base model quality but AUROC does improve slightly, the gap to fine-tuning stays large versus their worst fine-tuned model, and verbal elicitation is on par with weaker fine-tuning methods in discrimination; 'not usable by a scaffold with no training' is the researcher's inference, not a finding.
fix: Fine-tuned or probed confidence beats prompted confidence (Kapoor et al.): prompted-method ECE does not improve with base model quality, AUROC improves only slightly, and zero-shot prompting stays well behind their worst fine-tuned model (LLaMA-2 7B). A scaffold without training would be limited to prompted or sampled confidence (inference, not a measured result).

problem: Tian numbers match one table (TriviaQA 0.140 / 0.068 / 0.050); Xiong says white-box methods are better with a narrow gap, so 'close' is fair; the two papers pull in slightly different directions.

Dai and Wang numbers match (Top-3 78.2-92.1%, M-ratio 0.62-0.92), but Yoon et al. show the AUROC rise comes from REMOVING epistemic markers (the model then uses only two bins, 95% and 65%, so ECE worsens 0.042 to 0.109 while AUROC rises 0.782 to 0.837), not from epistemic markers coarsening confidence.
fix: Coarse scale choice hurts measurement: the three most frequent values hold 78.2 to 92.1% of 0-100 answers; baseline M-ratio ranges 0.62 to 0.92. AUROC can rise while ECE worsens when confidence is coarsened: in Yoon et al., removing epistemic markers pushed the model onto two bins (95% and 65%), so ECE went 0.042 to 0.109 while AUROC went 0.782 to 0.837 on TriviaQA.

problem: Kumaran et al. reported in the same paper (four evidence lines are one source); only Prasad and Nguyen is a second independent paper, and it supports just the debate-confidence clause.

Numbers are real but come from specific methods: ECE 46.94 to 25.49 with AUROC 65.71 to 61.20 is Wang et al.'s supervised CalibSFT alone (their confidence-aware RL then lifts OOD AUROC to over 71%), and Xuan et al.'s CAR raises AUROC in the main Table 2 (up to 17% relative); it lowers AUROC only in the Serper-API transfer test (Qwen2.5-7B 0.831 to 0.790, Qwen3-4B 0.825 to 0.765).
fix: Calibration training can lower ECE without raising AUROC, and the gain may not transfer: in Wang et al., supervised CalibSFT alone cut OOD ECE from 46.94 to 25.49 while OOD AUROC fell from 65.71 to 61.20 (confidence-aware RL later restored it above 71%); in Xuan et al., CAR lowers ECE and raises AUROC in the main tests but lowers AUROC in the real-API transfer test (Qwen2.5-7B 0.831 to 0.790, Qwen3-4B 0.825 to 0.765). Off-the-shelf reasoning models put their verbalized confidence on a few high values (fewer than 5% of responses below 0.5, 70-90% on fewer than 7 values).

problem: Absence of a single criterion is an inference: Veale et al. say Fauconnier and Turner give five non-orthogonal optimality constraints, and Turner's page says evidence is mostly in-sample generalisation tested out of sample while experiments (McCubbins and Turner 2013) exist but are hard.
The 56% smoked paprika figure is for GPT-4o asked for a general creative recipe, not a recipe merge (merges show fixation separately); 0.459 vs 0.738 is the v3 value.
The 75% agreement is on unanimous items only (panel majority agrees with humans 66% overall, n=96 on unanimous); ICC bands are 'fair to good' by Cicchetti.
Absence claim ('effect sizes unknown') cannot be proven by these sources; they do show LLM-panel judging (Schapiro, Lu), image tasks (Peng) and lay Prolific humans (Schapiro, N=75).
Peeperkorn calls the coherence relation with temperature 'moderate' (.240) and the novelty one 'weak' (.308); Terwiesch: GPT-4o diversity 0.618 (T=0) to 0.679 (T=1), nonsensical above 1.0, matching.

The 96.8 / 79.9 / 75.4% win rates are real but belong to MCTS-IR-E, informed rollouts guided by a static state evaluation (no minimax), against random-rollout MCTS-Solver; the paper itself says adding shallow searches into rollouts did not improve MCTS-IR, so these numbers do not show that a shallow minimax hybrid repairs trap blindness or that trap density drives the gain (hybrid vs alpha-beta win rates are 66.9% Breakthrough, 17.4% Catch the Lion, 26.9% Othello).
fix: MCTS is more susceptible to shallow traps than alpha-beta (Baier and Winands 2018; Ramanujan et al.). Evaluation-guided informed rollouts (MCTS-IR-E, no minimax) beat random-rollout MCTS-Solver at 96.8% in Catch the Lion, 79.9% in Othello and 75.4% in Breakthrough, so playout value matters; whether shallow-minimax hybrids specifically repair trap blindness is shown by the paper's separate hybrid experiments, not by these figures.

problem: Three evidence lines are the same Coquelin and Munos paper (arXiv cs/0703062 and its 2014 re-upload 1408.2028, UAI 2007) and the fourth is a Wikipedia page with no numbers. Content check: the paper does give a double-exponential bound with 10^156837 at D=20 for the square-root confidence sequence and a D-1 composed-exponential bound for the usual log sequence, so the 10^156837 figure belongs to the sqrt variant, not standard UCT.

Silver et al. show AlphaZero defeating Stockfish, but Baier and Winands (2018) say that regardless of the state evaluator MCTS remains more susceptible to traps than alpha-beta; the conclusion that the limit is value-model quality rather than the search loop is an inference, and the Feng et al. line (Game24 15.5 vs 19.1) is about LLM decoding, not chess.
fix: A learned policy/value network lets MCTS beat Stockfish (AlphaZero), so evaluator quality matters a great deal for chess-like games; Baier and Winands note deep RL evaluators seem to avoid traps well, yet MCTS stays more trap-susceptible than alpha-beta whatever the evaluator, so the weakness is reduced, not shown to be removed.

problem: Wu et al. (MATH, REBASE vs MCTS vs sampling) is a different task family and only supports the general direction; the ARC and code numbers all come from Inoue et al. (AB-MCTS), whose table matches exactly.
Stroebl et al. give the false-positive ceiling and optimal K often under 10 (K about 5 in Figure 4); Brown et al. support only the general plateau/false-positive point.

Qwen team confirm MC-estimation PRMs are significantly worse than LLM-as-judge and human-label PRMs, but in rStar the 24% is the share of RAP trajectories (LLaMA2-7B, GSM8K, 32 rounds) that are correct, a measure of generation quality, not the share judged correct by prompted self-evaluation; rStar separately says small models struggle to tell which steps or answers are right, without that number.
fix: Monte Carlo step-value labels are noisy (right answers can come from wrong steps), and PRMs trained on them did significantly worse than ones trained on LLM-as-judge or human labels (Qwen team). Prompted self-exploration with small models is also weak: after 32 RAP rounds only 24% of LLaMA2-7B trajectories on GSM8K are correct, and rStar reports small models have difficulty telling which steps or final answers are correct.

problem: Zhang et al. say extra search compute 'does not reliably improve' / 'does not necessarily yield' optimal plans, not that it never does; the sources are otherwise exact (tight MCTS row, RAP(20) 1.00/0.88/0.42).
fix: LLM tree planners degrade steeply with plan length: MCTS success under tight budget 1.00, 0.92, 0.50, 0.11, 0.05, 0.00 for L=2..12; RAP Blocksworld LLaMA-33B 1.00/0.88/0.42 for 2/4/6 steps at 20 iterations; extra expansions do not reliably yield optimal plans.

problem: Mancala c=2.5 and unfocused small-c tree are confirmed (single domain), but 'no safe default' and 'smoothness constants unknown for language' are not stated by Ramanujan-Selman or Coquelin-Munos (BAST just needs smoothness coefficients known/assumed); b06 and c03 are the same paper.
fix: UCT exploration constant matters: in Mancala c=2.5 was best, c=20 gave a minimax-like tree and small c an unfocused tree with weak play; the bound-based fix (BAST) requires smoothness coefficients to be known or assumed.

problem: Wang et al. show majority voting beating revision and mixture-of-agents only for reasoning models; for non-reasoning models (Llama-3.3-70B) external search occasionally surpasses majority voting, so the unqualified wording is too wide.
fix: Sampling accuracy saturates at a fixed limit set by the model's own output probabilities (Wu et al.); non-reasoning models hit a 'reasoning floor' that more inference compute does not lift, and among reasoning models, verifier-free simple majority voting beats sequential revision and mixture-of-agents (Wang et al.).

problem: Game of 24 numbers match Stechly et al. (5%, 3%, 36-38%, 42%), but LLM critique raised Blocksworld accuracy (40% to 55%), the 'shallow exhaustive code check vs LLM check' sentence is not in either source, and Zhao et al. show LLM self-verification at scale (Verification@200) beating majority voting and o1-Preview.
fix: In Stechly et al.'s GPT-4 tests, an LLM self-critique loop lowered accuracy on Game of 24 (5% to 3%) and Graph Coloring (16% to 2%) but not Blocksworld (40% to 55%), while a sound external verifier raised Game of 24 to 36-38% and plain k=25 sampling reached 42%; LLM self-verification can help when scaled over many samples (Zhao et al.).

problem: The 100-token PRM suffix (>0.9), 43% style share and 35-90% judge false positives are confirmed, but 'patching one family fixed that family only' is not supported: Zhao et al. report Master-RM, trained with a small share of adversarial negatives, has near-0% false positives across all tested attacks.
fix: Search against a learned evaluator has exploitable blind spots: optimized 100-token suffixes lift PRM reward above 0.9 on flawed reasoning, 43% of an RL reward gain is stylistic, and judge false positives reach up to 35% (punctuation, GPT-4o) and 60-90% ('Thought process:', open 70B+ models) under master keys; a judge trained with adversarial negatives (Master-RM) reached near-0% on the tested attacks.

problem: ReSCALE numbers (53.6/58.4/53.4) are exact, but SC-MCTS* only says the default C=1 led to 'potential failures'; the +5.27 is one ablation step (pseudo-random-reward base, Blocksworld step 6 hard mode), not evidence that default C=1 'failed'; 'decide whether more budget helps' is broader than either paper.
fix: AlphaZero-style LLM tree search declines at the largest budget on GSM8K (53.6%, below ReSCALE 58.4% and just above Best-of-N 53.4%), and in an SC-MCTS* ablation on Blocksworld (step 6, hard mode) tuning the UCT constant away from the commonly used default of 1 added 5.27 points.

problem: 'Turned DPLL into an industrial tool' is a narrative gloss only weakly supported (Wikipedia says CDCL made solvers powerful for real-world applications, tagged citation needed); Chaff's one-to-two-orders speed-up over GRASP/SATO and its engineering credit are exact.

G4SATBench findings are accurate (b09 and b10 are the same paper), but the general claim ignores that the original NeuroSAT paper reports generalisation to larger problems (25% of satisfiable SR(200)) and new domains by running more iterations, and G4SATBench says SR-trained models generalise better.
fix: G4SATBench finds that NeuroSAT and GGNN struggle to generalise across distributions in most cases and show limited generalisation to larger formulas (better when trained on SR), and that GNNs learn a heuristic akin to greedy local search and fail to learn the CDCL heuristic; the original NeuroSAT paper reported more favourable transfer to larger problems when run for more iterations.

problem: Totals 1281-1291 vs 1269 verified; the AESAT paper has no parameter-tuning baseline (no tuning/SMAC mention found).
Table columns garbled in text extraction but row values match (o1-full 81.0; Llama-3.1-405B large 1.5, X-large 0.0 with overall 32.6; GPT-4o majority 38.0 at N=32 from 31.7, oracle 60.3).
o4-mini puzzle 89.4 here vs 89.3 overall elsewhere in SATBench (rounding).

Lehman and Stanley found coarse behaviour grids barely hurt (except 4x4), which is a different setting from Kistemaker's supercell result; claim numbers (21/70, 29/70, 6/70, cell size vs mutation range) match Kistemaker.
Enhanced POET plateau comparison is against original POET (ANNECS plateau after ~20,000 iterations), not a no-archive control; HGM re-run shows DGM improves but is beaten by HGM.

Panickssery et al. report GPT-4 is 73.5% accurate at distinguishing its own summaries from other LLMs' and humans' (self-recognition), not that it picks its own text 73.5% of the time; the other numbers (72.7%, 92.2%, 0.833 vs 0.800, 61.1-71.4%) match.
fix: The judges used in LLM open-endedness systems are only moderately reliable: OMNI-EPIC success detector 72.7% agreement with 50 humans; ACD 92.2% of tasks valid; QDAIF human-AI agreement 0.833 vs human-human 0.800. Self-judging adds bias: GPT-4 is 73.5% accurate at recognising its own summaries and self-preference strength is linearly correlated with self-recognition; pairwise LLM judging reaches 61-71% on paper acceptance; judge-human agreement is lowest on similar-quality items.

problem: The sources compare goal-only RL with goal plus novelty/rarity bonuses (Song et al.: bonus needs a baseline, naive UCB did not help test performance; He et al.: GRPO sharpens and underperforms base sampling at large N; Yue et al.: base beats RL at large k), but none tests novelty-only RL, so 'beats either alone' is wider than the evidence.
fix: Adding a novelty bonus to goal-only LLM RL can help: an answer-novelty bonus needed a baseline to improve test pass@k (naive UCB did not), and rewarding rare-but-correct proofs raised pass@N where goal-only GRPO sharpened and lost to base sampling at large N; goal-only RL narrows coverage (base beats RL at large k, e.g. 128-256). Novelty-only LLM RL and adaptive-weight rules (as in NSRA-ES) were not tested in these sources.

problem: ExpeL ablation table columns are garbled in extraction but values 40.0/48.5/42.5/59.0 are consistent; Memento K=4 best is on DeepResearcher average F1 (64.5 vs 63.9-64.1 for larger K).
Table 1 of Huang et al. checked; gap-search statements match Kamoi, CorrectBench, Tsui.
Tsui's 14 models are open non-reasoning models (reasoning models show a small or negative blind spot); the 23.53%/11.11% figures use an oracle mistake location and PaLM 2 traces.

Zhang et al.'s abstract says GPT-5.4 'fails on 54%' but the body (intro and results) says accuracy fell from 100% to 54% on a 19-problem slice, i.e. it failed on 46%; the claim repeats the abstract's misstatement.
fix: Memory pollution and drift: online AWM workflows from unverified trajectories can degrade results, and add-all memory with a weak evaluator is flat or declining. Gap search: LLM consolidation itself erodes memory (GPT-5.4 dropped from 100% to 54% accuracy, i.e. failed 46% of a 19-problem ARC-AGI slice it solved without memory), and history-based deletion with a reliable evaluator helps.

problem: The arXiv link cs/0003051 given as 'Reiter (1987)' is actually Wassermann's 'Local Diagnosis' (it restates Reiter's definitions and the okY/okZ example); the theorem itself is confirmed by Wassermann, Pill et al. and Rodler.

Greiner et al. say the pruning rule applies only when some conflict is a strict superset of another, and the loss occurs when a smaller conflict is found after a larger one was used to label a node; the claim states the direction backwards ('a superset of a conflict seen earlier'). The LLM-contradictions-are-non-minimal part is flagged as inference and is not in the sources.
fix: The bug only bites when conflicts are non-minimal, i.e. when the conflict finder returns a conflict that is a proper subset of one already used to label a node (a smaller conflict arriving after a larger one); whether LLM-produced contradictions are often non-minimal is an unmeasured inference.

problem: The HER2+.SHORT counts, NP-completeness and depth-limit remarks all come from one survey (Gainer-Dewar and Vera-Licona; a06, a07, b04 are the same paper); Rodler independently supports only the hardness side.

Sources show ENT, SPL and MPS (most probable singleton) perform comparably (median savings 50/52/52%, not significantly different), so entropy/split are not shown to work 'best'; the 50/52/52% figures are DynamicHS runtime savings over HS-Tree, not a comparison among selection rules.
fix: In sequential diagnosis, queries chosen by entropy, split-in-half or most-probable-singleton heuristics all narrow diagnoses and gave similar DynamicHS median runtime savings over HS-Tree (50/52/52%); in ontology debugging, entropy-based query selection needed significantly fewer queries than split-in-half.

problem: Minor: 20.7% is an average over 11 models, not a single best score.

The 1989 paper says no experiment exceeded 220 cycles but also reports 402 cycles for the large Hamlet/Macbeth network, so 'max 220' is wrong; also all substantive sources are Holyoak and Thagard (same lab) plus Wikipedia.
fix: Analogical mapping is guided by three soft pressures at once (structural isomorphism, semantic similarity, pragmatic purpose), not a hard structural rule; Holyoak and Thagard's ACME constraint-satisfaction network usually settles in well under 100 cycles, with 220 cycles the most in their main examples and 402 cycles for the largest network (Hamlet/Macbeth, 730 units).

problem: Single study (the two paper entries are the same source; PAM is only context); numbers match the paper.
Numbers match; all sources are the same lab (Holyoak/Spellman), as the claim itself states.
ARCS PDF is an unreadable scan and the 38% column is garbled in OCR of Table 5; other numbers (69/33/13, Keane 88/12/86) match; sources are largely one lab.
StoryAnalogy human figure 85.7% not on abstract page (abstract says over 85%); other numbers match.
The 0.966/0.398 gzip rates are for Audio-8bit data in Yoran et al., not for K estimates of arbitrary strings; the 50-symbol limit comes from Gauvrit et al.
Table columns scrambled in PDF extraction; abstract-level 43.4%/16.4% and 21.9% adjusted confirmed, non-text adjusted rates 185.3/228.9/224.7 appear in the table.
K5 is a Coding Theorem Method estimate, not K itself.

ESTAR GPQA retention table is garbled in extraction (values seen 98.9-100.2%, one row 98.4%); the cross-method inference that the OOD drop is specific to CaRT is the researcher's hedged interpretation, not from the sources.
Chen's >92% is the paper's aggregate statement; its figure shows some set-model bars near 89-90%.
LYNX trains a hidden-state probe with conformal calibration, so it is not training-free; the sources do not call it training-free or answer-based. DEER, Answer Consistency and EAT numbers match.
fix: Training-free answer-based early exit saves large token shares with equal or slightly higher accuracy: DEER cuts CoT 19.1-80.1% with +0.3 to +5.0 accuracy over 11 models; Answer Consistency cuts over 40% of tokens on NQ; EAT 12-22% with no accuracy harm. A probe-based method that needs training (LYNX) reaches 35-70% fewer tokens with matched or better accuracy.

problem: Zhang et al. abstract stresses probes generalize to some OOD sets; the degradation OOD is in their section 4.3 (math to knowledge domain) and in thought calibration (60% to 20%).
Minor: DEER's appendix says averaging reduces false-positive probability but does not remove its dependence on noise, so 'does not fix' is slightly loose.
MediQ numbers match, but QuestBench's 80-90% vs 40-50% are question-selection accuracies on math (GSM-Q/GSME-Q) versus Logic-Q/Planning-Q, not solving versus finding the missing variable.
fix: Question-asking agents need a stop-asking rule: plain prompting to ask makes models worse than answering from initial info (MediQ); an abstention module gives +22.3% over basic interactive and +12.1% over non-interactive, still 10.3% below full info. QuestBench: models identify the right clarification question with over 80% accuracy on math tasks but only 40-50% on Logic-Q and Planning-Q, and struggle to pick the right question even when they can solve the fully specified problem.

problem: Abstract says selective generation improves the correct fraction among answered by 2-10% (en dash), not 210%; the second listed source (MediQ) does not address context sufficiency.
fix: Context sufficiency is a separate skill from answering: large models (Gemini 1.5 Pro, GPT-4o, Claude 3.5) answer well when context is sufficient but often answer wrongly instead of abstaining when it is not, while smaller models (Mistral 3, Gemma 2) hallucinate or abstain often even with sufficient context; sufficiency-guided selective generation raises the fraction of correct answers among those answered by 2-10% for Gemini, GPT and Gemma.

problem: The 21/29 eventual-solver figure is not stated in Wason's original text (it gives 6 first-time, 13 one-wrong, 9 two-plus, 1 none) and comes from Jhaveri et al.; 'replicated across many studies' is from Klayman and Ha's review.

Klayman and Ha show positive tests can also falsify when the hypothesized set merely overlaps or is disjoint from the true rule, not only when it is broader; positive tests fail only when the hypothesis is a strict subset of the rule.
fix: Positive testing is a general heuristic, not irrational by itself: a positive test can falsify a hypothesis when the hypothesis is broader than, overlaps, or is disjoint from the true rule, but it can never falsify when the hypothesis is a strict subset (narrower) of the true rule, where only negative tests can. Whether a test is informative depends on that set relation.

problem: Minor: Branchini control baseline was 36.7% not 20%; 20% baseline comes from Gale and Ball; Gorman abstract gives no rates.

SEP says Miller and Tichy showed in 1974 that Popper's verisimilitude definition is formally defective for false theories and Popper conceded the mistake but kept the concept as heuristic; Duhem-Quine is not named (Putnam and Lakatos are); the 'philosophers judged unworkable' line is not in the SEP pages; a03-a06 are all one SEP entry.
fix: Philosophically, falsification is never fully mechanical: Popper says acceptance of basic statements rests on a decision or agreement (like a jury verdict); a failed prediction does not show which assumption is at fault (Putnam; Lakatos's protective belt); and Miller and Tichy showed in 1974 that Popper's definition of verisimilitude is formally defective for false theories, which Popper partly conceded. Oaksford and Chater (1994) state that philosophers regarded strict falsificationism as unworkable.

problem: Neither listed source (Mayo abstracts, SEP Popper) contains the 44% vs 96% Registered Reports figures; they come from Scheel et al. (2021), which I confirmed (71 vs 152) but which is not in the evidence; Mayo PDF text was unreadable; 'change outcomes' is a causal reading of a between-paper-type comparison.
fix: Registered Reports in psychology reported a positive result for 44% of first hypotheses vs 96% in standard reports (N=71 vs 152; Scheel et al. 2021), a gap consistent with publication bias in standard papers when tests are not pre-committed. Mayo's minimal severity rule: a claim has not passed a severe test if little has been done to rule out flaws in taking the data as evidence for it.

problem: Minor: SWE-Mutation was read from a benchmark-list summary page, not the paper; the Mayo-severity link is the researcher's interpretation.
Jaynes PDF unreadable via fetch; Wikipedia and Drory confirm. Note Jaynes himself argued invariance selects 1/2, so 'no single answer' holds only absent a specified sampling process.

Haldane/Jeffreys/uniform forms and 4/5 rule of succession check out, and Jeffreys is reparameterisation-invariant, but the sources do not support calling it 'the default': Jaynes 1968 argues for 1/(t(1-t)) for total ignorance and Gelman et al. say no default prior is safe independent of the likelihood.
fix: For an unknown pass rate, the choice among Haldane (1/(t(1-t))), Jeffreys Beta(1/2,1/2) and uniform Beta(1,1) changes early estimates (the rule of succession gives 4/5 after 3 successes under uniform). Jeffreys is the choice that is invariant under reparameterisation, but Jaynes argues for Haldane as the ignorance prior and Gelman, Simpson and Betancourt argue that no default is safe without checking its implications for the likelihood.

problem: Minor: Gelman et al. posterior sd/99.2%/N(0,0.005) mean 0.002 verified in PDF text; the example concerns a sex-ratio survey and the claim omits that context.

Numbers 6/5/2 of 11 verified in Selby et al., but that is the only supporting paper (b19 and c07 are the same paper; AutoElicit does not address leakage), and dataset recognition shows possible contamination, not that scores were inflated.
fix: In Selby et al. (2025), given a single row, GPT-3.5 recognised 6 of 11 datasets, Gemini 1.5 Pro 5 and Llama 2 70B 2, so data leakage is a possible contaminant of tests of LLM prior knowledge (single study; inflation of scores not shown).

problem: Arora et al. find that on toy GPT-2/GINC models SFT mostly shifts the task prior while DPO also disrupts task knowledge; the real-model (Llama 3.1) evidence is inferred from fitted parameters and the authors say they do not claim LLMs are Bayesian learners; Xie et al. support only the in-context mixture framing.
fix: Bayesian scaling laws (Arora et al. 2025) find that in toy models SFT mostly shifts the model's task prior rather than its task knowledge (DPO also disturbs task knowledge), and fitted parameters on Llama 3.1 8B Base vs Instruct are read as further, non-conclusive evidence of the same; Xie et al. (2022) frame in-context learning as implicit Bayesian inference over a pretraining mixture of latent concepts with a prior.

problem: LP 'both' value and Belnap's four values are real, and Allen et al. use a bilateral (verify/refute) record, but no source calls this cheap: Allen et al. report macro-F1 +0.062 at a coverage cost of -0.456, and a14/b10 are the same paper.
fix: LP-style 'both' (glut) values and Belnap's four values let a record keep evidence for and against a claim separately instead of a single truth value; in Allen et al. (2025) a bilateral verify/refute judge raised macro-F1 by about 0.06 but lowered coverage by about 0.46, so it is not free.

problem: 53.7% (22 of 41) verified in Alxatib and Pelletier, but that means about half, not that gap and glut answers come from the same people; the Egre et al. 37% figure could not be opened (HAL blocked; abstract found says 'neither' is preferred to 'and', i.e. gaps over gluts); a11 and b02 are one paper.
fix: In Alxatib and Pelletier (2011), 53.7% (22 of 41) of those who judged 'neither tall nor not tall' true of the 5'11 man also judged 'tall and not tall' true, so gap and glut answers often come from the same people; Egre et al. report that 'neither' descriptions are nonetheless preferred to 'and' descriptions.

problem: Minor: WikiContradict figures (2.1-10.4% no cue; 10.4-43.8% with cue) verified in PDF table, PCBench 4.0-40.5% and 53.5-77.9% verified in paper; WikiContradict measures answers that reflect both passages, not noticing as such.
ContraDoc numbers verified in the paper (50.1/53.8/52.0/50.5%; GPT-4 recall 8.0% at 97% precision; top-5 evidence hit 70.2%); b17 and b18 are one paper.
