Minor: Gokul et al. figures (0.006-0.456 self-contradiction, 0.893 pair, high precision/lower recall) verified in PDF text on a synthetic dataset; 'precision above 0.9' not individually checked per model; ECon (high precision, weaker-model low recall) only partly corroborates.

Minor: 3.90 is the o3-mini proactive cost ratio on the easy subset in PCBench Table 2; the R1 'deliberated then silently used one side' is a single case study, not a rate; Fan et al. say reasoning models are slow to recognise the missing premise rather than never doing so.

Han et al. numbers (11.4-25.2%, mean 18.6%, gap 11.1, 920 per model, six 4B-14B models) verified; but the ECon '0.4-2.8 F1' comes only from the first dataset column of Table 16 and 2.8 is Mixtral, not a strong LLM (strong models there move 0.4-1.8); other columns of the table show drops of about 3-6 points.
fix: LLM conflict adjudication is order sensitive: reversing two contradictory documents flips the answer for 11.4-25.2% of items (mean 18.6%, accuracy gap 11.1 points, 920 paired predictions per model, six 4B-14B open models). Conflict detection in ECon changes less on the first dataset (about 0.4-1.8 F1 points for Claude 3 Sonnet, Llama-3 70B, GPT-4 and Llama-3 8B), but the paper says most detectors are order sensitive and larger drops appear in other columns of its Table 16.

problem: ECon 24%/38% chance and PCBench R1/o3-mini token numbers and 4.0-40.5% unprompted range are correct, but instructed critique rates across PCBench models range 53.5-77.9%, not 67.7-77.9% (e.g. Qwen3-8B-thinking 57.2, Llama-4/others 53.5-61.8).
fix: Unprompted LLMs often silently choose a side in conflicts (ECon: 24% of Sonnet and 38% of Haiku responses resolve by chance; PCBench unprompted premise critique 4.0-40.5%). An explicit premise-check instruction raises reporting to 53.5-77.9% across PCBench models (R1 67.7%, Gemini-2.0-flash-thinking 77.9%) and for some reasoning models cuts tokens (R1 2590 to 1014; o3-mini 1279 to 1023 on the easy set).

problem: All three supporting evidence lines (Woods-Walton, Walton, pragma-dialectics) are the same SEP Fallacies page; the Singh line does not address dialogue types. SEP also says Walton held the illicit-shift idea 'at one point' and later moved to other explanations, and does not state the 'sound in one dialogue type, fallacy in another' point (only that fallacies have sound counterparts under strategic maneuvering).

Jin (22.72-27.23 on LOGICCLIMATE) and Sourati (coarse 46.6/57.3, fine ~24) are right, but the CoCoLoFa numbers are misread: 0.05 is CoCoLoFa-trained BERT vs Reddit-trained BERT on Reddit (0.63 vs 0.68), 0.13 is Reddit-trained BERT vs CoCoLoFa-trained on CoCoLoFa (0.73 vs 0.86), and 0.19/0.09 are classification F1 deficits of CoCoLoFa-trained BERT/NLI vs Reddit-trained on Reddit, not scores on CoCoLoFa; the paper says CoCoLoFa-trained models generalize better.
fix: Fallacy detectors transfer poorly across datasets: on LOGICCLIMATE zero-shot transfer F1 is 22.72-27.23 (Jin), coarse 46.6-57.3 and fine about 24 (Sourati); in CoCoLoFa, BERT trained on Reddit scores 0.13 F1 below CoCoLoFa-trained BERT on CoCoLoFa (0.73 vs 0.86), while CoCoLoFa-trained BERT is only 0.05 below Reddit-trained BERT on Reddit detection (and 0.19 and 0.09 F1 lower for BERT and NLI in classification).

problem: Minor: 'valid class' is the native valid class; 16.6/58.9, 28% of 203 spans and level-2 0.093-0.144 per-annotator-as-gold all match, but the 58.9% comes from Singh's constructed matched negatives (single paper).

83.20 is the T5-3B score on Reddit, not Argotario; on Argotario GPT-4 (78.94) beats T5-3B (69.13) and T5-large (65.65). Other numbers (Reddit 79.10 vs 80.42, MAFALDA 48.38-49.78, Jeong LOGIC macro-F1 0.28) are right.
fix: Zero-shot single-round GPT-4 beats fine-tuned T5 on Argotario (78.94 vs 69.13 for T5-3B) and is close on Reddit (79.10 vs 83.20 for T5-3B and 80.42 for T5-large), but is far lower on harder ones (MAFALDA about 49 macro-F1; LOGIC 0.28 macro-F1 in Jeong et al.). Performance depends strongly on dataset.

problem: Pan GPT-4 MAFALDA 48.38/49.78 and MAFALDA GPT-3.5 0.627/0.201/0.138 vs human 0.749/0.352/0.186 verified (human figure is a 20-text sample by 4 annotators); Pan and MAFALDA are independent.

Lei & Huang GPT-3.5 accuracy (Reddit 65.29 to 70.76, LOGIC 42.28 to 47.99), Llama-2 LOGIC 69.36 to 74.16 and Jin Electra-StructAware +5.46 F1 all match; the Jin gain is a different method (logical-form hypothesis), not the tree.
Minor: Talk2AI percentages are quip-level detections by a classifier.

Lim & Perrault (95 of 780 None; accuracy 0.79 to 0.90), Xu (nine models, high FPR and near-zero FNR) and Singh (16.6% vs 58.9%) check out, but Xu does not show that adding a Prolog rule lifted classes: the starred rows in its Figure 3 are the SmartyPat-Bench-Augmented dataset (Prolog-generated, more explicit fallacy sentences), a different benchmark rather than a rule given to the model.
fix: LLM fallacy detectors give many unidentified outputs and false positives: GPT-4 returned None for 95 of 780 items (accuracy 0.79 rising to 0.90 after removing them); all nine models in Xu et al. show high false-positive and near-zero false-negative rates (accuracy is higher on the Prolog-generated, more explicit SmartyPat-Bench-Augmented set). Gap search: published false-positive rates are low mainly because the valid class holds few sound arguments that look like fallacies; scheme-matched sound arguments were flagged 58.9% (vs 16.6% native) by a fine-tuned encoder.

problem: RuozhiBench numbers (best model Claude-3-haiku 62% vs humans above 90%, 677 questions, 17 LLMs) are right but rest on one paper listed three times; DeflectBench measures refusal to generate fallacies (about 100 points across frames, over 80 across fallacy types within explicit framings), which does not show that fallacy-trap sets are hard for LLMs.
fix: Fallacy-trap questions are hard for LLMs: on RuozhiBench (677 questions, 17 LLMs) the best model scores 62% against humans above 90%. Separately, in DeflectBench (generating deflection fallacies) refusal depends on request framing: one prompt-frame change swings within-model refusal by nearly 100 points and changing the fallacy type by over 80 points.

problem: GPT-4 25% overall is stated in the later Mitchell et al. paper (2311.09247), not in the original ConceptARC table; ARC open-QA 0.119 is on the ARC-T text subset.

The final sentence (best representation depends on model type, pixel canvas for vision models, so no single rewrite step is robust) is not shown by VARC (one vision model trained from scratch, no cross-representation comparison).
fix: Part of the gap is representation: an object-based representation raises GPT-4 on the simplest ARC tasks from 13/50 to 23/50, and giving GPT-4 code execution removes the significant gap to humans on letter-string tasks (P=0.496). A vision-only model (VARC) using a pixel canvas reaches 54.5-60.4% on ARC-1, suggesting representation matters, but no source compares representations across model types.

problem: Human accuracy staying flat was tested only for the permuted-alphabet letter-string tasks (Lewis and Mitchell); Wu et al. (base, orientation) tested no humans, and indeed discuss that humans may also do worse under unfamiliar conditions.
fix: Counterfactual variants of letter-string analogies (permuted alphabets) lower LLM accuracy while human accuracy stays roughly flat (Lewis and Mitchell), and counterfactual tasks with changed base or code orientation also reduce LLM performance (Wu et al., no human comparison); early claims of emergent analogical reasoning in GPT-3 were not robust to these variants.

problem: Numbers are correct, but three of the four evidence lines are the same Akyurek et al. paper and the fourth (Li et al.) only repeats the 61.9% figure from it, so there is a single independent source.

The ~40% single-method figures are private/Kaggle leaderboard scores (Chollet et al.) while 56.75% is Li et al.'s ensemble on the public validation set, so they are not one like-for-like comparison; Li's own validation singles are about 35% (induction) and 43-57% (transduction).
fix: Induction (program writing) and transduction (direct answer) solve substantially different ARC tasks; the best single induction-only and transduction-only Kaggle submissions each score around 40% on the private set, and Li et al.'s ensemble of both reaches 56.75% on the public validation set (2 tries), so combining them beats either alone.

problem: Numbers check out (o3-medium 53.0 vs 3.0; NVARC 24.03%; Gemini 3 Pro harness 31% to 54% at $0.81 to $31), but both papers are by the same ARC Prize authors, so there is one independent source; also 'near saturated' is the authors' framing, not a measured result.
Minor: Mistral-Large-2 one-shot is 2.5% (not 1-2%) and GPT-4.1 in the 36-45% range is a closed model; 52% is SOAR's best, not the best of all ARC-AGI-1 systems.
Meta-analysis also reports a significant n-back-specific effect (g=0.15) vs treated controls; 'not replicated' is the overall picture, not every replication.
Each half rests on one paper (inverse scaling: Gema et al.; Raven text items: NeuroCognition); the R1 70% to 30% result is on the Misleading Math distractor-counting task, not Zebra.
Neither page is the 1976 paper itself (Cognito is a study-note summary naming 'Wood et al.'); critics-say-partly-alike is the reviewer's implication in Stone, not an explicit statement.

g=0.46 (144 studies, 333 outcomes), g=0.385 and the 2017 no-fading-effect finding are confirmed, but both meta-analyses are by the same Belland/Walker/Kim group, and no listed source mentions a 2014 preliminary version finding adaptive fading better.
UCO reports answer leakage of 35.2% for GPT-4o (33.1% is its solve rate), 46.6% for DeepSeek-V3 and 61.0% for Qwen2.5-72B, not 33-35% for large general models.
fix: Strong problem solvers are poor scaffolders and stock LLMs leak answers: Qwen2.5-Math-7B scores 0.88-0.91 on problem solving but only 0.06 win rate on scaffolding generation (MathTutorBench); large general models leak the solution in 35-61% of tutoring dialogues in UCO (GPT-4o 35.2%, DeepSeek-V3 46.6%, Qwen2.5-72B 61.0%); education-tuned SocraticLM scores low on error perception (0.14 in GuideEval).

problem: Minor: the ablation is 'without scaffold reward' (a ZPD-based reward); Dinucu-Jianu reports leak reduction via a penalty rather than a single headline number.
Numbers match HintMR (Hossain et al.); all quantitative figures come from this single paper, with SMART (KAIST) only supporting the general direction; test sets are 15-75 items.
Two-example fix applies to ZPD-SCA's context-learning setting; the 'simulators play weak students too well' part rests on Wu et al./Acquaye et al. framing, not a numeric result.
Small-model clause is wrong for Claude 3.5 Haiku (AIME 2024 10.0 to 36.7 with DC-Cu, AIME 2025 0.0 to 13.3); only GPT-4o-mini falls below baseline and Haiku's GPQA gain is small.
fix: Stored lessons act as self-scaffolds: Reflexion HumanEval 91% vs 80% (GPT-4 baseline); ExpeL insights and retrieved trajectories combine; ReasoningBank +8.3 points on WebArena overall (40.5 to 48.8, Gemini-2.5-flash) and 55.1 vs about 42 for no-memory best-of-5 on Shopping; Dynamic Cheatsheet doubled Claude 3.5 Sonnet on AIME 2024 (23.3 to 50.0) but about half of that came from the empty-memory prompt (36.7); Voyager skill library. Majority vote of 3 gave no gain (23.3). Smaller models are mixed: GPT-4o-mini falls below baseline on AIME 2024 (16.7 to 13.3), while Claude 3.5 Haiku gains on AIME but little on GPQA.

problem: ACE gains persist without ground-truth labels when execution outcomes supply feedback (57.2 vs 42.4), so gains do not require oracle labels; they require a reliable external signal.
fix: Intrinsic self-review without an outside signal does not help and lowers accuracy (Huang et al.: GPT-3.5 gains only with oracle labels, e.g. GSM8K 75.9 to 95.5); in agent settings ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet gain with execution feedback even without ground-truth labels but may degrade without any reliable feedback signal, so lessons need an external signal.

problem: Voyager's curriculum is automatic but not explicitly 'just beyond current skill' and Cui and Sachan figures were not checked numerically; STRETCH's table text says 0.06 SR over AZR (0.73) while an extracted table row shows 0.67.

Numbers verified (3.90 vs 3.43, N=451 after exclusions, Study 3 p=.146, Study 4 p=.026, ambivalence drop), but both papers are from Petty's lab (Bizer, Larsen, Petty; Teeny and Petty) and no outside replication is listed.
The 'memory load nullifies it' detail was not seen in an opened source (the press release only says the effect needs ability to think carefully); two of three papers are Petty-lab.
Wang and Zhang's two framings are described by the authors as logically equivalent but differ in instrumental versus cooperative wording of a voting task.
WildFrame reports r>=0.52 for all eleven LLMs; 0.52 to 0.61 is only the range across the GPT models (GPT-3.5 to GPT-5-mini), which the authors call the least human-correlated family.
fix: LLM framing sensitivity is not simply human-like in direction: allow/forbid shifts in Tjuatja 2024 were often opposite to humans (Llama2-7b -60.4, GPT-3.5 +25.3); Braun 2025 finds an LLM 'no' bias rather than human acquiescence; in WildFrame (eleven LLMs) all models correlate with human reframing shifts at r>=0.52 (GPT models lowest, 0.52 for GPT-3.5 to 0.61 for GPT-5-mini), so response to naturally occurring reframing is more human-like than the survey-bias results.

problem: Echterhoff's self-help result is on one prompt set/GPT-4 only; Dubois is a preprint; Chapala effect is limited to two of three models and most aggregate effects do not generalize across items.
Minor: CogBias backfire range in the extracted table is about 11.6 to 21.0 pp across the bottom five biases, not 13 to 21; CogBias is an under-review preprint.
Payne reports 'limited correlation' between EV calculation and framing size (and elsewhere says formal analysis correlates with an aggregate dampening), so 'uncorrelated' is slightly strong.

Mandel 'at least vs exactly' confound was not verifiable (OSF page does not render) and its reported Q values (p=.92) do not obviously show a confound; Kuhberger d=.31 and message-framing d=0.10 are cited in the 2023 review from earlier meta-analyses (Kuhberger 1998; O'Keefe and Jensen).

Sycophancy as 'a stance-cue effect close to oppose/support' is the researcher's interpretation; the quoted numbers (27%, 42% for GPT-4) match Sharma et al., where 42% is the lowest admit rate among the assistants.

Fansher, Shah and Helie is a new Tower of Hanoi study of computer vs mental presentation (its Experiment 2 replicates its own Experiment 1), not a replication of Zhang and Norman; the two entries a18/b08 are the same preprint.
fix: Moving part of a task's rules or state into an external, well-structured display lowers errors, steps and time for humans (Zhang & Norman 1994, N=18-36 per experiment). A later Tower of Hanoi study (Fansher, Shah & Helie, preprint) found that an external computer display improved completion (100% vs 91%) and progress, while move count did not differ significantly.

problem: Minor: the 20%/15% win rates are against CoT, where debate uses more compute, not strictly matched compute; matched-compute shortfall is vs self-consistency.
Wikipedia is a secondary summary of Prelec, so only one independent source; claim is a method description so this does not matter.

Consensus-is-not-verification does report models predict other models better than truth and SP/aggregation failing; the popularity paper (arXiv 2608.29257) never tests SP, so 'both make SP fail' is an inference, not a finding.
fix: Models are better at predicting what other models will say than at identifying what is true, and aggregation methods including Surprisingly Popular gave no reliable gain over a single sample (Denisov-Blanch et al. 2026); separately, LLMs systematically favour popular options and pick a popular wrong answer 66% of the time when all distractors are more popular than the correct one (Abdallah et al. 2026), which would plausibly hurt SP when the popular answer is wrong, but SP was not tested there.

problem: Table 2 of Luo and Liu: the heuristic variant (HMTS) fixed 48 of 149 on Spambase and 5 of 52 on Hill Valley; '1 of 64' on Hill Valley is the discriminative variant (DMTS), whose Spambase result is 70 of 76, so the claim mixes variants.
fix: Learned aggregation using confidence plus meta-prediction reached 64% success (RCR-Agg) when only 28% of respondents were individually correct (Shinitzky et al. 2022); Machine Truth Serum gains over majority vote on high-disagreement items vary widely by dataset and variant: heuristic MTS fixed 48 of 149 on Spambase (+32%) but 5 of 52 on Hill Valley (+9.8%), and discriminative MTS fixed 70 of 76 on Spambase but 1 of 64 on Hill Valley.

problem: Only Kim et al. carries the numbers; the second listed source (Consensus is Not Verification) supports the general point, not these figures.

Neither listed source (Hunt 2000 abstract, Emery and Clayton 2004) gives 5550 tools, 21 sites, 3 designs or between-population design differences; those figures come from Hunt and Gray 2003 (Proc R Soc B 270:867), which I verified but which is not cited.

Compound tool (4 of 8, transfer, 70.8% vs 20.8%, Fisher p values) and metatool criterion 16/20 are confirmed in von Bayern 2018 and Gruber 2019, but 'metatool use 4 of 7 on trial 1' is in neither listed source (it would come from Taylor et al. 2007, which is not cited); also Gruber 2019 shows 4 of 11 crows reaching 16/20 with few errors and others needing up to 46 trials, not a first-trial pass.
fix: Crows show tool-reasoning abilities: 4 of 8 naive crows built compound tools in the first construction test and transferred to new materials (von Bayern et al. 2018; uncombined tool tried first on 70.8% of close-food vs 20.8% of distant-food trials, per-bird Fisher p 0.037, 0.001, 0.100, 0.193), and wild-caught crows reached criterion (16/20) on out-of-sight multi-stage metatool problems, mostly after tens of trials (Gruber et al. 2019).

problem: The magpie paper supports 'significant only in late trials' and mentions (via Hennefield et al.) learning from success but not failure, but neither listed source reports a pooled analysis of 5 articles / 32+ experiments or a no-transfer finding; Jelbert 2015 is a narrative review that predates that meta-analysis.

Minor: the 42.4% is a share of errors in GPT-4's infeasible/non-efficient answers (200 analysed), not all attempts; 'LLMs pick the similar-looking distractor' is the authors' description of the older (2023) models only.
The r=0.038 and 10.69% figures come only from Na et al. 2010; Na 2020 is the same lab (corroboration, not independent), though the claim rests on one dataset's numbers.
Atari et al. preprint could not be fetched (OSF); the figures come from Tao et al. 2024, and AlKhamissi et al. supports the general point.

Wyrich et al. support 53.7% all-student of 95 and that almost no studies link design to comprehension theory in general, but say nothing specific on chunking or on pooled effect sizes for expertise; Issever et al. (EMIP reanalysis) does not address either, so the 'no pooled effect size' absence claim is unsupported (second source not opened for relevance, being off-topic).
fix: Of 95 code-comprehension experiments (1979-2019), 53.7% used all-student samples, and almost none linked their design to a comprehension theory (Wyrich et al. 2023); whether a pooled effect size exists for the expertise effect was not established by these sources.

problem: Minor: Li et al. is code summarization, and '22%' means significant Spearman correlation for at most 22% of 68 methods for any human-model pair.

cAST numbers confirmed; but Glasz et al. report LLM partitions beat all methods except Single Module (which aligned best with experts, near-perfect recall on MUMPS), and the least factual comments came from Single Module chunking (most limited context), not fixed-length chunking; fixed-length chunks merely had minimal overlap with expert split points.
fix: Structure-aware chunking beats fixed-size chunking in code RAG: cAST (RepoEval Pass@1 StarCoder2 GIST 57.9 vs 51.2; SWE-bench Lite Claude-3.7 BGE 16.3 vs 13.7, GIST 15.0 vs 14.7). In Glasz et al. (legacy MUMPS/ALC), LLM-chosen partitions matched expert partition points better than all other methods except single-module (subroutine) chunking, fixed-length chunks had minimal overlap with expert partitions, and single-module chunking, with the least context, gave the least factual comments.

problem: Beaty 2015 and Beaty 2016 review are same-lab (corroboration not independent), but the cooperation finding is also replicated by other labs in the review.
Sole supporting study is Kenett, Yoed et al. 2025 (one paper); the second listed source (Beaty 2019 review) only gives context.

Marek et al. 2022 supports small BWAS effects, underpower and inflation at typical (median ~25) samples; application to network-creativity studies is an inference, not shown directly. Beaty 2015 r=.44 N=25 text not located by search.
Minor: Padmakumar and He find the diversity loss comes from the InstructGPT-generated text (not GPT-3 co-writing); human-written portions were unaffected.

Mild: Peeperkorn finds temperature only weakly correlated with novelty; Meincke finds chain-of-thought (stepwise) prompting most diverse at fixed temperature 0.7, so the 'more than temperature' comparison is across studies, not head-to-head.
Huang et al. is a narrative review that pools nothing (g range is across independent comparisons, mostly AUT); Bellemare-Pepin supports the top-humans point.

Huys 2015 (PNAS) and Lally 2017 report the same 41 recruited / 37 analysed volunteers (Huys 2015: 'the same 37 subjects included there' for the fMRI report), so the '2015 sample' is not a fourth sample; independent samples are Huys 2012 (N=46), the Lally/Huys 2015 sample (N=37) and Faulkner 2022 (N=61, depressed and healthy), all one task from related labs.
fix: Humans cut a plan branch after a large early loss and choose the best path less often when it runs through that loss. Seen in three samples of one task from overlapping labs: Huys 2012 (N=46; pruning model predicts 91% of choices), the Lally 2017 / Huys 2015 sample (same N=37; 78% correct without a large loss vs 37% with one, d=2.06; 37/37 subjects prune in Huys 2015), and Faulkner 2022 (N=61, pruning model wins).

problem: Numbers are right (iBIC 2472 vs 2466; Faulkner reward weight 7.25 vs loss -2.60), but Lally et al. call loss aversion 'evident' and Pruning+Loss the best model (dIBIC 5.8, which they report as an improvement), and Huys 2012 found subjects about 1.4x more sensitive to punishments than rewards; the robust finding is that pruning beats loss-aversion-only models, not that loss weighting adds nothing.
fix: Pruning is not reducible to loss aversion: models with pruning beat models with loss weighting alone (Huys 2012, Lally 2017), and pruning remains after loss sensitivities are fitted. Loss weighting still adds a little: in Lally 2017 Pruning+Loss was the best model (iBIC 2466 vs 2472 for Pruning), Huys 2012 found punishments weighted about 1.4 times rewards although adding loss aversion to its best model did not improve parsimony, and in Faulkner 2022 the fitted large-gain weight (7.25) was about 2.8 times the large-loss weight (-2.60) in healthy controls.

problem: Minor: pruned choices were faster than OLL error trials but not significantly faster than OLL correct; Huys 2012 compared loss in first vs second half of the sequence at depth 4-5 (no difference at depth 6+), which the claim paraphrases loosely. Lally and Huys 2015 share one sample.
Minor: no-prune search found the answer in 4/20 games but its output heuristic returned only 1 (game score 5%).
Minor: ThinkPrune is RL-trained length limit rather than an internal-signal cut.

Content is supported, but both sources are the same Friston/Da Costa group; the evidence lines a15/a16/b05/b24 are one paper (b05 lists wrong authors Paul et al. 2024), and 2608.19202 and PMC13601584 do not bear on the claim.

UoT tables show open-set gains are often larger than closed-set gains (e.g. Llama3-70B MedDG DP 25.7 to UoT 50.6 in OS vs 60.2 to 64.3 in CS), BED-LLM gets +37.4 points in an open target space, and Mazzaccara's Celebrities +1.1 is a domain shift at the same 8-candidate size, not a larger set; BigBench success actually rose 17.2 to 31.0 while EIG fell.
fix: EIG-based question selection gains are not uniform across settings: in Mazzaccara et al. the DPO gain was only +1.1 points on Celebrities (out-of-domain) and on BigBench (29 candidates) success rose 17.2 to 31.0 percent while mean EIG fell 0.31 to 0.28; in UoT, open-set gains over direct prompting are not systematically smaller than closed-set gains, and BED-LLM gains 37.4 points in an open target space.

problem: In BED-LLM Table 1 Implicit Maximization recovers little of the gain (e.g. Celebrities GPT-4o: prompt-only 45, implicit 50, BED-LLM 86; the paper says it 'works much less well'), and predictive entropy recovers only part (about 30 to 80 percent) of the gap.
fix: Cheaper substitutes recover only part of the gain: in BED-LLM's 20 Questions ablations, predictive entropy lands between Prompt-Only and full EIG (e.g. Animals GPT-4o-mini 44 / 79 / 88 percent; Celebrities GPT-4o 45 / 64 / 86), and LLM-judged Implicit Maximization beats Prompt-Only only modestly and works much less well than full EIG; separately, Piriyakulkij et al. show expected-entropy minimisation and expected model change are equivalent in their setup.

problem: Li et al. (GATE) elicit with prompted LMs (open-ended questions, edge cases) and do not use an EIG objective; their comparison is against supervised learning, pool-based active learning and user-written prompts, with significance only in content recommendation and email validation.
fix: Preference elicitation: EIG/BOED-based question selection beat vanilla and ReAct prompting in a simulated shopping task (Piriyakulkij), OPEN (BOED) beat LM-only and BOED baselines in user studies (Handa), and BED-LLM beat prompt-only in simulated movie recommendation though prompt-only was a stronger baseline there; separately, non-EIG LM-driven elicitation (GATE, Li et al.) beat supervised, pool-based active learning and user-written prompts with significance in only 2 of 3 domains.

problem: Numbers and paper descriptions check out; 'Wen' is named in the claim but has no listed source, and 'only two measured tests' is an absence-of-evidence statement from a literature search, not something the sources prove.

The paper says the one premature commitment to the wrong model happened with full expected information gain (one failure in 64 games), not with state-only gain; the eLife paper (Schwartenbeck 2019) is about state vs parameter exploration and does not report these rule-discovery numbers; the PMC article is in Nat Commun (2026), same Friston group.
fix: In a Friston-group simulation of 64 games (32 trials each), expected information gain over models and parameters cut mean rule-discovery time from 28.5 to 19.4 trials and raised cumulative score from 89.2 to 150; removing all information gain dropped the score from 150 to 51, and the single failure with full information gain was a premature commitment to the wrong model (one simulation by one group).

problem: Claim is fully supported only by Piriyakulkij et al. (2024), including the entropy/model-change equivalence; STaR-GATE is a fine-tuning method, not scaffold-only EIG selection, so there is no second independent source (the 'tokens not fixed' remark is an author caveat).
Mouse age (adolescent) not confirmed on the fetched page; Diering et al. used a different mouse preparation, so the 'this population' wording is loose.

Yang 2014 and Li 2017 are the same Gan lab; the V1 potentiation point comes from a review (Puentes-Mestril and Aton, Aton lab data) which says sleep-dependent, not strictly required; the 'poor analogy' conclusion is interpretive.

Every listed source is the Tononi/Cirelli group (the 2019 review, their 2014 review, Nere 2013 modelling); Gulati 2017 and Gonzalez-Rueda 2018 are only seen through that review (and the review is dated 2019, not 2020); numbers match the review.
Minor: the Huber 2012 TMS slope result is frontal cortex, so 'all indices motor-cortex based' is slightly loose; Huber is reported via the review only.

All stated numbers come from a single Tononi/Cirelli-lab paper (Nere 2013 I; verified 80/90/95%, S/N 4/9/19, 87/75/53/94%); the extra-wake and sleep-potentiation S/N are 0.25 and 0.33 not 0; Capone 2019 is independent but gives none of these numbers.

The two spiking-net papers are the same Massey/Hubin/Nichele group, so there are two independent groups, not three; Robinson's p<=0.5 equals p=0 detail not checked in the text, the paper reports a trend up to p=0.75 and down at 0.9.

Both facts check out, but the 1% freezing control in Golden et al. is not down-scaling, and the same control found that freezing 5% gave modest results and 10% fully preserved Task 1 while blocking Task 2; so 'pruning needs something to replay' is the researcher's inference, not a result.
fix: In Robinson et al. (class-incremental CIFAR-100), accuracy collapsed at every downscaling fraction p without generative replay; in the Golden et al. spiking model, freezing 1% of Task-1 weights let Task 2 be learned but did not preserve Task 1 (10% preserved Task 1 but blocked Task 2), whereas interleaved sleep replay preserved both; this suggests, but does not show, that pruning-type protection needs replay.

problem: Minor: combined deletion for RegAgent kept 890 records (66.58), so '188-323 records' covers only the other three agents; Mem0 accuracy is a few points below full context; RSPM and FadeMem are single-group simulations or benchmarks.

Xiong et al. say history-based deletion with a coarse GPT-4o-mini evaluator gave a clear gain on EHRAgent but degraded AgentDriver (unstable, not simply 'did not help'); other figures (ACE 76.1/66.7 vs base 70.7, DC small-model quote, 36.92 to 47.37, add-all 32.32) verified.
fix: Pruning helps only with a reliable utility signal. Xiong 2025: with a weak coarse evaluator history-based deletion was unstable (gain on EHRAgent, worse on AgentDriver) and errors propagate via experience-following; ACE degrades without ground truth or execution feedback and can be polluted; Dynamic Cheatsheet: small models leave memory with flawed or incomplete strategies and gain little. A judge fine-tuned on 300 labelled outcomes lifted AgentDriver from 36.92 to 47.37 (add-all 32.32); ACE kept its gain with one harmful reflector update in five (76.1 vs base 70.7) but fell to 66.7 when every update was harmful. No threshold on judge accuracy has been measured.

problem: SCM and SleepGate are single-author small or synthetic tests as stated, but FadeMem (LoCoMo, Multi-Session Chat) and RSPM (LoCoMo-10, +7.6 points) also report public benchmarks, and the current ZenBrain v4 abstract is a correction release reporting mostly null ablations and LongMemEval_S (about 91% of full-context accuracy), not large gains; the 37%/47.4% figures are not on the current page.
fix: Sleep-inspired LLM memory papers (SCM, SleepGate, ZenBrain, RSPM, FadeMem) are mostly single-author or single-group preprints: SCM and SleepGate report gains on self-built or synthetic tests (8-test suite; a 793K-parameter transformer on a synthetic interference task); RSPM adds a simulated SWE-bench arm plus LoCoMo-10 (+7.6 points) and one conversation with a 19.5-point loss; FadeMem uses its own LTI-Bench plus LoCoMo and MSC; ZenBrain's latest version retracts earlier headline gains. None found has an independent replication on a real LLM agent task stream.

problem: Xiong numbers exact. Dynamic Cheatsheet is internally inconsistent: its text says GPT-4o full-history 6.7% on AIME 2024 but Table 2 lists 13.3 (baseline 20.0 either way); the ACE source listed does not bear on this claim.
Minor: Tolman says the strip map carries over less well, not that it fails outright, and SR-TD is a cached predictive map rather than a literal single route.

Park 2020 numbers verified (282 trained, 82 passed, 33 scanned, 27 analysed, 93.6 percent); Constantinescu 2016 confirmed only as existing and showing gridlike conceptual coding, its own numbers not checked; generalising to 'humans' from the 29 percent who passed training is the claim's own caveat.
Minor: the GAVEL 38.6 to 99.4 is on BEHAVIOR-1K multi-task planning, a different setting from MAP, and the Hybrid-WM and GAVEL papers are not in the same task family as MAP.
Minor: the self-consistency 56.5 greedy CoT uses Wei's same exemplars, so it is a re-run by an overlapping group, not an independent replication.
Minor: LaMDA 68B already gains (5.7->8.2) so 'below roughly 100B' is the paper's own approximation; 'modern models past threshold' is the researcher's inference.
Minor: Wei SingleOp is +3.0 for LaMDA 137B and 0/-2.1 for PaLM 540B/GPT-175B (small-or-negative); CSQA 68.8->64.6 is the first of two answer-extraction variants (other is 72.6->64.0).
Minor: all three ablations come from one paper (Wei); Lanham independently covers only the filler-token one.

SVAMP +11.0, AQuA +12.2, StrategyQA +6.4, ARC-c +3.9 are code-davinci-002 gains (the abstract's headline numbers), not PaLM; PaLM-540B is SVAMP +7.6, AQuA +12.5. Also Stechly says self-consistency was 'generally worse' (5 samples), and '40x tokens' is 40 sampled paths, not a measured token cost.
fix: Self-consistency (sample many chains, majority vote) adds large gains over greedy CoT: PaLM-540B GSM8K 56.5 -> 74.4 (+17.9), AQuA +12.5, SVAMP +7.6; code-davinci-002 gets SVAMP +11.0, AQuA +12.2, StrategyQA +6.4, ARC-c +3.9. It samples 40 paths (about 40x the generation cost), and on Blocksworld table-to-stack (5 samples) it was generally worse than plain CoT.

problem: Minor: invalid-reasoning exemplars retain 81% (39.5/48.5) on GSM8K; wrong-answer cost 3.2 points average across benchmarks (the claim reads as an AIME-linked pair but is correctly flagged as training, not prompting).
Minor: 39.5->23.3 is no-CoT vs zero-shot CoT accuracy in the biased context; GSM-NoOp 'up to 65%' is the maximum drop across models.
Minor: Balachandran says R1 and Claude 3.7 are within 3% accuracy on AIME 25 (not equal); 34.5 is quoted as a percent gap by Hassid.

Minor: the linear-step regular-language result needs projected pre-norm and standard complexity conjectures; Feng et al. prove a compatible but different (arithmetic/DP) result rather than the same hierarchy.
Minor: R1 70%->30% is the 'natural overthinking' setup only; CatAttack is adversarial trigger search (R1 transfer rate about 20%), not an inverse-scaling measurement.

All listed sources (Nuxoll and Laird 2012, Derbinsky/Li/Laird 2012, Laird 2022) are from the Laird Soar group, so the demonstrated capabilities (action modelling, decision evaluation, virtual sensing) rest on one lab's own toy-domain demos; the findings themselves match the papers, with learning curves given only as graphs.

Minor: Nuxoll 2004 says unbiased matching gave only moderately-better-than-random scores and the activation-biased match performed significantly better; 'retrieval with the wrong cue is the main failure' is a synthesis (Nuxoll notes identical cues for every move, RMM calls retrieval the bottleneck), not a single quoted finding.
Minor: Laird 2022 (section 5) states this directly; the Soar manual RL chapter only says Q-values are numeric-indifferent preferences, and the second Laird listing is the same paper.

Minor: Nuxoll and Laird 2012 say memory consolidation, forgetting and generalisation are not included; Soar manual says epmem has no forgetting; Laird 2022 says no generalisation; all from one lab and some are version-specific.

Minor: +22/+20 are Reflexion's abstract-level gains over strong baselines (ALFWorld 12 trials); +8 is Reflexion vs episodic-only on 100 HotPotQA questions with ground-truth context; ExpeL/ReasoningBank are related but do not restate these numbers.

Minor: ExpeL's task-similarity retrieval (59.0) vs random (42.5) is a single ALFWorld ablation; 63.6 is the best plain RAG (GTE) and 70.4 RMM, 90.2 oracle (Gemini-1.5-Flash); the not-tested-in-LLM-agents statement is an absence claim no source can confirm.
Minor: the Hu comparison uses different benchmark/metrics from the Mem0 paper, and the Mem0 paper is a vendor paper; the numbers all match.

LoCoMo F1 32.4 is the best of the limited-context base models (GPT-4-turbo, 4K); the same paper reports long-context GPT-3.5-16K at 37.8 and RAG GPT-3.5-16K up to about 41.4 overall, so 32.4 is not the best model overall. LongMemEval and key/time-expansion numbers check out.
fix: Long-term chat memory is hard: LongMemEval shows about a 30% drop for long context (GPT-4o 0.870 to 0.606), commercial ChatGPT 0.5773 vs offline reading 0.9184; on LoCoMo the best base model (GPT-4-turbo, 4K context) reaches F1 32.4 and long-context or RAG variants about 38-41, vs human 87.9. Fact-augmented keys +9.4% recall, time-aware query expansion +6.8% to 11.3% recall.

problem: CoALA, Pink et al. and Wray/Kirk/Laird are indeed conceptual or position papers with no experiments, but none of them can establish that no study exists; the universal negative is unsupported by the listed sources.
fix: We found no published study that runs Soar episodic memory or Soar-RL against an LLM-agent memory on one benchmark; the Soar-to-LLM link in the sources read (CoALA, Pink et al. position paper, Wray/Kirk/Laird design patterns) is conceptual.

problem: Minor: ReasoningBank's simulated-judge result is read from a figure (flat across 70-90%, best at 100%) on one WebArena-Shopping subset with one judge model.

All numbers (number game R2=0.95, logical concepts R2=.81, Zendo .57 vs .10) come from two papers by the same lab (Ellis 2023; Piriyakulkij, Langenfeld, Le, Ellis 2024), and the Wong et al. papers are conceptual with no matching numbers; the figures themselves match the sources, and the 'far better than direct LLM' contrast is vs GPT-4 / ReAct baselines from those same papers.

Minor: MMToM-QA numbers (75.3/76.7 vs GPT-4V 44.0, human 93.0 multimodal) and BToM 0.93 (goal attributions; 0.92 for belief statements) match, but they come from two different papers with overlapping MIT authors (Tenenbaum, Zhi-Xuan), and in the BToM paper the LLM translates belief sentences rather than supplying likelihoods.

Minor: 'no matched-token EIG vs diverse-sampling test exists' is an absence claim no source can confirm; Pruned UoT (4.7k tokens) vs CoT-SC (4.6k) is roughly, not exactly, matched; k=10 'close match' is stated for mean human performance in the Grand et al. text and figures.

Sources are position papers (Griffiths 2020; Griffiths, Zhu, Grant, McCoy 2023 argue Bayesian and neural models sit at different Marr levels and are complementary; Perfors et al. 2011 proposes rational process models as a bridge), so 'best used' is the authors' argument, not an established finding, and two of the three authors are one lab.
fix: Griffiths and colleagues argue that Bayesian models are useful at the computational level for describing what a network implicitly assumes (priors, inductive biases), with resource-rational or rational process models proposed as the bridge to process-level accounts (Griffiths 2020; Griffiths et al. 2023; Perfors et al. 2011); this is a position, not an empirical result.

problem: Minor: Kim et al. compares different models' errors while Brown et al. and Chen et al. concern repeated samples of one model, so 'LLM samples are not independent voters' blends two kinds of dependence; the Vul et al. comparison is the researcher's inference (Vul is not among the sources).

Santo et al. 2024 and Schapiro et al. 2025 are indeed purely theoretical (no experiments), but the Wiggins source is only a Wikipedia citation, and Schapiro et al. also cite Toivanen et al. 2018, who describe an implemented transformational architecture for a song generator, so 'all formalisations are theory with no agent experiment' is an unsupported universal.
fix: Transformational creativity has been formalised as a meta-level change of the rules, representation or hypothesis space (Wiggins 2006; Espirito Santo et al. 2024; Schapiro et al. 2025); the Santo and Schapiro papers are theory with no agent experiment, but Toivanen et al. 2018 describe an implemented song-generation architecture with meta-level modules, and Wiggins' framework was seen only through a citation.

problem: Minor: Jones & Love and Marcus & Davis were not among the opened sources (Bowers & Davis states the post-hoc/unfalsifiable critique directly); Perfors et al. propose 'rational process models', with 'resource-rational' wording coming from Griffiths' later papers.

CreativeBench never mentions transformational creativity (it only covers combinatorial and exploratory), AGC-Bench only lists it as a harder-to-assess aspect in its limitations, and only Franceschelli-Musolesi explicitly calls testing it open; OMEGA/T-UoT proxies were not opened.
fix: No benchmark found in this search measures transformational creativity directly: CreativeBench covers only combinatorial and exploratory creativity, AGC-Bench lists transformational creativity as an aspect that remains harder to assess, and Franceschelli and Musolesi call testing for it an open, possibly unsolvable problem.

problem: Minor: numbers listed in human-vs-LLM order (human 4.84, LLM 5.64), and the execution study used 43 completed projects, not N=49.

Numbers match, but dz +1.40 is a composite creativity score (not novelty alone), the 0.5-0.75 temperature sweet spot is from one agent benchmark (InnoGym), CreativeBench says reasoning significantly helps exploratory tasks, and Peeperkorn finds temperature only weakly linked to novelty.
fix: Asking models to be creative raised composite creativity scores far more (dz +1.40, 18 models) than enabling reasoning (dz +0.34, 10 models); in the InnoGym agent benchmark mid-range temperature (0.5-0.75) gave near-optimal performance with higher novelty; in CreativeBench reasoning gave almost no benefit on combinatorial tasks but a significant benefit on exploratory tasks, and another study finds temperature only weakly related to story novelty.

problem: Minor: DGM 20.0 to 50.0 is on a SWE-bench subset, and ADAS +13.6 is F1 on DROP versus hand-designed baselines.

Sources show asymptotic polynomial-rate failure and a double-exponential worst case for UCT, but Kocsis-Szepesvari only say 'some constant C' (no huge constants are shown), and the LLM-budget implication is the researcher's inference.
fix: UCT guarantees are asymptotic: root failure probability falls at a polynomial rate with an unspecified constant, and Coquelin and Munos show a worst case needing exp(exp(D)) rounds before the best branch is first seen; the paper does not analyse budgets of tens of rollouts, so treat the theory as design motivation only.

problem: Minor: rStar-Math shows 'saturation or slow improvement' at 64 trajectories only on MATH, AIME and Olympiad Bench (College Math keeps improving); the 6-simulation result is for Ms. Pacman.
Minor: RAP 48.8 is the text figure while the table lists RAP(1) 48.6; the RAP vs SC(10) comparison is not compute-matched; Wu et al. MCTS test is on MATH.
Minor: REBASE reached higher (not equal) accuracy with about 7x less compute; 'dozens of times more tokens' is Wu et al.'s background statement, not their own measurement.

Minor: headline 'search helps on hard problems' holds for levels 3-4 only; on level 5 no method made progress, and Liu et al. show the pattern depends on policy size; all of Snell's support is one paper.
Minor: LATS appendix Table 11 labels are garbled/inconsistent with main Table 8 (which gives the quoted 0.63/0.37/0.42); the prompted-vs-learned Game24 numbers are for TS-LLM with LLaMA-SFT policy.
Minor: PG-TD 26.70 vs 25.19 is the APPS introductory pass rate for the GPT-Neo/GPT-2 setup; SWE-Search 23% is the reported mean relative gain.
Minor: the 'more reliable as teacher than run-time engine' framing is the researcher's synthesis; the quoted numbers all match.

A universal negative contradicted by its own evidence: LATS does report a 3-value exploration-weight ablation (w=0.5, 1, 2); and 'width matters more than c' is unsupported, since the 0.432 vs 0.402 width gap (std ~0.015-0.02, w=3 gives 0.429) was never compared against any c effect.
fix: Few LLM-MCTS papers sweep the UCT constant: LATS ablates the exploration weight at three values on HotPotQA (w=0.5 gave 0.55 EM vs 0.63 at w=1; w=2 gave no gain), TS-LLM chose c_init from only {0.3, 3.0}, and SWE-Search uses c=1.41 with no sweep found. For fixed-width MCTS on LiveCodeBench (DeepSeek-V3) width 5 scored 0.432, width 3 0.429 and width 10 0.402, so performance is sensitive to width at least at the larger setting.

problem: Minor: a02 and b08 are the same Wikipedia page, so only two independent sources; in the non-termination case the set is satisfiable but the prover never shows it.

All four listed sources are the one Suda 2021 paper (the 'cross-reading' entry cites other papers but links the same arXiv id), so the general 'helps most when mixed, fails as full replacement' rests on a single study; its numbers (net-only 190 solved = 25% of 756; layered 1:1 1032 = 136%, 1:2 1036 = 137%) are correct.
fix: In Suda (2021), Vampire on an SMT-LIB subset solved only 25% of the baseline count with a neural-net-only clause queue but 136-137% with the net layered as a second queue next to the stock queue.

problem: ENIGMA-NG (2019) and ENIGMA Anonymous (2020) are by the same group (Jakubuv, Chvalovsky, Suda, Urban), so they count as one lab; all numbers check out (1256 vs 1197 on MPTP2078; 24,347 vs 23,262 on Mizar40 at 10 s; GNN had higher TPR).
fix: Within one research group's two ENIGMA papers, boosted trees beat a recursive neural net (MPTP2078, 10 s: 1256 vs 1197 solved) and a GNN (Mizar40, 10 s: 24,347 vs 23,262) on solved counts, although the GNN had better held-out accuracy; no independent group has replicated this.

problem: The Vampire study notes one exception (a TPTP-trained model still improves over default elsewhere), and the TRAIL authors read their 11%/3% transfer losses as evidence of relatively domain-general features, which does not support 'dataset-specific'; TRAIL is also a different system (Beagle RL, Mizar-derived sets only).
fix: In a Vampire neural-guidance study, a model trained on one benchmark family usually scores below the unguided default on the others (with one exception, a TPTP-trained model), and a single model trained on all four sets nearly matches the dedicated models (95-101%); in TRAIL (a Beagle-based RL prover) transfer between two Mizar-derived sets lost only 11% and 3%.

problem: Numbers match, but all three sources are the same Piepenbrock et al. 2022 paper (single-study result); the 3.3% baseline is one random run vs 100 runs for 9,923.

Numbers match, but 'translation is the main loss' is general while the evidence is mainly AR-LSAT; on FOLIO the same Logic-LM pipeline executes and scores 94.2% of executable cases, so translation loss is not shown to dominate everywhere.
fix: On hard first-order tasks, translation to formal logic is a major loss in LLM-plus-solver pipelines: GPT-4o Logic-LM on AR-LSAT produced executable programs for only 33.8% of problems (51.3% accuracy on those), its translation accuracy falls as formula complexity rises, and LINC syntax errors fall with model strength (13% GPT-4, 24% GPT-3.5, 38% StarCoder+) while missing-information and mis-encoding errors remain; on easier sets like FOLIO the loss is small.

problem: Minor: RND is a prediction-error bonus rather than a literal count, and 31.6 vs 16.5 is 'nearly double'.
Minor: the ICM/RND 'avoid counting uncontrollable noise' part is argued by their authors (RND is not shown immune to a noisy TV).

The RND paper does not tie 'dancing with skulls' to the noisy-TV effect (it suggests dangerous states are rarely seen, in Montezuma and Pitfall); the noisy-TV link there is for the dynamics-error agent oscillating between rooms, and the Unity-maze noisy-TV test is on random-feature and inverse-dynamics curiosity, not ICM exactly.
fix: Prediction-error bonuses can stall on unpredictable states: a noisy TV in a Unity maze drastically slows curiosity learning (inverse-dynamics and random-feature agents, though they sometimes converge if run long), and a forward-dynamics-error agent is significantly worse than RND on Montezuma, Private Eye and Solaris, oscillating between rooms because sticky actions make prediction error irreducible; separately, RND agents that exhaust extrinsic reward keep interacting with dangerous objects ('dancing with skulls'), which the authors do not attribute to noise.

problem: Minor: Go-Explore scores assume deterministic training/simulator resets and Go-Explore itself picks cells by visit counts; its own table lists RND at 11,540 (the 8,152 is RND's original paper mean); NGU and Agent57 are the same lab.

Krishnamurthy numbers check out (>60% suffix failures for basic GPT-4, T=100; only one GPT-4 configuration, summarised history with CoT, truly succeeded), but Monea 2025 tests positive-only subsampled episodes, not code-made summaries, and Harris-Slivkins find summaries help only on medium-difficulty tasks with LLMs still worse than linear regression, so the 'all agree' conclusion is too strong.
fix: GPT-4 with a basic prompt shows suffix failure (best arm never chosen after early rounds) in over 60% of bandit replicates at T=100, and only one GPT-4 configuration (chain-of-thought with an externally summarised history) explored well; EVOLvE finds summary statistics in the prompt beat raw history, Harris and Slivkins find summaries help on medium-difficulty tasks but LLMs still trail linear regression at exploitation, and Monea et al. find showing only positive subsampled episodes works, which points the same way but is not a summary.

problem: Minor: the 'about 30% above base at small k' is from the Oat-Zero/DAPO comparison (Fig. 11), and the 26.1-to-42.5 training pass@1 figure is on the training set; the claim's 'indirect evidence' framing is the researcher's.

Minor: ELLM compares against RND, APT and a novelty baseline (not count-based bonuses), and says such bonuses have 'limited benefits' rather than 'waste effort'; ELLM wins on three of four Housekeep tasks; Voyager's 93% (random curriculum) and 73% (no self-verification) check out.

Numbers match (AUC@64 AIME 0.160 vs 0.131 base and 0.116 SimpleRL; over 50% verifier-efficiency gain for Qwen-2.5-14B), but no source says exact text is always new or that embedding hashes collapse (Hu et al. only call embedding distance a poor diversity proxy), the hidden-state bonus is not a semantic key, and Song et al. use final-answer outcome keys, not semantic ones.
fix: Two LLM-exploration papers use a semantic signal rather than text: an LLM-judged strategy cluster with an inverse-cluster-size reward (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct AIME AUC@64 0.131 base, 0.116 SimpleRL, 0.160 ours) and a hidden-state elliptical (covariance) bonus (over 50% better verifier efficiency, Qwen-2.5-14B-Instruct, at inference time); Hu et al. call token entropy and embedding distance poor proxies for strategy diversity, and Song et al. find a final-answer count bonus helps pass@k only in refined forms.

problem: The 1980-82 CYRUS reports show worked examples on narrow Vance/Muskie data and list the human validity of E-MOPs as an open question, but 'no quantitative test exists' is a universal negative not shown by these sources, the authors cite existing human evidence (Williams and Hollan) for its elaboration-style retrieval, and UNIMEM (a follow-up system) was evaluated with parameter sweeps; nothing opened covers IPP's own evaluation.
fix: In the sources read, early dynamic-memory CBR (CYRUS E-MOPs) organised episodes under generalised norms with discriminating indices and was demonstrated through worked examples on a narrow hand-built domain (events in the lives of two US Secretaries of State); its authors list the psychological validity of E-MOPs as open, and no quantitative accuracy or human test of CYRUS or IPP was found in these sources.

problem: Kolodner thesis and Kolodner & Barsalou are the same author/lab and both describe CYRUS; the only other source (HyDE, numbers verified) is a dense-retrieval analogue that does not support the CYRUS claim itself.
All four evidence lines are the same Memento paper (arXiv 2508.16153; numbers 59.9/72.2 to 66.6/80.4 and HLE 17.4 to 24.4 verified); one study, so the general claim has no independent support.
Memento (K=4 64.5 F1, K=32 63.9), DS-Agent (more than one example case adds interference) and CBR-RAG (k=3 0.9141) verified; DS-Agent actually favours exactly one case.
ExpeL ablation verified (HotpotQA 36 vs 31, ALFWorld 50 vs 55, full 39/59); AWM (35.5 vs 23.5) only supports the abstraction part, not the combination.

Three evidence lines are the same ReasoningBank paper (numbers 48.8/44.1/42.1/40.5 verified, author list mislabelled 'Zhao'); AWM paper is a baseline and never compares against ReasoningBank, so only one independent source.
Minor: AWM on Claude-3.7 is not a weak backbone; all numbers verified (Reflexion starchat 0.26/0.26, DC 16.7 to 13.3, AWM 40.8 vs 41.7, Gemma 17.1/16.0/24.1).

r=0.717/0.563 and the AIME-25/GPQA remark verified in Evo-Memory only; Dynamic Cheatsheet does not report a similarity correlation and itself shows large gains on AIME-25 (+30) and GPQA-Diamond (+9) for Claude 3.5 Sonnet, so the recurring-structure/low-similarity generalisation is not supported across sources.
fix: In Evo-Memory, ReMem's gain over the History baseline correlates with within-dataset task similarity (Pearson r=0.717 on Gemini 2.5 Flash, 0.563 on Claude 3.7 Sonnet), and low-similarity datasets such as AIME-25 and GPQA show smaller gains there.

problem: Minor: long-context models in MemoryAgentBench span 42.2-60.6 (not 48.8-60.6); direction unchanged; Mem0 latency reduction is 91.6%.
Both evidence lines are the same paper (Hu et al., arXiv 2402.17709; 30.2% vs 92% and RFFT >95% on 12-digit verified, but no second study).

Hatalis et al. only say comprehensive benchmarks for CBR-augmented agents remain an open challenge and report only DS-Agent 100%/99%; Wikipedia says nothing on benchmarks, so a universal 'no benchmark yet' rests on one 2025 review.
fix: A 2025 review (Hatalis et al.) states that comprehensive benchmarks for the distinctive capabilities of CBR-augmented LLM agents remain an open challenge, and reports only one figure (DS-Agent 100% development success, 99% one-pass deployment, taken from Guo et al.).

problem: Minor: Dupre's Property 1 needs only a fully predictive model; closure is a separate route (Poole's Theorem 3.2 needs a different encoding per framework, for acyclic domains).
Neither source gives the definition: Wikipedia's section mentions Ab(S) but not minimality or consistency, and Theseider Dupre uses mode assignments, not minimal Ab sets.
Minor: 0.38 is GPT-4 with ordinary chain of thought (vanilla 0.27); golden chain gives 0.83.
Pooled medians 79.96 vs 42.50, GPT-4 41.67 on syllogism abduction and ART 68.9 vs 91.4 verified.
Elenchos itself says the 86.5 percent is consistent with premature commitment rather than proving it.
OpenRCA 2.0's 20.7 percent is an average over all cases, not broken down by fault count; its multi-fault link is only qualitative.
RCAgent compression and MedMAS-DDx (small gains) are weaker support than EviRCA.

Only Kim et al. rank interpretation hallucination as the most frequent pitfall (71.2 percent of runs); ORCA-bench (7-40 percent of reports) and Roy et al. (4-40 percent of predictions, only 4 percent for ReAct) report hallucination rates but not that it is the leading failure.
fix: Hallucinated interpretation of retrieved data is the most frequent pitfall in Kim et al. (71.2 percent of runs); ORCA-bench finds invented root causes in 7 to 40 percent of reports and Roy et al. find hallucination in 4 to 40 percent of predictions depending on the agent.

problem: GEAR's 20 percent consistent hypotheses for 70B-class models is verified, but Theseider Dupre says Cordier rejected parametrised assumptions for possible hypothesis proliferation in a methodology, not that weak models proliferate hypotheses.
fix: Single gold answers hide underdetermination: in GEAR, 70B-class models give only about 20 percent consistent hypotheses (consistent ones cover about 95 percent of the sample space); separately, in model-based diagnosis Cordier rejected parametrised assumptions because of potential proliferation of hypotheses.

problem: The two Lovett et al. papers (2006 proceedings and 2009 journal) are one research group, and Goldstone and Medin / Sloutsky and Yarlas data are only read second-hand through them; incremental-mapping models are all this one group's.

Stevenson et al. numbers verified (GPT-4o 0.85/0.63/0.48; adults 0.88/0.91/0.89), but Webb et al. show GPT-3 generalizing letter strings to concepts and Musker et al. report LLMs matching humans in several conditions, so a general failure to transfer is not supported.
fix: In letter-string analogies (Stevenson et al.), GPT-4o accuracy fell from 0.85 with the Latin alphabet to 0.63 with Greek and 0.48 with symbols, while adults stayed at 0.88-0.91; other work finds LLMs match humans in several analogy conditions, so transfer failure is task-dependent.

problem: Lu et al. verified (permutations 88.7 vs 51.6 percent on SST-2; 175B vs 2.7B correlation 0.05); Chen et al. concerns premise order, not model-size transfer.
Accuracy drop of 27% is an average over six datasets (Claude 1.3); final clause is an inference, hedged with 'may'.
Numbers match; 'grounded' label is loose since Self-Refine uses model-generated feedback, and Voyager's self-verification is also LLM-based.

8.62 is the gain of CR (GPT-3.5, FOLIO-wiki) over Direct prompting (CoT gain is +4.31, so over CoT it is about 4.3); neither paper tests an explicit structured store versus free-text context (lost-in-the-middle only compares input positions).
fix: Models lose over 20% accuracy when the answer sits in the middle of a long context (Liu et al., GPT-3.5 multi-document QA), and Cumulative Reasoning, which accumulates verified propositions, improves FOLIO-wiki accuracy by up to 8.62 points over direct prompting and about 4.3 points over CoT (GPT-3.5-turbo); this suggests but does not show that an explicit proposition store beats long free-text context.

problem: Opielka et al. is about antonym-type concept vectors from ICL heads, not analogy per se; 38.4% is a best case (Gemma-7B) of incorrect cases fixed by replacing the first pair.
Guo et al. counts are per benchmark (14/17 MedQA, 14/17 JAMA CC, 16/17 MedMCQA); 'up to 30%' is a maximum average.
BeliefShift's trade-off is about personalising vs fact-grounded models; AGM-Bench does not frame a trade-off itself, only inertia and collateral damage.
Kuhn et al. App. B: 61% (hot, T=1.5) vs over 92% (cooler) is the accuracy of the semantic-equivalence clustering, not the accuracy of sampled answers.
fix: Entropy signals have limits: a model that is consistently wrong has low semantic entropy (an inference from the definition; Farquhar et al. say it detects only confabulation); sampling temperature trades accuracy against diversity (best AUROC at T=0.5, Kuhn Fig 3b, TriviaQA/OPT-30B); at T=1.5 semantic-equivalence classification accuracy falls to 61% vs over 92% at lower temperatures; tests are mostly factual QA (TriviaQA, CoQA), not multi-step reasoning.

problem: Li et al. say LM-led elicitation is 'often' more informative than user-written prompts (claim drops 'often'); Handa et al. and Li et al. share several authors (Tamkin, Goodman, Andreas, B. Li), so they are one research group, though the two findings are separate.
Second source (BED-LLM) just cites Bertolazzi et al. and Zhang et al., so 'other work agrees' rests on a citing sentence, not independent evidence.
'No study compares stop rules for EIG-based probe selection' is an absence claim that opened sources cannot establish.
Early-stopping SC shows lower entropy for correct vs incorrect voted answers (mean difference), so 'mostly correct' is a mild gloss; the closing recommendation is the notes' inference.

Papadimitriou-Tsitsiklis result is only second-hand via Bernstein et al.; Madani abstract confirms undecidability of infinite-horizon planning (policy-existence wording is from the paper's body, not fully verified).

The Tag numbers match (Perseus -6.17, PBVI -9.18, QMDP -16.9) but no source states '10-100x lower cost at near-equal quality' as a general result; Perseus actually beats PBVI on Tag, speedups differ by problem (about 36x vs PBVI on Tag), and POMCP scored 20.01 vs SARSOP 21.56 on RockSample(11,11).
fix: Point-based and sampling planners (PBVI, Perseus, SARSOP, POMCP, DESPOT) plan over sampled or reachable beliefs only and reach comparable or better reward than earlier solvers at much lower cost on benchmarks (e.g. Tag: Perseus -6.17 in 1,670 s vs PBVI -9.18 in 59,772 s, QMDP -16.9; POMCP 20.01 in 1 s per action vs SARSOP 21.56 with about 1,000 s offline on RockSample(11,11)).

problem: QMDP is not literally 'observation as state' (it uses the belief with Q-MDP values); the Tag numbers (-16.769 vs -6.17 to -9.18) match.
Ni et al. report better sample efficiency and asymptote than 6 specialised methods on 18 of 21 environments ('matches or beats'), slightly stronger than 'matches'.
Krishnamurthy et al. is not needed for the cited numbers; EVOLvE (50.2 vs 27.5, 65.6 vs 28.3) and Lindenbauer (53.8 vs 54.8; +13% to +15% turns) match.

All supporting numbers come from a single paper (Qiu et al., opened three times under different ids); Imran et al. (BCC vs scale) does not test multi-round plateaus, so the generalisation rests on one study.
fix: In one study (Qiu et al. 2025: 624 simulated users, flight-preference task, 5 rounds) off-the-shelf LLMs update beliefs poorly, most plateau after round 1; Bayesian assistant final accuracy 81% vs about 36-58% for the LLMs and humans in the figure labels; chain of thought, numeric formats, 30 rounds and base models did not fix it.

problem: 38.1% described as relative gain is the note's reconstruction; paper only says 'success rate by 38.1%'. Sample is n=3 runs per cell (Appendix H) as stated.

Numbers match (40/55/88; 5/3/36; 97.09% FNR; 87 to 99% verifier accuracy, 17x tokens) but all sources are the Kambhampati group (Valmeekam, Stechly, Kambhampati), so this is one lab, not independent confirmation.
fix: A sound external verifier beats self-critique in one lab's studies (Valmeekam, Stechly, Kambhampati et al.): Blocksworld GPT-4 generator 40%, LLM+LLM 55%, LLM+VAL 88% (100 instances); Game of 24 standard 5%, LLM+LLM 3%, sound verifier 36%; GPT-4 as Mystery Blocksworld verifier has 97% false-negative rate; a 99%-accurate CoT verifier left a 6 point gap at 17x tokens. No independent lab has replicated these here.

problem: 'Much higher compute' rests on the authors' limitations note (multiple LLM calls), no measured ratio; UCT 0.0 is under a 120 s runtime bound.
Kambhampati et al. say LLM-Modulo with a VAL verifier reaches only about 10% on Mystery Blocksworld; 28.3% is GPT-4o one-shot without any verifier.
fix: Search helps only when the LLM can propose plausible actions: with a VAL verifier in the loop Mystery Blocksworld reaches only about 10% (one-shot GPT-4o alone scores 28.3%), and LLM-MCTS wins where the world model is simpler than the policy (e.g. multiplication via 1-digit tables).

problem: Shai et al. report R2 = 0.95 for the RRXOR belief-state geometry (vs 0.31 for next-token geometry), not for Mess3; no Mess3 R2 of 0.95 is stated.
fix: Transformers trained on hidden-Markov data linearly encode the Bayes belief-state geometry (R2 = 0.95 on RRXOR; Mess3 also recovered, Shai et al. 2024) and Decision-Pretrained Transformers behave like posterior sampling (Lee et al. 2023); this is training-time evidence, not prompt-time.

problem: Final sentence on LLM planner comparisons (N 20-40, one seed) is the notes' inference; BSE uses N=40/25 paired seeds and UoT n=3 runs per cell; DESPOT authors' own POMCP runs scored below published values.
SEP matches the progressive/degenerating definition; the ad hoc1/ad hoc2 labels could not be checked in the Lakatos text (archive.org copy not downloadable) and rest on a search summary.

SEP confirms Halley (72 years) and Copernicus parallax (1838) and Branahl/Johansson confirm the 'wait indefinitely' objection; the Prout 1815 to about 1911 dates could not be checked in the opened sources.

The 'about 54% pooled correct' is Yang & Johnson-Laird Exp 1 correct rate over ALL quantified illusions (possibility 23%, impossibility 67%), not illusions of impossibility alone; other numbers (15/91 N=20, 19/95, 6/83 N=80 r=.87) check out.
fix: Illusory inferences are systematic: confident, uniform errors on problems where reasoning from true cases only gives a wrong answer. Found with propositional, embedded-disjunction, quantified, modal and conditional problems. Human rates from originals: modal 15% correct vs 91% on controls (N=20), embedded disjunctions 19% vs 95%, conditionals 6% vs 83% (N=80, Spanish lab, r=.87, only partly independent of the Johnson-Laird network). Illusions of impossibility are weaker than illusions of possibility (quantified problems, Yang & Johnson-Laird: 67% vs 23% correct; 54% pooled over both kinds). LLMs also produce the predicted fallacies on disjunction problems (d01, d02), though those tests are by a rival theory's authors and have no matched controls. Gap pass: an independent lab (Sable-Meyer & Mascarenhas 2021, N=64 and 70 analysed) found the disjunction illusion again with controls at 87%/26% and 90%/20% accepted, and showed it is triggered by knowledge links, not only word overlap (d24).

problem: Cited confidence values match Goldvarg and Johnson-Laird, Espino et al. and Khemlani and Johnson-Laird; JL&S 1999 not opened; note Yang and Johnson-Laird found a small reliable confidence gap (.13), and 4 of 5 sources are one lab.

Numbers match (80/21, 92/51, 98/72/8), but every source is a Johnson-Laird-lab paper (Bucciarelli, Khemlani, Goodwin, all co-authored by the theory's author); no outside lab replicates the model-count effect, and the relational 98/72/8 is cited from earlier work.

In Bucciarelli and Johnson-Laird, no-valid-conclusion items (50%, 41% in Exp 2) are harder than one-model items (80%) but easier than multiple-model items (21%), so it is not 'the hard case' for humans; the LLM part (rarely say 'nothing follows', ICL does not fix it) is supported by Eisape et al. and Bertolazzi et al.
fix: 'Nothing follows' is a hard case for humans and a very hard one for LLMs. Humans do worse on no-valid-conclusion items (50% in Exp 1) than on one-model items (80%), though better than on multiple-model items (21%) (Bucciarelli & Johnson-Laird); LLMs rarely produce it (PaLM 2, Pythia, LLaMA) and drift to form-based (atmosphere) answers; in-context examples did not fix it for the open models.

problem: Numbers verified (5.6 vs 1.1 unbiased, 56% violations N=39, 53% vs 8% cited second-hand from Girotto and Gonzalez), but both papers are Johnson-Laird-lab work testing his own theory; the Bayesian rescue figure is only a citation; the notes' 'r=.76' is actually R2.

51/21 and 74/92 match Johnson-Laird 2010 (a self-review of one cited study); but the 228 experiments show people select instances, counterexamples or both (not simply 'default confirming'), and the feedback switch comes from the repeated selection task, not the 228-study meta-analysis; both sources are model-theory authors' work.
fix: In Wason selection tasks people select instances of the hypothesis, its potential counterexamples, or both, depending on content and instructions (meta-analysis of 228 experiments, Ragni & Kola 2018); with feedback in the repeated selection task they switched from instances to potential counterexamples. When judging given conclusions, counterexample use was higher and correct rejection lower for conclusions merely consistent with the premises than for inconsistent ones (use 51% vs 21%; correct rejection 74% vs 92%; Johnson-Laird 2010, citing one study).

problem: Mondorf and Plank (31.7% Llama-2-70B sound, symbolic strategy only occasional) and Eisape et al. (NVC accuracy near 0%) match; note Zephyr-7B uses the symbolic strategy most often among tested models, and the closing design inference is the notes' own.

Chen et al. say permuting premise order 'can cause' a drop of over 30% (a maximum, not a drop shown for each listed model); the 14%, 7% and +4% figures (11 LLMs), and the 13-22% moral-judgment order effects match their abstracts.
fix: Premise order and counterfactual content hurt LLM deduction. Permuting premise order can cause accuracy drops of over 30% (Chen et al. 2024; models tested include GPT-4-turbo, GPT-3.5, PaLM 2-L, Gemini 1.0 Pro). Premises that contradict world knowledge cost an average 14% across 11 models; a flag-and-reason prompt cut the gap to 7% and raised overall accuracy 4%. Note the Johnson-Laird view predicts order effects (model construction is serial) and belief effects (believable conclusions stop search), but neither paper tests it. Gap pass: no 2025-26 premise-order measurement on frontier or reasoning models for deduction was found; d26 is training-based on 7B-70B models and d27 shows order effects of 13-22% in frontier models on moral judgments only.

problem: Numbers match (Dong et al. 47.27->56.64, 77.39->80.01, 111 and 51 tasks; Jha et al. 19/20 vs 2/20), but Dong's feedback was only 'your answer is not correct' (no counterexample), and the Jha figures are GPT-4 baseline success by problem size, not a measured effect of counterexample feedback, so 'counterexample feedback helps but is weak' is not shown.
fix: An external checker telling ChatGPT that its answer is wrong (no counterexample content) improved it only slowly: gpt-3.5 rose from 47.27% to 56.64% and gpt-4o from 77.39% to 80.01% on 256 syllogism satisfiability tasks over up to 10 rounds, with 111 and 51 tasks never solved (Dong et al.). Separately, in blocks-world planning GPT-4 alone solved 19/20 problems at 3 blocks and 2/20 at 10 blocks, and Jha et al. use solver counterexamples in an LLM loop, but that paper's baseline numbers here do not measure how much counterexample feedback helps.

problem: Oaksford and Chater 1994 and Sperber et al. 1995 (independent labs) support the 4% and ~10% logical rates; the 46%/33% modal figures come from Johnson-Laird and Wason (1970), quoted second-hand, while the 34-task pooled counts support the general pattern.

Klayman and Ha (positive test strategy as general default heuristic; fails when H lies inside T) and Wason 1960 (29 subjects, 6 correct first time) match; the conditions for soundness rest on the single Klayman and Ha paper.
Jhaveri et al. (6% to 78%, eleven LLMs, I:C correlates with success) and Bertolazzi et al. (12 LLMs, Spearman -0.779, p=0.003) match; two independent groups.

Numbers match, but the general claim is too strong: in FalsifyBench the smallest reasoning models (GPT-5-Nano 12%, Qwen3.5-9B 21%) did worse than all instruction-tuned models; Jhaveri's Gemini-2.5-Pro vs small non-thinking comparison confounds scale (thinking helped Qwen3 but without a consistent rise in disconfirming tests); and on WILT the best model (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, 14/50) is not a reasoning model, with o1-mini 13 and o1-preview 12.
fix: Larger reasoning (thinking) models generally do better at rule discovery and falsify more: GPT-5.2-Chat 75 percent and GPT-OSS-120B 68 percent vs 33 to 41 percent for instruction-tuned models (FalsifyBench), although the smallest reasoning models (GPT-5-Nano 12%, Qwen3.5-9B 21%) did worse than all instruction-tuned ones; Gemini-2.5-Pro (thinking) 0.73 vs 0.06 to 0.33 for small non-thinking models (Jhaveri, confounded with scale). On WILT no model solves more than 14 of 50 and the best (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) is not a reasoning model.

problem: Dasgupta et al. (z>2.2 for Chinchilla, PaLM 2-L, GPT-3.5, humans; marginal 1.78) and Seals and Shalin (chance 1/6, mostly 0.06-0.29) match, but Seals and Shalin found that social content does benefit LLMs (significant social-rule by content interaction; realistic social > realistic non-social), only less than in humans (about 30% vs about 70%), so 'weak or absent' overstates.
fix: LLMs show the human content effect on the Wason task: realistic rules beat arbitrary ones (Chinchilla, PaLM 2-L, GPT-3.5 and humans, all z>2.2; only marginal for PaLM 2-M and Flan-PaLM 2). Small open models mostly fail the standard form (0.06 to 0.29, chance 1/6). In one study the social-rule advantage in LLMs was real but much smaller than in humans (about 30% vs about 70% solved).

problem: Numbers check (Maegherman n=27: 22.2% correct, 40.7% confirming only; maths majors and mathematicians under 50% in Dasgupta et al.; Swann and Giuliano F(1,47)=4.161), but the judges' task was a leaves-and-pot variation, not the abstract task, with n=27 and the thesis itself calls 22% a relatively good result against the typical under 10%.
fix: Confirmatory choices remain common in trained people: in a small survey (n=27) of Dutch judges on a Wason variant, 40.7% chose only the confirming option and 22.2% gave the correct confirming-plus-falsifying pair (the thesis reads this as relatively good versus the typical under 10%); undergraduate maths majors and academic mathematicians scored under 50% on the arbitrary abstract task (Dasgupta et al., citing others); and in social interviews people favour confirmatory questions, especially when certain (Swann and Giuliano).

problem: Parab et al. (4.3% of semantically wrong hypotheses yielded a program passing the training examples, 5,500 trials GPT-4o) and Moghe and Chin (N=1 never above 45.5%, N=5 57.5% pass@2, refinement only -0.75pp) match; Chari and Pattanaik's EIG result is about a support mismatch with the generator, so the EIG sentence is the notes' inference, and Parab also finds the summarizer step loses about a quarter of correct hypotheses.

Cosmides et al. 2010 ('only 5-30%' on indicative rules, 65-80% on social contracts) and Klauer et al. 2007 ('typically fewer than 10%' P and not-Q) support it; the 5-30% range is Cosmides' summary, not a pooled meta-analysis, and Fiddick and Cosmides sources share a lab.

Fiddick 2003 (realistic rules failed to replicate Wason and Shapiro; Manktelow and Evans 1979), Cosmides et al. 2010 and Kroger et al. 1993 (permission 47% vs arbitrary 5% only with violation-checking plus explicit negatives) support it; Fiddick and Cosmides are the same theoretical camp, while Kroger/Cheng/Holyoak and Sperber/Girotto are independent rivals.

Cosmides 2010 (64/46/26 additive factors, 5-30% indicative), Cosmides 1989 pages via 2010 summary, and Gigerenzer and Hug (n=93, 94% vs 44%) match; minor slip: Cosmides' familiar descriptive control was 46%/38%, just above the stated 45% top of the control range; the claim already flags that 65-80 is one lab's spread.

Sperber and Girotto 2002 Exp 2 (N=120, 33%/43% vs 10%/0% P and not-Q) and Gigerenzer and Hug 1992 (perspective flips P and not-Q 75% to not-P and Q 61%) match; independent labs; note Sperber and Girotto's cheater cells were below Fiddick et al.'s original (33% vs 66% failed replication).

Lampinen et al. (Wason z>2.2, NLI no effect with ceiling, item-level t(832)=3.49, t(345)=4.98) and Ando et al. NeuBAROCO (GPT-3.5 31.37% inconsistent vs 61.05% symbolic) match; the NLI null is partly due to ceiling effects, and the claim omits that stronger models show little belief effect (see K12).

Lampinen et al. (Chinchilla 5-shot Wason content effects exaggerated), Bertolazzi et al. 2025 (CE 0.348 to 0.096; 0.213 to 0.014 with CoT) and Bertolazzi et al. 2024 (LLaMA-3 8B 70.74 to 52.59, LLaMA-2-inst 7B 32.22 to 19.26) match; 'ICL often cut accuracy' rests on other sources I did not open.

Cosine 0.48-0.64 vs 0.10-0.17, debias vector CE 0.348 to 0.072, and K-CAST up to 15% absolute match, but 'not reachable by a text scaffold' is contradicted by the same Bertolazzi et al. paper, where chain-of-thought alone cut CE 0.348 to 0.096 and 0.213 to 0.014; also the two Bertolazzi entries are versions of one paper.
fix: Validity and plausibility are linearly encoded and aligned inside open models (cosine 0.48 to 0.64 vs 0.10 to 0.17 for controls); a debias vector cut CE from 0.348 to 0.072 and conditional activation steering (K-CAST) gave up to 15 points absolute on models that static steering could not fix. Chain-of-thought prompting alone also cut CE substantially in strong open models (0.348 to 0.096), so text prompting reaches part of the effect, while steering offers a further internal lever.

problem: GSM-Symbolic found accuracy falls when numbers (or names plus numbers) change, but changing names alone leaves GSM8K performance near the name-changed distribution (only extra variance); the 65% figure is a maximum and Wu et al. report 'substantial and consistent' degradation over 11 tasks (not verified per task).
fix: Models are brittle to surface content beyond logic tasks: changing numerical values lowers GSM accuracy (changing names alone mainly adds variance), adding one irrelevant but plausible clause drops accuracy by up to 65 percent (GSM-NoOp), and on counterfactual variants of 11 tasks performance degrades substantially and consistently relative to the default versions (Wu et al.).

problem: Ahn and Graham (n=22; control P and not-Q .18), Macchi et al. (control 4%/10%; Necessarily 66%/77%) and Kroger et al. (47% vs 5%) match; minor slip: n=130 is Macchi's Exp 1 control sample, the 'necessarily' groups are smaller (N=82 combined), and Ahn and Graham's 50% is a mean over three explicated conditions rather than the same measure as the control's 18% P and not-Q.

FOLIO 93.8 vs 74.1 (81 items), Symbolic Tree ChatGPT 71.8 vs 53.7, and Phi-3-mini over 65% NoOp drop all match; slip: the 65% drop is for the irrelevant clause (NoOp), not for name or number swaps, and name-only swaps do not clearly lower accuracy.

Eisape et al. (about 75% vs about 50%, near 0% on 'nothing follows', 30 samples at temp 0.5, binary discrimination markedly higher on those items) and Bertolazzi et al. (pretrained LLaMA/Pythia rarely say 'nothing follows') match; the 'does this conclusion follow' wording is the notes' description of Eisape's binary-validity method.

Wu et al. (93.8 vs 74.1 on 81 FOLIO items; consistent drops on 11 tasks), Tang et al. (70.1 vs 71.8), and Saparov and He (true ontology allows skipping hops) match; Kim et al. only report 'evidence of partial contamination' from extra attention heads, so 'inject world knowledge' is stated more firmly than the paper; 'so it was using memory' is Tang's inference.

Ozeki et al. (87/90 = 96.67%, 77.78 to 83.33; GPT-3.5 58.89 to 52.22/54.44), FregeLogic (Z3 74.7%, invalid 97.6, valid 52.2), LINC (syntax errors 38/24/13%) and Kartac et al. (95.83 vs 84.17, +11.7) all match; the closing 'weak link depends on size and data' is the notes' synthesis, and the Z3 figure comes from one SemEval system paper.

Kim et al. (recovery fails on belief-inconsistent data, 'suggesting' extra heads), Bertolazzi et al. (cosine 0.48-0.64 vs 0.10-0.17, alignment tracks content effect) and Valentino et al.
